One Book of Dom Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, On Ecclesiastical Writers, or on men illustrious in the Church through their writings; with two appendices of those who either were not noticed by Trithemius, or in our intervening age have become, or still are, most distinguished by their writings. Carefully purged of the innumerable errors with which it has hitherto swarmed, and illustrated and enlarged throughout with many small additions marked with the sign †.

The former of these appendices was recently produced in France; the latter is now newly added, by Balthazar Werlin of Colmar.

With a most faithful index, from which the quality of this edition can conveniently be judged at once, on the first page.

Cologne, from the workshop of Peter Quentel, in the month of March, in the year 1546. With privilege.

In Praise of This Most Noble Work, an Epigram by Dom Sebastian Brant.

Whoever you are who wish to know the approved writers of the Church, and whatever distinction each one has, read this epitome of the learned Abbot Johannes of Sponheim, whom his eloquent life commends.

As he restores the ancient doctrines of the fathers of the order, and renews the sacred rights of Benedict, so he takes care to bring together the scattered names of the writers of old and to collect them in one book.

He sets down a catalogue, by which he reckons the times, and what that venerable company of authors wrote. He rescues from decay so many worthy names of men, whom devouring time had lately held beneath its feet.

And it is a wonder that one man could either read in order so many worthy men, or call to mind such great men; so that I am quite inclined to doubt whether, if perhaps he did not read them all, yet a great part of them all may have seemed to him to have been seen.

Therefore I rightly place this great-souled and distinguished man also among the number of the learned.

Index of Ecclesiastical Writers, Compiled Recently and Newly in This Volume by Johannes Trithemius and Others, Faithfully Gathered and Carefully Arranged by Barth. Laurens.

Mirari te dicis Alberte amantissime, ꝙ profeffores secularium li- terarum qui nihil ecclesiasticum scripferūt, inter viros illustres ecclesiasticos qđ scriptores pofuerim, cum haꝑ rerum scri- ptores, Hieronymus, Gennadius, lsidorus, Honorius, Sigebertus, & reliqui doctorẽ cęsores, id minime feciffe inueniatur: indignum iu dicans vt secularibus disciplinis intenti, qui nihil ad ecclefie vni- uerfalís aedificationem laborarũt, inter ecclesiafticos scriptores lo cum fortiantur, Non miror ꝙ miraris: mirantur et caeteri. Tibi er go respõdendo, satisfecerim oĩbus qui eadem opinione tenentur, Et primo quidem cur alij non fecerint, quod me feciffe miraris, ni hil ad me pertinet: ego vero quare fecerim quod illi non fecerunt, breuiter narrabo, Equidem bonarum artium ꝓfeffores, in fide ca- tholica manentes, philosophos, oratores, atque poetas, qui vtile ̄ honefum in sua facultate quippiam scripfitant, indignos catalo go ilustrium virorum nequā cēseo, quos iuuare ecclesiam fujs lu- cubrationibꝰ non ignoro, Neq́ enim fatis eruditum in diuinis scri pturis quenq̃ dici poffe arbitror, vbi secularis literaturae disciplinā ignorarit. Quomodo autem eam difce theologus, fi non fit q tra diderit; Quis nefciat quantū Christianus et fidelis philofophus ,p¬ sit ecclefia, qui gentiliũ errores destruit, argumenta ̄ fallaces syl¬ logismos aperit, dogmata infidelium cōfundit: Lege veterum hi¬ storias, ̄ inuenies gefta fidē adstruere verbis. Quoties orthodoxi philofophi calliditatem hereticorum disputado defruxerint, gen tiles fuperarint, schifmaticos vicerint? Quid multis vtar; Omnis theologorum schola, à philosophia iam studēdi sumit exordium, adeo vt theologus effe non posfit, qui prius philosophus apud eos non extiterit. Responsive letter of the reverend father and lord Johannes of Trittenheim, abbot of Sponheim, to the venerable and most learned man Father Albert Morderer, giving an account why he placed many professors of secular letters among ecclesiastical writers.

[unclear] Brother Johannes of Trittenheim, abbot in Sponheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, sends greeting to Brother Albert Morderer, of the Observant Order of Minorites, his friend. You say, most beloved Albert, that you wonder that I have placed professors of secular letters, who wrote nothing ecclesiastical, among the illustrious ecclesiastical men whom I have called writers, since Jerome, Gennadius, Isidore, Honorius, Sigebert, and the remaining learned censors of writers on such matters are found not to have done this at all; judging it unworthy that those devoted to secular disciplines, who labored in nothing for the edification of the universal Church, should obtain a place among ecclesiastical writers. I do not wonder that you wonder; the others wonder too. Therefore, by answering you, I shall satisfy all who hold the same opinion.

And first, indeed, why others did not do what you wonder that I have done does not concern me; but why I did what they did not do, I shall briefly explain. Indeed, I by no means consider professors of the good arts, remaining in the Catholic faith, philosophers, orators, and poets, who have written anything useful and honorable in their field, unworthy of the catalogue of illustrious men, for I know that they assist the Church by their lucubrations. Nor do I think that anyone can be called sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures when he is ignorant of the discipline of secular literature. But how will a theologian learn it, if there is no one who has transmitted it? Who does not know how much a Christian and faithful philosopher can do for the Church, one who destroys the errors of the gentiles, exposes arguments and fallacious syllogisms, and confounds the doctrines of unbelievers? Read the histories of the ancients, and you will find that deeds confirm faith by words. How often have orthodox philosophers destroyed the cunning of heretics by disputation, overcome gentiles, conquered schismatics? Why should I use many words? Every school of theologians now takes the beginning of study from philosophy, to such an extent that one cannot be a theologian unless he has first been a philosopher among them. What shall I say about orators, without whose teaching

15
infructuosum antiqui omnem censebant theologum, quippe qui bona quae didicisset, alijs p̄suadere non potuerit. Rhetor enim figu- ras scripturarum reserat, tropos dilucidat, dissoluit nodos, colores ostēdit, dubia enucleat, vmbras verborum efficit claras. Qui dum oratoris assumit officium, facile haereticoꝛum allegationes destru¬ et, atqꝫ conuincet errores. Quis deniqꝫ boni oratoꝛis laudes digne prosequi valeat; si quantum in perfuadendo possit, diligenter pen¬ fat: O vtinam omnes theologi nostri temporis, oꝛatoriā colerent: quantum in ecclesia Dei suis exhortationibus fructum produce¬ re possent? Theologus orator, animos auditoꝛum seuroꝛum in pote¬ state sua habere dicitur, ad cuius persuasiones ad ea quae sancta cru¬ dis, qui omnes poetas vna sententiā damnant, mēdaces eos asseren¬ tes atqꝫ turpiloquos; quasi non possint esse veraces boni, qui car¬ mina veterum imitatūr poetarum. Abfit, poetam bonum esse non posse atqꝫ veracem, qui sanctos patres, Augustinū, Hieronymum, Sedulium, Prudentium, Bedam, aliosqꝫ innumerabiles, in hac arte habuit pręcessores. Sed non est mei officij, neqꝫ huius temporis, ho¬ rum ignauīa redarguere. Vt ergo claudam epiftolam, ego philo¬ sophos, oratoꝛes, poetas, ceterarumqꝫ bonarum artium cultores fi¬ deles Christianos, qui aliuid vtile scripserunt, ecclesiasticis scri¬ ptoribus connumerandos existimai, triplici ratione: Prima, q̄ eo¬ rum opuscula ad scientiam sanctorū scripturarum, non modicum cōducere posse arbitratũ sum. Secunda, q̄ verifimile mihi visum fit, eos aliqua ecclesiastisice scripsisse quae me lateant. Vltima, q̄ oc¬ casionem sibi per nos datam intelligant, vt ecclesiastice deinceps scribentes, locum succeptum condignis laboribus exornent. Tan¬ tos ergo viros, ecclesie catholicae tam vtiles, tu ne reijciendos exi¬ stimas? Abfit à nobis, vt tam temeratam illis iniuriam irrogemus, qua nos credant aemulationis studio prouocatos, non ratione pie¬ tatis. Deniqꝫ nobis cauendū illud qđ vulgo iactatur puerbiū, Sciē¬ tia non habet inimicum, nisi ignorātem. His itaqꝫ breuiter tibi re¬ spondere volui, vt scires non fine causa factum, quod factum ante mirabaris. Vale, nostri memor ad Deū in orationibꝰ tuis. IN CHRI sto patri et amp; domino, Dn.Iohāni de Dalburg, diuina prouidentia Vor- matiensi episcopo:F.Iohānes, voca- tus abbas in Spanheim, ordinis san cti Benedicti, modicū id quod est. Consueuerunt olim veteres,Re- uerendiss.pater,si qđ operis noui cudissent, vt robur et firmitatem acciperet perpetuam, id viris dicare praestan tibus,quatenus aemulorum lingua venenata,lumine ma iestatis reuerberata,dentem praui morsus nusquam va- luisset infigere.Nec eos fallebat opinio quae ex humili- tate processit,cum doctis semper praesulibus amica sit in subditos laudibus attollenda benignitas,quae bono- rum studia remunerat,prauorū coercet. Hoc nostri quo que vetustatis exemplum pro posse imitātes, opera quae scriptitāt, dicata ecclesiarū praelatis ac viris doctioribus solēt submittere,vt eorum authoritate comprobata,se- cure valeant in publicum prodire.In lucem enim sine ti more prodeunt,quae testimonio pōtificis fulciūtur.Neo

the ancients judged every theologian unfruitful, since he could not persuade others of the good things he had learned. For the rhetorician opens up the figures of the Scriptures, makes tropes clear, unties knots, shows colors, explains uncertainties, and makes the shadows of words clear. When he assumes the office of an orator, he will easily destroy the allegations of heretics and refute their errors. Finally, who could worthily recount the praises of a good orator, if he carefully weighs how much power there is in persuasion? O would that all the theologians of our time cultivated oratory: how much fruit they could produce in the Church of God by their exhortations. The theologian who is an orator is said to have the minds of his own hearers in his power; at whose persuasions, toward those things that are holy, [unclear]. [Unclear] untrained men, who condemn all poets in a single judgment, asserting that they are liars and foul-spoken; as if men who imitate the poems of the ancient poets could not be truthful and good. Far be it that a poet cannot be good and truthful, one who has had as his predecessors in this art the holy fathers Augustine, Jerome, Sedulius, Prudentius, Bede, and countless others. But it is not my office, nor the business of this time, to rebuke their sloth. Therefore, to close the letter: I have thought that philosophers, orators, poets, and faithful Christian cultivators of the other good arts, who have written something useful, should be counted among ecclesiastical writers, for three reasons. First, because I judged that their little works could contribute not a little to the knowledge of the holy Scriptures. Second, because it seemed likely to me that they had written some ecclesiastical works which are unknown to me. Last, because they should understand that an occasion has been given them by us, so that, writing henceforth ecclesiastically, they may adorn the place they have received with fitting labors. Do you therefore think that such great men, so useful to the Catholic Church, should be rejected? Far be it from us to inflict upon them so rash an injury, by which they might believe that we were provoked by zeal of rivalry, not by the reason of piety. Finally, we must beware of that proverb commonly tossed about: Knowledge has no enemy except the ignorant man. Thus I wished to answer you briefly, so that you might know that what you previously wondered at had not been done without cause. Farewell, remembering us before God in your prayers. From Spanheim, the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the year of the Lord 1492.

Letter of the Venerable and Distinguished Father in Christ, Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Johannes von Dalberg, Bishop of Worms.

To the most reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord Johannes von Dalberg, by divine providence Bishop of Worms: Brother Johannes, called abbot in Spanheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, offers the little that he is.

It was formerly the custom of the ancients, most reverend father, if they had fashioned some new work, to dedicate it to eminent men, so that it might receive lasting strength and firmness, and so that the poisonous tongue of rivals, beaten back by the light of majesty, could nowhere succeed in fastening the tooth of wicked biting. Nor were they deceived in the opinion that proceeded from humility, since among learned prelates a kindness friendly to subjects must always be lifted up with praises, a kindness which rewards the studies of the good and restrains those of the wicked. Imitating as far as we can this example of antiquity, men of our own time also are accustomed to submit the works they write, dedicated to prelates of churches and to more learned men, so that, approved by their authority, they may be able to go forth securely into public. For those things go forth into the light without fear which are supported by the testimony of a bishop.

PRO-

To the Bishop of Worms.

For indeed no one, unless foolish, readily accuses what he knows has been approved by the judgment of greater men. The innocence of the sheep rests safely when the compassion of a good shepherd watches over it. Since, therefore, the examples of the ancients are incentives to virtue for us, it is fitting that we imitate the holy conduct of those whose praises we sing, so that, while we profit from them and others from us, the order of the ecclesiastical hierarchy may continue inviolate. And although I am too slight a man to trust that anyone might take pleasure in my little works, nevertheless I have resolved humbly to offer what I have into the Lord’s treasury, in which the widow’s two coins are rightly preferred to the riches of Croesus.

Accordingly, when recently, at the urging of friends, I had gathered together with much labor a book On Ecclesiastical Writers, as the work itself bears witness, I resolved, lest I stray from the footsteps of the ancients, to submit this labor of mine to some most learned man, eminent in ecclesiastical dignity, by whose authority and goodwill it might pass through the teeth of the envious without being bitten. And when much thought had arisen in me as to whom I should [dedicate?] this same little lucubration so that it would be more welcome, many presented themselves to me as I hesitated, men concerning whose learning and goodwill no small promised hope was strong; among them you, most reverend father, appeared to me as preferable, more eminent, and more learned, you who surpass all in learning and exceed everyone in erudition. In you the nobility of a high lineage shines forth, episcopal authority stands eminent, integrity of conduct is seen, and every kind of knowledge of the liberal arts is praised. Could we find such a man anywhere besides you, in whom

Dedicatory Letter.

all these things come together at once? Among the Germans, most reverend father, I know no one equal to you, in whom such lineage, dignity, and erudition shine forth. I do not speak into your ear; let the Almighty be witness; nor do I aim to seem a flattering panegyrist, since all Germany knows you as a man most skilled in every respect. The learned honor you; nobles and princes respect you. You are to us what Plato is said to have been to Antimachus. Whoever is approved by your eloquence is deservedly judged learned. By public report, which does not lie, we have learned how deep a knowledge of sacred letters abounds in you, how penetrating an interpretation of law, and finally how great a charm, sweetness, and grace in speaking and delivering orations, so that we do not hesitate to compare you with the most learned men whom we have mentioned in the catalogue. The speeches you are said to have delivered bear most clearly witness to this; your letters bear witness; many epigrams bear witness. Indeed, the most illustrious fame of your name has become known with praise not only to our Germans but also to Italians and Frenchmen.

Hence it entered my mind that I should inscribe to you, so great a bishop, the work On Ecclesiastical Writers submitted to you, and dedicate it to your name, so that I might rest secure under the shadow of your pontifical eminence. But while I behold in you the splendor of flashing light, I am struck with awe, drawn back, and wholly shaken by fear of your great majesty, lest perhaps I, wholly inferior to you, a lofty and most learned father, in knowledge, merit, and dignity, should displease you in the very matter by which I presumed to please. For I know your many occupations; I am not unaware of your sacred studies, which I ought not to have troubled with my trifles.

Dedicatory Letter.

But your learning gives me courage, which your kindness and humanity render lovable to all, since it recoils from no one’s letters and judges no one unworthy of its address. Therefore I approach your Highness, although I am the lowest of men; I humbly submit the present little work to you; I appoint you its judge and defender. Accept, I beg you, most reverend and most learned father, this lucubration of ours, such as it is; examine it, judge it, defend it; and, if you judge it worthy, follow it with kindly favor. And you who turn over the writings of the ancients in continual reading, deign also, when there is leisure, to inspect their catalogue.

I, however, have not yet shared the present little work with anyone, nor shall I share it until I know that it has been approved by the testimony of your authority. Friends await it; printers are waiting for it; but I judge the opinion of your Fatherhood to be preferred to all. May your most merciful Fatherhood, I pray, pardon me for having presumed to bring my [trifles?] to ears occupied with difficult matters, because I have such confidence in your humanity, gentleness, and kindness that it is scarcely possible to doubt the benevolent reception of our catalogue. And I shall count it among the greatest delights if I learn that you take pleasure in my little lucubrations. Farewell, most reverend father; keep me, your most devoted servant, commended to you together with the volume sent. From Spanheim, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord 1492.

Prologue of the Author to the Catalogue or Following Book

Often, at the urging of many people, I have been asked to complete, when at last an opportunity should present itself, the book on ecclesiastical writers which I had once begun, for the purpose of gaining knowledge of books. I confess that I delayed for a long time, lest, if I presumed to undertake so arduous a matter unskillfully, I should provoke the hatred of rivals through my own levity.

But now, since to the request of friends there has been added the counsel of learned men, who by their arguments encouraged me to take up this task, I could no longer resist their petitions, especially since this little work of ours is supported by the patronage of such great men. For why should I fear the hatred of detractors, when I see that a refuge among the learned lies open to me? There will be, I do not doubt, some who will judge this labor of ours worthy of praise; there will also be some who, with a zeal of rivalry, will disparage it. What then? Shall we therefore abandon the exercises of good works, lest we provoke the hatred of rivals? Far from it. Whoever does not imitate the wicked offends them; but whoever fears to offend the envious does wrong to the good. And indeed it is praiseworthy to have displeased the wicked, who are accustomed to love nothing unless it is matched to their own morals.

Now therefore, my friends and timely exactors, receive the book composed on ecclesiastical writers, which with diligent prayers you so greatly desired to be brought to completion. I have done what I could, and have expended my ready strength on this work, although in many things the capacity itself is less than the desire. For I, after the manner of those who see dimly, entered this wood under the guidance of the fathers who went before, and, gathering from their little works the several things suited to my purpose, I carried them together into this bundle. Many writers also, found by long investigation, I have inserted into our Catalogue with great toil and expense.

Do not be surprised, excellent reader, if in the annotations and titles of books my opinion does not always agree with yours. Who, amid so manifold a variety of books, could enumerate the opinions of individuals, let alone make them agree? You will therefore grant pardon if at times you find a volume designated in one way or another differently from what your opinion holds. For it was not possible for me everywhere to express the differences of individuals. For, as I have already said, I followed the footsteps of the fathers, and where they disagreed, I embraced what I believed to be truer. But if you find something else that rests on a more solid truth, I shall gladly yield to your judgment.

It pleased me, moreover, to proceed by a new manner of writing, so that the reader himself might more easily find knowledge of the books from their beginnings. Beginning, therefore, with the disciples of the apostles down to the last year of Emperor Frederick III, namely the year of the Lord 1493, I have carried down the catalogue of illustrious men; in it I have recorded not the names, ranks, writings, and times of all men, but only of those whom I found, placing opposite them the beginnings of the titles of the volumes; those not seen I have passed over with a blank space. The times in which certain men flourished I could not find at will; nevertheless, as it seemed to me, I placed them in a suitable position. And in each defect let the knowledge of one who knows supply what is lacking, namely that he may compute the times of individuals and restore those transposed to their proper places.

I confess that I have also deliberately passed over several men whose writings are not easily found, nor their times. I know, too, that there are still many very learned men living, who are said to be publishing various little works; but since I do not have certain knowledge of them, I prefer to pass them over in silence rather than think uncertain things. And, to use the words of Jerome, those still-living writers who have been omitted by me in this catalogue should blame not me but themselves, since they preferred to hide their writings rather than have them come into the light. But I believe that, content with their writings and talent, they will not care about the losses caused by my silence. For even of those whom I found, I wished to portray not praises, but books. This, indeed, the labor of a more prolix volume would demand.

Go now, therefore, into the world, work completed by our labor; go, and dispense to lovers of books the treasure which you contain. What do you fear? Why do you tremble? Why do you delay? Do not be afraid to go forth in public; do not fear the hatred of rivals, supported by the patronage of so many saints. Come, book, slight indeed in talent, but a revealer of great matters: why is it that, as though sluggish and useless, you are afraid? Go forth confidently. A thousand will praise you, while scarcely one disparages you. The love of God, with which you were written, I pray may mercifully excuse you, together with your author, always and everywhere. End.

Of the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Dom Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim, On Ecclesiastical Writers, one book, with two supplements down to these times.

Clement, the fourth bishop of the holy Roman Church ordained after blessed Peter, as some think, a Roman by nation, a holy man and beloved of God, adorned also with beauty of character, whose life and passion are contained in ecclesiastical writings, sat in the pontificate nine years and ten days. He was banished into exile for the faith of Christ with steadfast spirit, in the one hundred third year of the Lord. This most blessed martyr is said to have written, in the person of the Roman Church, several letters full of faith and learning, of which the principal ones are extant:

Two letters to the church of the Corinthians. Clement to the lord James.

Besides these, ten books of the itinerary of his life. When in the city of Rome.

Also one book of the disputation of Peter.

These last two volumes, however, are counted among the apocrypha, as is clear in distinction 15, Sancta Romana. Other letters of his are also circulated, but they are apocryphal.

Addition:

He compiled the Apostolic Canons, an epitome of the kerygmata. All are extant in Greek in the Vatican Library.

Dionysius the Areopagite, an Athenian, a distinguished philosopher, converted to the faith by blessed Paul the Apostle, was ordained the first bishop of Athens, as some think, a man of eminent holiness and incomparable learning. After the death of the apostles, blessed Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, sent him with Rusticus the priest and Eleutherius the deacon into France to preach the word of God to the nations, another bishop having been ordained in his place. On Ecclesiastical Writers

many excellent little works, of which among the Latins I find only the following:

On the Celestial Hierarchy, one book; On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, one book; On the Divine Names, one book; On Mystical Theology, one book; On Symbolic Theology, one book; To Gaius, four letters; To Dorotheus the minister, one letter; To Sosipater the priest, one letter; To Polycarp, one letter; To Demophilus, one letter; To St. John the Evangelist, two letters; To Apollophanes the philosopher, three letters; On the death of Paul, to Timothy, four letters.

These are the writings of blessed Dionysius that I find among the Latins; whatever more he published has remained among the Greeks. But since the aforesaid little works were covered with great obscurity, they were made clear by the explanation of the following fathers. Of these John Scotus, a monk of our order, was the first to translate and polish them; then Hugh of St. Victor, Rupert of Lincoln, Albertus Magnus, Dionysius the Carthusian, and many others, of whom no recollection is now at hand.

Blessed Dionysius suffered in the territory of Paris, together with the companions named above, under the emperor Domitian, in the year of the Lord 96, in the ninth indiction, and in the ninetieth year of his age. He was buried at Paris in a church consecrated to his name, shining with miracles.

Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, philosopher, disciple of Sotion the Stoic, uncle of the poet Lucan, was a man of most continent life. Since he is celebrated by the testimony of blessed Jerome, I have therefore placed him in the catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers, because he was a very close friend of the apostle Paul, and composed many elegant works for the instruction of moral life. This man Nero Caesar, that ill-starred ruler, killed two years before Peter and Paul were crowned; Nero had once been his most unworthy pupil. Of his little works I have found the following:

On the Training of Character, one book; On the Four Virtues, one book; On the Remedies of Fortune, one book; ten books of Declamations; On Clemency, to Nero, two books.

The Abbot of Spanheim.

On Benefits to Brutus, seven books. On Anger, to Novatus, three books. On Providence, one book. On the Happy Life, to Gallio, one book. On Consolation, to Marcia, one book. On Consolation, to his mother, one book. On Tranquillity of Life, one book. That Injury Does Not Befall the Wise Man, four books. On the Brevity of Life, one book. On Moral Studies, one book. On Natural Questions, seven books. Of Suasory Sentences, one book. Of Controversies, five books. On Poverty, one book. To Polybius, of Consolation, one book. On the Games of Seneca, one book. On Abundance of Words, one book. On Marriage, one book. Of Tragedies, ten books. On the Death of Claudius, one book. Of Letters to St. Paul, one book. “I believe you, Paul, now.” Of Letters to Lucilius, twenty-two books. “Therefore do this, my Lucilius.”

These are the works of Seneca’s writings that I have been able to find at present. He is also said to have written some other little works, which have not yet come into our hands. He was certainly a most ardent lover of wisdom, and a zealous seeker of it, and of so retentive a memory that, when two thousand names had been read before him, he soon recited them from memory. Moreover, when a certain poet had composed two hundred verses and, after putting them onto a sheet, was reciting them in order before Nero, Seneca at once, using his memory instead of the volume, repeated the same verses one by one, beginning from the last and proceeding in reverse order as far as the first. He is read to have held in memory the names of all his fellow citizens. He flourished at Rome in the times of the apostle Paul, under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Marcellus, son of Marcus, prefect of the city of Rome, once a disciple of Simon Magus, sufficiently instructed in secular letters, converted to the faith of Jesus Christ by the preaching of the blessed apostle Peter, composed many things for the benefit of the Church of God. For, at the request of Christians, he wrote:

On the Conflict of St. Peter and Simon Magus, one book. To the saints Nereus and Achilleus, one book. On the Acts of Peter and Paul, one book. On the Arts of Simon, one book. On the Death of Saint Petronilla, one book. On the Passion of Saint Felicula, one book. On the Passion of Saint Nicomedes, one book.

He also published other things concerning the deeds of the saints, which have not come to our knowledge. He flourished at Rome in the times of St. Peter the apostle, in the year of the Lord 50.

Linus, the first bishop of the city of Rome after blessed Peter, a Tuscan by nation, a man of most holy conduct, held the pontificate for eleven years, three months, and twelve days. Since he was a very learned man, beloved by God, he wrote in the Greek language concerning the holy apostles Peter and Paul, who suffered on one day:

The Martyrdom, one book. And certain letters.

At length, by Saturninus the prefect, whose daughter he had freed from a demon, he was punished by a capital sentence and became a martyr on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Galba, in the year of the Lord 70.

Philo the Jew, an Alexandrian by nation, of the race of priests, is placed by blessed Jerome among ecclesiastical writers for this reason: because in his little works he is very often engaged in praise of Christians. When he had been sent to Rome as envoy of his people, he is remembered as having had the friendship of the blessed apostle Peter; for this reason also he adorned with his praises the followers at Alexandria of Saint Mark, Peter’s disciple. He was a man most learned in every respect, regarded as another Plato, so that it was commonly said: either Plato imitates Philo, or Philo imitates Plato. For so great a likeness of thought and expression between them is reported. He wrote very elegant books, of which the following are given below:

On the Life of the Wise Man, one book. On the Conduct of Life, one book. On the Confusion of Languages, one book. On the Nature of Quadrupeds, one book. On Those Things Which We Attest by Sense, one book. On Education, one book. On the Succession of [generation?], one book. On the Change of Names, one book. On the Heir of Divine Things, one book. On the Division of Unequal Things, one book. On the Three Virtues, one book. On the Nature of Invention, one book. On Covenants, one book. Adam Begot Three Sons, one book. On [unclear] On

On the Contemplative Life, book 1. On the Reason of Animals, book 1. On Agriculture, books 2. That Every Fool Becomes a Slave, book 1. He is read to have written many other things as well, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Nero, in the year of the Lord 50.

Josephus the Jew, by nation a Jerusalemite, by religion a priest, son of the priest Mattathias, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished writer of the times, whom I would not place in our catalogue unless the Church read his writings and Blessed Jerome had done so before: after the destruction of Jerusalem he was captured by the emperors Vespasian and Titus and brought to Rome; because of the excellence of his talent he was magnificently honored by the senate and people of Rome. Although he remained a Jew, nevertheless he often praised the race of Christians, and in the eighteenth book of the Antiquities he set down a notable testimony concerning our Lord Jesus Christ. His volumes were held in such authority among the Romans, while he was still alive, that they were handed over to the public libraries; and after his death he was granted a bronze statue by the senate and people. Of his little works I have seen only the following:

The Jewish War, books 7. Antiquities of the World, books 24. To write the history Against Apion, book 1. sufficiently, as I think On the Power of Speaking, book 1.

He flourished at Rome under the emperors Vespasian and Titus, and remained among men down to the times of the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 100.

He described the contest of the sufferings of the seven sons of one mother, with their mother.

Ignatius, the third bishop of the church of Antioch after Blessed Peter, a man of outstanding holiness and a most singularly fervent lover of our Lord Jesus Christ, was accustomed to say, as Dionysius bears witness: “My love has been crucified.” This most blessed prelate, since he was a learned and zealous preacher of the divine word, wrote several elegant letters full of fervor, in which he showed himself to have been a lover of holy martyrdom. Among these the following are considered the more important:

To the Church of the Ephesians, one letter. To the Magnesians, letter 1. To the Trojans, letter 1. To the Ro-

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

To the Romans, letter 1. To Saint John, letters 2. To the holy elder John To the Blessed Virgin, letter 1. To Mary, bearer of Christ, her To the Philadelphians, letter 1. To Polycarp, letter 1.

He suffered at Rome under the emperor Trajan, in the year of the Lord 111.

Papias, hearer and disciple of Saint John, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, a most steadfast propagator and defender of the Christian faith, disciple and zealous imitator of the holy apostles, wrote little works of authority not to be despised. Among these there exists a distinguished work, divided into five volumes, which he titled thus: Explanation of the Sayings of the Lord, books 5. Other things which he wrote we have not seen. He first invented the novelty of the thousand years, after which he dreamed that Christ would reign again in the flesh with the elect upon the earth; those who afterwards spread this error were called Chiliasts, from the thousand.

He flourished in the times of Caesar Trajan, in the year of the Lord 100 and thereabout.

Hegesippus, a Jew by nation, converted to the faith of Christ, shone forth as admirable in teaching and holiness in the Church of God; his feast has a place in the martyrology with the other saints. He wrote several little works of excellent talent, of which I have found only this: from the time of the Lord’s Passion down to his own age, a distinguished work, History of Ecclesiastical Acts, books 5. In the Parthian war, which between I have seen no other work of his.

He flourished near the apostolic times, under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 160.

Justin, converted from being a philosopher to the catholic faith, a distinguished lover and worshipper of Christ, when in the city of Rome he rebuked Crescens the Cynic, who was blaspheming Christians, as gluttonous and afraid of death, and as a follower of luxury and lusts, was accused before the senate through that man’s plots, because he was a Christian, and was crowned with martyrdom for Christ. He wrote many distinguished little works in defense of our faith, of which these are reported:

Against the Gentiles, to Antoninus, book 1. On the Soul, book 1. To Aurelius, Against the Gentiles, book 1. The Pre-noted Psalter, book 1. Likewise Against the Gentiles, book 1. Against Trypho the Jew, book 1. Corrections Against the Gentiles, book 1. Against Marcion, book 1. On the Monarchy of God, book 1. Against All Heresies, book 1. Others

Abbot of Spanheim.

He composed, besides, many other works which have not come to our knowledge. He flourished under Antoninus Pius, in the year of the Lord 150.

Quadratus, an Athenian, bishop after the martyr Publius, once a hearer and disciple of the holy apostles, a man steadfast and of incomparable learning, labored much for the usefulness of the Christian faith, made much progress, and gathered into the unity of the faith the church dispersed by fear of persecution. Since he was an eminent teacher, he wrote, among other things, on behalf of the Christians to the emperor Hadrian, an Apologeticum full of instruction, 1 book. And other works unknown to us. At last he suffered for the defense of the catholic faith on the seventh day before the Kalends of June. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Aristides, an Athenian philosopher, a man most learned in secular letters and very studious in the divine scriptures, shone forth distinguished by such eloquence that he offered the nations a marvel of himself; under the garb of a philosopher he bore both Christian faith and Christian conduct, and shone forth renowned by reputation, not without holiness. He wrote an Apologeticum on behalf of the Christians to the emperor Hadrian, 1 book. And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Hadrian, in the year of the Lord 120.

Melito the Asian, bishop of Sardis, a man learned in the divine scriptures and venerable no less for holiness than for doctrine, shone forth renowned among catholic preachers. For the usefulness of the church of the faithful he wrote many distinguished volumes, of which these are reported:

On Easter, 2 books. On the Life of the Prophets, 4 books. On the Church, 1 book. On the Fallen, 1 book. On the Lord’s Day, 1 book. On the Body and the Soul, 1 book. On the Senses, 1 book. On Baptism, 1 book. On Faith, 1 book. On Truth, 1 book. On Hospitality, 1 book. On the Generation of Christ, 1 book. The book entitled Key, 1. On the Prophet, 1 book. On the Devil, 1 book. Of Selections, 6 books. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. On the Passing of Saint Mary, 1 book. Melito, servant of Christ,

He also published other small works, which age has not permitted to come down to our memory. Tertullian, mentioning in a certain passage this man’s elegant and declamatory talent, says that he was regarded by our people as a prophet. It should indeed be noted that the book On the Passing of Saint Mary ascribed to him is reckoned among the apocrypha, in distinction 15, Sancta Romana. He flourished under the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 160.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Theophilus, sixth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man very devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in talent and speech, and an excellent declaimer, wrote many volumes for the benefit of the faithful, and shone forth as an excellent expounder of the Lord’s discourses. Of his little works the following are reported:

Against Marcion, one book. Commentaries on the Gospels, four books.

To Autolycus, three books. On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book.

He also composed several other short treatises pertaining to the edification of the Catholic Church, which among the Latins are rarely found together. He was ordained bishop in the year of the Lord 173, indiction II.

Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, a learned man and distinguished defender of the Christian faith, eminent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, in which he showed himself a man not so much learned as zealous. Among them these are reported:

Apologetic for the Christians, two books. On Truth, three books.

Against the Cataphrygians, five books.

But he also published some other works, knowledge of which antiquity has taken from us. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 165.

Dionysius, bishop of the church of the Corinthians, a most eloquent man and very learned in the divine Scriptures, a most vigilant shepherd of Christ’s flock, was of such concern and diligence that he instructed not only the people of his own city with salutary teachings, but also, by letters, summoned the peoples of foreign cities to constancy in the faith. These letters are indeed reported to be so useful and lengthy that they may not improperly be called books; of them the following are listed:

To the Lacedaemonians, one letter. To the Athenians, one letter.

To the Nicomedians, one letter. To the Cretans, one letter.

To the Gnosians, one letter. To the Pope and the Romans, one letter.

To the Amastrians, one letter. To Chrysophora, a woman, one letter.

He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 170, not without a reputation for sanctity, and wrote various works.

Tatian, heresiarch, hearer and follower of Justin Martyr, did not depart from his side for as long as [unclear]. But afterward, when Saint Justin had been crowned, puffed up with swelling eloquence, he founded a new heresy, which is called that of the Encratites, which Severus later enlarged; from him those of the same party

[unclear] heretics were called Severians. They abominate flesh, do not drink wine, do not accept the Old Testament, and do not believe in the resurrection. Tatian, however, wrote almost countless volumes, though they have not come to my knowledge. For because of the teacher's error, even his writings, despised, perished. There survives, with Jerome as witness, a distinguished volume of his, which he entitled Against the Gentiles, book 1. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus, in the year of the Lord 170.

Philip, bishop of Crete, that is, of the city of [Gortyna?], whom Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, placed above, mentions in his letter which he had written to the church of that same city, a noble and learned man, published for the benefit of believers volumes sufficiently instructive, as they say, which have by no means come into our hands. There survives one book of his, Against Marcion. He also wrote certain letters to various persons and various treatises, which have still by no means come into our hands. He flourished in the year of the Lord 170, in the times of the emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus.

Modestus, a man indeed of flourishing talent, although it is unknown to us what dignity or rank he held, wrote, as blessed Jerome witnesses, little works not contemptible in their reading, in which the abundant vein of his talent is seen. Of these there survives a distinguished volume, Against Marcion, book 1. The rest are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 175.

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon in Gaul after the triumph of blessed Photinus the martyr, formerly a hearer of Polycarp the martyr, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and very learned, sent as legate to Rome under Pope Eleutherius, was approved as most illustrious no less in holiness than in doctrine. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which these are reported: Against the Gentiles, one book. On the Monarchy of God, book 1. On Discipline, book 1. On the Ogdoad, book 1. To Blastus on Schism, book 1. On Easter, to Pope Victor, book 1. Against Heresies, book 1, Insofar as the truth re[unclear]. On Apostolic Preaching, one book. Of Various Treatises, one book. He also wrote many other things, which have still by no means come to my knowledge. At last, when persecution was raging against the Christians, with all fer[unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear] with the people of his city he was crowned with martyrdom for the Catholic faith on the fourth calends of July. He flourished under Marcus Antoninus, in the year of the Lord 175.

Theodotion, by origin an Ephesian, once a pupil of Tatian the philosopher while he was still faithful, a man certainly most learned from every source, and the third interpreter of the divine Scriptures, besides the translation of the Scriptures which he made Latin from the Hebrew, also wrote certain other little works, which however have not yet come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Commodus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Rhodon, an Asian by race, once a hearer and pupil of Tatian, most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, is said to have written many works in the Greek language, copies of which are rarely found among our people. Of these, however, the more important are reported to be those which we have set down:

Against Marcion, 3 books. To Callition, 1 book. Against the Cataphrygians, 1 book. On the Hexameron, 6 books.

He flourished under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Clement, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, hearer and pupil of Pantaenus the Stoic, once a Christian philosopher, who after him held the ecclesiastical school at Alexandria for many years, was a devout, learned, and most eloquent man. He wrote many distinguished volumes, of which these are reported:

Stromata, that is, Varieties, 1 book. On Disputation, 1 book. Against the Nations, [unclear] books. On the Salvation of a Rich Man, 1 book. The Pedagogue, 3 books. On Detraction, 1 book. On Easter, [unclear] book. Against Those Judaizing, [unclear] books. On Fasting, 1 book. On Ecclesiastical Canons, 1 book.

He also published many letters and various treatises, whose titles we do not know. He flourished in the times of the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Melciades, whom Rhodon remembered in his work which he composed against the Cataphrygians, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, the mad prophets, a man most learned in secular letters and exercised by constant study in the divine Scriptures, wrote not a few little works for the edification of the faithful, of which the following are reported:

Against the Nations, 1 book. Against the Jews, 1 book. Against the Nations, 1 book. An Apologetic for Our Faith, 1 book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Marcus Antoninus Commodus, in the year of the Lord 170. Apol-

The Abbot of Sponheim

Apollonius, a certain learned and most eloquent man, distinguished no less in life than in eloquence, a most valiant overthrower of heretical depravity, composed many things for our faith, and often refuted the madness of Montanus in words and writings, as is clear to those reading that notable volume which he is said to have composed with the greatest charms of eloquence:

Against Montanus, 1 book.

But he published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 180.

Serapion, formerly an anchorite and the eighth bishop of the church of Antioch, a man of keen intellect, very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge, is reported to have fashioned several little works for the [unclear] of believers, in which he shows himself a learned man and a most vigorous defender of the Christian faith. Of their number there are:

To Domnon Judaizing, one book. To Carinus on Montanus, 1 book. On the Gospel under the Name of Peter, 1 book. Of brief but numerous letters, one book.

He was ordained bishop of the aforesaid city under Commodus, ruler of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 193, in the first indiction.

Apollonius, a senator of the city of Rome, a man most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, venerable no less for sanctity than for knowledge, when before the senate he had been denounced as a Christian and refused to deny Christ, received sentence of death, since an old law among them prevailed that Christians were not to be released without denial, once they had been brought before their judgment. Among other things he wrote:

An Apologetic for Our Faith, 1 book.

When he had recited this in order before the senate, he was beheaded. He flourished at Rome under the rulers Commodus and Severus, in the year of the Lord 190.

Tertullian, presbyter, by origin a Carthaginian of the African province, his father being a centurion, a proconsular man, a man of keen and vehement intellect, most learned both in the divine and in secular writings, since indeed at Carthage he gloriously taught rhetoric for many years, wrote almost countless little works in the Latin language, in which he strongly crushed the errors of the heretics. The most blessed martyr Cyprian held this man’s writings in such veneration that he let no day pass without reading them; for he was accustomed to say to his secretary, “Give me the master,” meaning Tertullian. At last he slipped into the error of Montanus

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He is called apocryphal, because his little works are counted among the apocrypha, Distinction XV, Sancta Romana. And although he erred in some matters, nevertheless he wrote well on many, as his volumes attest. Of these I have seen: On the Patience of God, one book, “I confess to the Lord God”; Against Praxeas, one book; Against Marcion, five books; Against the Jews, [unclear]; Against All Heresies, one book; On the Prescriptions of Heretics, one book; Against Hermogenes, one book; Against the Valentinians, one book; On the Flesh of Christ, one book; On the Resurrection of the Flesh, one book; On the Soldier’s Crown, one book; To the Martyrs, one book; On Repentance, one book; On the Veiling of Virgins, one book; On Women’s Dress, one book; On the Adornment of Women, one book; To His Wife, two books; On Persecution, to Fabius, one book; To Scapula, one book; an Exhortation to Chastity, one book; On Monogamy, one book; On the Pallium, one book; On Spectacles, one book; On Fasts, one book; On Ecstasy, one book; Against Apollonius, one book; On Modesty, one book.

He also wrote many other things and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands at all; and he lived studiously even to old age and senescence. He flourished in the times of the emperor Severus, in the year of the Lord 200.

Origen, who is also Adamantius, a priest, Alexandrian by nation, son of the martyr Leonides, once a disciple of Clement of Alexandria, was a man of great and excellent talent, so that in zeal and learning he never had his equal. In the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, when a persecution was set in motion against the Christians and his father Leonides was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, he was left poor with his widowed mother and six brothers, being about seventeen years old.

The Abbot of Spanheim

For the treasury had seized all their substance because of their confession of Christ, so that they no longer had anything from which they might live. And although the number of years was reckoned slight in the young man, nevertheless his learning was already wonderful, and his constancy in the Christian faith admirable. For he had resolved to die bravely with his father, the faithful Leonides, for the faith of Christ, had it not happened that, by his mother’s stratagem, he was preserved for the usefulness of the Church, since he was to become a great teacher. For when, early in the morning, he had resolved to run to his father at the place of contest on the preceding day, his garments were taken away by his mother during the night, and the doors of the chamber were locked, and he was forced to remain at home.

When, however, he had grown into a man, he resolved to lead the apostolic life, and, proclaiming the word of God in the region around him, he went about barefoot for many years. Finally, he never slept on a bed stuffed with feathers; he abstained completely from wine and meat, except in illness; he was intent on serving God devotedly with fasts, vigils, prayers, and continual studies and expositions of the divine Scriptures. Also, according to Christ’s counsel, he was accustomed to wear only one tunic, and, having become a despiser of all worldly things, he took no thought for the morrow. Out of love of chastity, so that he might dare to preach safely to women, he had himself castrated, although in this deed zeal remained without knowledge.

Because of his learning, eloquence, and apostolic life, Mammaea, the most Christian mother of the emperor Alexander, when she was seized with a desire to hear him, came from Alexandria to Antioch, and heard his honey-sweet doctrine with great admiration. He was so intent upon the study of the divine Scriptures that he never took either food or sleep unless one [unclear] of the brothers had first delivered a reading of the Scriptures while all listened. He knew the New and Old Testament by heart like another Ezra, and when already an old man, contrary to his age, he learned the Hebrew language; and with wonderful zeal he brought together into one all the editions of the interpreters, besides the Septuagint.

In dictating editions of the Scriptures he had so admirable a memory and subtlety that, with incredible speed of utterance, he wore out seven notaries and the same number of girls, very swift in writing, besides other young men, all at the same time writing different things from his mouth. And although he was held, and was, so great and distinguished a teacher among all ecclesiastical men, nevertheless he is marked by great errors, by which either he himself was foolish, or he was corrupted by others inserting false things into his writings. The opinion of learned men about Origen was always varied, some asserting that he was a heretic, others affirming that a fraud had been imposed upon him. It is not to be wondered

On Ecclesiastical Writers

... it is not [unclear], if he erred as the first man without an example, who expounded so many volumes without a preceding teacher. Yet it is our part, not only concerning Origen, but concerning any writers whatsoever, to think with the holy Roman Church and to despise superfluous opinions. He published, moreover, almost infinite volumes, of which I have seen only the following translated into Latin:

On Genesis, 16 homilies. “In the beginning God made...” “It seems to me one...”

On Exodus, 15 homilies. “As on the last day...” “As on the last days...”

On Numbers, 28 homilies. “In Numbers not all...” “The Lord gave a name...”

On Joshua, 26 homilies. “God for doing good...”

On Judges, 9 homilies. “As long as King Uzziah...”

On the beginning of [Idida?], 2 homilies. “Not from the beginning only...”

On Isaiah the prophet, 9 homilies.

On Jeremiah the prophet, 4 books.

On Ezekiel, 14 homilies.

Likewise on the Gospel of Matthew, 26 homilies.

On the Song of Songs, 4 books. “As formerly among the people...” “Concerning the Song of Songs...”

On the number 150. “Blessed is the man,” this psalm.

Against Heretics, 5 books. “Adamantius said, who...”

Against Celsus the philosopher, 8 books.

Periarchon, 4 books. “All who believe...”

On the Epistle to the Romans, 15 books. “Because the rest of the Apostle Paul...”

On the beginning of John, 1 book.

He also composed many other works, which have not come into our hands. There are those who write that they have read six thousand treatises of Origen, a number both large and unknown to the Latins. Nor is there any doubt that many little works of his have lately been translated, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading. He died an old man and poor, buried at Tyre, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 261, the ninth indiction, in the seventieth year of his age.

Ammonius of Alexandria, the most celebrated of all men of his time, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language certain distinguished volumes, by which he left the memory of himself to posterity; of their number the following are extant:

On the Harmony of Jesus and Moses, 1 book.

Of the Evangelical Canons, 1 book. “In the first canon four...”

One from Four, 1 book. “Since indeed many...”

And certain other things. The most impious Porphyry, a pagan philosopher and the bitterest enemy of Christians, falsely accuses him of having denied the faith and become a heathen, though it is established that he remained a devoted Christian until death. He flourished under Alexander, son of Mammaea, in the year of the Lord 230.

Ambrose, a hearer of Origen, first a Marcionite and afterward corrected by Origen himself, an outstanding confessor of the Christian faith, also deserved to be promoted to the office of deacon. He was certainly a most learned man and a zealous lover of books; with him furnishing the expenses, notaries, and copyists, our Adamantius composed almost infinite volumes. He was so great an admirer of his studies that day and night he urged him on, in words and in writings, to write something new, so that in a certain familiar letter he is named by Origen as the taskmaster of the work. He used to say that he never went to bed in Origen’s presence, nor took food, unless first one of the brethren who was always present had sounded forth in the letters of the sacred offering. He wrote, concerning his conversion, giving thanks, to Origen:

Epistles, 1 book.

And certain other things. He flourished with Origen in the year of the Lord 230.

Tryphon, a hearer and disciple of Origen, to whom some of Origen’s letters are extant, a man most learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Greek language certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are extant:

On the Red Heifer in Deuteronomy, 1 book.

On the Quality of Sacrifices, 1 book.

On the Dove and the Turtle-Dove, 1 book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 230.

Minucius Felix, an advocate, Roman by nationality, a man most learned in secular letters and zealous in divine readings, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote in the Latin language certain distinguished little works, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these there is extant a dialogue between a Christian and a heretic, which Octa-

On Ecclesiastical Writers

The eighth is entitled, one book. On Fate, against the Astrologers, one book. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 230.

Beryllus, bishop of Bostra in Arabia, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and exceptionally instructed in secular letters, after he had governed the church gloriously for some time, at last fell into the heresy of the Paulianists, who denied that Christ existed before Mary; but, corrected by Origen, he wrote many things, of which there survives a Dialogue held among them, one book; Letters to Various Persons, one book; and certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Alexander, in the year of the Lord 254.

Hippolytus, bishop of a certain city whose name Jerome did not specify, certainly a man both studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, wrote many and almost incredible volumes, so that Ambrose, of whom we have already made mention above, used to urge Origen to imitate him, and strongly encouraged him to expound the divine Scriptures, providing him, as we have said, with seven copyists, the same number of very swift girls for writing, and a considerable number of book-copyists, with their costs and expenses. You would have seen a beautiful and delightful contest, in which each of the two greatly desired to surpass the other in the publication of books. The following are reported among the works of Hippolytus: On the Hexameron, six books; On the Apocalypse, one book; On Genesis, one book; On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book; On Exodus, one book; On Ecclesiastes, one book; On the Song of Songs, one book; On the Antichrist, one book; On the Prophet Zechariah, one book; Against Marcion, one book; On Daniel, one book; Against All Heresies, three books. He also published many and varied treatises on the Psalms, as well as homilies and sermons almost innumerable, and many other works still unknown to us. He flourished under the prince Alexander, in the year of the Lord 220.

Alexander, bishop of Cappadocia, when out of desire for the holy places he was traveling to Jerusalem, was there, by divine revelation, ordained bishop after Saint Narcissus. Illustrious for much holiness and learning, he shone forth, and at last, for the faith of Christ, under Decius, a most impious tyrant, completed his martyrdom. He wrote many elegant letters to various persons, among which the following are chiefly reported: On the Peace of the Church, to the Aaronites, one letter; For Origen against Demetrius, one letter; To the Antiochenes, a letter; To Origen, several letters. COrnelius, Romanae vrbis post Petrum XXII. episcopꝰ, patria Romanꝰ, patre Castino, post Fabiani gloriosum martyrium Papa creatus, sedit in cathedra Petri annis duobus, vir doctꝰ atque sanctissimus, donec tandem etiam ipse martyrio coronatus, trāsiuit carne solutus ad superos. Scripsit aīt plures ad vtilitatem ecclesiasticam epistolas, de quibus ego duntaxat reperi subiectas: Ad Fabium Antiochenum episcopum: De synodis epist.i. De Nouatiano epist.i. Ad eundē de Nouatianis lib.i. De gestis synodi epi.i. Ad Cyprianũ Carthaginẽn epifcopum plures scripsit epistolas, &amp; alias ad alios. Claruit sub Decio tyrãno principe, anno dn̄ii 255. CYprianus, ecclesie Carthaginensis in Aphrica episcopus, vir doctus atqꝫ sanctassimꝰ, multis annis rhetoricam gloriofe do- cuit, &amp; in omni literatura seculari doctor magnificus fuit. De- inde persuadente presbytero Caecilio, à quo fortitus est cognomẽ, adfide m Christi conuerfus, omnem substantiam suam pauperibꝰ ero

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He suffered at Caesarea under Decius, in the year of the Lord 253, in the first indiction.

Julius Africanus, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, historiographer, and distinguished theologian, and a most ardent lover of divine Scripture and of books, founded by his own efforts and at his own expense a notable library at Caesarea in Palestine, in which he gathered many volumes both of secular and of divine writings. He also wrote several very useful little works, of which the following are reported:

Five books of Chronicles. One book On Easter.

One book On the Holy Trinity. One book On the Sabbath.

One book On Circumcision. One book To Origen on Susanna.

One book On Attalus. One book To Aristides the Philosopher.

And he is said to have composed many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Marcus Aurelius, in the year of the Lord 220.

Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, a hearer and disciple of Origen, a learned and holy man, both wrote many things and, while living, shone forth with miracles. While still a young man, seeking the study of secular philosophy with his brother Athenodorus, he placed himself under the school of Origen; by him, together with his brother, he was gradually, as if imperceptibly, converted to the faith of Christ, and became a most learned and most holy man. Of his writings there survives:

One book, a Panegyric addressed to Origen. One book of Interpretations on Ecclesiastes.

And several letters. He flourished under the emperor Gordian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Cornelius, the twenty-second bishop of the city of Rome after Peter, a Roman by birth, his father being Castinus, was made pope after the glorious martyrdom of Fabian and sat in the chair of Peter for two years, a learned and most holy man, until at last he too, crowned with martyrdom, passed, released from the flesh, to those above. He wrote several letters for the benefit of the Church; of these I have found only the following:

To Fabius, bishop of Antioch:

One letter On Synods. One letter On Novatian.

To the same, one book On the Novatians. One letter On the Acts of the Synod.

He wrote several letters to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, and others to other persons. He flourished under the tyrant emperor Decius, in the year of the Lord 255.

Cyprian, bishop of the church of Carthage in Africa, a learned and most holy man, taught rhetoric gloriously for many years, and was a magnificent teacher in all secular literature. Then, at the persuasion of the presbyter Caecilius, from whom he obtained his surname, he was converted to the faith of Christ, [unclear] all his substance to the poor

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...he distributed. And not long afterward, having been chosen priest, he was also ordained bishop. Since he was zealous in the divine Scriptures, he usefully published many things for the edification of the faithful, and composed the following volumes in the Latin language, namely:

On the Grace of God, to Donatus, one book: “You admonish well, Donatus...” Against Demetrianus, one book: “You, barking at and against...” [unclear], one book: “Many and great are...” On Piety and Almsgiving, one book: “You desired, Fortunatus...” On the Praise of Martyrdom, one book: “Be zealous for what is good...” On Zeal and Envy, one book: “Let us speak of patience...” On the Good of Patience, one book: “And if among very many...” On Mortality, one book: “The evangelical precepts...” On Virginity, one book: “Discipline, guardian of hope...” On the Lapsed, one book: “Peace, behold, most beloved...” On the Sacrament of the Cup, one book: “Cyprian to his brother Caecilius...” On the Unity of the Church, one book: “Since the Lord warns and...” On the Lord’s Prayer, one book: “The chief evangelical...” On the Vanity of Idols, one book: “That idols are not gods...” On the Life of Clerics, one book: “I had indeed promised you...” On the Two Mountains, one book: “The proof of the chapters...” To Antonianus concerning Novatus, one book: “We have received the first letters...” On the Jews, to Quirinus, two books: “The Jews into offense...” To Pope Cornelius, eight letters: “We have learned, dear brother...” On Gamblers, one book. To Julianus his friend, one book.

He is said to have composed letters to various people and also many other works, which have not come into our hands. The little book On the Twelve Abuses of the Age, ascribed by many to Cyprian, does not have the flavor of his style. At length he suffered martyrdom under Valerian, on the same day as Cornelius at Rome, but not in the same year, namely in the year of the Lord 249, in the twelfth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.

Pontius the priest, hearer and disciple of blessed Cyprian, a learned and holy man and an outstanding declaimer, after the glorious triumph of his master came into Gaul and at the city of Cymerla won the palm of martyrdom for the faith of Christ. This Pontius, by his honey-flowing preaching and industry, converted the two emperors Philips to Christ, and persuaded them, the first of the Roman rulers, to renounce idols. He also wrote, in an elegant style, a notable volume, which contains:

The Life of Saint Cyprian, one book: “Cla[unclear]...”

Abbot of Sponheim

He flourished under the emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 240.

Dionysius, the thirteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, once a hearer and disciple of Origen, while he was still a priest held the public school under Heraclas, and gained great glory for his learning. For he was a man most learned in every science of doctrines, a distinguished philosopher, rhetorician, and theologian. Agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and of the African synod concerning the rebaptizing of heretics, he wrote very many letters on that matter to various people, of which the following are reported among the number:

On Penance, to Flavianus, one letter. To the Romans, one letter. To Saint Pope Sixtus, two letters. To the priests Philemon and Dionysius, two letters. Against Nepos the Chiliast, one book. To Pope Dionysius, one letter composed. Against Sabellius, four books. To Novatian the heretic, one letter: “Dionysius to Novatian...” To Ammon, bishop of Berenice, one letter. To Pope Dionysius, four books. To Telephorus, one letter. To Dionysius and Didymus, one letter. To the Laodiceans, on Penance, one letter. To Euphranor, one letter. To the Armenians, on Penance, one book. To Origen, on Martyrdom, one letter. On the Order of Sins, one letter. To the Alexandrians, on Exile, one letter. A Canon on Penance, one book. On Easter. On Nature, to Timothy, one book. To Heraclas, bishop in Egypt, one book. On Temptations, one book. Commentaries on Ecclesiastes, one book. To Basilides also several letters of his are reported.

An outstanding letter of his against Paul of Samosata is extant, which he had written a few days before his death. He also composed many other works for ecclesiastical utility, which are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Gallus and Volusianus, in the year of the Lord 255.

Novatian, priest of the Roman church, attempted to seize the episcopal chair against Cornelius; when he could not do so, he stirred up the first schism in the Roman Church and established the heresy of the Novatians, refusing to receive penitent apostates and rebaptizing those duly baptized. The author of this error was Novatus, Cyprian’s priest. Now Novatian wrote:

On Easter, one book. On Jewish Foods, one book. On the Sabbath, one book. On Urgency, one book. On [unclear]...
