On Ecclesiastical Writers

On Circumcision, one book. On Attalus, one book. On the Priest, one book. On the Holy Trinity, one book. On Prayer, one book. Several letters to various persons. He is said, moreover, to have written some other works, which have not come to my notice. He flourished in the times of the emperor Philip, in the year of the Lord 250.

Malchion, presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and very eloquent man, since indeed he taught rhetoric in that same city for many years with the greatest success, published some distinguished little works, which in his own time seemed greatly useful for the defense of the Christian faith against heretics. Of these there survives an excellent work of dialogues:

Against Paul of Samosata, one book.

To Pope Dionysius, from the synod, one epistle.

He flourished under the rulers Claudius and Aurelian, in the year of the Lord 270.

Victorinus, bishop of [Pictavium?], a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, furnished with Greek and Latin eloquence, wrote many distinguished little works, in which he magnificently exercised his talent. He was an eminent preacher of the divine word, and at last is read to have been crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ. Of his writings the following are reported:

On Genesis, one book. On Habakkuk, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Ecclesiastes, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. On the prophet Isaiah, one book. On the Apocalypse, one book. On Ezekiel, one book. Against All Heresies, one book.

And many others. He flourished in the times of the rulers Valerian and Gallienus, in the year of the Lord 270.

Pamphilus, presbyter of Eusebius of Caesarea, gathered so many books at Caesarea out of love for the Scriptures that in all the world at that time no library was more celebrated. Indeed he copied out a large part of Origen’s books with his own hand and placed them in that same Caesarean library. From him Eusebius obtained the surname Pamphili. But before Eusebius began to write, he wrote little works of authority not to be despised, of which I have found only:

Against the Mathematicians, one book.

An Apology for Origen, one book.

He is also reported to have written certain letters full of faith and learning. At last, after blessed studies and many labors for the church of God, he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ at Caesarea in Palestine, under the persecution of Maximian, who ruled around the years of the Lord 240.

Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures and second to none in secular letters in his own time, an eminent rhetorician, astronomer, and geometer, left many distinguished little works of his talent; yet very few of them have come to our notice. There survives his notable volume, entitled:

On Easter, one book. On Arithmetic Instruction, ten books.

He flourished under the rulers Probus and Carus, in the year 285.

Three sermons by the same author, On Death, in Greek, are preserved in Italy, namely at Rome, as some will have it.

Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia in Syria, a learned man and a keen disputant, wrote some little works in the Syriac language, which among the Latins are rarely found. At the end of [Persia?] he disputed vigorously against Mani the heresiarch, and confounded all his arguments, although he could not call him back from error. He wrote that same disputation:

Against Mani, one book.

Other works, however, are unknown to us. He flourished under the rulers Aurelian and Probus, in the year of the Lord 280.

Lucian, presbyter of the church of Antioch and afterwards bishop of Nicomedia, a learned and eloquent man, was of excellent talent in delivering homilies to the people, and venerable no less for his life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures. Under the persecution of Maximian he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ, and was buried at Helenopolis in Bithynia. He wrote, among other things:

On Our Faith, one book.

And various other treatises, sermons, homilies, and letters. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Pierius, presbyter of the church of Alexandria, a man of such learning and eloquence that he was called the younger Origen, was most excellent in delivering homilies to the people. Under Theonas, bishop of the Alexandrians, shining most brightly in life and doctrine, he was an eminent cultivator of voluntary poverty for the love of Christ, and an admirable teacher of the people. He wrote countless treatises, which, however, have not come to our notice. There survives his very long treatise, delivered to the people on the vigil of Easter:

On the prophet Hosea, [unclear].

32
22 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. <Illegible reason="faded" extent="ca. 1 word"/> Hileas episcopus Thebaidae ciuitatis in Aegypto, vir nobilis atqꝫ doctissimus, nō minus moribus quàm eruditione scriptu- rarum insignis, post multos labores, & editos pro vtilitate fi- delium varios tractatus, tandem sub Maximiano imperatore pro fide Christi martyr effectus, euolauit ad superos. De cuius scriptis extat disputatio habita Contra iudicem iniquum li.i. De laude martyrum li.i. Alia quae scripsit, nobis incognita sunt, quanuis multa ferantur à patribus. Claruit sub Maximiano principe, Anno domini 240. A Rnobiꝰ presbyter, philosophus et rhetor insignis, cū adhuc gētilis rhetoricā doceret, diuina miseratiōe vocatus, Chria- nũ se ceꝑit p̄iteri. Cumqꝫ ad eẜos accedēs, se baptizari ex- peteret, nō credebāt, veriti ne vir seculari tumēs eloquentia, sacra- mentis fidei conaretur illudere, & ideo sententiam differebant. Ar nobius vero cernens sibi fidem minime adhiberi, in argumentum synceritatīs suꝝ, scripsit et obtulit episcopis insigne vosumen Aduersum Gentes li.i.7. In Pfalterium quoque li.i. De retoricainstitutione li.i. Alia quoqꝫ multa edidit, quae ad notitiam meam venerunt, Docuit in Aphrica retoricam sub Diocletiano principe. habuit multos egregios et nobiles discipulos, ꝗ viri doctissimi euaserunt. Claruit ergo circa annos domini nostri Iesu Christi 500. † Scripsit et in aliquot euangelistarum locos annotatiunculas. I Ohānes Climachus, qͦd Latine sonat scholasticus, abbas mon- tis Sinai, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus et eruditus, ingenio excellens, mitis et humilis, vita et conuerfatione deuotos atqꝫ sanctissimus, cum adhuc sexdecim esset annoꝝ, mundū cum suis oblectamentis deseruit, & in dicto coenobio monachū se fieri in- stantissime petijt, & obtinuit. Deinde post annos decem et nouem cum iam solitarius pugnare et vincere secundum regulam mona- chorum didicisset, cum licentia abbatis sui etrum petijt, in qua multis annis in omni sanctitate folus cum Deo habitauit. Postre- mo cum vita eius sanctissima oībus innotuisset, ynanimi oīm con- fensu in abbatē eligitur, & renités, ad coenobiiū reuocatur. Scripsit ad Iohannē abbatē de Raythu opus celeberrimū, & ꝓ institutione monachoꝝ valde accōmodū, habēs fermones triginta, qͦd p̄notat De triginta gradibus li.i. A bono et superbono Ad

On Ecclesiastical Writers, 22

[unclear]

Phileas, bishop of the city of [unclear] in Egypt, a noble and very learned man, distinguished no less for his character than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, after many labors and various treatises published for the benefit of the faithful, at last under the emperor Maximian was made a martyr for the faith of Christ and flew to the heavenly ones. Of his writings there is extant a disputation held

Against an Unjust Judge, one book. On the Praise of Martyrs, one book.

Other things that he wrote are unknown to us, although many are reported by the fathers. He flourished under the emperor Maximian, in the year of the Lord 240.

Arnobius the priest, an eminent philosopher and rhetorician, while he was still a pagan teaching rhetoric, was called by divine mercy and began to profess himself a Christian. And when, approaching them, he sought to be baptized, they did not believe him, fearing that a man swollen with worldly eloquence was trying to mock the sacraments of the faith; and therefore they postponed their decision. But Arnobius, seeing that no trust at all was being placed in him, as proof of his sincerity wrote and offered to the bishops an excellent volume:

Against the Nations, seven books.

Also On the Psalter, one book.

On the Teaching of Rhetoric, one book.

He also published many other things, which have come to my knowledge. He taught rhetoric in Africa under the emperor Diocletian. He had many excellent and noble pupils, who became very learned men. He therefore flourished around the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 500.

He also wrote brief annotations on some passages of the evangelists.

John Climacus, which in Latin means Scholasticus, abbot of Mount Sinai, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, excellent in talent, gentle and humble, in life and conduct devout and most holy: when he was still sixteen years old, he left the world with its pleasures, and very earnestly sought, and obtained, to be made a monk in the said monastery. Then, after nineteen years, when he had already learned, according to the rule of monks, to fight and conquer as a solitary, with the permission of his abbot he sought a desert place, in which for many years he lived alone with God in all holiness. Finally, when his most holy life had become known to all, by the unanimous consent of all he was elected abbot, and, though reluctant, was recalled to the monastery. He wrote to John, abbot of Raythu, a very celebrated work, and one very suitable for the instruction of monks, containing thirty sermons, which he entitled

On the Thirty Steps, one book.

The Abbot of Spanheim.

To Pastor, Sermons, one book: “In the lower book indeed ...” Several letters to monks, one book. And certain other things.

In certain places, especially where he treats of the impassibility of the mortified spiritual man, he is censured by modern theologians, as is found in certain treatises in John Gerson. He flourished around the times of Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, brothers and emperors, who reigned in the year of the Lord 346.

Ildephonsus, bishop of the see of Toledo after St. Eugenius, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant either of secular literature, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and above all the bishops of his time fluent and eloquent, worthy of God and most holy in life and conduct. For he was endowed with constancy in the fear of God, devoted in religion, abundant in compunction, grave in gait, praiseworthy in honor, singular in patience, renowned for his talent in discourse, supreme in wisdom. When, while still a boy, he had been touched by the divine spirit, despising the guilty world and the affections of his parents, he sought the monastery of Agali, and there for many years fittingly showed himself a monk. He also built a convent of virgins in the little village of Deibia, which he endowed from the wealth of his parents. Then, made abbot of the monastery of Agali, he trained the manners of the monks, administered its property, and preserved its life. After this, by princely violence he was brought back to Toledo, and there, after the death of his predecessor, was appointed bishop in his place. He wrote many distinguished little works, of which the following are reported:

On the Holy Trinity, one book. On His Own Weakness, one book. Various Hymns, one book. Annotations on Sacred Matters, one book. Many Epigrams, one book. Annotations on the Sacraments, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And very many other things.

When this most blessed prelate Ildephonsus had completed to the end the book on the virginity of Mary, the most pure Mother of God, whom he was always accustomed to serve most devotedly with all the zeal he could, the most holy Lady of the world appeared to him, holding that book in her hands and giving him thanks for such service, which she affirmed was most pleasing to her. Firmianus Lactantius, once a hearer and disciple of Arnobius the rhetorician, a man abundantly learned in secular letters and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, so that in the art of speaking he easily held the first place after Cicero, taught rhetoric gloriously, first at Nicomedia, then at Rome under Diocletian, having been summoned by him. There, when through lack of pupils he had fallen into poverty, at last, already an old man, he became tutor in Gaul to Caesar Crispus, son of Constantine. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which these are reported:

On the Divine Institutes, one book. “To the great and excellent...” book 1. “Although in the first book...” On the Origin of Error, book 1. “I should like it to be explained to me...” On False Wisdom, book 1. “As I was reflecting and when...” On True Wisdom, book 1. “There is no doubt with me...” On Justice, to Constantine, book 1. “Because it was the duty undertaken...” On True Worship, book 1. “It is well...” On the Blessed Life, book 1. “I have often observed, Do...” book 1. “How little I am one who...” On the Wrath of God, to Donatus, book 1. Letters to Probus, 4 books. Letters to Severus, two books. A Symposium in hexameter verse, one book. An Epitome against the Gentiles, book 1. The Grammarian, inscribed book 1. On Paradise, in hexameters, book 1. “There is a happy place in the first...” He says that he wrote not a few other things besides, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished under the emperor Constantine, to whom he was very dear, in the year of the Lord 320.

Eusebius, bishop of the church of Caesarea in Palestine, surnamed Pamphilus, once a disciple of Dorotheus the eunuch, a very learned man, most devoted to the divine Scriptures and, together with the martyr Pamphilus, a most diligent restorer of the ecclesiastical library: although he was an Arian, when he came to the first council of the Fathers held at Nicaea, he laid aside his error; and, following the opinion of the Fathers, by their command he composed the creed which is called Nicene and offered it to them to read and confirm as testimony of his own most pure faith. In it he vigorously crushed the errors of the Arians, and nothing has been either added to or subtracted from his edition, but to the present day it is publicly sung in the Church of God. Thereafter, persevering in the orthodox faith, he was most holily brought to his end. He wrote in Greek many excellent volumes, of which the following, that is, are current among the Latins:

Against Porphyry, 30 books. On Isaiah the Prophet, 10 books. Books of Gospel Expositions, 20. On Evangelical Preparation, 14 books. “Since what becomes Christians...” Ecclesiastical History, 10 books. “The successions of the saints...” Chronicle Epitome, book 1. “Moses of the Hebrew race...” Theophanies, 5 books. Topics, book 1. On the Life of Pamphilus, 3 books. Martyrology, book 1. On the Disagreement of the Evangelists, one book. Apology for Origen, 6 books. On the whole Psalter, book 1. He also composed many other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under the emperor Constantine the Great, to whom he was very dear because of his exceptional learning and holiness of life, in the year of the Lord 320.

Rheticius, bishop of the Aedui at Autun, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and in his time a teacher of renowned reputation, is said to have written not a few little works, and especially commentaries on various books; but we remember that few have come to our knowledge, namely:

On the Song of Songs, book 1. Against Novatian, book 1. Saint Jerome censures his exposition on the Song as inept. He flourished in Gaul under Constantine the Great, in the year of the Lord 320.

James, surnamed the Wise, bishop of Nisibis, a city of the Persians, a man of great learning and incomparable holiness, one of the number of the confessors victorious under the persecutor Maximian, attended the Council of Nicaea and condemned the most impious Arius by opposing the homoousion. This man of most holy conduct often delivered the city entrusted to him from many dangers by his prayers. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, not a few little works in the Syriac tongue, of which these are reported:

On the Resurrection, one book. On Life after Death, one book. On Humility, one book. On Patience, one book. On Penitence, one book. On Satisfaction, one book. On Virginity, one book. On the Perception of the Soul, one book. On Circumcision, one book. On the Blessing of Unleavened Bread, one book. On Christ, that he is the Son of God, one book. On Chastity, one book. Against the Gentiles, one book. On the Conversion of the Tabernacle, one book. On the Persecution of the Gentiles, one book. On the Kingdom of the Persians, one book. Of Christians, one book. He flourished under the great prince Constantine, in the year of the Lord 350.

Methodius, bishop of Olympus in Lycia and afterwards of Tyre, learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, an eminent confessor and defender of the Christian faith and a diligent emulator of evangelical perfection, after the publication of many volumes, was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ in Chalcis of Greece under the last persecution, or, as others affirm, under Decius and Valerian. He wrote not a few volumes in a polished and well-composed style, among which the following are reported:

Against Porphyry, one book. On the Resurrection, one book. On the Departure of the Soul, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. Also a Chronicle, one book. "For it must be known, brothers..." On the Pythoness, one book. A Symposium on the Ten Virgins, one book. He flourished under the great prince Constantine, or, as others prefer, under Decius and Valerian, in the year of the Lord 255.

Antony, monk and abbot, Egyptian by nation, a most holy man and distinguished inhabitant of the desert, whose praises the whole world proclaims, furnished many with a rule of religious and blessed life. Although he had not learned letters, yet he was so learned in the divine Scriptures that none of the teachers presumed to prefer himself to him. He had memory in place of books, understanding and sense in place of letters, grace in place of the study of reading. In the Egyptian language he dictated various letters, of apostolic meaning and speech, to diverse monasteries; among these there survives that distinguished one:

To the Arsenoites, one letter. To other monasteries, six letters.

He wrote [unclear].

Eius vitam beatus Athanasius, episcopus Alexandrinus, insigni vo lumine Gręco sermone descripit. Claruit sub Constantino Magno filijs eius regnantibus, anno domini 330. multis coruscans miraculis. I Vencus presbyter natione Hispanus, vir nobilis atque doctif- simus, philosophus, poeta, rhetor theologus insignis, non minus conuersatione quàm scientia scripturarum ecclesie ve nerabilis, edidit pro aedificatione legētium, tam metro quàm pro fa multa praeclara volumina:sed pauca eorum ad notitiam meam peruenerunt. Legi opus infigne, quod hexametris pentametrisc versibus composuit De quatuor Euangelijs lib.4. De Sacramentis lib.2. Caetera quae composuisse dicitur, ad manus nostras non venerunt. Claruit sub Constantinô Magno filijs eiꝰ, anno dn̄i 330. E Antiochenus genere Pamphylius, primo Beriae Syriae, ac deinde doctus sanctus, multa pro catholica fide ab Arrianis sustinuit it incommoda. In exilio naque Traianopolim Thraciarum relegatus, ibidem moritur, cuiꝰ Ariani ecclesiam inuadẽtes, multis eam annis tenuerũt. Scripsit autem maxime contra Arrianos plurima opuscula, aliosque diuersos varios tractatus, scilicet Aduersum Arrianos lib.5. De anima lib.I. Aduersum Origenem lib.II. Epistolas pene innūerabiliū lib.II. Claruit tēporibus Cōstantini filior̃ eius, anno dn̄i 340. A Thanasius, Alexandrinae vrbis nonufdecimus episcopus, vir sanctus, atque in diuinis scripturis doctiffimus, multas profide catholicae perfecutiões ab Arrianis suftinuit. Totus siqui dem orbis illi anguftus erat, Arrianis vbique perfequentibus, q nusquam tutus, nufquãm videbatur effe securus. Nam inimi ci hominis, domeftici ejus erāt. Fugiens ergo à facie imꝑatoris Arria nores, venit ad Treuerim vrbem Galliarum, à sancto Maximino archiepiscopo honorifice susceptus, septem annis apud monasteriu S. Maximi mini Treueri in crypta offenditur. In hoc loco multis annis (vt diximꝰ) latitans, folē nō viditibique symbolũ, Quicūque vult faluꝰ effe, d ij com 27 28 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. composuit, donec tandem à quadam puella proditus, Dei nutu fu- ga lapsus est. Cuius gesta si quis plenius agnoscere desiderat, tri par- titam historiam legat. Scripsit autem Graeco sermone pene infini- ta opufcula, de quibus apud Latinos subiecta reperi: De vnitate Trinitatis li.i. De proprijs perfonis trinitatis li.i. De hominis assumptione li.i. De nominibus trinitatis li.i. De vnica substantia trinitatis li.i. De beatitudine fidei li.i. De ꝓfessione regulae catholice li.i. De vnitate fidei li.i. De patre &; filio &; spũ sancto li.i. De trinitate &; spiritu sancto li.i. Ad Luciferum episcopum li.i. Contra obiecta Arrianorum li.i. Altercationẽ contra Arriũ et amp;c. li.i. Contra Valentē et amp; Vrfatium li.i. De virginitate li.i. Ad ep̃os Aegypti et amp; Libye li.i. De spiritu sancta li.i. Contra Gentes li.i. Contra Arrianos li.i. Aduerfus eosdem li.i. De patris et amp; filij homousion li.i. Dialogum cum Arriano li.i. Exhortatorium ad monachos li.i. Vitam sancti Antonij li.i. Symbolum fidei suae li.i. In omnes epistolas Pauli li.i. De perfeione Arrianorum li.i. De fuga et amp; exilio suo li.i. Epistolas plures ad diuerfos edidit, sermones quoqꝫ et amp; varios tra- ctatus, qui vel neum translati sunt in Latinum, vel ad notitiam meam non venerunt. The Abbot of Sponheim.

He also wrote a celebrated work in two books, entitled Melissa (that is, The Little Bee).

Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, described his life in Greek discourse in a notable volume.

He flourished under Constantine the Great, when his sons were reigning, in the year of the Lord 330, shining with many miracles.

Juvencus, a priest, a Spaniard by nation, a noble and most learned man, a philosopher, poet, rhetorician, and distinguished theologian, venerable to the Church no less in manner of life than in knowledge of the Scriptures, published for the edification of readers many excellent volumes, both in verse and in prose; but few of them have come to my knowledge. I have read the notable work that he composed in hexameter and pentameter verses:

On the Four Gospels, 4 books.

On the Sacraments, 2 books.

The other works that he is said to have composed have not come into our hands.

He flourished under Constantine the Great and his sons, in the year of the Lord 330.

Eustathius of Antioch, a Pamphylian by birth, first [bishop?] of Beroea in Syria, and then [unclear], learned and holy, endured many troubles from the Arians on behalf of the Catholic faith. For, having been banished into exile to Trajanopolis in Thrace, he died there; when the Arians invaded his church, they held it for many years. He wrote many small works, chiefly against the Arians, and various other diverse treatises, namely: Against the Arians, 5 books; On the Soul, 1 book; Against Origen, 2 books; Letters, almost innumerable, 2 books.

He flourished in the times of Constantine and his sons, in the year of the Lord 340.

Athanasius, the nineteenth bishop of the city of Alexandria, a holy man and most learned in the divine Scriptures, endured many persecutions from the Arians for the Catholic faith. Indeed, the whole world was narrow for him, with the Arians persecuting him everywhere, so that he seemed nowhere safe, nowhere secure. For a man’s enemies were those of his own household. Therefore, fleeing from the face of the Arian emperor, he came to Trier, a city of the Gauls, was honorably received by Saint Maximinus the archbishop, and for seven years [was hidden?] in a crypt at the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier. In this place, hiding for many years, as we have said, he did not see the sun, and there he composed the creed Whoever wishes to be saved, until at last, betrayed by a certain girl, by the will of God he escaped in flight. If anyone desires to know his deeds more fully, let him read the Tripartite History. He wrote in Greek discourse almost innumerable small works, of which I have found the following among the Latins:

On the Unity of the Trinity, 1 book.

On the Proper Persons of the Trinity, 1 book.

On the Assumption of Man, 1 book.

On the Names of the Trinity, 1 book.

On the Single Substance of the Trinity, 1 book.

On the Blessedness of Faith, 1 book.

On the Profession of the Catholic Rule, 1 book.

On the Unity of Faith, 1 book.

On the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, 1 book.

On the Trinity and the Holy Spirit, 1 book.

To Bishop Lucifer, 1 book.

Against the Objections of the Arians, 1 book.

A Disputation against Arius, etc., 1 book.

Against Valens and Ursacius, 1 book.

On Virginity, 1 book.

To the Bishops of Egypt and Libya, 1 book.

On the Holy Spirit, 1 book.

Against the Gentiles, 1 book.

Against the Arians, 1 book.

Against the Same, 1 book.

On the Homoousion of the Father and the Son, 1 book.

A Dialogue with an Arian, 1 book.

An Exhortation to Monks, 1 book.

The Life of Saint Antony, 1 book.

The Creed of His Faith, 1 book.

On All the Epistles of Paul, 1 book.

On the Persecution by the Arians, 1 book.

On His Flight and Exile, 1 book.

He published several letters to various persons, and also sermons and various treatises, which either have not yet been translated into Latin or have not come to my knowledge. He died in the time of the emperors Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 379, in the forty-sixth year of his priesthood, on the sixth day before the Nones of May, in the seventh indiction.

There are extant at Rome, in the Vatican Library, thirty-two sermons in Greek, and

The Abbot of Spanheim

And a treatise to Antiochus, on very many necessary questions which are doubtful in the sacred writings and ought to be known by all Christians.

Theodore, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an excellent declaimer of well-composed speech, published commentaries of no contemptible reading on the sacred volumes, of which the following are reported:

On the Psalter, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.

He is said also to have written some other works, but they have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Constantine II, in the year of the Lord 340.

Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man most learned in the divine writings, and in declaiming homilies to the people second to none in his time, a rhetorician and theologian most celebrated in the opinion of all, is said to have written many, almost innumerable, little works; but we have been able to find only the titles and numbers of a few, namely:

Against the Gentiles, one book. Of many homilies, one book. Against the Jews, one book. Sermons to the people.

He flourished while Constantine and his brothers were reigning, in the year of the Lord 550.

Triphyllius, bishop of Ledra or Leucotheon in Cyprus, a man most learned both in divine and in secular writings, and easily the most eloquent of all prelates in his age, is said to have written not a few volumes and to have expounded the divine writings in many ways; but I do not recall that anything of his works has come into our hands. His exposition is reported:

On the Song of Songs, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Constantius, in the year of the Lord 340.

Serapion, formerly a monk, bishop of Thmuis, and a very close friend of the blessed abbot Antony, a man of such great learning and eloquence that, on account of the excellence of his talent, he obtained the surname Scholasticus, is said to have written many little works, of which the following are extant:

Against the Manichaean, one book. On the Titles of the Psalms, one book. Several letters to various persons. He flourished under the prince Constantius, in the year of the Lord 540.

Acacius, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, a man indeed practiced in the divine Scriptures, but corrupted by Arian impiety, was held in such reverence by the emperor Constantius that he obtained the appointment of Felix, an Arian presbyter, as bishop at Rome in the place of Pope Liberius. This Acacius, because he was one-eyed, was called Monoculus. He wrote many varied treatises, which would truly have been useful if they had had a Catholic author. Of these, the more important are reported to be those which we set forth below:

On Ecclesiastes, seventeen books. Sethematon, sixteen books. Symicton, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 350.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, a man very venerable in morals, life, and doctrine, endured many wrongs from the Arians for the faith of Christ. For, through the faction of Saturninus, bishop of Arles, he was banished from the synod of Beziers into Phrygia, and for four years bore a hard exile with steadfast spirit; there, by his prayers, he is read to have called a dead man back to life. Since he was a man most learned in every respect, he composed many little works, of which the following are reported in number:

Against Dioscorus, one book. Against Valens and Ursatius, one book. On the Holy Trinity against the Arians, twelve books. “As I look about me” A Defense of the Catholic Faith, one book. “God, who is everywhere” Against the Arians, one book. “To the most beloved brothers” On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. “The step which Matthew” On the Synods, to the bishops of the Gauls, one book. “I had resolved” On some Psalms, forty-two treatises. On the Psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” twenty-two treatises. To the emperor Constantius, fifteen books. “The time for speaking now” Of Hymns, one book. Of Mysteries, one book. On the Book of Job, one book. Against Auxentius, one book. “To the most blessed and glorious” On Heresies, one book. On the Song of Songs, one book. Chronicles, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He also published some other works which have not come into our hands. At length, after returning to his city from his exile, he died under the emperor Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 371, in the fourteenth indiction; his feast is celebrated on the Ides of January.

Victorinus the African, a man of consular rank, the most celebrated rhetorician of all in his time, who in the city of Rome under the emperor Constantine taught rhetoric for a long time, where on account of the excellence of his learning he earned a bronze statue in the Forum of Trajan, having been converted to the faith of Christ in his old age, published many works on the sacred Scriptures,

Against the Arians, one book. On the Holy Trinity, one book. Its opening: “In the first discourse.” Against Heretics, one book. Its opening: “Logos,” or [unclear]. On the homoousion also, one book. Its opening: “He lives, and life [is] one.” On the Trinity, of hymns, one book. Its opening: “Be present, true light.” On the Epistles of the apostle Paul, one book. And certain other works. He flourished at Rome under the emperor Constantine, in the year of the Lord 360.

Titus, bishop of Botra, otherwise Bostrinus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, sharp and forceful in talent, is said to have fashioned many little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Of these, the following are given in number:

Against the Manichaeans, [unclear] books. A Commentary on the Gospel, one book. And many others. He flourished in the year of the Lord 340, and died under the emperor Valens.

Damasus the pope, Spanish by nation, sat after Liberius in the chair of Peter for eighteen years; a man most learned in divine matters and excellently instructed in secular letters, a very celebrated rhetorician and poet, and most skilled in composing verses; subtle in talent, devout in life and most holy, very dear to the priest Saint Jerome. He wrote various little works in both genres, of which the following are extant:

Deeds of the Supreme Pontiffs, one book. Its opening: “The blessed apostle Peter.” On Faith against Heretics, one book. Its opening: “Since after the Nicene council.” Letters to Various Persons, one book. Its opening: “Damasus the bishop.” Various poems. And other works. He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

Brocardium, or Book of Brocards, on properties.

Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, a man devoted to and learned in the divine writings, and by far most learned in grammatical instruction, sharp and forceful in talent, clear in speech, wrote certain distinguished volumes in defense of the Catholic faith, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these there is extant a very celebrated work:

Against the mad Porphyry, thirty books. And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

He also wrote a work in verse, embracing the whole Scripture of the Hebrews.

On the Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Didymus of Alexandria, blind from early childhood and on that account wholly ignorant even of the elements, furnished so great a marvel of himself that he learned perfectly dialectic and geometry, which especially require sight. In the divine Scriptures he was most learned, the teacher of blessed Jerome and very close friend of Saint Antony; sharp in talent and more distinguished in life. He wrote the following works in Greek:

Against the Arians, seven books. On Doctrines also, one book. On the Canonical Epistles, seven books. On the Holy Spirit, one book. On the Book of Saint Job, one book. On Hosea, to Jerome, three books. On Isaiah the prophet, ten books. On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On Zechariah, to the same, five books. On the Psalter also, one book. On the Gospel of John, one book. And certain other works. He flourished as an octogenarian under the emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 395.

[unclear]

Optatus, bishop of Milevis, African by nation, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, devout in life and Catholic, is said to have written certain distinguished little works in defense of our faith, in which he magnificently exercised his abundant talent. Of these there is said to be extant a large and notable volume, which he wrote:

Against the Donatists, six books. And several letters. And many other works. He flourished under the princes Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370.

[unclear]

Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a most learned and most holy man, was of such authority among the Greeks that no one, however slightly learned, ever dared to contradict his teaching or writings in anything. He wrote many distinguished little works in Greek, but few of them have come into our hands:

On the Holy Spirit, one book. Against Eunomius, one book. On the Hexaemeron, eleven homilies. Its opening: “In the beginning,” etc. [unclear] Rule of Monks, one book. Its opening: “The human race.” Exhortation of Monks, one book. Its opening: “Hear, my son, the admonition.” On the Instruction of Boys, one book. On Faith, one book. On Hidden Speech, one book. To a Fallen Virgin, one book. The Abbot of Sponheim.

Many homilies, namely twenty-nine.

In addition he composed other treatises, sermons, and letters for various [unclear].

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 380.

He also wrote an Exposition on Isaiah; likewise On the Soul, On Natural Principles and Causes, Several Chapters on the Divine Nature, On Synods, and Origen’s Philocalia.

Ephrem, a monk and distinguished inhabitant of the desert, and deacon of the church of Edessa, ordained priest by blessed Basil, because of his humility never approached to perform the divine mysteries, although he was held worthy before God and men. Nevertheless, so far as pertained to his office, in admonishing the people he delivered countless homilies. He, as is read in the Lives of the Holy Fathers, was seen to have received from an angel a book written in golden letters; whence immediately on the next day, and thereafter, with the Holy Spirit speaking in him, he had such grace in declaiming that he found no one like himself in his time. He wrote in the Syrian tongue, for the instruction of readers, certain devout little works, of which the following are found among the Latins, namely:

On the Holy Spirit, one book. On Compunction of Heart, one book. On Contrition of Heart, one book. On Repentance, one book. On the Struggles of the World, one book. On the Day of Judgment, one book. On the Resurrection, one book. On the Blessedness of the Soul, one book. On Thoughts, one homily. On Severe Preaching, one homily. On the Celebration of the Mysteries, one homily. Lament over the City of Edessa, one book.

He also published not a few other works, especially sermons and homilies to the people, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Valentinian and Valens, a very close friend of blessed Basil, as you may find in his Legend, in the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, bishop of Emesa ([Nyssenus?]), brother of blessed Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, a man very zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, stirred by his brother’s zeal, also himself wrote some little works in the Greek language, of which I have found among our writers only these:

[unclear]

54 On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Image and Creation of Man, one book. “Man from the soul [unclear].” Against Eunomius, two books.

He flourished, younger than his brother, under the emperors Valentinian and Valens, and composed various works, in the year of the Lord 380.

Gregory, from monk made bishop of Nazianzus, a man of such great learning, integrity, and eloquence that not even his adversaries dared in any way to contradict the things that were said by him, so that for the confirmation of authority it was enough that Gregory had merely said something. He, cultivator and lover of the monastic way of life, when on account of the excellence of his learning and the holiness of his life he was called to the episcopate, fled and hid himself, preferring to be abject in the house of the Lord rather than to be exalted among the crowd with perishable honors. But almighty God did not wish so bright a light to be hidden under the bushel of the aforesaid way of life, since it could be extended to the salvation of many. Found therefore by divine indication, he is led by the people to the episcopal see; and immediately, in excuse for his flight, a solemn homily is composed, in which he shows that the rule of souls is the art of arts. On account of his distinguished learning and holiness of life, he was called Gregory the Great before the blessed pope of the same name. He wrote many little works in the Greek language, of which the following are extant:

On the Death of His Brother Caesarius, one book. On the Praise of Maximus the Philosopher, one book. On the Praise of Cyprian the Martyr, one book. Against the Same, in Vituperation, one book. On the Praise of Athanasius the Bishop, one book. On Virginity, in hexameters, three books. On the Holy Spirit, one book. Apologetics, When He Had Fled, two books. “I have been conquered, and I confess.” On the Nativity of the Lord, one book. “Christ is born; glorify...” On the Second Epiphanies, one book. “Again my Jesus...” On the Holy Spirit on the Day of Pentecost, one book. “On the solemnity of this...” On Himself, Having Returned from the Field, one book. “I was longing for you...” On Jeremiah, with the emperor present, one book. “My belly pains me...” On the Reconciliation of a Monk, one book. “Our tongue [unclear].” On the Devastation by Hail, one book. “What praiseworthy [unclear].” Against Eunomius, two books. Against Julian the Apostate, one book.

He published many sermons and homilies, and various treatises on diverse subjects, since they have not come to my knowledge. At last, worn out by old age, when he perceived that he could no longer be equal to the governance of the people, after another bishop had been ordained in his place, he returned to the pursuit of the solitude he had left behind.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Eutropius, monk and priest, a man of most religious manner of life, very zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and fully instructed in secular letters, is said to have composed some little works, of which the following alone survive for us, known by their titles:

To two virgins, sisters, 2 books. And a Chronicle down to his own times, 1 book.

He flourished under the rulers Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 370. There are also some who write that he was a disciple of St. Augustine, and flourished in the year of the Lord 430.

Sychius, or perhaps more correctly Hesychius, priest and monk, once a hearer and disciple of the blessed bishop Gregory of Nazianzus, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, admonished by the example of his teacher, is said to have written many small works of explanation on the divine books; for he composed various volumes on both the New and the Old Testament, which have not yet come into our hands. I have read only that notable work of great size which he wrote to Eutychianus, the venerable deacon:

On Leviticus, 1 book. Venerable deacon ...

I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under the rulers Arcadius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 400.

Ambrose, bishop of Milan, Roman by birth, a man most celebrated for faith and holiness, easily the most learned of all in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, fully instructed in the Greek and Latin tongue, whose merit the whole world proclaims, whose books holy mother Church confirms with a great commendation of authority. In expounding and explaining the divine scriptures he surpassed all teachers; no earthly power could ever break his faith, so that when many bishops were banished into exile for the faith, no one ever dared to touch Ambrose. For he was like a hammer of heretics, a most steadfast assailant, and while his tongue spoke in the faith of Christ, no human authority could ever impose silence on it. Always ready to undergo any dangers for the faith, with the Lord protecting him, he escaped everywhere free and unharmed. He wrote many very clear little works, of which I have found only those set down below:

On Circumcision, one book. “No small [unclear].” On the Synagogue, to Theodosius, one book. “The army always with continual [unclear].” The Revelation of Gervasius and Protasius, two books. “To the lady sister, of life and [unclear].” On the Passion of Saint Agnes, one book. “Ambrose to virgins [unclear].” On Choosing a Pontiff, one book. On Judgments, one book. On holy Job, one book. On the Forty-Two Stations, one book. Of hymns and prefaces, [unclear] books. On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. On the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” two books. “Although also by mystical [unclear].” Letters to various persons, ten books. “You admonish well, brother.” On the Gospel of Luke, ten books. “About to write on the book of the Gospel [unclear].” Of many sermons, [unclear] books. “We gladly preach [unclear].” On certain Psalms, six books.

He also published some other works, which have not come to my knowledge. Finally, he is said to have made Hegesippus and certain others Latin from the Greek. He flourished under the most merciful emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, known and familiar to blessed Ambrose of Milan, whom Saint Augustine mentions in a certain letter to Quodvultdeus, wrote for the common benefit certain excellent little works, of which I do not recall that any has come into our hands. There is said to be an outstanding work of his, as blessed Augustine, in the place cited above, attests, which he wrote:

On 156 Heresies, one book. “The Simonians from Simon [unclear].”

The rest I have not seen. He flourished under the most Christian emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 380.

Evagrius, monk, disciple of Saint Macarius the Egyptian, afterward bishop of Antioch, a man in every respect most learned, instructed in both secular and divine writings, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, even in the episcopate preserving the austerity of his former life, was of such abstinence that he was regarded as a marvel. He was the first to commit the life of the holy fathers to writing, and from his own vein he published many little works. Of these, however, very few have come to my knowledge. The following are reported as his:

To the Anchorites, very useful, one book. On the Eight Principal Vices, one book. Also to the Cenobites, [unclear], one book. Exhortations to a Virgin, [unclear] books. He made the Life of Antony Latin, one book. “The presbyter Evagrius [unclear].” On the Life of the Holy Fathers, one book. [unclear] Commentaries on the Proverbs of Solomon.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

He also wrote many other works, and translated from Greek into Latin works unknown to us. He flourished under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Maximus, bishop of Constantinople, an Alexandrian by nation, a distinguished philosopher and theologian, in whose praise Gregory Nazianzen published a book, having suffered many injuries from the Arians [unclear], and at last driven from his bishopric, wrote much against them. Of these there survives an excellent work addressed to Gratian:

Against the Arians, one book. The rest are unknown to me. He flourished in Greece under the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 380.

Ambrose, a priest, an Alexandrian by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of Didymus the Blind, learned the divine Scriptures magnificently while he expounded them, and composed various explanations of them, which at that time were held in great esteem among the Greeks. Of these the following are current among us:

Commentaries on Job, one book. Against Apollinaris of Laodicea, one book.

He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in the year of the Lord [400?].

Petronius, bishop of Bologna, a monk in manner of life, very learned and eloquent in the divine Scriptures, and revered no less for holiness than for knowledge, because he shone with many miracles in life and after death, as is read in his history, wrote, among other works:

On the Life of the Holy Fathers, one book. On the Ordination of a Bishop, one book.

And other works unknown to us. He died under Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year of the Lord 383, in the thirteenth indiction.

Pachomius (Gennadius calls him Pachumius), abbot and a most magnificent founder of the monks of his time, founder of many monasteries, and a man of most holy manner of life, shining with many miracles in life and after death, since he was a learned man and instructed in the divine Scriptures, wrote many letters for the edification of the brothers; of these the following are reported:

To Cornelius the abbot, a letter. To the provosts of the monasteries, a letter. To Syrus the abbot, a letter. To the brothers working outside, a letter.

Also a Rule for Monks, one book.

He flourished under the emperors Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a Christian poet, a man most learned in secular literature and sufficiently skilled in the divine Scriptures, excellent in meter and prose, having been held for fifty-seven years by the loves of the world, read and expounded many little works of the poets, and from his own vein wrote many profound poems.

Of the Abbot of Spanheim

But at last, in old age, having rejected the vanity of the world, he betook himself to the sacred Scriptures, and in verse and prose expounded many hidden things of both Testaments. He wrote many little works; among these, with the measure of the meter supplied, I found the following:

Against Symmachus the Idolater, one book. “Paul, herald of God.”

On Compunction, one book. “The faithful old man first.”

On the Divinity, one book. “God is three supreme things.”

Against the Patripassians, one book. “There are very many, but.”

Against the Sabellians, one book. “Yield, profaner.”

Against the Jews, one book. “These things, if Jewish, if in.”

Against the Homuncionites, one book. “There are some who [unclear] with Jewish [unclear].”

Against the Phantastics, one book. “There is reward for the work [unclear].”

On the Origin of Sins, one book.

On the Hexaemeron, six books.

Of Various Hymns, two books. “The winged messenger of day [announces] the light.”

Praises of Saint Lawrence, two books. “Blessed martyr, look forth.” “Romanus, brave man of Christ.”

Praises of Romanus against the Gentiles, one book. “The ancient [unclear] of shrines.”

Of Histories, one book. “Eve was a dove.”

On the Nature of the Soul, one book. “Here a doubter meets.”

On the Resurrection of the Flesh, one book. “I ask for my own in Christ.”

On the Martyrs, one book. “Written things are in heaven.”

He also wrote not a few letters.

The Hamartigenia, one book. “Whatever errs [that] souls.”

On the Hope of Pardon, or his prayer, one book. “Brothers, Ephebus the digger.”

Against the Marcionites, one book. “O [unclear] parent.”

Peristephanon, one book. “Whither does [unclear] hurl you.”

Enchiridion of the New and Old Testament, which some also call [Diptychaion?].

John, monk and priest of Damascus, a learned and holy man, of whom marvelous things are told, held in great esteem because of the excellence of his doctrine and the purity of his life, appointed [unclear] of the monks at Constantinople, turned many away from iniquity. He wrote in the Greek language some little works of profound meaning, but few of them have come into our hands. I have read only that excellent work [unclear].

40 On Ecclesiastical Writers

Four books of The Tradition of the Orthodox Faith. “No one has ever seen God.” One book of the History of Barlaam and Josaphat. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He also wrote one book On Logic; one book, Introduction of Dignities; one book On the Two Wills and Operations in Christ, etc.; an epistle or one book On the Trisagion; one book On the Hundred Heresies; one book On the Dispute of a Christian and a Saracen; one book of very compunctive hymns; one sermon On Those Who Have Departed Hence in Christ, That They Are Greatly Helped by Sacred Offices and by the Good Deeds of the Living. Of all these works, together with certain others, recently printed at Cologne by the Quentel presses, a good part had nowhere been printed before these days, so that you may readily believe the Abbot when he says that he had not seen them; but as to the time at which he asserts this author lived, and likewise as to the other Damascene placed below in his own place, you will not readily believe him.

He flourished under Theodosius, that most devout prince, in the year of the Lord 390.

Ticonius the African, whom blessed Augustine, in the first book On Christian Doctrine, records as having belonged to the Donatist party, although in certain matters he disagreed with them, was certainly a sharp-witted man and very much practiced in the divine Scriptures. He wrote not a few little works, of which these are reported, namely: one book On Civil War; one book, an exposition of diverse causes; one book On the Apocalypse of John; one book of rules for sacred Scripture; several letters to various persons; and many other things.

He flourished when Theodosius and his sons were ruling, in the year of the Lord 390.

Heraclides the monk, a man holy in conduct and distinguished in learning in the divine Scriptures, a most diligent investigator and imitator of the holy fathers, anchorites and monks, who, like a resourceful bee, gathering from the way of life of each one the flowers of virtues into the little hive of his breast, produced the honey of spiritual sweetness. Among other things, for the edification of readers, he wrote an outstanding work on the life and conduct of the holy fathers living in the desert or in a monastery under a rule, whose title is:

Paradise, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Gratian, in the year of the Lord 580.

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, a man very studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and sufficiently imbued with secular letters, and worthy of the priesthood no less by his way of life than by his knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote, among other things, a useful work On the Holy Spirit.

The Abbot of Spanheim

One book On the Holy Spirit.

Of the other things which he is said to have composed, nothing has come to my knowledge.

There are, however, extant in Italy sermons by the same author, which follow: On the Life and Miracles of Basil the Great; On the Sinful Woman Who Anointed the Lord, Against the Pharisee; That One Must Not Despair; certain orations and hymns, all in Greek.

He flourished in the times of the devout emperor Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis, a city of Cyprus, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures, was of such sanctity that he deserved to be illumined by the spirit of prophecy and to become a worker of many miracles. He was a very close friend of blessed Jerome and wrote several letters to him. If anyone desires to know his deeds, let him read the Tripartite History. He composed some little works, of which these are reported:

One book On the Eighty Heresies. “The Simonians, from Simon.” Two books Against All Heresies. One book On the Errors of Origen. One book To Theophilus of Alexandria. One book of letters to various persons. “To the lord, most beloved son.” And certain other things.

He flourished under Theodosius, that most religious prince, in the year 390.

There is extant by the same Epiphanius a Greek book, translated by Albanus Torinus, On the Life of the Prophets and Evangelists.

Theophilus, the twenty-first bishop of the church of Alexandria, a man devoted to the Scriptures, a very fierce opponent of the Origenists, who is said to have had great discord with Saint John Chrysostom and, after he had been driven from the episcopate by intrigues, to have compelled him to die in exile, as is contained more fully in the histories of the ancients. He is reported to have written certain little works, of which few have come to my knowledge. There is extant his one book of letters to various persons on various matters. “To the lord most beloved, a.” One book On Easter.

He also produced many other things, as is gathered from the letter of blessed Jerome directed to him, in which he asks that they be sent to him either to be read or to be translated. He flourished under the princes Theodosius and Valentinian, in the year 390.

Antiochus, bishop of a certain city, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in secular letters, whose conduct commended his teaching to his people, wr[ote]

On Ecclesiastical Writers

...wrote for the edification of readers certain distinguished volumes, of which these are considered the more important:

Against Avarice, 2 books. On the Illumination of the Man Born Blind, 1 book. Several Homilies to the People, 1 book. And other works unknown to us. He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Arcadius, in the year 390.

Macarius, an Egyptian monk and formerly a disciple of the blessed father Antony, a devout man of most holy way of life, about whom many miracles are told, and how he even obtained the voices of the dead from tombs for the confirmation of the faith, sent to all religious men a useful letter, which is: To Monks, as one book. “In the first place indeed [unclear].” And other letters to others. He flourished in great holiness under the emperors Constantine and Constantius, in the year of the Lord 350. His deeds are contained in the Lives of the Fathers.

Faustinus, a priest, a man very learned in the sacred scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, of the Luciferian party, and for that reason deservedly blameworthy, wrote many excellent volumes, which are judged useful for the refutation of heretics; of these I have found only the titles of a few:

Against the Arians and Macedonians, 7 books. An Apology to Valentinian, one book.

He flourished under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 390.

Jerome, priest and monk, born of his father Eusebius, from the town of Stridon, a man learned in secular literature and, among all the doctors, most learned in the divine scriptures, remarkable for his knowledge of many languages, interpreter of the sacred law, hammer of heretics and most powerful assailant: he is the true evangelical steward, faithful and prudent, who, bringing forth from his treasury things new and old, and giving to his fellow servants in due season the measure of spiritual wheat, despoiled the proud Hebrews and enriched the humble Latins. He is the distinguished doctor of the Church of Christ, who, with his pious mother Rebecca, that is, the grace of God, brought forth the garments of Esau, wandering astray through the byways of errors, laid away idly at home, and clothed meek Jacob, faithful and serving Christ. He is Jerome, the sincere lover of Jesus Christ, who, passing no time idly, meditated day and night on the law of the Lord, and, scarcely allowing his body necessary sleep, always by day and night wrote, read, taught, or prayed, as the almost countless books that he published testify. This defender of truth, cultivator of virtue, most bitter enemy of vices,

Abbot of Spanheim

when he was a priest of the Roman Church and was steadfastly accusing the crimes of the clerics, withdrew from the city because of their envy; and coming into Judea, he visited the glorious sepulcher of the Lord, and, establishing for himself a dwelling-place beside the manger at Bethlehem, became known in glory to the whole world, divine providence arranging this, namely, that there the light of the world should rest where the true sun of righteousness had become known to human beings by being born. A holy and fitting inhabitant of the most holy place, firm in faith, kindled with charity, mature in conduct, who could not be led astray by prosperity, whom no adversity ever cast down from his holy purpose. But why do I, a foul praiser, touch the holy head of the man with impure lips? It would have been more humble for me to be silent than to speak insufficiently about so holy a man. Now therefore let us set down in order what we have found concerning his writings and little works; of these there are:

On Faith, to Damasus, 1 book. “We believe in God the Father.”

On the Faith of the Nicene Council, 1 book. “We believe in one God.” “Almighty God the Father.”

On the Essence of the Trinity, 1 book. “Very few days.”

Against Jovinian, 2 books.

Against Helvidius, 1 book. “Recently, asked by the brothers.”

Against Vigilantius, 1 book. “Many monsters in the world.” “It comes very near that he who.”

Against the Luciferian, 1 book. “Not boldly, as falsely.” “Already written to Ctesiphon.” “About ten years ago.” “If according to the apostle Paul.” “Both by your letters and those of many.” “Having read the letters of your prudence.” “That up to now to you.” “Never, Oceanus, would he himself.” “To the most blessed Pope Damasus.” “You sent me a volume.” “In the previous letter which.” “In the seventy-seventh Psalm, which.” “Among the letters of your Blessedness.” “My son Apodemius.” “You ask me that for you.” “Now in the very moment of departure.” [unclear]

On the Same, 1 book. On Virginity and Marriage, 1 book. On the Vision of Isaiah, 1 book. On Melchizedek, 1 book. On True Circumcision, 1 book. On the Forty-Two Stations, 1 book. On the Prodigal Son, 1 book. On Twelve Questions, 1 book. On Eleven Questions, 1 book. On Anna and Joachim, 1 book. On the Resurrection of the Flesh, 1 book.

These are the writings of the most blessed doctor Jerome which at present occurred to us to record. Nor do we doubt that he wrote more, which are not contained in this catalogue, chiefly for this reason: that they either remained unknown to us or dispersed among many things. For among all the doctors of the Church none was of more benefit than Jerome, who, besides innumerable small works, translated the Old Testament from Hebrew into Latin, corrected the New according to the Greek truth, and faithfully offered it to the Church to be read. He also made many volumes of the Greeks Latin, namely those of Origen, Josephus the Jew, Eusebius of Caesarea, Didymus of Alexandria, Victorinus the martyr, and others.

At last, after many labors, full of days, he died under the rulers Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 422, in the fifth indiction, on the last day of the month of September, at the hour of Compline, in the ninety-ninth year of his age; he was buried at Bethlehem, shining with many miracles. Eusebius, his disciple, described his life.

47 The Abbot of Spanheim

Audientius, a Spanish bishop, a man having a mind exercised in the divine Scriptures, wrote against the Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians, yet with his principal intention against the Photinians, who afterward were called Bonosians, an outstanding work, which is entitled On the Faith against Heretics, one book.

He also published certain other works, which have come to my knowledge.

Rufinus the monk, priest of the church of Aquileia, an eloquent man, very learned in the divine Scriptures, skilled in Greek and Latin speech, was of no small reputation among the ecclesiastical doctors. Although his writings are many, nevertheless they are counted among the apocrypha, distinction 15, Sancta Romana, because he wrote invective letters against the most holy man Jerome, as can be understood from the reading of them. But afterward, when they returned into the concord of brotherly love, the little works of Rufinus were made authentic, insofar as they were not contrary to the sayings of Jerome. Concerning the writings of Rufinus, therefore, the following are reported:

On the prophet Hosea, one book. On the prophet Amos [unclear]. On the prophet Joel, one book. “To me indeed, most faithful...” On his faith, to Bishop Laurentius, one book. “I have read your writings...” Invectives against Jerome, one book. “I heard certain persons, when...” On his faith, to Anastasius, one book. On the sacraments, one book. On the blessings of the patriarchs, one book. Additions to the Ecclesiastical History, two books. An exhortation to Proba, one book. [unclear]. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius. Letters to various persons, two books.

He is said to have composed many other things besides, but they have not come into our hands. He also translated into Latin the volumes of many Greeks, namely of Clement, Origen, Basil, Gregory the Great, bishop, Pamphilus the martyr, Eusebius of Caesarea, Evagrius, Sixtus the philosopher, and many others, all of which he marked with his own prefaces and prefixed letters. He flourished in the times of the emperors Arcadius and Honorius; he wrote many and various works, in the year of the Lord 400.

John, bishop of Constantinople, once, while still a priest at Antioch, a hearer and disciple of Eusebius, bishop of Nyssa, who because of the charm of his speech is named Chrysostom, that is, “golden mouth,” a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, was of excellent ability in delivering homilies to the people, distinguished no less for holiness than for learning, and was held by the people in great reverence and love. This most blessed bishop endured many wrongs from Theophilus of Alexandria, and by his fraudulent and deceitful machinations [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On charity, one homily: “Charity [is] the best [unclear].” Of exhortation to the good life, one homily: “[unclear].” To Theodorus the monk, one book: “[unclear].” To Cyriacus the bishop, on exile, one book: “[unclear].”

He is also said to have written many homilies, sermons, and innumerable letters, which have not come into our hands.

Letters, two books. Thirty-five homilies at the beginning of Lent. Ethics. Expositions on Isaiah. Two manuscript sermons on Jeremiah are extant at Bologna in the library of San Salvatore. At Rome, in the papal library, four Greek volumes are preserved. A homily on προστυχὴ, [unclear], from the third up to the thirty-eighth.

At length, after many labors and holy exercises, through the deceit of Theophilus of Alexandria and of the empress Eudoxia, he died in exile in Pontus, on the Kalends of February, in the year of the Lord 411, in the ninth indiction.

Severianus, bishop of Gabala, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, and an admirable teacher in delivering homilies to the people, was of incredible eloquence; whence he was frequently summoned by the emperor Arcadius to Constantinople by the aforesaid blessed bishop John, to preach. To him Saint John commended his people when he was being driven into exile, venerating not only his doctrine but the merit of his life. Severianus, however, commending himself to the people more than was fitting, supplied kindling for discord between him and John. But when the patriarch returned from exile, they returned to the bonds of brotherly love, as the homily delivered above in the church of Constantinople testifies. Of the writings of Severianus, a most learned man, few are possessed among the Latins; still fewer have come into our hands.

On the Epistle to the Galatians, one book. On baptism and Epiphany, one book. In the church of Constantinople, one homily. On the advent of the Lord, [unclear]. On the death of the innocents, one homily: “To what end zeal tends, to what [unclear].”

There are extant among us certain other homilies of his, brief indeed, but very useful. Concerning his other little works, though many are reported, I have as yet found nothing. He flourished under Arcadius and Honorius, at the time of John Chrysostom, in the year of the Lord 406.

Vitellius Afer, defending the Donatist schism, a man indeed well exercised in the divine Scriptures, would have composed doctrine useful enough if he had remained in ecclesiastical unity. But because he denounced true Catholics as persecutors and, as it were, betrayers, he was deservedly despised together with his volumes. The following volumes from his writings are extant:

Against the nations, one book. That the servants of God are hated by the world, one book. A complaint against our own people, one book. He is said to have composed many other volumes besides, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Constans, son of Constantine the Great, emperor, in the year of the Lord 360.

Theodotus, presbyter of the church of Antioch, a learned and eloquent man, and practiced in the reading of the ancient authors, wrote against the Apollinarists and Eunomians a most elegant volume, in which by very clear reasoning and authority he refuted the depraved doctrines of the heretics. He entitled this magnificent and notable work:

On the incarnation of the Lord, fifteen books.

He is said to have written many other things also, which have not come to my knowledge.

Acrobius, presbyter, and afterward hidden bishop of the Donatists in the city of Rome, while he was still a presbyter in the Church of God, wrote to the confessors and to the virgins of Christ a volume, moral indeed, but very necessary, of doctrine; in it he chiefly deals with and treats [unclear]. To show that there is one principle, and that nothing material was created from any other source than God, he wrote a sufficiently elegant and notable work, which he entitled On the natures of primordial things, one book.

He flourished first among our people at Rome, afterward among his own Donatists, the Montenses of Africa.

Heliodorus, once a presbyter, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, sufficiently sharp in disputation and of a vehement intellect in the scholastic manner, [unclear].

[Unclear], after the death of [unclear], provost of his monasteries, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, a vigorous governor of regular discipline, and venerable no less for sanctity than for doctrine, wrote lucid sermons on the holy Scriptures to the monasteries:

Letters of exhortation, three.

He is said also to have written several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Theodorus the monk, disciple of blessed Pachomius, and, after the death of that man, [unclear], distinguished both in life and in learning, wrote for the instruction of monks a work seasoned with divine salt and furnished with the instruments of the whole monastic discipline, which we may entitle [unclear].

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Instruction of Monks, one book. If he wrote anything more, I do not know. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, in the year of the Lord 420.

John Cassian, a Scythian by nation, formerly a hearer and disciple of blessed John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople, and ordained deacon by him, after some years was expelled by the same man for I know not what cause. Consecrated priest at Marseilles, he founded two monasteries, one of men and one of women, in which a great fervor of regular discipline remained for many years. With experience as his teacher he wrote several little works, in which the grace of eloquence is apparent even in the translator. Among these are counted: at the request of Leo the archdeacon, afterward bishop of the city of Rome, he wrote against Nestorius the heretic:

On the Incarnation of the Lord, seven books. On the Institutes of Monks, four books. “On the institutes and [unclear]” On the Eight Capital Vices, eight books. “The fifth, with [unclear] helping us” Conferences of the Holy Fathers, twenty-four books. “When in the desert of Scete”

In these conferences of the saints there is useful and necessary instruction for monks; but because he is censured by blessed Prosper on certain points concerning freedom of the will, his little works are counted among the apocrypha. At length, after the publication of many books, he died at Marseilles, not without a reputation for sanctity, while Theodosius and Valentinian were reigning, in the year of the Lord 455.

Lucian, priest of the church of Jerusalem, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and most holy in life and conduct, to whom in the times of Honorius and Theodosius almighty God revealed the place of the tomb and relics of the most holy protomartyr Stephen, is said to have written some little works. Of these there survives a lengthy letter:

On the Discovery of Saint Stephen, one book. “Lucian the priest”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He wrote that revelation itself in the Greek language; Avitus, a priest Spanish by birth, translated it into the Latin tongue and, with his own letter added, sent it through Orosius to the easterners to be read. He flourished under the emperors Honorius and Theodosius, around the year of the Lord 410.

Severus the priest, surnamed Sulpicius, born from the province of Aquitaine, a man noble in birth and letters and distinguished by love of poverty and humility, dear also to the holy men Martin, bishop of Tours, and Paulinus, bishop of Nola, in his old age was deceived by the Pelagians; and recognizing the fault of loquacity, [he kept] silence until dea-

Vnde sine dubio mentiri conuincitur, qui se Augu- stinum inuenisse totum confitetur. Cunctos enim scriptores nu mero librorum vtilitate praecedit, qui plusquam mille tractatus insignes compofuit. Nemo sic profunde sacram scripturam, vt Au gustinus, explanauit. Christianos mores nemo sic vtiliter instituit, nec fidem catholicam aliquis eo ardentius defensauit. ABBOT OF SPONHEIM. [running head]

…held [silence] until death, that the sin which he had contracted by speaking he might wholesomely amend by keeping silence. He wrote little works of no contemptible reading, of which the following are reported: On the life of St Martin the bishop: 3 books. ["Very many of mortals…"] The Conference of Postumianus and Gallus: 4 books. ["When into one place I…"] Of letters to [his] Sister: 1 book. Of letters to various [persons]: 1 book. To Paulinus, bishop of Nola: 2 books. He is said to have written also some others, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished with Saint Martin, archbishop of Tours, under the princes Arcadius [and] Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.

Ausonius, bishop of Bordeaux, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, second to none of his time in secular letters, excelling in verse [and] prose, shone forth renowned no less for sanctity than for erudition; who at Trier, in a council under the prince Maximus, together with the saints Martin, Ambrose of Milan, [and] Jerome the presbyter, did many illustrious things. He wrote there, among other metrical [works], a distinguished little work, which is entitled: The Moselle: 1 book. On the praise of the same homeland: 1 book. But he is reported to have written many other little works, which have by no means come to us. He flourished under Maximus, in the year of the Lord 410.

Augustine, bishop of Hippo, a Carthaginian by nation, in Africa, a man most erudite of all the learned, both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, eloquent in speech, renowned in eloquence, profound in sense, most holy in life [and] conversation; he wrote so many little works that I should believe no one able either to read or to have them all. Whence without doubt he is convicted of lying who confesses that he has found the whole of Augustine. For he precedes all writers in the number [and] usefulness of [his] books, who composed more than a thousand distinguished treatises. No one so profoundly explained sacred Scripture as Augustine. No one so usefully instituted Christian morals, nor did anyone defend the catholic faith more ardently than he. The king led [him] into the wine-cellar, and clothed [him] with such fortitude that he strongly laid low all the adversaries of the faith with the sword of his mouth. If you have him as a teacher, even with the rest lacking, he himself suffices you. Now therefore, of the many books which he published, let us mark down even a few: On the Holy Trinity: 15 books. ["[You who are] about to read these [things]…"] On the City of God: 22 books. ["The most glorious city…"] On the predestination of the saints: 2 books. ["[That] the Apostle indeed said…"] [page 92:] On Genesis according to the letter: 12 books. On Genesis, unfinished: 1 book. On Genesis against the Manichees: 2 books. On the Academics: 3 books. On the blessed life: 1 book. On order: 3 books. Of Soliloquies: 2 books. On the morals of the catholic Church: 2 books. On the quantity of the soul: 1 book. On free will: 3 books. On the teacher: 1 book. On music: 6 books. On true religion: 1 book. On the usefulness of believing: 1 book. On the two souls: 1 book. Acts with Fortunatus the Manichee: 1 book. On faith and the creed: 1 book. On the Lord's sermon on the mount: 2 books. On eighty-three questions: 1 book. A Psalm against the party of Donatus: 1 book. Against the letter of Donatus: 1 book. Against Adamantius: 1 book. On lying: 1 book. Against lying: 1 book. To Simplicianus the bishop: 2 books. Against the letter of the Foundation: 1 book. On the Christian struggle: 1 book. On Christian doctrine: 4 books. Against the party of Donatus: 13 books. Of Confessions: 13 books. Against Faustus the Manichee: 2 books. Against Felix the Manichee: 1 book. On the nature of the good: 1 book. Against Secundinus: 1 book. Against Hilary: 1 book. Questions of the Gospels: 3 books. Of Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans: 1 book. On the Epistle to the Romans, an unfinished work: 1 book. On Ecclesiastical Writers

Of an exhortation to the candidates, one treatise. On the ascension of the Lord, two treatises. On Saint Perpetua and Felicity, one treatise. On Saint Vincent, two treatises. On spiritual almsgiving, one treatise. On bodily alms, one treatise. On Samson, one treatise. On Susanna and Joseph, one treatise. On the dedication of the temple, two treatises. Sermons on various subjects, 200, one book. Letters, more than 200, one book.

There is extant also a certain sermon on the mercy of God at Mount Saint John, a monastery of the Benedictines in the Rheingau.

He published many other works as well; if anyone desires to know them more fully, let him read the list of his books edited by Possidius, from which we have taken many items. Jacobus de Voragine, bishop of Genoa, writes in his treatise which he composed on the books of Augustine that the number of his books, treatises, sermons, and letters rises beyond one thousand thirty. And he concludes thus: And therefore no one has ever been found who was able to find all the books of Augustine. And Possidius says: He lies who declares that he has read you entire, Augustine.

But in this work I have deliberately omitted certain treatises which are ascribed by many to blessed Augustine. Among these is the book On the Spirit and the Soul, in whose seventh chapter Boethius is cited, though he was born a long time after Augustine. But the style itself does not have the savor of Augustine. Likewise the book which has now been printed under Augustine’s name, On True and False Penitence, is falsely ascribed to him, since in the seventh chapter, toward the end, Augustine himself is cited. The book On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices, which begins “The apostolic voice,” echoes the style of Pope Gregory, and agrees with the older copies. Likewise the book On the Ladder of Paradise, whose beginning is “When on a certain day,” is in the ancient copies inscribed to blessed Bernard, whose spirit and manner of speech it seems to express.

Why should I strive at length? So many treatises and sermons are falsely inscribed to blessed Augustine that a review of them would require its own volume. Nor is it my place to sit as judge and deprive of their titles things that belong to another. Let the prudent reader carefully consider what is to be done or held by him in these matters.

Saint doctor Augustine died in the city of Hippo when it was being besieged by the Vandals, in the year of the Lord 430, in the thirteenth indiction, in the seventy-sixth year of his age and the fortieth of his priesthood, according to Marianus Scotus, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the third month of the city’s siege. While answering, amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals, the books of Julian the Manichaean at the very end of his days, he persevered gloriously in defense of the Christian faith. He made no testament, because there was nothing from which he might make one
