Abbot of Spanheim.

Constitutions of his order, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

Albertus Galeoti, by country a Parmese, a professor of canon and civil law and a famous interpreter, subtle in intellect, cautious in counsel, and scholastic in speech, who, because of his learning and experience in affairs, was counted among the chief doctors by the old jurists, wrote certain minor works in law not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with immortal praise. Of these there survives:

The Summa Margarita of Questions, one book. “When I, Albertus Gal...” And Declarations of Judgments, one book. And certain other diverse works, unknown to us, are held by various persons.

Odofredus of Benevento, a hearer of Azo of Bologna and afterwards the teacher of Jacobus Balduini, a man most skilled in both laws, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, who left many distinguished disciples after him, was held in great authority among the ancients because of his teaching and erudition both in law and in the other humane letters. Many minor works of his are reported, by which he made his name known to posterity:

On the Formation of Libels, one book. “After the work of the notary...” On Judicial Order, one book. “As Christ...” On the Art of the Notariate, one book. And other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Johannes de Blanoso, Burgundian by nation, a man most learned in both laws and sufficiently instructed in the precepts of the secular philosophers, keen and ready in intellect, wrote in clear speech minor works not to be scorned by the professors of this faculty, by which the fame of his name became known far and wide both to those then present and to those who would come after. Of these there survives a volume of great utility, which he entitled:

On the Actions of Advocates, one book. “I, Johannes de Blanoso...” And Various Questions. But the other works which he composed have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes, Teutonic by name and nation, born from the city of Freiburg, bishop of Bosnia in Hungary, of the Order of Preachers, a man much exercised in the divine Scriptures, learned in law, and excellently skilled in secular philosophy, who because of his learning and holiness of life had been taken from the order to the episcopate, which he later abandoned and returned to his order, and after Raymond was appointed master general of the order, did many good things. He wrote a notable Summa for Confessors, five books. “Since new matters of doubts...” And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1150. He was buried in his convent at Strasbourg, once shining, as they say, with many miracles.

Innocent, Pope IV, previously called Symbaldus, an Italian by nation, born from the city of Genoa, sat in the pontificate after Celestine IV for eleven years, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and in law, a lover of religious, who celebrated the general Council of Lyons, in which, with the consent of the fathers, he deposed Frederick from the empire and established many things for the utility of the Church. He nevertheless wrote certain excellent minor works, by whose publication he is worthily numbered among ecclesiastical writers, to be transmitted with them to the knowledge of posterity. Against Petrus de Vineis:

On Ecclesiastical Power, one book. An Apparatus on the Decretals, five books. “It is read in Ezekiel...” The Rule of the Poor Clares, one book. “The form of life of the order...” The Authentics also, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And certain other things. He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Rolandinus de Romanciis, a most celebrated professor and interpreter of both laws, and nobly learned in secular philosophy, who was not among the least with the old jurists, wrote in that faculty certain excellent minor works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I found only the Summa:

On the Order of Crimes, one book. “The little book begins...” Determinations and Questions. The rest, which he is said to have composed, have not come to my knowledge.

Bernardus, priest of Compostela, intimate and chaplain of Pope Innocent IV, a man most learned in law, prompted by the zeal of that same pontiff, wrote certain excellent minor works in law, which are held in great authority in these times among jurists. Of these I have been able to find few, namely an eminent Apparatus:

On the Decretals, five books. “At the beginning of this book...” Ca-

The Cases of the Decretals, 5 books. “The peaceful king, pious [unclear]…” I have seen nothing of the rest. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1250.

[Guido?] de Suzaria, a doctor most skilled in law and sufficiently instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, among the ancients expert in these matters enjoyed great authority. He is said to have produced certain distinguished little works in law, among which there exists a notable Summa, which he entitled, in 4 books, On the Ordering of Cases. Various Declarations also. And many other works, which have not yet come into our hands.

Bartholomaeus Brixiensis, professor and interpreter of canon law, most [unclear] and excellently learned in the other disciplines of secular literature, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote various distinguished little works both in law and on other matters, by which he gave his name to immortality. Of these the following are reported: A Repertory of the Decretum, 3 books. “Since with favoring [unclear]…” Disputations on the Decretals, 5 books. A Chronicle of Italy, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And certain other works. The same man wrote additions to the glosses of the Decretum. Also Sunday and Friday Questions, 91 in number. He also produced a history of times.

Johannes de Deo, professor and eminent expositor of both laws, and sufficiently learned in the disciplines of philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who among the ancients was of great authority, wrote many various little works in both laws, through which the memory of his name came to the knowledge of many. Of these only a few have reached my knowledge. For I have found only the following: A Summa of Cavillations, 7 books. “For the honor of the highest [unclear]…” Another work entitled Judgment, 4 books. “At the beginning may [unclear] be present…” A Table of the Decretum, 2 books. “The book of decretals [unclear]…” A Concordance of the Decretum and the Decretals, 1 book. “For those willing, promptly…” Various Questions. He taught in the city of Bologna, where he composed the aforesaid works and others, from [unclear]

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Hugo Barchinonensis, of the Order of Preachers, cardinal priest of the title of Santa Sabina of the holy Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who before his entry into the order had been master of sacred theology and had had many distinguished pupils, wrote several excellent little works, by which he consecrated his name to immortality. Shining no less brightly in conduct and religion than in knowledge, he remained the same in dignity as he had been before. Of his books these are reported: On Genesis, 1 book. On Exodus, 1 book. On Leviticus, 1 book. On Numbers, 1 book. On Deuteronomy, 1 book. On Joshua, 1 book. On Judges, 1 book. On the Books of Ruth, 1 book. On Kings, 4 books. On Chronicles, 1 book. He also composed several other works, which have not yet come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Jacobus Baldeuini, formerly a hearer of Odofredus Beneventanus, a very distinguished man, professor and eminent interpreter of civil law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported: On the Code, 2 books. On the Old Digest, 11 books. On the New Digest, 3 books. On the Infortiatum, 4 books. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240. Da-

23 ABBAS SPANHEIMENSIS. 187 D Auid, ordinis (vt ferunt) Minoꝝ, natione Teutonicus, vir in diuinis scripturis exercitat⁹, vita et cōuersatione infignis, in declamandis sermonibus ad populum, excellentis ingenij fu̇it. Scripsit quaedam aperto fermone opuscula, quorum lectio deuo tis fratribus non est contemnenda, de quibus extant subiecta: Ad nouitios De cōpositione hoīs exterioris, lib.i. De cōpositione hoiis interioris, lib.i. Sermones de tempore lib.i. Sermones de Sanctis lib.i. Et quaedam alia. Claruit non longe post B. Franciscum, sepultus est in Augusta. H Vmbertus, ordinis Praedicatorum quintus magister genera lis ꝓ patria Viennensis, Hugonis Barchinonensis theologi qͥn dam auditor, vir in diuiuis scripturis erudit⁹, declamator egregius, vita euangelicus, conscientia purus, actione praecipuus, eloquio dulcis, ad persuađendum idoneus, qui Hugonem olim su um praeceptorem sacrae theologiae, pertraxit ad ordinem: scripsit quaedam deuota opuscula, qui bus nomen eius ad notitiam posteriori tatis deuenit. E quibus ista feruntur: Sup regulam S. Augustini lib.i. Summa praedicantium lib.i. Gesta fratrũm Praedicatorum lib.i. De officijs sui ordinis lib.i. De tribus substãtialibꝰ religio, lib.i. Epistolarum ad diuerfos lib.i. Claruit imperio vacante, anno domini 1250. V Incentius Gallus, natione Burgundus, ordinis Praedictatoꝝ dictus Bellouacẽsis, vir in diuinis scriptoris studiosus exer citatus, ac vetere lectione diues, ingenio subtilis, fermone cōpositus, tantum literis studiū adhibuit, vt nullis vnquam laboribus, vigilans vel occupationibꝰ ab eaꝝ cultura potuerit auocari, qn semꝑ aut legeret, aut scriberet, aut prędicaret. Tantus itaqꝫ fuit, vt post se neceđ habuerit parē, si ardua quae scripsit opuscula, ex mul tis laboriose collecta, aequa lance cũ coeteris põderemus. Alia insuper nonnulla edidit, quae ad notitiā meam non venerunt. Claruit sub Frederico imperatore secundo, Anno domini 1240. A lexander de Hales, natione Anglicus, ordinis Minorum, p̄ceptor Eustathij cardinalis, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus, &amp; in seculari philosophia nulli suo tempore secundus, ingenio subtilis, &amp; clarus eloquio, cum esset doctor sacrarum literarum in gymnasio Parisiensi, vt coelestis philosophie verus ef ficeretur discipulus, ordinem pauperū Christi intrauit, qē sua etuditione et amp; sanctitate mirabiliter illustrauit. Scripsit iubente Innocentio papa quarto, insigne opus quatuor voluminibus partitum, multa vtiliter complectens, quod prenotauit Summam theologiae li.4. Qm̃ sicut dicit Boethius Reuerendo in Christo Caetera eius non vidi. Dicitur autem ꝙ tam vetus quàm nouum testamẽtum ex magna parte postillauerit, &amp; de concordia iuris diuiń et amp; humani multa subtiliter differuerit, aliaqƺ composuerit varia, quae ad manus nostras non venerunt. Claruit sub Frederico secundo, Anno domni 1240. I ohannes de Rupella, ordinis fratrꝰ Minorum, sacrae theologie magister Parisiensis, in diuinis scripturi eruditus, &amp; in philosophia Aristotelica magnifice doctꝰ, qui se cum Alexandro de Hales, in declaratione regulę Minorum ad ministrum generalem subiscripsit: edidit qđam praeclara opuscula, qbus nominis fui famam ad posterioritatibꝰ notitiā transmisit. E q̄bus subiecta ferūtur Super sententias li.4. Summa virtutum et amp; vitiorum li.i. De anima quoque li.i. Cla

The Abbot of Sponheim.

David, of the Order, as they say, of Minors, German by nation, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in life and conduct, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works in a plain style, the reading of which is not to be despised by devout brothers. Of these the following are extant:

To novices. On the composition of the outer man, one book. On the composition of the inner man, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain others.

He flourished not long after Blessed Francis; he is buried at Augsburg.

Humbert, of the Order of Preachers, the fifth master general, from his homeland a man of Vienne, formerly a pupil of Hugh of Barcelona the theologian, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding preacher, evangelical in life, pure in conscience, excellent in action, sweet in speech, fit for persuasion, who once drew Hugh, his own teacher of sacred theology, into the order: he wrote certain devout little works, by which his name came to the knowledge of posterity. Among them these are reported:

On the Rule of Saint Augustine, one book. A Summary for Preachers, one book. The Deeds of the Friars Preachers, one book. On the offices of his order, one book. On the three substantial things of religion, one book. Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Vincent the Gaul, Burgundian by nation, of the Order of Preachers, called of Beauvais, a man devoted to and practiced in the divine writings, and rich in ancient reading, subtle in intellect, ordered in speech, applied so much zeal to letters that he could never be called away from their cultivation by any labors, vigils, or occupations, since he was always either reading, writing, or preaching. Accordingly he was so great that after himself he necessarily had an equal, if we were to weigh with the others, in an even balance, the arduous little works that he wrote, laboriously collected from many sources. For, at his request and with the king of the Franks supplying the expenses, he brought together with the greatest labors a great and admirable work of Mirrors concerning everything, so to speak, knowable, in many volumes, which he entitled and divided thus:

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Historical Mirror, 32 books. God is a substance in Natural Mirror, 53 books. Since the multitude in the book Moral Mirror, 5 books. In all your things remember Doctrinal Mirror, 4 books. Since the multitude in the book Also On the Grace of God, 40 books. The book of the generation and [unclear] On the Praises of Saint Mary, 7 books. If God with prophetic mouth [unclear] On the Praises of Saint John the Evangelist. Blessed John the evangelist [unclear] On the Education of Boys, 1 book. You have sons; instruct them [unclear] A Consolation on the Dead, 1 book. First, therefore, attend Letters to various persons, 1 book. He also published some other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Alexander of Hales, English by nation, of the Order of Minors, teacher of Cardinal Eustathius, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none in his time in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, when he was a doctor of sacred letters in the Parisian school, entered the order of the poor of Christ so that he might become a true disciple of heavenly philosophy; he wonderfully adorned it by his learning and holiness. At the command of Pope Innocent IV he wrote a distinguished work divided into four volumes, usefully embracing many things, which he entitled:

Summa of Theology, 4 books. Since, as Boethius says. To the reverend in Christ [unclear]. The rest of his works I have not seen.

It is said, however, that he annotated both the Old and the New Testament for the most part, and discussed many matters subtly concerning the concord of divine and human law, and composed various other works, which have not come into our hands.

He flourished under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

John of La Rochelle, of the Order of the Friars Minor, master of sacred theology at Paris, learned in the divine Scriptures and magnificently taught in Aristotelian philosophy, who, together with Alexander of Hales, subscribed himself in the declaration of the Rule of the Minors to the minister general: he published certain excellent little works, by which he transmitted the fame of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. A Summary of virtues and vices, 1 book. Also On the Soul, 1 book.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He flourished under Frederick, the second emperor, in the year of the Lord 1250.

Henry, archbishop of Embrun and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, commonly called the Ostian, a man most skilled in both laws, who, on account of the excellence of his talent and learning, was held in esteem by Pope Alexander IV, wrote certain little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the distinguished work known to all, On the Titles of the Decretals, in five books. “Alpha and omega, one in [unclear].” Also a concise Summa, in one book.

The other works that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1259.

[Unclear], a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly taught in the disciplines of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works not to be despised, of which the following are reported: for at the command of Pope Alexander IV he arranged, in a very useful style, through the cycle of the year, Sermons, in two books; On the Sentences, in four books; Quodlibets, in one book. “It is asked how virtue...”

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1250.

[Unclear], a man exercised by long study in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent and clear in eloquence, who in his own time, because of his learning and erudition, was of great reputation, wrote at the request of the provost and clerics of the church of Lille, On the Psalter, in one book, and certain letters.

He also published several other works, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

Alexander, called de Villa Dei, of Dol as his native place, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Minor, a man certainly trained in every direction, a grammarian, philosopher, astronomer, and distinguished calculator, wrote not a few little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Of these I have so far found only the following: a volume written in leonine verse on grammar, whose use today is constant in boys’ schools, [unclear] so useful, because of the weakness of the younger age and the sloth of teachers. On Ecclesiastical Writers

The Doctrinale puerorum, [unclear]. “I prepare to write for little clerics...” On the ecclesiastical computus, one book. “Although now at the end of time...” On the sphere, one book. On the art of numbering, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, sermons, letters, and various treatises, which have not yet come into our hands.

He flourished with great piety and learning under Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1240.

Eustathius, who is Bonaventura, born at Bagnoregio, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, and afterwards bishop of Albano, cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, formerly a hearer and disciple of Alexander of Hales, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, devout and most holy in life and conduct: when his teacher Alexander contemplated his intellect, his natural gift, and the purity of his life, he used to say: “In Brother Bonaventura Adam does not seem to have sinned.” He wrote many profound and most devout little works, in which, bringing forth burning words, he no less kindles the reader’s affection in the love of Christ than he enlightens the intellect with holy teachings. For he easily surpasses all the doctors of his time in the usefulness of his works, if you attend to the spirit of divine love and Christian devotion speaking in him. He is profound, not wordy; subtle, not curious; eloquent, not empty; bringing forth words that are flaming, not puffed up. Hence he is read more safely, understood more easily by one who loves, more sweetly retained the more often he is read, and more fruitfully. Many set forth doctrine; many, though few, preach devotion; by writing books they have taught both. But Bonaventura surpassed many, and few [equaled him], since his doctrine instructs devotion, and devotion instructs doctrine. Therefore, if you wish to be called devout, be attentive to his little works. These are:

On the Sentences, [unclear] books. “The depths of rivers...” Breviloquium, one book. “Tell me, I ask, O man...” Soliloquium, one book. “In the beginning, first...” Itinerary of the Mind into God, one book. “I am fixed with Christ...” The Tree of Life, one book. “Since, my beloved brother...” Exhortation to a Brother, one book. “Every best gift...” On the Reduction of the Arts, The Rule of Those Making [unclear]: a small good, one book. “Behold, I have described it to you...”

Philippus, chancellor of Paris, a man learned in the divine scriptures and nobly instructed in secular philosophy, since he was a famous master of sacred letters, presided gloriously for a long time over the theological school at Paris, where by lecturing to his students and preaching to the people he instructed them magnificently. He wrote two or three elegant sermons on each of the psalms, 1 book; a Summa of theology, 1 book.

He also published many other works, which by no means have come to our knowledge.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Albertus, bishop of Regensburg, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, a Swabian by homeland, originating from Lauingen, a man very studious and learned in the divine scriptures, and in secular philosophy second to none in his time; subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout and most holy in life and conduct. Because of his teaching and learning he was called Magnus. He taught sacred letters and Aristotelian philosophy for many years, first at Paris, later at Cologne, where among others he had Thomas Aquinas as an excellent pupil. Then, having been assumed to the episcopate of the church of Regensburg, after he had governed it for some years, he left it, and out of love for saving study returned to his convent at Cologne, where he continued teaching and writing until the end of his life. He wrote many and almost countless little works, of which the following are reported:

Summa of Theology, 4 books. On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Four Coeval Things, 1 book. On Man, 1 book. On the Good, 1 book. On the Spiritual Life, 1 book. On the Office of the Mass, 1 book. He wrote commentaries on the books of Aristotle, and composed many other works which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished at Paris in the year of the Lord 1257. He died under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280, in the eighth indiction, in the eightieth year of his age, and was buried in the middle of the choir of his convent at Cologne. And after him there arose no man like him, who was so learned, educated, and expert in all letters, sciences, and matters. But as to his being accused of necromancy, this man beloved by God suffers injustice.

Simon of Tournai, priest, learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly instructed in secular philosophy, a very acute dialectician and most skilled in all the liberal arts, having been made master of the theological school, taught for many years in the university of Paris, where he instructed very many hearers. But while he follows Aristotle too much, he is found to have erred in certain matters. He wrote, however, a certain little work of his own talent: On Athanasius, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book. On the Creed, 1 book. He also published some other works which have not come to my knowledge.

Thomas, of the counts of Aquino, of the Order of Preachers, hearer and disciple of Albert the Great in the convent at Cologne, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, notable in life and conduct, easily obtained primacy among all the doctors of his time. Like another Augustine, he gave himself wholly to the study of Scripture, spending day and night in its love and practice, and wrote so many and such great volumes that among the moderns he has few equals either in number or in usefulness

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On sense and intellect, one book. It begins: Concerning consideration...

On the discovery of the middle term, one book. It begins: Since the principle of a syllogism...

On the nature of light, one book. It begins: It must be considered concerning [unclear].

On the nature of place, one book. It begins: For knowing the nature...

On universals, two books. It begins: Concerning universals much...

On intellect and the intelligible, one book. It begins: It must be known that of the nature...

The agreement of his own sayings, one book. It begins: Many shall pass through...

And many sermons, one book.

Against William of Saint-Amour, one book.

At the command of Pope Urban IV he composed the office for the feast of the Body of Christ. He commented on all the books of Aristotle and Porphyry. He also published many other works, both on divine scriptures and on secular philosophy, which have by no means come into our hands.

He died under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1274, in the second indiction. And he was canonized by Pope John XXII.

Thomas of Cantimpre, a Brabanter by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a certain disciple, as they say, of Albert the Great, a devout man, excellently learned both in divine scriptures and in secular letters, ready in talent, scholastic in eloquence, is said to have written certain distinguished volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant a work on mystical bees, which he entitled The Universal Good, one book. It begins: To the reverend in Christ...

On the nature of things, one book.

The life of Saint Christina, one book.

And other works which I have not seen.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270. And there are those who write that he had knowledge of the Greek language and translated the books of Aristotle that are now in use in the schools.

Alfonso, king of Castile and Leon, a philosopher and astronomer most excellent among all men of his time, subtle in talent and distinguished in speech, an outstanding lover and cultivator of letters, after a long vacancy of the Roman Empire, had been elected king of the Romans against Richard, brother of the king of England; and since he was a good and prudent man, when Richard died in the fifteenth year of his election, with a view to peace he voluntarily yielded before Pope Gregory X and freely renounced every right that he had had in his election. He wrote very useful and elegant works:

Abbot of Spanheim

Astronomical tables, one book.

Letters to various persons, one book.

He flourished in the time of the vacant Empire, in the year of the Lord 1270.

[unclear]

Peter, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a Gaul by nation, and provincial prior in France of the same religious order, a man learned in divine scriptures by long study and not ignorant of secular philosophy, acute in talent and ready in speech, was apt in delivering sermons to the people. Hence, for the use of readers, he composed, through the cycle of the year, sermons not to be despised:

Sermons for the season, one book.

Sermons also on the saints, one book.

But he is said also to have written some other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Peter of Tarentaise, of the Order of Preachers, and, after Gregory X, canonically consecrated pope under the name Innocent V, sat in the supreme pontificate for only five months. Certainly he was a man most learned in divine scriptures and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, who taught theology excellently for many years and acquired great praise for his learning. He wrote many distinguished little works, by which he made his name known both to those then present and to those who would come afterward. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, one book. It begins: Do you know the order...

On all the epistles of Paul, one book. It begins: To inquire into the principles of things...

On the Psalms also, one book.

John of Ascoli, from Ascoli, of the Order of Friars Minor, minister general after Saint Bonaventure, a man learned in divine scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, was sent to Constantinople by Pope Gregory X. By his exhortations he brought the Greeks back to obedience to the Roman Church, and persuaded them to come with him to the Council of Lyons. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, works not to be despised:

Sermons for the season, one book.

Sermons on the saints, one book.

Several letters to various persons, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished while the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1170.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Rupert of Rusia, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, inasmuch as he taught theology excellently for many years and left after him many distinguished disciples, wrote several excellent little works by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant, addressed to Haymo the Englishman, minister general of his order, a man likewise most learned, a Declaration, one book.

On the Rule of St. Francis, four books. Also on the Sentences, four books. Various sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Udalric of Argentina, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, formerly a hearer and disciple of Albert the Great, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, composed little works not to be despised in reading, by which he became known to both present and future generations. Of these there are extant: A Summa of Theology, one book.

On the Sentences, four books. Also On the Soul, one book. And many other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Haymo, an Englishman by nation, minister general of the order of friars, a man trained by long study in the holy Scriptures, who, having obtained the magisterial chair of the theological faculty, instructed many disciples in it, and who, by order of Pope Alexander IV, corrected and rubricated the Roman Breviary, is reported, among other things, to have written briefly:

On the Sentences, one book. And certain sermons, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1279.

Otto, bishop of Freising in Bavaria in Germany, and, as some write, nephew of the emperor Frederick I, a German by nation, whom Pope Pius II, citing him in a certain oration, commends, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not meanly instructed in secular letters, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, wrote certain little works not contemptible in reading, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there is extant a distinguished work, to be pursued with every praise:

Histories, one book. And other things which I have not seen. He flo[unclear]

Abbot of Spanheim

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

Peter the Spaniard, a Portuguese, bishop of Tusculum and cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, and finally supreme pontiff after Hadrian V, a man very learned in medicine and magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, sat in the pontificate for only eight months. He wrote little works not to be despised by physicians, of which the following are reported:

Thesaurus pauperum, one book. On Problems, one book. Canons of Medicine, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And certain other things, namely several treatises in dialectic, already long very well known commonly.

He flourished in the pontificate under the name John XXI, in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1275.

William, a citizen of Piacenza, a learned doctor of the art of medicine and not ignorant of other humane letters, who, hired at a public salary at Verona, maintained a school in that faculty for many years and instructed several excellent disciples, wrote little works not to be despised by professors of this science, by which he made his name known to both present and future generations. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume which he wished to be entitled:

On Universal Medicine, four books. Also On Surgery, one book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William, bishop of Paris, by native land an Auvergnat, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent and open in eloquence, and venerable no less in conduct than in knowledge, composed not a few works of his learning, by which, showing himself both a learned and devout master, he rendered the memory of his name immortal. Of these the following are reported: a distinguished volume, entitled:

On the Holy Trinity, one book. On the First Principle, one book. On the Sacraments, one book. I shall add still four [unclear], one book. Summa of Vices, one book. Why God Became Man, one book. In the Order of Divine [unclear], one book. On Good and Evil, one book. Summa of Virtues, one book. On the Profession of Novices, one book. On Faith and Laws, one book. On the Works of Virtues, one book. On Human Souls, one book. [unclear] On the Tri[unclear] On the Universe, one book. 401 On the Gift of Knowledge, one book. 203

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Thirty Remedies for Temptations, 1 book. Against the Plurality of Benefices, 1 book. On the Cloister of the Soul, 1 book. On Divine Rhetoric, 1 book. On Penance, 1 book. On Demons, 1 book. On the Psalter, 1 book. On Ecclesiastes, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, [unclear] books. He also published certain other works which have by no means come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Frederick II, in the year of the Lord 1230.

John Valeis, otherwise Galensis, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, who for a long time taught theology with distinction in the school of Paris, was of such great learning and eloquence that he was called the Tree of Life. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come into our hands. For I found a notable volume, which I judge very necessary and useful for preachers of the word of God, which most people call the Communiloquium, because it contains something concerning every estate; but he himself entitled it: Sum of Collations, 7 books. "Since the doctor or preacher ..." On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Ordering of Life, 1 book. "Since in every undertaking ..." Handful of Flowers, 1 book. "Abstinence is good in ..." On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. On Diverse Subjects, 1 book. Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

And note that this book of John is called the Handful of Flowers, whose prologue begins, "Poor little Ruth"; he began it, but, prevented by death, did not finish it, but Brother Thomas of Ireland afterwards completed the same work. The book itself begins thus, according to alphabetical order: "Abstinence is good in food to receive with thanksgiving," etc. He flourished in the times of Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William Durandus, bishop of Mende, once a hearer and disciple of Henry of Ostia, whom they call the Speculator, a most pious doctor in law and very zealous for ecclesiastical observance, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, wrote to Ottobono, cardinal of St. Hadrian, afterwards supreme pontiff, Hadrian V, an outstanding work divided into three volumes, which he entitled: Mirror of Law, 3 books. "Reverend in Christ ..." Rationale of Divine Offices, 8 books. "Whatever things in the ecclesiastical ..." Repertory of Law, 1 book. "By the rust of the first-formed man ..." And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, and completed his work the Rationale of Divine Offices, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord 1286.

James of Belusio, a very distinguished doctor of both laws and a careful interpreter, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in counsel and knowledge, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, is said to have written certain excellent little works in law, by which he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity; of these I have not yet been able to see any. His works are said to be: On the Authentics, 1 book. On the View of Fiefs, 1 book. Additions on the Novels, 1 book. And many other works. And various disputations. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Lyons, of the Order of Friars Preachers, as they say, bishop of the same church, a man much learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, of sweet intellect and subtle speech, not over-curious, yet orderly, was quite outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He is said to have written certain little works, by which he magnificently instructed both those then present and those who would come afterwards; of these they report: On the Sentences, 4 books. Sum of Virtues, 5 books. "Since concerning individual useful things ..." Sum of Vices, 8 books. "About to speak of individual vices ..." Sermons to the People, 1 book. He is said to have written many other works also, which have not come to my knowledge.

William of Ware, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, teacher of John Scotus of the same order, a man sufficiently learned in the divine Scriptures and, through long study, very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy, in the manner of modern theologians, wrote certain works of his intellect not to be despised, by which he made himself known to posterity. Of these there are extant: On the Sentences, 1 book. "Since, according to the testimony of Blessed Augustine ..." Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

204 On Ecclesiastical Writers

He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Gerard, a monk of the monastery of St Quentin in the Isle, a man devoted to the Holy Scriptures and skilled through continual exercise, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain little works not to be despised in reading, by which he made his name known to those present and those to come. Among these is said to be a history of the translation of the crown and of part of the Lord's cross, which relics Louis, king of France, obtained from the emperor of Constantinople and transferred to Paris. He also wrote concerning blessed Elizabeth the Landgravine:

Miracles after her death, four books. Responsories and chants concerning the same, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280. And in both kinds of literature he composed various little works.

William Lamarensis, of the order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by long use and exercise, and also, according to the custom of that time, sufficiently skilled in secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, composed various little works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Correctory of the works of Thomas, one book. Additions on Bonaventure, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1289.

Richard, archbishop of Reims in Gaul, of the order of Friars Minor, excellently learned in the Holy Scriptures, inferior to none of the doctors of his time in delivering sermons to the people, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, is said to have written many excellent volumes, by which he rendered himself useful to those then present and known to those to come; but I do not recall that any of them has come into our hands. The following are reported as his:

Sermons for the season, one book. Also sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

William of Samuco, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary Ever-[unclear]

The Abbot of Sponheim

[unclear] learned in the Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, venerable no less in manner of life than in learning, published several little works of great usefulness, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported: a certain little work not useless to spiritual persons, which he entitled:

Decretals of religious, one book. On the Sentences, one book. On the rule of his order, one book. Chronicle of his order, one book. And many other things.

He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Aegidius of Rome, of the order of the Hermit Friars of St Augustine, prior general and afterward archbishop of Bourges, formerly a hearer of blessed Thomas Aquinas, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct, wrote almost innumerable little works, of which few have come into our hands. The following are reported as his:

[unclear], two books. On the Hexaemeron, “Let your voice sound in my ears,” one book. On the body of Christ, one book. On the measure of angels, “Because among the other things which,” one book. “That concerning the measure of angels,” one book. On the knowledge of angels. The question: “Whether angels,” one book. [unclear], one book. Distinction of the articles of faith, one book. On Ecclesiastical Writers

On predestination, one book. “To the noble knight, lord ...” The Theory of Being and Essence, one book. “Every being either is ...” On the Soul, as the Philosopher attests ... On generation and corruption, one book. “I am dust ...” In which are set forth ... On original sin, one book. “Of theological truth ...” On the formation of the human body, one book. “It will not please him when ...” On ecclesiastical power, five books. “Why have you disparaged ...” [unclear] [unclear], one book. And not a few other works. A Compendium of Theology, six books. On the Renunciation of the Pope, one book. Against the Corrupter of Thomas, one book. Various Sermons, two books. On all the books of Aristotle. Notable Letters. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

[unclear], chaplain of the pontiff, as they say, a man nobly learned in canon law and secular philosophy, excellent in talent and distinguished in eloquence, who in his own time was considered not least among the doctors of this faculty, wrote some little works not to be despised in their reading, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a notable Summa, sufficiently widely circulated:

On the Titles of the Decretals, five books. “The diversity of glosses in ...” Various Questions, one book. Other works which he is said to have composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Guido de Baysio, archdeacon of Bologna, a man most skilled in both laws, acute in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, whose authority among the professors of this science has endured greatly down to the present day, wrote many distinguished volumes, by which, so to speak, he rendered the memory of his name immortal. Of these only a few have so far come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following: a very large and highly notable volume, which he entitled Rosarium:

On the Decree, three books. “Reverend in Christ ...” On the Decretals, five books. He flourished under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Thaddaeus, a Florentine by nation, a most skilled doctor of the medical art, who taught that science excellently at Bologna for certain years, hired at a public salary, gathered an almost incredible treasure and acquired a great reputation for his experience. For when he was called by some prince, he wished to have no less than fifty gold coins as his daily wage. Once called by Pope Honorius IV, he refused to come until one hundred gold coins per day were appointed for him; when the pope had been cured of a most serious illness, he bestowed ten thousand gold coins on him. He wrote:

On the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, one book. On the Prognostics of the same, one book. On the Work on Acute Diseases of the same, one book. On Galen’s Techne, one book. On the Isagoge of Johannitius, one book. On Preserving Health, one book. Various Counsels, one book. And certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280. And at last, an octogenarian, he died at Bologna.

John of Parma, born from the territories of Bologna, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man learned in the divine scriptures, devout in life and conduct, and an outstanding lover of holy poverty, who from the Parisian school, where he had lectured on the Sentences, was elected general in his absence, is said to have written many and various treatises, by which his name has come down to our memory. Of these I have found only:

On the Sentences, four books. On the Conduct of Religious, two books. He flourished while the Empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

John Christophori, of the Order of Friars Preachers, exercised in the scriptures by long and continual study and nobly learned in secular philosophy, ready in talent and scholastic in speech, is said to have fashioned many little works on the holy scriptures; their publication made him, useful to those then present, known to those to come. For over a long time he expounded the divine writings publicly by lecturing and explained them with subtle understanding. From his commentaries the following volumes are reported, namely:

On the Gospel of Matthew, one book. On Mark, one book. On Luke, one book. On John, one book. On all the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books. And many other works.

208 On Ecclesiastical Writers

He flourished while the empire was vacant, in the year of the Lord 1260.

Hambaldus, a Roman by nationality, professor of sacred theology and an outstanding interpreter of the Scriptures, subtle and forceful in intellect, and quite capable in disputing and solving their difficult questions, is said to have written certain excellent little works for the instruction of his disciples, by which he made his name known. Among these there are extant: On the Sentences, one book. Quodlibets, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Rudolph, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Henry of Ghent, archdeacon of Tournai, German by nationality, a man among all the doctors of his time most learned in the divine Scriptures, and very subtle in Aristotelian philosophy, was of such reputation and authority in the University of Paris that he was called the Solemn Doctor throughout the whole Christian world. For he was subtle in intellect and most acute in scholastic disputations, as his excellent works testify. Of these I have found only the following at present:

Summa of Theology, one book. On the Sentences, two books. To the Sacred Virgins, beginning “Concerning virginity,” one book. On Penance, one book. On the Metaphysics, three books. On the books of the Physics, five books. On Metaphysics, four books. He indeed composed many other things, but they have not come to my knowledge.

He died under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1293, in the sixth indiction, on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul, and was buried at Tournai in the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God.

Hugolinus, patriarch of Constantinople, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man trained by long study in the divine writings and sufficiently learned, subtle in intellect, almost scholastic, noteworthy in character and life, is said to have written certain excellent little works, of not contemptible reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following, among others, are reckoned the better ones:

On the Sentences, three books. Quodlibets, six books. On the Difference of Idioms, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Adolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Arlotus, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, Tuscan by nationality, a man excellently learned in the divine writings and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, a subtle dialectician and a most acute disputant, who won great praise for his learning by writing variously, was of excellent talent in declaiming sermons to the people. He is said to have assembled the Concordances of the New and Old Testament into one volume, one book. Various Sermons, one book.

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of Emperor Adolf, in the year 1290.

The Abbot of Sponheim

James, bishop of Genoa, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man trained in the divine Scriptures, who because of his frequent citations of them was called Vorago, quick in intellect and clear in speech, was quite capable in declaiming sermons to the people. He wrote not a few little works for the use of readers, by which he made his name known. Of these a few have come to my knowledge, which I have also set down below: A volume of great size on the life and deeds of many saints, which he entitled the Golden Legend or Mirror of Saints, but which is now commonly called the Legend or

Lombardic History, one book. The whole present time [unclear]. “As I consider, the days [unclear].” On Saint Mary, one book.

Chronicle of the Genoese, one book.

On the Little Works of Saint Augustine, one book. “Sacred Scripture [unclear].” Sermons on the Season, one book.

“Following his footsteps [unclear] outstanding, in intellect [unclear] as I consider, the days [unclear].” Sermons on the Saints, one book.

An excellent preacher of the Word, distinguished in intellect and clear [unclear], he taught the people in truth, and, with the Holy Spirit working together, he brought the hearts of many to the love of Christ. He wrote sermons not to be despised, which he delivered to the people:

Sermons on the Season, one book.

He is also said to have written a number of other things, which have not come into our hands.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Conrad of Halberstadt, German by nationality, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man nobly learned both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher and theologian not worthless, since by lecturing publicly in that faculty he taught many and acquired great praise for his learning, wrote certain things in both

On Ecclesiastical Writers

... not to be despised in learning, by which he brought his name down to the memory of posterity. But few of them have become known to me. For I have found only:

A Summa for Students, 3 books. “This little work into three ...” Also On the Trivium, 1 book. “In three [unclear] ...” A Lecture on Job, 1 book. “Until the time [unclear] ...” Also Sermons, 1 book.

He is also said to have written commentaries on several books of the Bible, which, however, have not yet come into our hands. He is also said to have been the first to arrange concordances of the whole Bible of the New and Old Testament.

Richard of Middleton, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed both in philosophy and in canon law, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, subtle and ready in resolving questions and doubts concerning the Scriptures, is said to have written many very distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

On the Sentences, 4 books. “He brought forth hidden things ...” On the distinctions of the Decretum, 1 book. “All our fathers under ...” On the Order of Judgments, 1 book. On the Epistles of Paul, 4 books.

It is said, moreover, that he issued elegant commentaries and lectures on several books of sacred Scripture, but they have not come into our hands. He flourished in the times of the emperor Adolf and Pope Nicholas IV, in the year of the Lord 1290.

Nicholas of Bibra, German by nation, a man nobly learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher and distinguished poet, who at Erfurt in his time was held in esteem, acquired great glory for his learning and wrote not a few little works both in meter and in prose, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have seen only a work whose title is hidden, which he composed at Erfurt in verse and in prose:

On Avoiding Evil, 1 book. “Hearer of the poem ...” Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He flourished at Erfurt under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

John of Paris, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a theologian most learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, since, indeed, having ascended the magisterial chair in both branches of learning in the university of Paris, he taught publicly for a long time and left not a few disciples, is said to have written certain distinguished little works, by which he made himself useful to those then present and afterwards known to those to come. Of these I have found only a work not to be despised:

On the Sentences, 4 books.

Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished under the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1280.

Abbot of Spanheim

Nicholas the Frenchman, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, seventh prior general, a learned and holy man, who, after he had ruled his order vigorously for almost twenty years, as far as he was able, yielded his office for love of Christ and returned to the quiet of the hermitage, where he persevered in holy conduct until death, wrote, among other things, a mournful work lamenting the state of his order, when the brothers had been expelled from the Holy Land, which he entitled:

The Fiery Arrow, 1 book.

He wrote other things also. He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1270.

Matthew of Aquasparta, otherwise Aquasputa, of the Order of Friars Minor, twelfth minister general, and afterwards bishop of Porto and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, a man most learned in these divine Scriptures and, according to the custom of this time, magnificently instructed in secular philosophy, composed certain distinguished little works of excellent talent, by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these the following are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Inventory of Sentences, 1 book. On the Epistle to the Romans, 1 book. Several Sermons, 1 book.

And certain other things. He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1390.

William Peraldus, French by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and also sufficiently excellently instructed in secular letters, especially in Aristotelian philosophy, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, was of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people. He issued, in both faculties, several instructive volumes, by which he made his name known not only to those then present, but also to those to come. Of these there are extant:

Summa of Virtues and Vices, 2 books. On the Instruction of Religious, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

And very many other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

218 On Ecclesiastical Writers

Garcias, Spanish by nation, a man most practiced in both laws, subtle in intellect, ready and cautious in counsel, acute in resolving questions of cases, held in esteem among the professors of this faculty in his time, extended his name by teaching and writing. For he is said to have written several small works both in the laws and in canon law, which have not come into our hands. There are extant by him:

On the Decretals, five books.

And several works in the laws.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Rudolf, in the year of the Lord 1290.

[Nicolaus?] IV, pope, of the order of the Friars Minor, [Hieronymus?] [unclear], sat after Honorius IV in the chair of Peter for four years: a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not meanly instructed in secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and venerable no less for goodness of life than for learning. He wrote a sufficiently excellent work:

On the Sentences, four books.

And certain sermons.

He is also said to have published useful commentaries on several books of the Bible. He died at Rome, the empire being vacant after Rudolf’s death, in the year of the Lord 1291, in the fourth indiction.

Boniface VIII, pope, Campanian by nation, previously called Benedict, sat after the renunciation of Celestine V in the chair of Peter for eight years and nine months; a man indeed learned, but excessively arrogant and ambitious. By what means he acquired the pontificate, the chronographers have not passed over in silence. Since he was very skilled in law and saw that new varieties of cases were daily arising in the contentious forum which could not be determined through the Decretals, he composed, through three men most learned in law, new constitutions, which he wished to be called:

The Sixth of the Decretals of the Most Holy Roman [Church], one book.

Letters, several, to various persons, one book.

He died under the emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1305, indiction 1. Concerning him it had previously been prophesied: “He entered like a fox, lived like a lion, died like a dog.”

Guilhelmus Mandagoti, archdeacon of Nimes, afterward archbishop of Embrun, and of the most holy church

SImon monachus Haffligemeh,ordinis S.Benedicti,vir in diui- nis scripturis studiofissimus et amp; eruditus,inagenio subtilis et amp; cla- rus eloquio,confilium diui legislatorii nostri Benedictĩ,q̇ mo nachus diuinas scripturas amare iubetur,ita conuertit in practi- cam,vt nihil dulcius in hac vita fuerit quàm facras literas legere, &amp; sanctoꝝ patrum opuscula sedulo studio reuoluere,Abbreuiauit Moralia Gregorij papae lib.10. In Cantica scripsit fermones lib.i. Visionem cuiufdam conuersi lib.i. Sermones plures lib.i. Epi

The Abbot of Spanheim.

... finally cardinal of the Roman Church, a man highly skilled in both laws, one of those who, by order of Pope Boniface VIII, issued the Sixth Book of the Decretals, as is clear at the beginning of that same volume. In that faculty he wrote works not to be despised, by which he preserved his name for immortality. Of these I have seen only the notable work which he wrote while he still held the office of archdeacon in the church of Nîmes, to Berengarius, succentor of the church of Béziers and afterwards bishop:

On the election of prelates, book 1. “Because while elections in ...” Exposition of the same, book 1. “Since I am not the author of that ...”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Berengarius, succentor of the church of Béziers and afterwards bishop, and at last cardinal of the most holy Roman Church, to whom the aforesaid Guilhelmus Mandagoti, while both were still established in minor orders, composed the book On the Elections of Prelates, another of those who, at the command of Boniface VIII, compiled the Sixth Book of the Decretals, a man very learned in the same legal faculty, while he was still succentor, wrote to that same Guilhelmus, then archdeacon of Nîmes, a notable work on the Summa of Hostiensis according to alphabetical order; since it is, as it were, a clarifying glossary of that same Summa, he entitled it:

The Eye, book 1. On the sentence of excommunication, book 1.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1309.

Richardus de Senis, vice-chancellor of the Roman Church, and afterwards [unclear], in the praise of all [unclear] very celebrated in his time, the third of those who compiled the Sixth Book of the Decretals by order of Pope Boniface VIII, whose name is expressly contained at the beginning of that same volume, is reported to have written several works in law; but I do not remember that any of them have come into our hands. Let the studious reader inquire after them.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Dinus Mugelanus, professor of both laws and a notable expounder, subtle in intellect, and very ready and acute in disputing and resolving doubtful matters and questions of law, who by teaching and writing acquired great glory for himself among all the doctors of Italy, published many distinguished works in his faculty, among which the following are reported. By command of Lord Pope Boniface VIII he was the first after the archdeacon to write elegantly:

On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, book 1. On the Code, 10 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. Many Consilia, book 1.

Besides these he also published not a few other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He also wrote On Interest; On Prescriptions; On Successions from Intestacy; On the Method of Arguing; Contrary Glosses and their Agreements.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Johannes Duns, a Scot by birth, of the Order of Friars Minor, once a hearer of Alexander of Hales the Englishman at Paris, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and very learned in Aristotelian philosophy, and so profound that his writings are penetrable [unclear], and for that reason also less commonly used, published certain instructive volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. “Desiring ... Around the prologue ...” Quodlibets, book 1. “All difficult matters ...” On the Knowledge of God, book 1. “Because the highest ... for us ...” Questions on the Metaphysics, book 1. Sermons on the season, book 1. “There shall be signs,” etc. “In this ...” Sermons on the saints, book 1.

He is said to have written commentaries on the Gospel and the Apostle, and to have composed various other treatises, which have not come to my knowledge.

He died in the time of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1398, in the sixth indiction, and was buried at Cologne among the Friars Minor.

Simon, monk of Hasnon [unclear], of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man most devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, so put into practice the counsel of our divine lawgiver Benedict, by which the monk is commanded to love the divine Scriptures, that nothing in this life was sweeter to him than to read the sacred writings and to turn over with diligent study the works of the holy fathers. He abridged:

The Moralia of Pope Gregory, 10 books. On the Song of Songs he wrote sermons, book 1. The vision of a certain convert, book 1. Several sermons, book 1.

Epi...

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Also letters to various persons, 1 book. And many other things.

He also collected excerpts from the sermons of blessed Pope Gregory on Ezekiel; also from the Conferences of the holy fathers, from Richard of Saint Victor’s On the Contemplation of the Twelve Patriarchs, and various worthwhile things from various authors.

Peter de Bella Parthica, otherwise Pertica, a Burgundian by nation, a man most skilled in both civil and canon law, subtle and acute in intellect, and very ready in disputing and resolving doubtful questions of law, wrote many excellent volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Code, 9 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. One Hundred Disputations, 1 book. Several Opinions. And certain other things.

He flourished at the same time as Dinus Mugelanus, under Emperor Albert and Pope Boniface VIII, in the year of the Lord 1300.

[Rainerus?] of Pisa, otherwise Rainerius, an Italian by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and learned in the holy Scriptures, and sufficiently skilled in canon law, quick in intellect, scholastic in speech, cautious in counsel, venerable no less for religion than for learning, in order to provide a path in hearing confessions for his brothers who were less experienced in law, wrote a great and distinguished Summa on cases, in two large volumes according to alphabetical order, which he entitled:

Pantheologia, 2 books. 'Absolution. Concerning abso[unclear]' And certain other things.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Gerard, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a German by nation, lector of the convent of Liege, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer in making sermons to the people, distinguished in intellect and adorned with scholastic eloquence, wrote a very useful treatise for devout religious persons, teaching the seven dispositions to be made concerning the heart, and sagaciously gathering from the divine Scriptures on every side many things pertaining to edification, which he entitled:

On the Teaching of the Heart, 1 book. 'Prepare your hearts.' Sermons for the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

In addition he published certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

James de Arena, a native of Parma, a very celebrated jurist in both laws, profound in intellect, scholastic in speech, whose opinions in explaining the laws, as Bartolus testifies, were so proper and fitting that [unclear] concerning civil understanding many excellent little works, by which he transmitted his name to the perpetual memory of posterity:

On the Code, 9 books. On the New Digest, 24 books. On the Old Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On Excuses, 1 book. Various Disputations, 1 book.

But he also published several other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

John of San Gimignano, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man studious and especially learned in the divine Scriptures, distinguished in intellect and clear in speech, of excellent industry in declaiming sermons to the people, acquired great praise and fruit of doctrine in the salvation of souls. He wrote, among other things:

On the Similitudes of Things, 1 book. Sermons for the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Various Conferences, 1 book.

In addition he is said to have written certain other things, which have not come to me.

Peter of Dacia, a philosopher, calculator, and astronomer, the most excellent and celebrated among all men of his time, subtle in intellect and clear in speech, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures and of the Greek language, is said to have written many little works in astronomy and the art of calculation, which are judged not useless for ecclesiastical computation, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge.

On Calculation or Computation, 1 book. Also a Calendar, 1 book. And of his tables, 1 book.

The rest, although there are many things that he composed, have nevertheless not come to me.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Nicholas of Naples, a man skilled and very learned in civil law, nobly instructed also in other secular letters, whose authority among the professors of this faculty flourished in no small measure in his time, wrote several little works on the laws, of which

The Abbot of Sponheim.

By the publication of books he entrusted his name to immortality. But I have been able to find only the titles of the following:

On the Code, 9 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books.

Of the other things which he is said to have composed, I have so far been able to find nothing certain. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Hubertinus of Casale, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of Johannes of Parma, minister general, a devout man, sufficiently learned in the holy Scriptures, when he saw that his order was falling away from its first institution, began certain new separations under the appearance of reform, and obtained that they be confirmed by the supreme pontiff. Yet at the petitions of the custodians and ministers they were immediately revoked by the same pope, because they appeared to have been undertaken to the grave scandal and division of the order. Therefore Hubertinus, moved by this, entered the Order of the Carthusians. He wrote a very distinguished and notable volume, useful to religious and devout persons, which he entitled:

The Tree of the Life of the Crucified, 5 books. Sermons; Letters. To all true [servants?] of Christ. And certain other things.

Certain Catholic doctors warn us that Hubertinus, in the aforesaid volume, in certain places, especially where he takes up the Canticle of Simeon, must be read cautiously, because on certain articles he thinks otherwise than the Church, mother of us all. Yet the author himself is to be excused, because it had not yet been determined. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Jacobus of Ravenna, born in the province of Lorraine, a man most learned in civil law and the sacred canons, and easily the most skilled of all in his time both in divine Scriptures and in secular letters, professor of sacred Scripture, a distinguished philosopher and dialectician, who, as Cinus says, converted what had been handed down by the elders in a simple sense into the dialectical mode of arguing. He wrote many small works in both laws, of which the following are reported:

On the Code, 9 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. Various Disputations, 1 book.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Alanus de Insulis, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and in secular letters second to none in his time, a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, and poet, who for a long time gloriously presided over the ecclesiastical school at Paris, where, shining brightly in every divine and human science, he deserved to be called Universal, wrote in verse and prose almost innumerable little works, by which the memory of his name was made immortal among posterity. But few of them have come to my knowledge. For I have found only the following under their titles:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Quodlibets also, 1 book. The Eye of Sacred Scripture, 1 book. On Doctrine also, 5 books. On the Five Books of Moses, 5 books. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On Penance, to the father of Bourges, 1 book. On Mystical Equivocal Terms, 1 book. On the Six Wings of the Cherubim, 1 book. On the Complaint of Nature, 1 book. A Summa of Virtues and Vices, 1 book. On Parables, 1 book. On the Art of Preaching, 1 book. Anticlaudianus, 1 book. On the Natures of Animals, 1 book. Several Sermons, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

To the most reverend father and... Every science rests upon its own rules. Since many, for the adorning... By the grace of God, to the father of Bourges [unclear] From Phoebus, Phoebe [unclear]

And he wrote some dialogues.

Finally, he is said to have produced notable commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, especially on the prophets, on the Gospel, and on the Apostle; concerning these I have so far been able to find nothing. Certain marvelous things are told about him, to which I neither lend credence nor rashly deny it. He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Guilhelmus, a monk of the monastery of Hafligemen[unclear], of the Order of Saint Benedict, German by nation, and for some time prior in the same monastery, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and learned by long practice, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, strong in verse and prose, published in both kinds of writing certain little works not to be scorned, by which he [perpetuated?] the memory of his name; among these are
