ABBAS SPANHEIMENSIS. Sermones non inutiles lib.i. Vifiones cuiufdam monialis lib.i. De vita sanctae Lutgardis lib.i. Alia vero quae cõposuit, ad notitiã meam adhuc minime venerũt. Ranciscus Accursius, natione Italus, patria Florẽtinus, Accur si doctißimi viri filius, vir ipse in iure ciuili egregie doctꝰ, atque in alijs secularis philosophiae diiciplinis multum eruditꝰ, cuius oꝑa magnae authoritatis extant apud huiusce facultatis pro- fessores, docendo scribendo tempora sua clara reddidit, nomẽ suum immortalitati donauit. De cuius opusculis nihil adhuc vide re potui. Feruntur eius variae Disputationes quoque lib.i. Et alia plura. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore, anno domini 1300. Martinꝰ de Fano, vtriusque iuris profefor interpres omniũ suo tẽpore celeberrimꝰ, Iohãnis Andreę Bononien̄ p̃ceptor, ingenio subtilis eloqo clarꝰ, in perorãdis causis iudiciali bus acutissimus: scripfit in sua facultate egregia volumina, quibus nomen suum etiã pofteritati notificauit, e quibus tantum reperi De actionibus lib.i. Ego quidem Martinus De iudicio causaque lib.i. Quoniam plerique principa De alijs nihil vidi. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore, anno dominj 1500. A libertus Patauinus, ordinis fratrū Eremitarū sancti Au- gustini, Aegidij Romani quandam auditor atque discipulus, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosus eruditus, seculariũ lite rarum non ignarus, in declamandis ad populum sermonibus excel lentis ingenij fuit, multos ab iniquitate ad semitam iustitiae sua ẜdicatioẽ cõuertit. Scripsit multa p̃clara volumina, qbus se p̃sen- tibus tũc vtilẽ, posteris memorabilē effecit. de qbus īsta ferũtur: In Genefim lib.i. In Exodum lib.i. In Leuticum lib.i. In Numeros lib.i. In Deuteronomiũ lib.i. In Euangelium lib.i. In epistolas Pauli lib.i. Sermones de tẽpore li.i. Sermones de sanctis lib.i. Sermones per quadragefimam lib.i. Et quãdam alia. Claruit tẽporibus Alberti imperatoris, anno domini 1500. cc ij Dis 228 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. D Inus de Garbo, patria Florentinus, artis medicinae peritissi- mus doctor, atque in secularis philosophiae institutionibus no biliter eruditus, ingenio subtilis clarus eloquior edidit in sua facultate studentibus non contemnenda opuscula, quib⁹ me- moriã sui noīs ad notitiā posteritatis transmisit, e quib⁹ feruntur Commentaria in Galenum. De malitia variae complexionis, lib.i. In Hippocratem de natura foetus,lib.i. Diuersarum quaestionum lib.i. In Auicennam quoque lib.i. In philosophia etiā varia. Et quaedam alia. Huius pater Brunus in arte chirurgica peritissimus fuit medicus, qui hunc Dinum Thadaeo medico Florentino tradidit in ea scien tia erudiendum. Claruit sub Alberto imperatore, Anno domini 1300. G Vilielmus de Cumo,natione Gallus,iuris ciuilis consultissi- mus interpres,ingenio subtilis clarus eloquio,q;in ea fa- cultate suo tempore paucos habuit doctiores,docēdo scri- bendo Aurelianense gymnasium magnifice illustrauit. Edidit p̄- festoribus legum non spernenda opuscula , quib⁹ nomẽ suum po- steris notificauit Super ff.veteri lib.24. Super Codice quoque lib.9. Et alia diuersa. Claruit sub Henrico imperatore 7.Anno domini 1310. I Acobus de Viterbio,archiepiscopus Neapolitanus, ordinis fra- trum eremitarũ sancti Augustini,vir indiuinis scripturis eru- ditus, secularis literaturę non ignarus, ingenio subtilis, cla- rus eloquior nec minus conuersatione quàm scientia venerabilis; scripsit ad aedificationem legendium non contemnenda opufcula, quibus nominis sui memoriam ad posteros cum gloria transmi- fit,e quibus ego adhuc nullum videre merui.Fertur autem eius ad Clementem papam quintum, De regimine Chr̄ianoꝝ lib.i. Super sententias lib.4. Quodlibeta quoque lib.i. Et nonnulla alia. Claruit temporibus Henrici Lutzelburgenfis imperatoris septi- mi, Clementis papae quinti,Anno domini 1316. Hen

Abbot of Spanheim.

Non-useless sermons, one book. Visions of a certain nun, one book. On the life of Saint Lutgardis, one book. But other things which he composed have not yet come at all to my knowledge.

Franciscus Accursius, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, son of the most learned man Accursius, himself a man excellently learned in civil law and much instructed in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, whose works survive with great authority among the professors of this faculty, made his own times illustrious by teaching and writing, and gave his name to immortality. Of his little works I have as yet been able to see nothing. Various works of his are reported:

Disputations also, one book. And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Martinus de Fano, a professor and interpreter of both laws, most celebrated among all in his own time, the teacher of Johannes Andreae of Bologna, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, and most acute in pleading legal cases, wrote distinguished volumes in his faculty, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only:

On actions, one book. “I indeed, Martinus...” On judgment and cause, one book. “Since very many principal...”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Albertus Patavinus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, once a hearer and disciple of Aegidius Romanus, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, and by his preaching converted many from iniquity to the path of justice. He wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made himself useful to those then present and memorable to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On Genesis, one book. On Exodus, one book. On Leviticus, one book. On Numbers, one book. On Deuteronomy, one book. On the Gospel, one book. On the Epistles of Paul, one book. Sermons for the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Sermons throughout Lent, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Dinus de Garbo, Florentine by homeland, a most skilled doctor of the art of medicine, and nobly instructed in the institutions of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, published in his faculty little works not to be despised by students, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported:

Commentaries on Galen. On the malice of varied complexion, one book. On Hippocrates, On the nature of the fetus, one book. A book of various questions, one book. On Avicenna also, one book. Various things also in philosophy. And certain other things.

His father Brunus was a physician most skilled in the art of surgery; he entrusted this Dinus to the Florentine physician Thadaeus to be instructed in that science.

He flourished under Emperor Albert, in the year of the Lord 1300.

Guilielmus de Cumo, French by nation, a most learned interpreter of civil law, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, who in that faculty had few more learned than himself in his own time, magnificently adorned the school of Orleans by teaching and writing. He published little works not to be scorned by professors of the laws, by which he made his name known to posterity:

On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the Code also, 9 books. And various other things.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Jacobus de Viterbio, archbishop of Naples, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, renowned in eloquence, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, wrote little works not to be despised for the edification of readers, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with glory. I have as yet deserved to see none of these. But the following work of his addressed to Pope Clement V is reported:

On the government of Christians, one book. On the Sentences, 4 books. Quodlibets also, one book. And some other things.

He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and of Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1316.

De quibus fe- runtur praecipua: De sacramentis lib.i. Summa de casibus lib.i. De=

Abbot of Spanheim.

Henry of Brussels, a monk of the monastery of Affligem of the order of the blessed father Benedict, a man devoted to divine Scripture and skilled through continual practice, an excellent philosopher and computist, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote several commendable little works, by which in his own time he became known far and wide. Of these there are reported:

On the Method of Computation, one book. A Calendar on Incensions, one book.

And certain other works, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

Alexander of Alexandria, the sixteenth minister general of the order of friars, a man most learned in the divine writings, and second to none in his own time in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, profound in sense and understanding, composed certain little works in each science, by which, exercising his talent, he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Various Questions, one book.

On Aristotle's Metaphysics, twelve books. On the books On the Soul, three books.

He also commented on other books of Aristotle and wrote various works. He flourished under the emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Eckard, a German by nation, of the order, as some will have it, of Preachers, a man learned in the divine writings and, in Aristotelian philosophy, the most learned of all in his time, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence; but, while pursuing philosophy too much, he everywhere curiously mixed in novelty of terms contrary to the custom of theologians and introduced various errors, among which there survive seventeen articles condemned by the supreme pontiff and revoked at the end of his life by the same master Eckard. Many of these are contained in his exposition on the Gospel of John. Finally, the masters of the theological faculty of the school of Heidelberg, in the year of the Lord 1430, publicly declared the same errors, with certain others, condemned. Eleven articles, however, were left as suspect, all of which were customarily appended separately to his little works as a precaution. Nevertheless, where he wrote in Catholic fashion, he gave quite profound and useful teachings. Among his books I have found:

On the Sentences, one book.

On Genesis, one book.

On Exodus, one book.

On the book of Wisdom, one book.

On the Song of Songs, one book.

The beginning of this writing: These are the names, etc.; because Love, etc.; The judge always [unclear] ij In

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Gospel of John, one book. In the beginning, etc. [unclear]

On the Lord's Prayer, one book. Our Father. Before Sunday

A sermon in the chapter of the Preachers, one book. I as a fruitful vine

Of his Positions, one book. Blessed be God the Father

Sermons for the season, one book. The God of peace and love

Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in his time especially in Austria, where he was held most famous in teaching and preaching; he wrote many other volumes.

Richard Malumbra, a native of Cremona, formerly a hearer and disciple of Jacobus de Arena, a man not moderately learned in imperial law, sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, who for many years publicly taught the laws in the school of Bologna, where he acquired no small praise for his learning. Although he was the most learned of all the doctors of his time, nevertheless he is read to have been condemned of heresy. He wrote many volumes in explanation of civil law:

On the Code, nine books. On the Institutes, four books.

On the Digest, fifty books. Various Questions, one book.

And many other works.

He flourished under the emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Lampertinus de Ramponibus, a man most learned in both laws and nobly educated in the other arts of humanity, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, and notable for the practice of many virtues, wrote in that faculty many splendid volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise. Of these there are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

On the New Digest, twelve books. On the Infortiatum, fourteen books.

And certain other works.

He flourished under Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

William of Montlaudun, as they report, abbot of the monastery of Poitiers, of the order of the blessed father Benedict, a man excellently learned in divine Scripture, not ignorant of secular letters, especially Aristotelian philosophy and pontifical law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, published several little works of great authority, by which he made known to posterity the memory of his name. Of these the principal are reported:

On the Sacraments, one book. A Summa on Cases, one book. On

Vido, Ferrariensis ecclesiae presbyter, & postea (vt ferunt) episcopus, vir in diuinis scripturis lõgo studio exercitatus, & verterum lectione diues, atque in secularibus literis nobiliter doctorus, philosophus et poeta insignis: scripsit tam metro quàm ꝓsanon contemnendae lectionis plura opusacula, quibus nomen suumnotificauit. De quibus ego tantum volumen carmine scriptum reperi ad Clementem papam quintum, super nouum et vetus testamẽtum, imitatus Petrum de Riga, quod praenotauit Margaritam Bibliae lib.1. Petrus de Saxonia, natione Teutonicus, ordinis fratrum Minorum, in scripturis sanctis eruditus, & secularis philosophiae nonignarus, atque in iure canonicò nobiliter doctus; ingenio clarus, sermone scholasticus, diuini verbi praedicator egregius: scriꝑfit ingenij sui quaedam praeclara volumina, que suo tempore inpriçio habebantur. E quibus extat opus cõfessoribus vtile, Summa casuum lib.1. Sermones de tempore lib.1.Sermones de sanctis lib.1.Caetera q̃ composuisse dicitur, ad notitiam meam non venerũt. Scripserat antea in sua facultate nonnulla opuscula, quibus nomen notificavit.E quibus extat commentumIn Techni Galeni, lib.1.Et quaedam alia. Scripsitqꝫ multa praeclara opuscula, qbus nomen fu- um magnifice dilatauit. E quibus extant Super Sententias lib.4. Qui diasciplinati homi Venite, adscendamus lib.i. Nondū erant abysli, Sermones de tempore lib.i. Sermones de sanctis lib.i. Et alia quae non vidi. Claruit ante pontificatum suum Parisiis legens sententias, tempo ribus Ludouici Bauari imperatoris quarti, anno dñi 1317. <Emphasis type="italic">G</Emphasis>Entilis Fulginas, medicinae professor insignis, atqꝫ in alijs se- cularis philosophiae disciplinis magnifice doctus, cuius in ea facultate peritia non modica erat: scripsit in medicinis mul- ta (vt ferunt) egregia volumina, quibus nomē suum non folū tunc presentibus, sed etiam posteris cum laude notum fecit. Sed nihil eo rum vidi. Feruntur autem In Auicennam commentariorum lib.i. De gradibus medicinae lib.i. Et quedam alia. †Confiliorum in omnes morbos lib.i. Claruit sub Henrico imperatore VII. anno dn̄i 1310. <Initial type="simple">D</Initial>Antes Aligerus, natione Italus, patria Florētinus, vir tam in diuinis scripturis quàm in secularibꝰ literis omniū suo tem pore studiosissimus; scripsit metro prosa multa praeclara vo lumina, quibus nomen suum ad posteros trāfmisit. Pulsus patria omnibus diebus suis, exulauit in Gallia aliquandiu, postea apud Aragonum regem, de sua calamitate varia composuit. De cui- us opusculis ista feruntur: Comoediarum lib.i. De monarchia mundi lib.i. Epistolae plures, Et quaedam alia. †Eiusdem disputatio de aqua terra. Moritur tandem exul apud Rauēnam, sub Ludouico Bauaro im- pe

Abbot of Spanheim.

Various Declarations. Moreover he published many other small works, especially in law, and arranged various glosses on the canons, about which I have nowhere been able to find anything.

Vido, priest of the church of Ferrara and afterwards, as they say, bishop, a man trained by long study in the divine Scriptures, rich in reading of the ancients, and nobly learned in secular letters, an eminent philosopher and poet, wrote several small works, both in verse and in prose, not to be despised in reading, by which he made his name known. Of these I have found only a volume written in verse to Pope Clement V, on the New and Old Testament, imitating Peter of Riga, which he entitled The Pearl of the Bible, one book. Its noble beginning [unclear]. I have seen nothing of the others.

He flourished in the times of Henry of Luxembourg, the seventh emperor, and Pope Clement V, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Peter of Saxony, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, learned in the holy Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, and nobly learned in canon law, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, an excellent preacher of the divine word, wrote certain excellent volumes of his own ability, which in his time were held in esteem. Of these there is extant a work useful for confessors: A Summa of Cases, one book; Sermons on the Season, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book. The rest that he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Crufianus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, once a hearer and disciple of the physician Thadaeus, a man learned and instructed in philosophy and medicine, but by no means fortunate, and for that reason bidding farewell to the world and entering the Carthusian order, usefully exchanged the art of the flesh for the medicine of the spirit. He had previously written some small works in his own faculty, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a commentary On the Techne of Galen, one book, and certain others.

He flourished in the Carthusian order in the time of Albert, Roman emperor, in the year of the Lord 1300. And afterwards he is said to have written various treatises pertaining to spiritual edification.

Peter of Verberia, called Aureoli, of the Order of Friars Minor and archbishop of Aix, doctor of the Parisian school, very learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in Aristotelian philosophy according to the custom of this time, was subtle in intellect, an acute disputant, and excellent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote many excellent small works, by which he magnificently spread his name. Of these there are extant On the Sentences, four books; [unclear], Come, let us go up, one book; The abysses were not yet, one book; Sermons on the Season, one book; Sermons on the Saints, one book; and others that I have not seen.

He flourished before his pontificate, reading the Sentences at Paris, in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1317.

Gentilis of Foligno, an eminent professor of medicine and magnificently learned in the other disciplines of secular philosophy, whose skill in that faculty was not slight, wrote in medicine many excellent volumes, as they say, by which he made his name known with praise not only to those then present but also to posterity. But I have seen none of them. There are reported to be: commentaries On Avicenna, one book; On the Degrees of Medicine, one book; and certain others. Counsels on All Diseases, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Henry VII, in the year of the Lord 1310.

Dantes Aligerus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, a man in his time most studious of all in both the divine Scriptures and secular letters, wrote many excellent volumes in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Driven from his homeland for all his days, he lived in exile in Gaul for some time; afterwards, at the court of the king of Aragon, he composed various works about his calamity. Of his small works these are reported: Comedies, one book; On the Monarchy of the World, one book; several letters; and certain others. Also by him, a disputation On Water and Earth.

At last he died in exile at Ravenna, under Louis the Bavarian, empe-

Et alia plura. Summam theologiae p̄claram inchoauit, quam tamen morte prae- uentus imperfectam dereliquit. Moritur sub Ludouico Bauaro imperatore quarto, anno domini 1517. indictione decimaquinta, in Auinione sepultus. Iohannes de Columna, patria Romanus, ordinis fratrum Praedi- catorū, archiepiscopus Messanensis, vir in diuinis scripturis ex- ercitatum habēs ingenium, nec secularium literarum ignarus, historiarum transacti temporis sagacissimus perscrutator: scripsit ingenij nobilis non spernenda opuscula, quibus nomen suum po- steris notificauit. E quibus extat volumen, quod praenotauit Mare historiarum, lib. 10. Epistolae ad diuersos lib. 1. Alia qͦꝗ nōnulla edidit, quae ad notitiā meam minime venerūt. Martinus ordinis fratrum Prędicatorum, domini Papę vrbis Romae poenitentiarius, &̄ postea (vt ferunt) cuiusdam vrbis episcopus, vir in scripturis sanctis studiosus &̄ eruditus, &̄ se- culariū litteraꝝ nō ignarus, in declandis ad populū sermonibus excellentis ingenij fuit. Scripsit quaedā praeclara opulēcula, ꝗbus no- minis sui memoriā ad posteros trāsmisit. E quibus ego tantū vidi Tabulam decreti lib. 1. Inter alia quacunque fi Chronicam succinctam lib.2. Qm̃ scire tēpora summo Sermones de tempore lib.1. Scientes quia hora est De diuerfis miraculis lib.1. Ore confessio fit ad salu De ceteris nihil vidi. Claruit sub Ludouico imperatore quarto, anno dn̄i 1520. Sunt qui scribāt, hunc Martinum ordinis diui patris nostri Bene- dicti extitisse, quos (mea sentēta) nominis Mariani Scoti ordinis nostrī, cuius suprà memini, similitudo festilit, qui et ipse chronicā scripsit. Sunt item aliꝫ, qui Cisterniensis ordinis collegio cum exi- stiment aggregandū, qͦs aut ignoratia reꝝ obfuscauit, aut liuor. Abbot of Spanheim.

225

emperor IV, in the year of the Lord 1321, in the fourth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Michael of Cesena, the seventeenth minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, and venerable no less for religion than for knowledge, produced in the holy writings works of exposition not to be despised, by which he became known far and wide both to those then living and now to posterity. Of these I have so far been able to find very few, namely:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the prophet Ezekiel, 1 book. Sermons for the season, 1 book. Sermons on the saints, 1 book. He produced readings and commentaries on many books of the Bible, which I have not yet seen.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bertrand, of the Order of Friars Minor, by country a Milanese, born of a noble family, and, as some think, cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church, a man certainly exceptionally learned in the divine Scriptures and not moderately instructed in secular philosophy, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote several works of great usefulness, among which I have found:

On the Sentences, 1 book. Sermons on the Gospels, 1 book. “They shall see the Son,” etc. [unclear] Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

The rest that he composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1325.

Gerard of Bologna, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, the eleventh prior general, doctor of Paris, most learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, venerable no less for his way of life than for his knowledge, who governed his order vigorously for twenty years, wrote several volumes of reading not to be despised, by which he transmitted the memory of his name also to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 1 book. Quodlibets, 1 book. Ordinary Questions, 1 book. Sermons for the season, 1 book.

226 On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Sermons on the saints, 1 book. And many others.

He began a very distinguished Summa of theology, which, however, overtaken by death, he left unfinished.

He died under Louis the Bavarian, emperor IV, in the year of the Lord 1317, in the fifteenth indiction, and was buried at Avignon.

John of Colonna, by country a Roman, of the Order of Friars Preachers, archbishop of Messina, a man possessing a practiced intellect in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, a very sagacious investigator of the histories of past time, wrote works of noble intellect not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there survives the volume which he entitled:

Sea of Histories, 10 books. Letters to various persons, 1 book.

He also produced some other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Martin, of the Order of Friars Preachers, penitentiary of the lord pope of the city of Rome, and afterwards, as they report, bishop of a certain city, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these I have seen only:

A Table of the Decretum, 1 book. “Among any other things” [unclear] A Brief Chronicle, 2 books. “Since to know the times is a very great” [unclear] Sermons for the season, 1 book. “Knowing that it is the hour” On Various Miracles, 1 book. “Confession is made with the mouth unto salvation”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

There are some who write that this Martin belonged to the order of our holy father Benedict. In my opinion the likeness of the name of Marianus Scotus, of our order, whom I mentioned above, has deceived them, for he too wrote a chronicle. There are likewise others who think that he should be assigned to the community of the Cistercian Order; these either ignorance of matters has darkened, or envy.

Gerard Odonis, of the Order of Friars Minor, the eighteenth minister general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed in scholastic philosophy, subtle in intellect, apt in speech, and quite fit for disputation, is said to have composed certain works in the holy Scriptures, of which few have become known to me:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Also On Logic, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book.

Nicholas of Lyra, English by nation, of the Order of the Friars Minor, a man most devoted to the holy Scriptures and skilled through long practice, scholastic in speech, and no less venerable in conduct than in knowledge, wrote many distinguished little works on the sacred volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. How useful and how necessary these are for all who desire to learn sacred Scripture no one knows better than one who has exercised himself in reading them. For there are some who think him to be despised because of the simplicity of his eloquence; they seem to me both vain and unlearned, and unworthy of the sacred knowledge of saving philosophy, since they disparage ecclesiastical simplicity and embrace words, not things.

[Guido?], of [the order of] Mary ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, the twelfth Prior general, and afterward bishop of the churches of Mende and Elne, a man most erudite in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in talent, sweet in eloquence, a keen disputant, distinguished no less in conversation than in knowledge: he wrote many illustrious little works, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: A tripartite work—polished [and] distinguished—on the perfection of the catholic life, to Pope John XXII: [—] book[s]. On the Sentences: 4 books. Six Quodlibets: 1 book. ["In our first dispu[tation]…"] Whether the Word in divine [matters]… Ordinary Questions: 1 book. On the concord of the evangelists: 3 books. To the cardinal of Albano: 1 book. On the books of the Physics: 8 books. Questions on the soul: [—] book[s]. [page 268:] He composed also several others, which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and John XXII, pope, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Augustine of Ancona, of the order of the hermit-brothers of St Augustine, a man studious and erudite in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, prompt in talent, and scholastic in speech, wrote many volumes of no contemptible reading, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported: To Pope John XXII, a work not small, On ecclesiastical power: 4 books. ["To the most holy and reverend…"] On the Sentences: 4 books. Quodlibets also: 5 books. On the Holy Spirit against the Greeks: 6 books. On the ten strings: 7 books. On the entrance into the promised land: 8 books. On the powers of the soul: 9 books. On the resurrection; On Matthew: 10 books. On Mark; On Luke also: 11 books. On John; On "Missus est" [the Annunciation]: 12 books. On the Magnificat; On the Epistles of Paul: 13 books. On the canonical Epistles; On the Acts of the Apostles: 14 books. On the Apocalypse. And several others. He began a distinguished volume from the writings of the divine father Augustine, which he entitled the Milleloquium; but, prevented by death, he left [it] unfinished; which afterward Bartholomew of Urbino, of the same order, completed. He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, emperor, the fourth, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Peter of Abano, an Italian by nation, of Padua by country, a man studious [and] erudite in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, a physician of most celebrated repute, subtle in talent, renowned for [his] knowledge of many languages, is reported to have elaborated many little works, both in philosophy and in medicine, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. But there are [those] who write that he was a magician, [and] had shown many wonders through that superstitious art; whether [this be] true, [I know not]. Claruit Ludouici imperatoris quarti, Iohãnis Papae vicefimise cundi temporibus, anno domini 1320. <Initial type="simple">I</Initial> Rancifcus Marionis, ordinis fratrum Minorum, Iohannis Sco ti quondam auditor, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditissimus, in praeceptis philosophorum nobiliter doctus, ingenio subtilis, ore facundus, stylo compositus, studio cõtinuus, ad disputandas foluenas q̃ scripturarum questiōnes satis acutus valde idoneus; scripsit ingenij sui non pauca praeclara volumina, in quibꝰ se doctriffimum ostendit, nomen suum cum gloria ad posteros transmisit. de quibus ista feruntur: Super Sententias lib.i. The Abbot of Spanheim.

...divided into ten distinctions, which he entitled:

On Medicine of Every Kind, book I. To Pope John XXII, book II. On the Book of John Mesue, book III. On Aristotle's Problems, book IV. And certain other works.

He translated Galen On Black Bile and On the Regimen of Health, together with many others.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Sibertus de Beka, a German by nation, from Gelderland by homeland, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior provincial of Lower Germany, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently trained both in canon law and in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect and brilliant in eloquence, who shone in his time no less by his manner of life than by his learning, wrote certain commendable small works, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are reported:

On the Sentences, book II. A Summary of Censures of the New Law, book III. On the Rule of His Order, book IV. And certain other works.

He also corrected the ordinal of his order with sagacious purpose.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Clement, the fifth pope, born in Gascony, formerly called Bernard, bishop of Bordeaux, sat after Benedict XI in the chair of Peter for eight years and ten months. He was a learned and energetic man; at his command the Order of Templars was destroyed throughout the whole world on one day. He celebrated the Council of Vienne, in which he established many things for the benefit of the Church. He composed the seventh book of the Decretals, which John XXII, his successor, published, as is stated at the beginning of the same. It is commonly called:

The Code of the Clementines, book I. The foundations of the Catholic faith...

He died while Henry VII was governing the Roman Empire, in the year of the Lord 1314, in the twelfth indiction.

Petrus de Perpiniano, called Rimi, a Catalan by nation, of the Order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and a subtle expounder of scholastic philosophy, quick in intellect and an excellent declaimer, published many small works of reading not to be despised. By exercising in them the abundant vein of his talent, he made his name known even to posterity. Of these there are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, book I. On the Whole Psalter, book I. Various Sermons, book I.

But concerning other works that he composed, nothing has ever come to my knowledge.

Dericus, of the Order of Friars Minor, a holy and learned man, an excellent preacher of the divine word, because of his most fervent love for it took up a pilgrimage, penetrated Asia and India, where by preaching and teaching and proclaiming the faith of Christ, he converted many from iniquity to the path of justice. His most holy life was confirmed by many signs both in the flesh and after death. Among the other small works of his talent he wrote:

A History of His Pilgrimage, book I. Also Various Sermons, book I. And certain letters.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Franciscus Marionis, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly trained in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, composed in style, constant in study, sufficiently acute and very fit for disputing and resolving questions of the Scriptures, wrote not a few distinguished volumes of his talent, in which he showed himself most learned and transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, book I. Concerning the proemium of the first... On Formalities, book I. Various Questions, book I. Sermons on the Season, book I. Sermons on the Saints, book I.

He is also said to have composed certain commentaries on the divine volumes and some diverse treatises, which have not yet at all come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Bonaventura of Padua, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, formerly prior general, and thereafter cardinal priest of the most holy Roman Church of the title of Saint Cecilia, a man in the divine [unclear]...

Abbot of Spanheim.

learned in the Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, ready in talent, distinguished in eloquence, no less reverend for his manner of life than for his knowledge, of great reputation in delivering sermons to the people; and, since he most vigorously defended the liberty of the Church against tyrants, he was at last pierced by an arrow by the lord of Carrara and was crowned with martyrdom. He wrote very useful and elegant works:

Sermons for the season, one book. “The desired one will come [unclear]” Sermons on the saints, one book. “But far be it from me to glory” And certain other things.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

William Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, formerly a disciple of John Scotus, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly taught in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain small works on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Acting and writing against John XXII, who condemned the heresy of the Fraticelli, together with Peter of Piceno, whom Emperor Louis had set up as an idol and had caused to be called Nicholas V, and declaring him to be a heretic, he was excommunicated by him. Fleeing to Emperor Louis, likewise excommunicated, he said to him: “O Emperor, defend me with the sword, and I shall defend you with the word.” And so he remained excommunicated with the excommunicated man until the end of his life; at last, at his death, he was absolved. He was a most bitter assailant of Scotus, his master, and attacked almost all his sayings. He wrote:

Against John XXII on the poverty of Christ and the apostles An Apology, one book. On the Sentences, four books. Quodlibets, also one book. On the Supporters of Heretics, seven books. “In all curious matters” On the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320. And he was buried in the convent of his order in the province of Noricum, which is now called Bavaria, of which Emperor Louis had previously been duke.

Alvarus, of the Order of Friars Minor, Spanish by nation, a hearer of John Scotus, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, held in esteem by John XXIII, acted against William Ockham the Englishman in writings and in words. He published certain very distinguished volumes of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them there survives a great and notable work, describing the defects of ecclesiastical persons, which he entitled:

On the Lamentation of the Church, one book. Likewise The Mirror of Kings, one book. “In the name of our Lord Jesus” On the Sentences, four books. An Apology, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished at the same time as Ockham, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Matthew Silvaticus, of Mantua by homeland, noble by birth, a physician by art and profession, in which faculty in his time he was held to be both learned and experienced before many others, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote in that science volumes not to be despised, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only the notable work, addressed to Robert, king of Sicily and a physician, on all simple medicines and their properties, which he entitled:

Pandects, one book. “Aaron in Greek, in Arabic” I have seen nothing of the rest.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

A certain hearer and disciple of John Scotus in the schools of Paris, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly taught in secular philosophy, and also not ignorant of both pontifical and imperial law, is said to have composed certain distinguished little works, by which, exercising his talent, he also made his name known to posterity; but I have seen none of them. They are said to be:

On the Sentences, one book. Disputed Questions, one book. And certain other things.

Durandus of Saint-Pourcain, of the Order of Friars Preachers, and afterward, as they say, bishop of Le Puy, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not meanly instructed in secular philosophy, ready in talent and distinguished in eloquence, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, first a defender of the writings of Saint Thomas Aquinas, but afterward their most bitter assailant. to deny rashly: he wrote certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these are reported:

Erenus de Boyo, a Briton by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man in every respect most learned, an eminent professor of sacred scripture, of sharp and vigorous talent, quite capable in solving questions of the scriptures, is reported to have written some distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is found, as his people report, an excellent work:

On the Sentences, 4 books. And Various Questions. But he is said to have composed certain other works, which have not come to my knowledge.

Rupert, of the order of the Preaching Friars, a man learned through long practice in the divine scriptures, a subtle and profound interpreter of scholastic philosophy, an acute disputant, an outstanding declaimer, sharp in talent, scholastic in speech, published certain little works not to be despised; by exercising his talent fruitfully and usefully in them, he made his name known not only to the present but also to the future. Of these there survive:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. In addition, he adorned many books of Aristotle with most elegant commentaries. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1320.

Stephanus de Ast, of the order of the Friars Minor, a man nobly learned in the divine scriptures, an eminent philosopher and jurist, distinguished in knowledge, profound in talent, cautious in counsel, firm in judgment, composed in speech, is reported to have forged various little works of his excellent talent, by which he made his name known to those present as well as to those to come. Of these I have seen only the necessary work:

A Summary on Cases, 8 books. “Therefore, about to speak in this first [unclear]” Of the rest I have seen nothing. He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord 1550.

Johannes de Alerio, a Toulousain by nation, of the order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the thirteenth prior general, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, and venerable no less for fervor in religion than for learning, governed the Carmelite order vigorously for nine years. He published several distinguished volumes, by which he showed the abundant grace of his talent. Of these there survive:

On the Sentences, 4 books. A Reading on Ecclesiasticus, 1 book. And several others. He was elected general of his order at Montpellier in the general chapter, on the day of Pentecost, under Louis the fourth emperor and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1321, in the fourth indiction.

Johannes de Regno, a Frenchman by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the Toulouse convent, a man learned in the holy scriptures and not ignorant of secular learning, ready in talent, scholastic in speech, outstanding in delivering sermons to the people, published besides many volumes, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. A Lenten Work, 1 book. The rest, however, which he is said to have composed have not come to my knowledge.

Stephanus de Provincia, professor and excellent interpreter of both laws, and sufficiently instructed both in the divine scriptures and in secular letters, distinguished in talent and eloquence, whose learning was approved among his contemporaries, wrote certain volumes [not?] to be neglected, by exercising his talent gloriously in which he also transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is an excellent work:

On the Clementines, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book. Of the rest I have found nothing. He flourished around the times of Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Claruit temporibus Ludouici imperatoris quarti, &amp; Iohannis pa pae 22. anno domini i330. <Illegible reason="faded" extent="ca. 1 word"/> I Ohannes de Lignerijꝫ, philosophus et amp; astronomus om̄ium suo tempore celeberrimus, qui hanc disciplinā à memoria homī- num iam pene abrasam, magnifice instaurauit, in gymnasio Pa risiensi eruditionis suae laudes ingentes acquisiuit, vihi huiuse fa- cultatis cooperatores et amp; cōsocios habuit, viros mathematica esci- entię doctrissimos, Iohannē de Muris et amp; Ber nar-

The Abbot of Sponheim.

...of our time, although he was bound by the ties of a wife, nevertheless devoted incredible zeal to letters, so that nothing could have been sweeter to him than to write something for the edification of posterity. His distinguished volumes testify to this, by which he secured eternal remembrance for his name. Of these I have had the privilege of seeing a few:

On the Decretals, 5 books. On the Novellae in two forms, 1 book. “Because it is preposterous...” Additions to the Speculum, 2 books. The work entitled Mercuriale, 1 book. “I, Johannes And...” A Summa on betrothals and marriage, 1 book. On the Clementines, 4 books. “Since frequently in the forum...” On the praises of Saint Jerome, 1 book. “Johannes Gratiosum...” On the tree of consanguinity, 4 books. “Jerome continually...” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He died at last of the plague and was buried at Bologna, under Charles IV, emperor, and Clement VI, pope, in the year of the Lord 1348, in the first indiction.

[Unclear], formerly hearer and disciple of the most famous man Cinus of Mugello, and a close friend of Johannes Andreae, a man certainly most learned in civil law among all men of his time, subtle in intellect, ready and very abundant in knowledge, published many little works in that faculty, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, 9 books. On the first part of the Old Digest, 1 book. On the second part, 1 book. Additions on the remaining parts, 2 books. And many other things. He also wrote consilia.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Monaldus, of the Order of Friars Minor, a theologian and very learned jurist, subtle in intellect, cautious in knowledge, scholastic in speech, of excellent industry and virtue in delivering sermons to the people, published, for the benefit of the simple, little works not to be despised even by the learned, by which he usefully provided both for those then present and for those to come long afterward. Of these the following are reported:

A necessary and very beautiful Summa of canon law, 4 books. “Since one ignorant...” Questions on the Sentences, 4 books. Various sermons, 1 book. And many other things, which have by no means come to our knowledge.

[Unclear], an Italian by nation, formerly hearer of the very learned man Dinus of Mugello, and a very close friend of Johannes Andreae, a man very skilled in both laws, and also excellently imbued with the disciplines of philosophy, who for many years was a consistorial advocate and acquired great praise and glory for his learning, wrote some distinguished little works in both laws, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

A volume of consilia, 1 book. “In the name of the Lord, Amen...” Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He is said to have left after him many lectures in civil law, which I have not yet seen.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1320.

[Unclear] Johannes de Blomendal, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, was an eminent teacher in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote, for the edification of the faithful, volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have so far found only:

Sermons on the temporal cycle, 1 book. “Take your weapons, your quiver...” Sermons on the saints, 1 book. Sermons for Lent, 1 book.

He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

[Unclear] Guido de Monte Rocherii, a man very studious in the sacred Scriptures and rich in reading of the ancients, clear in intellect, scholastic in speech, wrote little works of his talent not to be despised, by which he made the memory of his name known also among posterity. Of these I have seen only that well-known work circulated in print, which, composing it for the guidance of simple priests, he wished to be entitled:

The Manipulus curatorum, 3 books. “Since, as the prophet says...” I could not find other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV, emperor, and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

[Unclear] Johannes de Ligneriis, the most celebrated philosopher and astronomer of all men in his time, who magnificently restored this discipline, now almost erased from human memory, acquired immense praise for his learning in the school of Paris, where he had as collaborators and associates in this faculty men most learned in mathematical knowledge, Johannes de Muris and Ber-

De sphaera quoque lib.i. De caeteris nihil reperi. Claruit temporibus Ludouici Bauari imperatoris quarti, Iohā- nis papae 22. anno domini 1330. Iohannes Danck de Saxonia, natione Teutonicus, Iohannis de Lignerij supradicti contemporaneus, studiorum eius confo- cius, vir vndecūque doctissimus, philosophus astronomus in- ter omnes fui temporis celebrimus, ingenio subtilis praefans, edidit multa praeclara admiranda opuscula, quibus nomen fu- um cum gloria transmisit ad posteros. Sed ego hucufque paucissi- ma inueni Canones Eclipsales lib.i. Eclipsis folis quantitatē Canones tabularum lib.i. Tempus quarti adspe De astrolabio lib.i. De incensionibus lib.i. Iohannes Calderini, natione Italus, patria Bononienfis, Iohan- nis Andreae quondā auditor atque discipulus, canonici iuris p̄- feffor, celeberrimus interprets, philosophiae secularis diui- narum scripturaꝝ nō ignarus, ingenio promptus, aptus eloque scripfit in sua facultate non pauca volumina, quibus ingeniū fu- um sedula exercitatione comprobās, ad memoriā posteritatis no- men men suum transmisit.E quibus reperi opus magnum &; infigne,tribus voluminibus non paruis distinctum, quod praenotauit Repertorium iuris lib.i.A.Hęc dictio à, interdũ Super decretalibus lib.i.Quãuis dubia plura cir De interdicto ecclesiastico lib.i.Confilia multa.lib.i.De alijs nihil vidi. Claruit sub Ludouico Bauaro imꝑatore quarto, Benedicto Papadecimo, anno domini 1340. The Abbot of Sponheim.

[unclear], notable philosophers and astronomers, who also themselves wrote various short works. But of the works of this John of Lignières, although he wrote many excellent things, I have seen very few, namely:

Canons of the first movable sphere, one book. “Of any given arc ...” Tables of the same, one book. On the sphere also, one book.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

John Danck of Saxony, German by nation, contemporary of the aforesaid John of Lignières and his companion in studies, a man most learned in every respect, the most celebrated philosopher and astronomer among all men of his time, excellent in subtle intellect, published many excellent and admirable short works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. But thus far I have found very few:

Eclipse Canons, one book. “The quantity of an eclipse of the sun ...” Canons of the tables, one book. “The time of the fourth aspect ...” On the astrolabe, one book. On burnings, one book.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and of Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1330.

Peter de Palude, French by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, an acute disputant and distinguished preacher, published certain excellent volumes on the holy Scriptures, by which he bestowed his name upon immortality. Among these are reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Various Questions, one book. And various Sermons, one book. And many other things.

He is also said to have adorned many books of the Bible with his commentaries, that is, to have expounded them.

John Calderini, Italian by nation, from Bologna, once a hearer and disciple of John Andreae, professor of canon law, a very celebrated interpreter, not ignorant of secular philosophy and of the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, apt in speech, wrote no few volumes in his faculty. By these, proving his intellect through diligent exercise, he transmitted his name to the memory of posterity. Among these I have found a great and notable work, divided into three not small volumes, which he entitled:

Repertory of Law, one book. “A. This word a, sometimes ...” On the Decretals, one book. “Although many doubtful matters ...” On ecclesiastical interdict, one book. Many opinions, one book.

Of the other things I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Paul de Liazariis, a hearer of John Andreae of Bologna and fellow student of John Calderini, a man most skilled in both laws, nobly instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, who among the doctors of law in his time was not [unclear], wrote, among the other short works of his intellect, a notable volume which is called:

On the Clementines, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, the fourth emperor, and of Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Lupold of Bebenburg, bishop of Bamberg, German by nation, as they report once a hearer of John Andreae of Bologna, a very celebrated jurist, nobly learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, published short works not to be despised in reading, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great glory. Among these there is extant a notable work:

On the Zeal of the Christian Religion of the Old Princes of the Germans, one book. On the Rights of the Roman Empire, one book. And certain other volumes on diverse subjects, which have not come to me.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and of Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Nicholas of Modena, a man nobly learned in both laws, especially in the civil laws, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel, in order to leave to posterity monuments of his intellect, wrote certain excellent volumes in civil law, by which he had made himself useful to those then living, and known to those to come. Among these are reported:

On the Code, nine books. On the Old Digest, twenty-four books.

ABBOT OF SPANHEIM.

On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. And certain other works. He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Lapus de Castellione, abbot of San Miniato, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a jurist most learned among all men of his time, and imbued from early youth, as they say, with the disciplines of the philosophers, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding disputant of scholastic questions, whose authority among jurists is to be judged by no means slight, wrote several short works in his faculty, among which there is an excellent work:

Of his Allegations, 1 book. On the Clementines, 1 book. And many other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Guerricus, abbot of Igny, a man by no means slightly learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, sweetly composed in speech, fit for persuading, distinguished no less by love of regular observance in his way of life than by knowledge of the Scriptures, wrote, for the edification of simple devout brothers, short works not to be despised; by these, showing himself a useful and faithful shepherd of Christ’s sheep, he also made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only the work of sermons on the temporal cycle and on the saints through the circuit of the year, which he delivered:

To his brothers, 1 book. We await the Savior.

He also wrote letters. Concerning the rest, however, which he is said to have composed, I have not been able to find anything anywhere.

Henry of Urimaria, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, by nation, as they report, a German, a man most devoted to the holy Scriptures from boyhood and very learned, second to none in his time in Aristotelian philosophy, who for many years was an outstanding doctor in the Parisian academy, distinguished by celebrated doctrine, wrote many very famous volumes, among which the following are said to be:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Quodlibets, 1 book. On the Ten Commandments, 1 book. Flowers from the Collation of the Fathers, 2 books. Hear, Israel, the commandments. On the Perfection of Man, 1 book. Because many [unclear]. On the Incarnation of the Word, 1 book. On the Fourfold Instinct, 1 book. On Exemption, 1 book. Exposition on the Creed, on the celebration of Mass, 1 book. Sermons on the Temporal Cycle, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. On the books of the Ethics, 10 books. And many other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis, the fourth emperor, surnamed Bavarian, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

[Unclear], studious [unclear], and excellently learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher and historiographer, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in speech, is said to have fashioned some volumes of excellent doctrine, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the distinguished work of Histories excels:

16 books.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Bartholomaeus Pisanus, of the Order of Preachers, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, most skilled in both laws, and nobly learned in the knowledge of secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect, open in speech, cautious in knowledge and counsel, is said to have written certain very famous short works. Of these I have seen only the Summa, which he calls the Pisan, a work certainly not to be rejected, which a few years ago was in great use among confessors of the common people, which the author entitled:

Summa magistrucia, 1 book.

Concerning the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, and completed his Summa, as he himself testifies, in the year of the Lord [1338?].

Bartholomaeus Brixianus, of the Order of Preachers, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and by no means slightly learned in both laws, also an outstanding declaimer of sermons, and no less holy than learned, since he is said to have shone with miracles even in life, wrote, among the other monuments of his talent, a notable:

Summa on Cases, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Louis, the fourth emperor, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Abbot of Sponheim.

Ludolphus, of the Carthusian order, in the house of Strasbourg, a German by nation, sprung from Saxon land, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, gentle in disposition, sweet and composed in speech, and also distinguished in life and conduct, published certain excellent little works of great devotion and deep learning. By these, nobly exercising his talent, he bestowed his name upon immortality. Of these I have seen only the following:

A large and distinguished volume on the Gospel, which he entitled The Life of the Lord Jesus, 2 books.

Also On the Psalter, 1 book. Another foundation, lest... [unclear]

Other works of his are reported. As once manna... [unclear]

He flourished under the emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

[Unclear], a man very zealous in the divine Scriptures, exceedingly skilled, eminent in ability, no less distinguished in life than in learning and knowledge, published many excellent volumes, in which he showed the abundant vein of his talent and transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity with great praise and glory. Of these the following are reported:

On the First Book of the Sentences, 1 book.

A lecture On Genesis, 1 book.

A twofold Hexameron, 2 books.

On the Song of Songs, 1 book.

On the Matter of the Chaoticorum [unclear], 1 book.

On the Lord’s Prayer, in two ways, 2 books.

On the Ave Maria, 1 book.

Breviloquium, 1 book.

On the Four Senses of Scripture, 1 book.

Of the Exposition of the Mass, 1 book.

Manual for Priests, 1 book.

On the Capital Vices, 1 book.

The Cloister of the Soul, 1 book.

On the Conception of Saint Mary, 1 book.

On the Method of Study, 1 book.

Introduction to Law, 1 book.

On True and False Friendship, 1 book.

On the Canonical Hours, 1 book.

On the Five Senses, 1 book.

On the Forty-Two Mansions, 1 book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Against the Flagellants, 1 book. On the Comparison of the Mass, 1 book.

On the Division of Philosophy, in verse, 1 book.

On the chapter Omnis utriusque, 1 book.

Various sermons, 1 book. Preachable conferences, 1 book.

Various questions, 1 book. On Aristotle’s Rhetoric, 1 book.

He published besides many other works which have not come to my knowledge.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Louis IV and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

William de Kaiotho, of the order of Friars Preachers, provincial prior in France, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, subtle in talent and clear in speech, of excellent ability in delivering sermons to the people, wrote certain little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. He abbreviated the Summa of Johannes Teutonicus, which is called the Summa of Confessors, 1 book. What is simony, say... [unclear]

Various sermons, 1 book.

The rest of what he composed has by no means come to my knowledge.

Peter de Casa, of Limoges, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the fourteenth prior general, and afterwards bishop of Vaison, and finally, as they report, patriarch of Jerusalem, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in talent and clear in speech, learned and eloquent in delivering sermons to the people, published certain excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these are reported:

On the Sentences, 1 book. Sermons for the season, 1 book.

Sermons on the saints, 1 book.

And certain other works.

He flourished, and was elected prior general of his order from the convent of Limoges, under the emperor Louis IV and Pope John XXII, in the year of the Lord 1350, in the thirteenth indiction. He ruled his order energetically for twelve years.

Paulus of Perugia, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed in secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, published several little works of great authority. By exercising his brilliant talent in these, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity with great glory. Of these there exists a very celebrated and almost divine work, which he recited in the Parisian school:

The Abbot of Spanheim.

On the Sentences, 4 books. "Concerning the first [unclear]" Quodlibets also, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished at Paris and completed his lecture under Emperor Louis the Bavarian, the fourth, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1344, in the twelfth indiction. And not long after that same lecture of his he died at Paris and was buried there in the convent.

Bernardus Parentinus, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a man zealous in the divine Scriptures and skilled through long practice, and not moderately learned in the scholastic disciplines, subtle in intellect and distinguished in speech, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the instruction of simple priests certain volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these there is extant:

An Exposition of the Mass, 1 book. "Since the Wise Man cries out" Various sermons, 1 book. And several other things.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Osbertus, English by nation, of the Order of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man certainly most learned in the holy Scriptures, and exceptionally learned in secular philosophy, of acute and forceful intellect, scholastic in eloquence, subtle in debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures, wrote certain excellent little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, 4 books. "One conclusion having been proposed" Various determinations, 1 book. "It is asked whether [unclear]" Various sermons also, 1 book.

The rest that he composed have not been able to come to the knowledge of our reading.

Johannes Estuidi, English by nation, a man easily the most learned of all his time in secular letters, a philosopher and astronomer second to none, outstanding in intellect and sweet in speech, wrote certain excellent little works of his intellect, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of a later age. Of these there is extant a notable work of judicial astrology, concerning the accidents of the world, which is commonly called:

The English Summa, 2 books. "My intention in this book"

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished, and completed the same Summa, as he states at its beginning, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1347, in the fifteenth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Bernardus, abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in life, and a notable cultivator and propagator of regular observance, wrote for the edification of monks certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are extant:

The Mirror of Monks, 1 book. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book. "It is read in Proverbs" On Regular Precepts, 1 book. Sermons to the Brothers, 1 book.

He is also said to have composed many other things, which have by no means reached us.

Symon de Cremona, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in speech, quite excellent in delivering sermons to the people, since indeed at Venice he labored for a long time in this office, where by word and example he instructed very many, wrote for the instruction of simple preachers little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant. To Antonius, his brother, a priest, sermons:

On the Gospels, 1 book. "Lift up your heads, because" On the Epistles also, 1 book. "Let us cast away the works of darkness"

The rest that he composed have not yet come to the knowledge of our reading.

Petrus Raimundi de Insula Grassa, French by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, the fifteenth Prior General, who after Petrus de Casa, from Limoges, vigorously governed his order for fifteen years, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, wrote elegantly:

On the Sentences, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished and was elected general from the convent of Carcassonne in the province of Narbonne, under Emperor Louis IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1343, in the eleventh indiction.

Reinerus Foroliviensis, a jurist most celebrated of all in his time, the teacher of Bartolus de Saxoferrato, a man distinguished in intellect and speech, is said to have composed various little works in civil law

The Abbot of Spanheim.

... little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. But I have not been able to find any of them anywhere.

He died under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1358, in the eleventh indiction.

Simon of Cascia, of the order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man [unclear], zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, who indeed is said to have been illumined by the spirit of prophecy in the Florentine convent, published several volumes of great usefulness, in which he showed himself a learned and devout man. Among these I found an outstanding work on the whole Gospel, which is commonly entitled:

The Deeds of the Savior, one book. “From the good and super-good...”

On Christian Doctrine, one book. “The imitation of God in men...”

On Patience, one book. [unclear]

Exposition of the Creed, one book. [unclear]

On the Mirror of the Cross, one book. [unclear]

On the Discipline of Spiritual Men, one book. [unclear]

Letters to Various Persons, one book. [unclear]

And certain other works.

He ended his life under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 140[unclear].

Simon of Speyer, a German by nation, of the order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, master of Paris, most learned in the holy Scriptures, and nobly instructed in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse, taught theology for a long time with distinction in the school of Cologne, and won from all great praise for his learning. He wrote an outstanding volume:

On the Sentences, one book.

Against the Jews, also one book.

A Postil Read at Cologne, [unclear].

He published some other things recently, but they have by no means come to our knowledge.

Sertorius, whom some call Fortunerius, the nineteenth minister general of the order of Friars Minor, an Englishman by nation, from [Galenis?] by homeland, afterward archbishop of Ravenna, and finally patriarch of Grado and cardinal of the sacrosanct Roman Church, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, published certain distinguished volumes by which he made his name known also to posterity. Among these there is extant an outstanding work:

On Augustine’s City of God, twenty-two books.

Concerning the rest I have found nothing.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Finally, he is also said to have composed various treatises on the books of the Bible. He flourished, and was elected minister general of his order in the chapter at Marseille, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1356, in the ninth indiction.

Albericus Roxiatus, otherwise de Rosate, a native of Bergamo, a distinguished professor of both laws and a very renowned interpreter, excellently learned also in the other secular letters, quick in intellect and polished in speech, produced many instructive volumes on the laws, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with praise to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Code, 12 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 13 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the comedies of Dante, 1 book.

He also composed some other works which have not come to my knowledge. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [1340?].

Johannes de Saxonia, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and sufficiently instructed both in canon law and in scholastic philosophy, of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people, produced certain distinguished volumes of his intellect, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Among these there is extant:

A Summa on cases, 1 book.

And other works which I have not seen. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord [unclear].

Gerardus of Siena, Italian by nation, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man not moderately learned in the holy Scriptures and skilled in both laws by long practice, subtle and acute in intellect, whose learning his contemporary Johannes Andreas often praises and cites, wrote some excellent little works, by which he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Among these the following are reported as the more important:

On the First Book of the Sentences, 1 book. On contracts and usury, 1 book. On prescriptions, 1 book.

I have found nothing about the rest. He flourished with Johannes Andreas, under Louis the Bavarian, Emperor IV, and Pope Benedict XII, in the year of the Lord 1340.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Johannes de Rupe Scissa, of the Order of Friars Minor, very zealous in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, led astray by I do not know what spirit, not to say led on, began, as though a prophet, to predict the desolation of the Catholic Church and certain other terrible things; he was cast into prison by the ministers of his order, and a lying spirit was found in his mouth. In chains he wrote to a certain cardinal:

His Revelations, 1 book. Most reverend in Christ... Also on the Sentences, 4 books. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Gerardus, bishop of Savona, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a native of Bergamo, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in canon law, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, worthy no less in life than in doctrine, composed for the benefit of readers little works not to be despised; by usefully exercising his intellect in these, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Two quodlibets, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Two wings of the Cherubim... On the Epistle to the Hebrews, 1 book. On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, concerning religious houses, 1 book.

He says that he wrote many other little works, which have not come to my knowledge. In the Parisian school he ascended the magisterial chair. He flourished under Emperor Louis IV, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Thomas de Garbo, a native of Florence, son of the former physician Dino, a man learned and skilled in medicine, nobly instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, adhering to the footsteps of his most learned father, produced in his faculty little works not to be scorned by physicians, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these there is extant, very noteworthy:

A Summa of Medicine, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of Louis the Bavarian, fourth Emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1340.

Alphonsus, bishop of Seville, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of Saint Augustine, a man much learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, among ecclesiastical doctors in his time...

Concerning Ecclesiastical Writers

... most celebrated in [his] time, distinguished in talent and eloquence. He published several volumes of great authority, by which he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have found only a subtle and notable work:

On the Sentences, 4 books.

Of the rest I have learned nothing.

He flourished under Louis IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1340.

John de Bachone, an Englishman, of the order of the friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed both in canon law and in secular philosophy, shone brilliantly in the Paris school no less for his conduct than for his learning; and afterwards, promoted to the provincialate of England, he energetically governed his order by word and example. He wrote many notable volumes, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. On the Epistles of Paul, 14 books. On the Acts of the Apostles, 1 book. On the Canonical Epistles, 7 books. On the Apocalypse, 1 book. On the Sentences, 1 book. Various Quodlibets, 1 book. Mirror of His Order, 1 book. Defense of His Order, 1 book. Against the Jews, 1 book. On the Poverty of Christ, 1 book. On the Rule of His Order, 1 book.

He also published explanations on the books of blessed Augustine On the Holy Trinity and On the City of God, and on Anselm’s Why God Became Man and On the Incarnation of the Word; in all of these he exercised his talent splendidly.

He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John Eligerus de Gonderfluen, a German by nation, once a hearer of John of Saxony, the very famous astronomer, a man most learned in secular letters, the most celebrated philosopher and astronomer among all men of his time, and sufficiently imbued with the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote volumes in mathematical science not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Construction of the Astrolabe, 1 book. On the Usefulness of the Astrolabe, 1 book. On the Usefulness of the Quadrant, 1 book. On the Magnet also, 2 books. On the Astrogometer, 1 book.

King of the stars Ptolemy [unclear] With principal zeal [unclear] The uses of the new [unclear] A treatise on the magnet [unclear] The sum, with [unclear] bedewing us [unclear]

And many other works. He flourished in the times of Charles IV, emperor, and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

The Abbot of Spanheim

Rupert, a Frenchman by nation, of the order of the friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and excellently instructed in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent, apt in speech, published various little works on the holy Scriptures; by splendidly exercising his talent in them, he made the memory of his name known also to posterity. He was an excellent preacher of the divine word, and wrote many things useful to composers of sermons. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 2 books. On the Epistles of Paul, 3 books. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book.

He composed many other works besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Clement VI, pope, a Limousin by homeland, formerly called Peter Roger, abbot of Fécamp, of the order of Saint Benedict, sat in the chair of Peter after Benedict XII for ten years and six months. He was a man learned in the divine writings and not ignorant of secular letters, a notable doctor of canon law, venerable no less for his conduct than for his learning; in declaiming sermons to the people he was of excellent talent. He published certain distinguished little works, by which he showed the liveliness of his talent. Of these are reported:

Various Sermons, 1 book. On the Canonization of Ivo, 2 books. Rejoice and praise [unclear] On the Approval of King Charles, 3 books. Solomon will sit upon [unclear] Many Collations, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book.

He died and was buried at Avignon, under Charles IV, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1352, in the fifth indiction.
