On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Gregory of Rimini, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, prior general, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very well instructed in scholastic philosophy, distinguished in talent and eloquence, earned from everyone in the University of Paris great renown for his learning, since he shone forth as very celebrated in life and doctrine. He wrote some little works of no contemptible reading, of which the following are considered the more important:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Epistles of Paul the Apostle, 14 books. And certain other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Philip of Bergamo, prior of the monastery of Saint Mary of [Avantia?] in Padua, of the Order of our holy father Benedict, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote several little works of holy doctrine, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only a large volume On the Ethics of Cato, 1 book. He is also said to have written Sermons, To the glory and praise, 1 book.

The other things that he composed have by no means come to the knowledge of my reading.

John de Beka, German by nation, clerk of the church of Utrecht, a man very studious and learned in the holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, published certain little works of his talent not to be despised. Of these I have seen only a work written in a simple and clear style, addressed to lord John, bishop of the church of Utrecht, and William, duke of Holland, on the deeds of the bishops of Utrecht and the counts of Holland; carrying it down from the time of Saint Willibrord, the first bishop, as far as the year of the Lord 1346, he wished it to be entitled Chronicle of the Church of Utrecht, 1 book. Therefore from the year [unclear]. Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the times of Louis IV and likewise Charles IV, emperors, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Francis Petrarch, Tuscan by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and, in secular letters, by far the most learned of all his time, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most celebrated poet, who after a long silence called back the letters of humanity, dead, so to speak, from the lower world to the upper, shone forth distinguished no less for holy conduct than for knowledge. For out of love of Christ and of saving philosophy he took up the solitary life, in which, persevering until death in meditation, prayer, and writing, his fame was carried through the whole world. Of his little works I have found:

On the Solitary Life, 1 book. Few men have I known. [unclear], 2 books. Since things and fortunes. On the Remedies of Fortune, 1 book. Monica in tranquil [unclear]. What indeed are we doing now, 1 book. On the Seven Penitential Psalms, 1 book. On the Conflict of Cares, 1 book. The Life of Scipio Africanus, 1 book. Bucolics, in verse, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 8 books. Africa, to King Robert, 1 book. On the History of Griselda, 1 book. 1 book

254 On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear]

Richard de Bury, bishop of Durham, chancellor of Edward III, king of the English, to whom there is extant a letter of Francis Petrarch asking about the island of Thule, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, a singular and very celebrated lover of books, founded, with much expense and labor, a notable library in the University of Oxford, which with incredible zeal he established there for the public benefit of students. He wrote a very fine treatise on the love of books and the establishment of the said library, which has now been printed, and which he entitled in Greek:

Philobiblon, one book. Several letters, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

[unclear]

John Walsgram, an Englishman by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly trained in secular philosophy, subtle and acute in intellect, adorned with the master's insignia in the Parisian school, was very celebrated in lecturing and disputation. He wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant the notable work:

On the Sentences, four books.

The other things which he is said to have composed have not yet come to my knowledge.

Various questions, one book.

John de Saxo, of the order of Friars Minor, learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly trained both in canon law and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, an excellent preacher in delivering sermons to the people, and very famous in his time, published certain little works of reading not to be despised, which are necessary for the instruction of simple priests. Of these I have found only:

A summa of law, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1359.

[unclear]

Thomas of Argentina, a German by nation, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, after Gregory of Rimini prior general, a man most learned in the holy Scriptures and an outstanding cultivator of secular philosophy, distinguished by his life and the honesty of his conduct, who wonderfully raised up his order by word and example, wrote several distinguished volumes on the Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there is extant the most brilliant work:

On the Sentences, four books. “The abyss gave forth its voice.” Constitutions of his order, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

The Abbot of Sponheim

John Brammart of Aachen, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior provincial of Lower Germany, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and, according to the custom of the scholastics of this time, a very celebrated expounder of secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect and speech, an excellent teacher in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the benefit of the faithful little works not to be despised; by exercising his talent in them, he transmitted the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, four books. Various sermons, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henry of Erfurt, a German by nation, long exercised in the divine Scriptures and not moderately learned, and excellently trained in secular letters, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, wrote for the edification of the Church several volumes, by which he made his name and reputation known to many. Of these there is reported a work of histories:

On memorable deeds, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350.

John of Erfurt, a German by nation, a Thuringian by homeland, of the order of Friars Minor, an enlightened and skilled doctor in the divine Scriptures, nobly and excellently trained both in both laws and in secular philosophy, published several little works of great authority, in which he also entrusted the force of his most excellent talent to posterity. Of these I have seen only a great volume, which he entitled:

Table of law, one book. “As it is written,” two. A summa on cases, one book. “Asked by the brothers that...”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

Cllmannus Aquensis, natione Teutonicus, ordinis fratrum be- T atę Mariae semper virginis de monte Carmeli, sacrarum lite- rarum insignis professor, ingenio prestans et declamator egre- gius, atq́ in philosophia seculari, quam Aristotelicam appellant, satis admodũ eruditus, scripsit ad vtilitatem legentium non con- temnanda syntagmata, quibꝰ famam nominis sui ad longinquos destinauit. E quibꝰ fertur lectura vna singulariter notabilis, quam Coloniae legit publice, In euangelium Matthaei lib. 1. Super sententias quoq́ lib.4. Sermones etiam et varios in bibl̃ cõpofuisse di- citur: de quibus cum sim incertus, nihil possim iudicare. kk Bar

256 On Ecclesiastical Writers

He is also said to have composed elegant sermons, but they have not come to me.

John Tacephale, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Brethren of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a doctor learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters, subtle in intellect, composed in speech, the most celebrated preacher of sermons of all in his time, produced little works not to be despised in reading; by them, usefully exercising his talent, he transmitted his name with praise to the knowledge of posterity. Of these, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in his convent at Norwich, where, buried, he rests in peace.

Robert Holkoth, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of Preachers, a man most learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and also an excellent preacher of sermons, wrote many excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. “Whether every wayfarer...” On the Book of Wisdom, 1 book. “The Lord is my rock...” On the Seven Mortal Sins, 1 book. “This is the way; walk...” Moralizations, 1 book. “Theodosius concerning the life...” On the Immortality of the Soul, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. On Ecclesiasticus, unfinished, 1 book. And many other things.

He died of the plague after he had begun a reading on the Book of Ecclesiasticus, under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1349, in the second indiction.

Nicholas Dorhin, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Brethren of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine scriptures and excellently taught in secular philosophy, who in the University of Oxford, by reading and disputing, earned great praises from all, wrote little works not to be scorned in reading, by which he showed the rich, all-round grace of his very lively intellect. Of these there are extant:

On the Sentences, [unclear], 4 books. Determinations of Questions, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the school of Oxford, and wrote many various volumes.

The Abbot of Sponheim

Paul of Perugia, professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and excellently learned in other humane letters, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, was for a long time keeper and master of the library of Robert, king of Sicily, a most learned and studious prince. He wrote certain excellent little works by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a distinguished volume, in which there are many pleasant and useful things concerning the gods of the gentiles and of others, which he entitled:

Collections, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1350.

Bonominus, by nation a [Permonensian?], born from the town of Clusone, a learned physician and easily the most skilled of all in his time, and not moderately learned in the other disciplines of philosophy, most experienced in healing human bodies, wrote in that faculty little works not to be scorned, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. But I do not remember having seen any of them. The following, however, are said to be his:

On Poisons, 1 book. Of Various Questions, 1 book. And certain other things.

Tilmannus of Aachen, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brethren of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, distinguished professor of sacred letters, outstanding in intellect and an excellent preacher, and also sufficiently learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, wrote, for the benefit of readers, compilations not to be despised, by which he sent the fame of his name to distant places. Of these there is reported one notably remarkable reading, which he read publicly at Cologne:

On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. Also on the Sentences, 4 books.

He is also said to have composed sermons and various works on the Bible; since I am uncertain about them, I can make no judgment.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Bartholus of Sassoferrato, once a hearer and disciple of the doctors Cinus and Jacobus Butrigarius, a most celebrated jurist, one to whom earlier ages had had no equal in that faculty, subtle and keen in intellect, polished and eloquent in speech, published certain distinguished volumes, especially on the laws. How great an authority these have today among jurists, no one even lightly learned and experienced is ignorant. Among these are cited commentaries on civil law, as follows:

On the Code, 9 books. On the Old Digest, 24 books. On the New Digest, 12 books. On the Infortiatum, 14 books. On the Institutes, 4 books. Also the Tiberiadis, 1 book. Also Councils, 1 book. On the Guelphs and Ghibellines, 2 books.

And many other things.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1355, in the eighth indiction, and in the fifty-sixth year of his age.

Petrus Thomas, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, first bishop of Patti, then archbishop of Crete, and most recently patriarch of Constantinople, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, most holy in life and conduct, since he is read to have shone forth, living and dead, with many signs and miracles, was of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain distinguished volumes, of which these are cited:

On the Sentences, 3 books. Also various sermons, 2 books.

And certain similar things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Clement VI, in the year of the Lord 1350, and was buried in Cyprus.

Bartholomaeus, of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, English by nation, a man most studious in the divine Scriptures and not meanly learned, and sufficiently imbued with secular letters, and distinguished no less by religious conduct than by knowledge, published little works of no negligible authority, the reading of which is judged necessary for simpler brothers. Of these I have found only the volume which he entitled:

On the Properties of Things. When the properties of things ... [unclear] 19.

ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS. Sermones varios lib. 1. Alia qͦq; multa scripsisse dicit̃, sed ad manus nr̄as minime venerūt. Etrus Boherius abbas sanctꝭ Auiani, ordinis diui patris Bene- dicti, iure consultus et sacrarum scripturarum cultor egregie- us, ingenio subtilis, eloquio clarus, monasticae disciplinae mo- derator celeberrimus: edidit pro fratrum suorum eđificatione non nulla opuscula, quibus nomen suum ad posteros transmisit. E qui bus reperi tantum In regulam S.Benedicti lib.1. In speculum monachorum lib.I. De fignis locutionum lib.i. De caeteris nihil vidi. Qui cum esset decretoꝝ doctor celeberrimꝰ, regulam S.patris Be- nedicti, nouo et inusitato expositionis generē cōmentatus est, oīa illius non folũ capitula, sententias dogmata, sed etiā (qͥd amplio ris industriae est) verba, consilia p̄cepta, iuri pontificio conferens, mirabili subtilitate canonibus patrum approbauit. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quarti, Innocentiij pa- pae sexti, anno domini 1360. Iacobus de Altauilla,natione Teutonicus,patria Rinaugiensis, dioecesis Moguntineñ, sacrarū literarum professor doctiffimus, in seculari philosophia nobiliter eruditꝰ; ingenio subtilissimus, ser mone scholasticꝰ: edidit nõnulla in diuinis scripturis insignia opu scula, quibꝰ nomen suum ad pofteritatis notitiam deftnauit. E q̃ bus ego videre hucufqꝫ duntaxat merui volumen infigne, Super sententies lib.4. Quęstiones quoque varias lib.I. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quarti, Innocētij papę sexti, anno domini I360. IOhānes de Imenhufen, natione Teutonicus, vir in diuinis scri- pturis eruditꝰ, seculariū literaꝝ nō ignarus, ingenio prōptus, sciētia cautus, sermōe scholasticus, nō minus exēplo ꝗ̈ verbo doctor insignis: scripfte non spernēdae lectionis quaedam p̄clara volumina, quibꝰ magnificesuum exercitans ingenium, etiam no minis fui memoriā posteris notificauit. E quibus reperi tantum Super sententies lib. 4. Sermones elegantes lib.i. De alijs nihil vidi. kk ij Cla- 260 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. Claruit sub Carolo imperatore quarto, anno domini 1560. Etrus Berthorij, (taliàs Bercharij) natione Gallus, patria Pieta uiẽsis, Prior monasterii S.Eligij Parisiensis, ordinis diuì pr̄is Bindi cti, vir in diuinis scripturis studiosissi. &; valde eruditus, atqꝫ in secularibꝰ lr̄is egregie doctꝰ, in de clamãdis sermonibꝰ ad pplm ex- cellētis ingenij philosophus, historiologus, &; cosmographus infi¬ gnis: scripsit multa p̄clara volũina, ꝗbus nomē suū ad posteritatis notitiā cùm gloria transmisit. E quiꝓbus ista feruntur: Ad Iohan¬ nem de Pratis episcopum Praenestinum, facrosanctę ecclesię Ro¬ manę cardinalem, scripsit magnum &; egregium opus, quod in tribus voluminibus iam impressũ est, praedicatoribus simplici¬ oribus non inutile, quod Dictionariū appellant, sed ipse illud prę¬ notari voluit Repertorium morale lib.5. Reductorium quoque morale lib.4. Inductorum morale lib.3. Breuiarium historiarum Bibliae lib.1. Cosmographiam scripsit lib.1. Sermones varios lib.2. Et alia multa. Deniqꝫ ad instantiam Iohannis regis Franciae, Titum Liuium in Gallicam linguam convertit. Et notandum ꝙ trium operum mo¬ ralium, quae primo confignauimus loco, vnumquodqꝫ tribus ma¬ gnis voluminihus confat, q̄rorum reductorij moralis vna pars omnes libros Biblĩe historiales moraliter complectẽs impressa est, &amp; incipit à Genesi sic: Deus in mundi creatione et amp;c. Feruntur eius ad diuerfos epistolae, &amp; parui, sed multi, tractatus. Claruit temporibus Caroli imperatoris quarti, &amp; Innocentij papę sexti, anno domini 1569. Iohannes de Tambacho, natione Teutonicus, ordinis fratrũ Prędicatorum, vir in diuinis scripturis multum exercitus et doctus, secularis quoqꝫ philosophiae non ignarus, ingenio prae- stans et amp; eloquio, &amp; scholastico nitore compositus, edidit quãdam non spernenda volumina, quiꝓbus nomen suum posteris notifica- uit. E quiꝑus ego reperi tantum subiecta: Opus grande et amp; non abij ciendum, contra foeuictis aduerfae fortunae iacula, non minus vtile quàm iucundum, quod praenotari voluit Consolationem theologiae, lib.15. Quaecunqꝫ scripta funt De

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Various sermons, 1 book.

He says that he wrote many other things also, but they have by no means come into our hands.

Petrus Boherius, abbot of Saint Avianus, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a jurist and an outstanding cultivator of the sacred Scriptures, subtle in intellect, renowned in speech, a most celebrated governor of monastic discipline: for the edification of his brothers he published several little works, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. Of these I have found only:

On the Rule of Saint Benedict, 1 book. On the Mirror of Monks, 1 book. On the Signs of Speech, 1 book.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

Since he was a most celebrated doctor of decrees, he commented on the Rule of the holy father Benedict in a new and unusual kind of exposition, comparing all its chapters, opinions, and teachings, and even, what belongs to greater diligence, its words, counsels, and precepts, with pontifical law; with admirable subtlety he approved them by the canons of the fathers.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Jacobus de Altavilla, a German by nation, from Rinaugia, of the diocese of Mainz, a most learned professor of sacred letters, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, most subtle in intellect, scholastic in discourse: he published several distinguished little works on the divine Scriptures, by which he destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have hitherto been judged worthy to see only a distinguished volume:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Also Various Questions, 1 book.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Johannes de Imenhusen, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, ready in intellect, circumspect in knowledge, scholastic in speech, a distinguished teacher no less by example than by word: he wrote certain excellent volumes, of reading not to be despised, by which, exercising his magnificent intellect, he also made known to posterity the memory of his name. Of these I have found only:

On the Sentences, 4 books. Elegant Sermons, 1 book.

Of the others I have seen nothing.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

He flourished under Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1360.

Petrus Berthorius, otherwise Bercharius, a Frenchman by nation, from Poitiers, prior of the monastery of Saint Eligius at Paris, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a man most devoted to and very learned in the divine Scriptures, and outstandingly learned in secular letters; in preaching sermons to the people, a philosopher of excellent intellect, a distinguished historian and cosmographer: he wrote many excellent volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported. To Johannes de Pratis, bishop of Palestrina and cardinal of the holy Roman Church, he wrote a great and outstanding work, which has now been printed in three volumes, not useless to the simpler preachers; they call it the Dictionary, but he himself wished it to be entitled:

Moral Repertory, 5 books. Also Moral Reductory, 4 books. Moral Inductory, 3 books. Breviary of the Histories of the Bible, 1 book. He wrote a Cosmography, 1 book. Various Sermons, 2 books. And many other things.

Finally, at the request of John, king of France, he translated Titus Livius into the French language. And it should be noted that of the three moral works which we have set down in the first place, each consists of three large volumes; of these, one part of the Moral Reductory, embracing morally all the historical books of the Bible, has been printed, and it begins from Genesis thus: “God in the creation of the world,” etc. His letters to various persons are reported, and small but many treatises.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1369.

Johannes de Tambacho, a German by nation, of the order of Friars Preachers, a man much practiced and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also not ignorant of secular philosophy, distinguished in intellect and speech, and composed with scholastic refinement, published certain volumes not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these I have found only the following: a large work, and not to be rejected, against the missiles of adverse fortune for those [unclear], no less useful than pleasant, which he wished to be entitled:

The Consolation of Theology, 15 books. Whatever has been written

The Abbot of Spanheim.

On the sensible delights of paradise, one book, beginning: “In the delights of the paradise of God.” He published Sermons, one book. And certain other works. He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord [1360].

Leonard of [Giffoni?], of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, the twenty-fourth minister general, and afterward cardinal priest of the Roman Church, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and very skilled in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and renowned in eloquence, is said to have left many monuments of his intellect, of which I have found very few:

On the Sentences, four books. On the Song of Songs, one book. A Notable Summa, one book. Various Sermons, one book.

He flourished under the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

John Balistarii, a Catalan by birth, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, the seventeenth prior general, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, who governed his order sternly in deed and speech for sixteen years, composed distinguished monuments of his intellect, among which are reported:

On the Sentences, one book. On the War of the Church Militant, one book. Various Sermons, one book. And certain other works.

The aforementioned notable work on the mighty war of the Church militant and of Antichrist attacking it he sent dedicated to Pope Gregory XI.

He died in the times of the emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord [1374], in the second indiction, in his convent of Majorca.

John Boccaccio of Certaldo, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, easily the most learned of all men of his time in secular literature and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated poet, philosopher, and astronomer, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, published many distinguished volumes, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these the following are reported. To Robert, king of Sicily:

On the Genealogy of the Gods, one book, beginning: “If sufficiently from the things related, Lord...” On Illustrious Men, one book, beginning: “When I was inquiring...” On Famous Women, one book, beginning: “On the day before, of eminent women...” On the Heresies of the Bohemians, one book. On the Victories of Sigismund, one book. On the Wars of the Emperors, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On Mountains, one book, beginning: “I had arisen, indeed weary...” On Springs, one book, beginning: “After concerning mountains and...” On Rivers, one book, beginning: “By poetic invention...” On the Wars of the Florentines, one book. On the Rebellion of the Lands of the Church, one book. On the Victory of the Tartars, one book. On Pools and Marshes, one book, beginning: “Although sometimes from pools...” On the Names of the Sea, one book, beginning: “A modest amount of labor having been undertaken...” Of Bucolics, one book, beginning: “Tyndarus, it was not enough...” On the Capture of Constantinople, one book. Letters to Various Persons, one book. And many other works.

In the vernacular language, moreover, many books of his are extant, full of jests and vanities, such as the book of the Hundred Novels, Corbaccio, and Philostratus.

He died under the emperor Charles IV and Pope Gregory XI, in the year of the Lord 1375, in the thirteenth indiction, at the age of 62.

John of Hildesheim, German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, learned in the sacred Scriptures, nobly taught in secular literature, a theologian, philosopher, and distinguished poet, was of excellent intellect in declaiming sermons to the people. He was formerly at Avignon the familiar and devoted servant of Blessed Peter Thomas, the general and most holy man of whom we made mention above. He wrote many distinguished little works in verse and prose, by which he transmitted his name with glory to posterity. Among these the following are reported. To Florentius, bishop of Münster, he published a lengthy volume:

On the Three Holy Kings, one book, beginning: “When of the most venerable...” A Chronicle of Histories, one book. A Defense of His Order, one book. On Monsters in the Church, one book. On the Fountain of Life, one book. On Antichrist, one book. Against the Jews, one book. Against One Painting Shameful Things, one book. Eighty Letters, one book. Various Sermons, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

The Abbot of Spanheim.

John Maronis, English by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and subtly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in ability, and an excellent disputant of scholastic questions, composed certain distinguished little works commending his talent, by which he made his name known even to posterity. Among these there is said to be a notable work, which he entitled:

Table of Originals, 1 book. Against the Wycliffites, 1 book. And certain others.

He flourished in the school at Oxford, where by teaching, disputing, and writing he earned great praise from all, at about the time when the errors of John Wycliffe were condemned by the archbishop of Canterbury.

John Golein, Norman by homeland, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of the convent of Rouen, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, and sufficiently instructed in secular letters, subtle in ability and clear in eloquence, wrote little works of no contemptible authority, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of later generations. Among these there survives a notable work:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Office of the Mass, 1 book. “Sing to the Lord a song.” Various Questions.

He also published several other works besides, which have by no means come into our hands.

Henry of Dolendorp, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and perfectly instructed in the disciplines of worldly philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, acute in ability and very well suited for disputing and unraveling scholastic questions, wrote for the instruction of readers certain excellent volumes, of which I have found only:

On the Sentences, 4 books.

Of the rest I have found nothing.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Urban V, in the year of the Lord [1370?].

Gallus, abbot of the monastery of Aula Regia in Bohemia, of the order, as they say, of the Cistercians, German by nation, a man skilled in the divine Scriptures through long practice, and rich in the reading of the ancients, an excellent contemplator of divine things, subtle in ability, open and composed in eloquence, also distinguished in the conduct of regular life, published for the edification of his brothers certain excellent volumes, by which he sent his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among these there survives a great and notable dialogue between father and son, which he entitled:

Pomegranate, 3 books. “Son, as you approach the service...” Sermons to the Brothers, 1 book.

There is today great use of this volume, the Pomegranate, among the truly devout religious, because it is suitable for beginners, those advancing, and the perfect.

Richard, archbishop of Armagh, primate of Ireland, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy and canon law, distinguished in ability, scholastic in speech, of excellent industry in delivering sermons to the people, wrote several little works of his talent, by which he transmitted his name to posterity. When at one time he was preaching to the people on the matter of mendicancy, he set forth nine conclusions; offended by these, the brothers of the mendicant orders appealed before the people to the Apostolic See. Therefore, when both the archbishop and the brothers appeared at Avignon before Pope Innocent VI and the cardinals, in the year of the Lord 1347, on the eighth day of the month of November, Archbishop Richard publicly set forth, read, and pronounced [unclear] of those propositions, 1 book. “Judge not according...” He also wrote Sermons, 1 book. Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Charles IV and Pope Innocent VI, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Matthew of Krakow, Polish by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, ready in ability, scholastic in eloquence, who, having been raised to the master’s chair in the school at Prague, earned from all great praise for his learning, wrote many excellent little works, though only a few of them have come into our hands. I have seen his work addressed to Henry, bishop of the church of Warmia, not to be rejected, on predestination, that God made all things well; the interlocutors of this dialogue are father and son, which he entitled Ra-

Iohannes Fustinione Teutonicus, ex oppido Crutzēnach, in comitatu Spanheimensi oriundus, ordinis fratrum beatae Ma- riae semper virginis de monte Carmeli, Prior Argentineñ, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditus, secularium literarum non ignar⁹, in declamandũ fermonibus ad populum excellentis ingenij scri- psit ad instructionem simplicium praedicatorū, cum adhuc lector esset in conuentu Crutzēnachensi,non spernēda opufcula, quibus nomen suum ad notitiam posteritatis trāsmisit. The Abbot of Spanheim.

Rationale of divine works, seven books. “I should wish it to be declared how...” Also, On contracts, one book. On the transfer of [unclear]. On the celebration of Mass, one book. To the bishop of Warmia, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Sermons, conferences. He first flourished in the school at Prague; then, when he was driven out with other Germans by the Hussites, he taught letters for a time in the Parisian academy.

Johannes Fustinione, a German from the town of Kreuznach, born in the county of Spanheim, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Strasbourg, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular letters, of excellent ability in delivering sermons to the people, while he was still lector in the convent of Kreuznach wrote, for the instruction of simple preachers, little works not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. Weekday sermons through Lent, one book.

But of the rest that he composed, nothing has ever come into our hands. He is said to have flourished at Kreuznach around the times of Emperor Charles IV. His aforesaid sermons, Fustgin, are held in the original in the convent of Kreuznach.

[Gerardus?] Magnus of Deventer, a German by nation, of the diocese of Utrecht, a man excellently learned both in the divine scriptures and in canon law, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, who first founded at Deventer the house of the Brothers whom they call “of the Common Life,” wrote several little works of no contemptible reading, by which, exercising his talent, he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. For he was famous throughout all Germany not only for learning, but also for a religious life and praiseworthy conduct. Of his little works these are reported:

On contracts and usuries, one book. On the instruction of novices, one book. On the leasing of pastoral care, one book. “It is asked whether someone can...” On internal conduct, one book. On the governance of nuns, one book. On the inconveniences of marriage, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Various sermons, one book. And many other things.

He died under Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1384, in the seventh indiction, in the forty-fourth year of his age.

William of Califford, an Englishman by nation, of the order of the brothers of most blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, in [unclear], distinguished, of excellent and vigorous ability in delivering sermons to the people, wrote little works not to be despised for preachers of the divine word, by which he made his name known to many. Of these there are extant:

A certain notable lecture, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book.

He flourished in the academy of Cambridge in England, where by writing, teaching, and disputing he won great glory for his learning.

Franciscus Martini, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, a Catalan by nation, a man learned in the divine scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, an outstanding declaimer, published with much diligence an excellent volume, furnished on the holy and most pure conception of the glorious Virgin Mary, mother of God, which he entitled:

Compendium, seven books. And certain other things.

He flourished in the convent of Barcelona, where at the beginning of the aforesaid golden work he states that he compiled it in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Jacobus de Lusanna, of the order of the Preaching Brothers of St. Dominic, bishop, as they report, of a certain city, a man most devoted to the divine scriptures, skilled by long practice, prompt in intellect, scholastic in speech, sufficiently outstanding in delivering sermons to the people, wrote little works of no contemptible usefulness, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there are reported:

On Genesis, one book. “In the beginning God created...” On Exodus, one book. “I will come to you and...” On Numbers, one book. On Deuteronomy, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. “As in the day, honorably...”

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Sermons on the saints, one book. Lenten sermons, one book. He also published many other things besides: lectures on the sacred books, collations, determinations, and various treatises, which have not come into our hands.

Conrad of Alzey, a town of the diocese of Mainz in the Palatinate, three [unclear] miles distant from Worms, a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular letters, a philosopher, poet, and mathematician, in his time most celebrated among the Germans, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, excellent in verse and in prose: he wrote in both styles certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known. Among these there is extant a volume, adorned with beautiful variety in verses and rhythms, entitled On the Most Holy and Most Pure Mary, Mother of God, and the Redemption of the Human Race:

The Work of Figures, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. Also Poems, one book. And many other things.

He flourished around the times of Emperor Charles IV, in the year of the Lord 1370.

Stephen Petringon, an Englishman by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, a most acute disputant, and very distinguished in delivering sermons to the people, published works not to be despised, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Among these are:

Against the Wycliffites, one book. A Repertory of Arguments, one book. A Certain Notable Lecture, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And not a few other things.

He flourished in the University of Oxford at the time when John Wyclif was burned.

Bertramus, bishop of Thefelicensis, of the order of Preachers, a German by nation, suffragan vicar in pontifical matters of the bishop of Metz, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most famous among the doctors of his time, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, also an excellent deliverer of sermons: he wrote to Cuno, archbishop of Trier, a distinguished work entitled:

On the Illusions of Demons, one book. "To the most reverend in Christ..." To the same, On the Schism, one book. "The wise seeking glory..." Various sermons, one book. And several other things.

He died under Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1387, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the tenth indiction, and was buried in his convent at Koblenz.

Thomas Lombe, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, a man learned in the holy Scriptures through long practice and continual study, and well instructed in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle and keen in intellect, who, having obtained the magisterial chair in the Oxford school, earned great praises for his learning, wrote an excellent work:

On the Sentences, four books. Against the Lollards, one book. On the Incarnation of the Lord, one book. Also Sermons, one book. And various questions. And certain other things.

He flourished in the University of Oxford, chiefly at the time when John Wyclif in England was exhumed and publicly burned.

Philip Riboti, a Catalan by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, and prior provincial of Catalonia, a man devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, venerable also in life and conduct, and an excellent lover and guardian of the Carmelite order, wrote for the edification of his brothers works not to be despised, in which, showing the fervor of his spiritual zeal toward his religion, he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among these there is extant a volume not to be rejected on the first institution, expansion, and confirmation of his order, which he entitled On the Special Deeds of the Carmelites:

On the Special Deeds of the Carmelites, ten books. "When the Israelite people..." On the Illustrious Men of the Carmelites, one book. Sermons and letters. He composed many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Nicholas Ritzonis, by homeland a Toulousain, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, and prior provincial in the kingdom of Sicily, a learned man, distinguished in life and conduct, and an excellent deliverer of sermons, subtle in intellect, brilliant in speech, published some works on Scripture, the reading of which will not be contemptible to preachers of the word. Among these are reported:

Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Qua-

174
ABBAS SPANHEIMENSIS. 169 Quadragesimale duplex lib.z. De caeteris quae composuit, ad notitiã meam adhuc nihil ꝑuenit. <Emphasis type="other">H</Emphasis>Enricus de Kalkar,natione Teutonicus,ordinis Carthusien- fis,&amp; Prior domus S.Barbarae in Colonia Agrippina, vir in diuinis scripturis illuminatum habens ingeniũ, secularium quoqꝫ literarum non ignarus,vita et amp; cõuersatione spectabilis,edi- dit non spernẽdae lectionis opuscula,quorum vsus religioẜs et amp; de- uotis fratribus admodum vtilis iudicatur. E quibus ĩta feruntur: Exercitorium monachale lib.i. Loquagium de rhetorica lib.i. Cantuagium de musica lib.i. De ortu ordinis fui lib.i. Et quedam alia,ad purgationem conscientiabꝰ maxime p̃tinẽtia. Claruit sub Venceslao imperatore,anno domini 1390. <Emphasis type="other">R</Emphasis>Ichardus Maidescoñ,ordinis fratrum B.Mariae semper virgi nis de monte Carmeli,natione Anglicus,vir in diuinis scri- pturis eruditissimꝰ,&amp; in philosophia seculari(quam Aristo- telicã vocãt)egregie doctus,in ingenio clarus, sermone scholasticus, &amp; declamator inigisis: scripsit multa commendanda opuscula, quibus nomen suum ad notitiam posteritatis transmisit.E quibus ego reperi Contra Lolhardos Vuicleff lib.i. Sermones de tempore lib.i. Sermones de sanƈtis lib.i. Caetera me latent. Claruit in gymnaẜio Oxonien̄,eo potissimum tempore, quo haere fis Iohannis Vuideffi pullulare incepit in Anglia,&amp; varia scripẜit. <Emphasis type="other">M</Emphasis>Arfilius de Ingen,natiõe Anglicus, vir in diuinis scripturis primus Heidelbergenẜs gymnaẜii plantator,quod Ruper- tus dux Bauariae ac comes Palatinus Rheni instituens,magnifice dotauit,&amp; Vrbanus papa fextus instar Parisiorum confirmãit,cà nonicus etiam(vt Vuimphelingius testatur) &amp; thesaurarius eccle fiae S.Andrea Coloniei:edidit non spernenda opuscula, quibus no men suum posteris notificauit.E quibus in bibliotheca Heidelber gen̄ hodie manu sua scripta habentur: Quaestiones sententiarum lib.4. Dialectica notabilis lib.i. II iij Com 270 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. Commentariorum in Aristotelem libri plures, Et quaedam alia. Moritur sub Venceslao imperatore, &amp; Bonifacio papa nono, ano domini 1394.decimotertio Calendas Septembris,indictione se cunda, Heidelbergae sepuitus in ecclesia sancti Petri.Sunt qui scribãt eum Germanum fuisse,quibus ego liberum concedo iudiciũ.Constat autem qđ de gymnasio Parisien̄ Heidelbergam fuerit euocatus pro vniuersitatis initio. Iohannes monachus Castelleñ coenobij, in dioecesi Eistetensi ordinis S.Benedicti,natione Teutonicus,vir indiuinis scripturis studiosus et amp; eruditus,ac secularium literarum non ignarus,ingenio excellẽs et amp; difertus eloquoĩ,theologus,philosophus et amp;rhetor insignis:scripsit multa et amp; praeclara volumina,quibus nomen suum ad posteritatis notitiam transmisit.E quibus ego reperi dunctaxat opus magnum et amp; clarissimum,in duobus voluminibus partitum,quod ingenti et amp; commendabili studio edidit, Super regulam sancti Benedicti lib.2. Breuiarium Bibliae lib.1. Sermones de tempore lib.3. Sermones de sanctis lib.4. De Passione dn̄i,sermones 42.lib.5. Epistoliarum ad diuerfos lib.6. Alia insuꝑ multa edidit,q̃ ad notitiã meam.adhuc non venerũt. COnradus de Monte puellarum,natione Teutonicus,Ratisponensis ecclesiae canonicus,vir indiuinis scripturis eruditus,&amp; in seculari philosophia doctissimꝰ, ingenio subtilis et amp; clarus eloquior:primo in gymnasio Erfordiensi rudimenta liberalium ar tium hauriens,se deinde ad vniuersitatẽ Parisiensem contulit,vbi philosophiam et amp; facras literas publice per octennium scholaribꝰ lectitans,doctoratus infulam cõsequutus est.Scripsit ad dominum Lupoldum epifcopum Bambergensem grande et amp;nobile opus,qđ praenotauit scundum Graecos Oeconomicam,lib.3.Omnes moralis philofMonasticam ad ducem Austriae lib.4.Politicam quoqꝫ lib.5.Quaestiones varias lib.6.Et alia multa. Claruit tẽporibus Venceslai imp.&amp; Vrbani papę 6.anno dn̄i 1390.Hen

Abbot of Spanheim.

A double Lenten work, 2 books. Of the other things that he composed, nothing has yet come to my knowledge.

Henry of Kalkar, a German by nation, of the Carthusian order, and prior of the house of St. Barbara in Cologne, a man who had an enlightened mind in the divine Scriptures, and was also not ignorant of secular letters, notable in life and conduct, published little works not to be despised in reading, the use of which is judged very useful for religious and devout brothers. Among them are reported:

The Monastic Exercise, 1 book. Loquagium on rhetoric, 1 book. Cantuagium on music, 1 book. On the origin of my order, 1 book. And certain other works, especially pertaining to the purification of consciences.

He flourished under the emperor Wenceslaus, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Richard Maidstone, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, English by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, and remarkably learned in secular philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, distinguished in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding declaimer, wrote many commendable little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them I have found:

Against the Lollards of Wycliffe, 1 book. Sermons on the season, 1 book. Sermons on the saints, 1 book. The rest are hidden from me.

He flourished in the Oxford school, especially at that time when the heresy of John Wycliffe began to sprout in England, and he wrote various things.

Marsilius of Inghen, English by nation, a man in the divine Scriptures, the first planter of the Heidelberg school, which Rupert, duke of Bavaria and count palatine of the Rhine, established and magnificently endowed, and which Pope Urban VI confirmed on the model of Paris; also, as Wimpheling testifies, canon and treasurer of the church of St. Andrew at Cologne: he published little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among them, in the Heidelberg library, written in his own hand, are held today:

Questions on the Sentences, 4 books. A notable dialectic, 1 book. Several books of commentaries on Aristotle, And certain other things.

He died under the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1394, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the second indiction, buried at Heidelberg in the church of St. Peter. There are some who write that he was German; I grant them freedom of judgment. It is established, however, that he was called from the Paris school to Heidelberg for the beginning of the university.

John, monk of the monastery of Castell, in the diocese of Eichstatt, of the order of St. Benedict, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular letters, excellent in intellect and eloquent in fluent speech, a distinguished theologian, philosopher, and rhetorician, wrote many and splendid volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Among them I have found only the great and very famous work, divided into two volumes, which he published with immense and commendable zeal:

On the Rule of St. Benedict, 2 books. A Breviary of the Bible, 1 book. Sermons on the season, 3 books. Sermons on the saints, 4 books. On the Passion of the Lord, 42 sermons, 5 books. Letters to various persons, 6 books. Besides these he published many other things, which have not yet come to my knowledge.

Conrad of Monte Puellarum, German by nation, canon of the church of Regensburg, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect and distinguished in eloquence: first absorbing the rudiments of the liberal arts in the Erfurt school, he then betook himself to the University of Paris, where, lecturing publicly to students on philosophy and sacred letters for eight years, he obtained the doctor's cap. He wrote for lord Lupold, bishop of Bamberg, a large and noble work, which he entitled, according to the Greeks:

Economics, 3 books. All of moral philoso[unclear] Monastics, to the duke of Austria, 4 books. And also Politics, 5 books. Various Questions, 6 books. And many other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Urban VI, in the year of the Lord 1390. Hen

Venerabilibus et amp; dif Super 6.decretalium lib.i. Super Clementinis lib.i. Mariae semp̃ virginis de monte Carmeli, nũcius et amp; legatus Bonifacij papae noni,in regnis Angliae,Hispaniae,Pontugaliae,Nauarrae,Ara= go-

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Henry Boyc, a Breton by nation, from the diocese of Leon, as he testifies at the beginning of his work on the Decretals, a man most learned in canon law and nobly trained in scholastic philosophy, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, expansive and abundant in judgment, wrote in that faculty volumes not to be despised, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Decretals, 5 books. “To the venerable and [unclear] ...” On the Sixth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the Clementines, 1 book.

He is also said to have published commentaries on the Decrees and various other treatises on different subjects, which have by no means come into our hands.

Johannes Rusbrock, prior of the regular canons of Groenendaal in Brabant, in the diocese of Cambrai, a German by nation, a man, as they say, devout but little learned, wrote in his native tongue, for the edification of the simple, certain little works which after his death were translated into Latin by another. In some matters they are excellent, but in others they are said by doctors to be erroneous. Concerning these Johannes Gerson, chancellor of Paris, composed advisements. Of them the following are reported:

On the Adornment of Spiritual Marriage, 5 books. “Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out ...” On the Progress of Religious, 1 book. Exhortatory Letters, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes Schodehoven, a German by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Mechelen, a man studious and learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote for the use of preachers of the word of God volumes not to be despised. Of these the following are extant:

A distinguished work on vices and virtues and every matter suitable for preaching, according to the order of the alphabet, in two volumes, which he entitled Polypodium, 2 books. “Many hide themselves ...” Various Sermons, 1 book.

He also published some other works, which have by no means come into our hands.

Michael Augrianus of Bologna, an Italian by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine scriptures and nobly trained in secular philosophy and canon law, whom Pope Urban VI first appointed vicar of the whole order, and who, finally elected general in the year of the Lord 1381, governed the order under obedience to Pope Urban for nine years. He wrote many excellent volumes, of which the following are reported:

To the Cardinal of Santa Maria in Trastevere, a distinguished and excellent work. On the Conception of Saint Mary, 1 book. On the Whole Psalter, 5 books. On the Sentences, 4 books. Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. Table of the Sentences, 1 book. On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book. Table of the Moralia of Gregory, 1 book. Table of the Decretum, 1 book. Lenten Sermons, 1 book. He began a Dictionary, 3 books. On Valerius Maximus, 1 book. On the Ethics of Aristotle, 1 book. And certain other works.

Prevented by death, he did not complete this divine work of the new dictionary, but brought it only from A to C inclusive, in three volumes. He died in the last year of the emperor Wenceslaus, under Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1396, on the calends of December, in the eighth indiction, and was honorably buried before the high altar of his convent at Bologna. May he rest in the peace of Christ.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Philippus Ferrarien[sis?] Tholosanus, bishop of the church of Pax in Spain, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine scriptures and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, quick in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, formerly preaching in the kingdom of Sicily, converted many from iniquity and brought forth for God great fruits of his learning. He wrote elegant:

Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. And certain other works.

There are some who write that he was raised to the honor of the cardinalate because of his extraordinary learning and the uprightness of his life; about this I am not certain.

Walter Disse, an Englishman by nation, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, nuncio and legate of Pope Boniface IX in the kingdoms of England, Spain, Portugal, Navarre, Arago-

176

Iohānis Hie- rofolymitani, vir in diuinis scriptoris eruditus, secularis phi- losophiae nō ignorans, sacrae paginae doctor infignis, declama- tor sermonũ egregius, ingenio acutus eloquio compositꝰ, edidit multa pręclara volumina, invniuersitate Parīsien lecturas plu- res elegantes pronunciauit. Claruit temporibus Venceslai imperatoris, &amp; Bonifacij Papae no- ni,anno domini 1390. N Icolaus de Gorra,ordinis fratrū san̄cti Do minici,vir in scripturis san̄c̃tis studiofissimꝰ,&amp;amp; nobiliter eru ditus,ingenio praestans,edidit scholastico et amp;amp; aperto sermone multa volumina,quoꝝ lectio his qui insitiui cupiūt in san̄ctis scriptu ptu

Abbot of Sponheim.

[unclear], and in the regions of Gascony, and in the other lands and kingdoms, preaching the Cross against the infidel schismatics, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, wrote little works not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Of these there are extant:

Against the Lollards, one book. Also On the Schism, one book. On Some Psalms, one book. Sermons de tempore, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. And certain others.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Gerard of Zutphen, German by nation, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant also of secular letters, subtle in intellect, distinguished in eloquence, and to be preferred no less for his manner of life than for his knowledge of the Scriptures, published certain little works pertaining to the instruction of devout brothers, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have seen only:

On Interior Reformation, one book, "A certain man descend[ed?]." On Spiritual [Ascension?], one book, "Blessed is the man whose..." Various sermons, one book.

John de [Hildinio?], of the order of the brethren of the Hospital of St. John of Jerusalem, a man learned in the divine writings, not ignorant of secular philosophy, an eminent doctor of sacred Scripture, an outstanding declaimer of sermons, sharp in intellect and composed in eloquence, published many excellent volumes and delivered several elegant lectures in the University of Paris. Of these the following are extant:

On the Gospel of Mark, one book, "He was made like a lion." On the Gospel of John, one book. On the Epistle to the Romans, one book. On the Epistle to the Corinthians, one book. On the Epistle to the Galatians, one book. On the Epistle to the Ephesians, one book. On the Epistle to the Philippians, one book. On the Epistle to the Colossians, one book. On the Epistles to the Thessalonians, one book.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

On the Epistles to Timothy, two books. On the Epistle to Titus, one book. On the Epistle to Philemon, two books. On the Epistle to the Hebrews, one book. On the Annunciation of the Lord, one book, "Hail Mary, full of grace." Various sermons, one book, "Instruct your son, because as..." And many other things.

He is said also to have written commentaries and lectures on many books of the Bible, which have not yet at all come into our hands.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Philip of Monte [Calerio?], of the order of the Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man practiced in the sacred Scriptures, a great and outstanding preacher of the word of God, wrote for the usefulness of those who serve in declamations little works not to be scorned; by nobly exercising his talent in them, he also destined his name for the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the following:

Sermons de tempore, one book, "There will be signs in the sun and [moon]." Sermons on the Saints, one book. Lenten sermons, one book.

He is said besides to have composed various other treatises and to have explained some of the divine books, but none of them has reached me.

John, surnamed Grossus, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin of Mount Carmel, the nineteenth prior general - some have the twenty-first - a native of Toulouse, a studious and learned man, wrote in plain speech volumes not to be despised; by exercising his talent magnificently in them, he made his name known also to posterity. Of these I have seen only the excellent work which, containing the institution and progress of the Carmelite order, is entitled Viridarium, three books, "By what things [unclear]." His sermons, one book, and certain other things are also reported.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Nicholas de Gorra, of the order of the Friars of Saint Dominic, a man most studious in the holy Scriptures and nobly learned, outstanding in intellect, published in scholastic and plain discourse many volumes, the reading of which, for those who wish to be instructed in the holy Scriptures...

177

ABBOT OF SPONHEIM.

[unclear], it will not be to be rejected; of these I remember that few have come into our hands. Of the many, however, the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Five Books of Moses, 5 books. On Isaiah the Prophet, 1 book. Likewise on Jeremiah, 1 book. On Ecclesiasticus, a large work, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. “He will give a blessing.” On the Gospel of Matthew, 1 book. On the Gospel of Mark, 1 book. “He gave [him?] as a light to the nations.” On the Gospel of Luke, 1 book. On the Gospel of John, 1 book. Various Sermons, 1 book. And certain other things.

He is said, moreover, to have issued noteworthy commentaries and readings on almost the whole Bible, which have not come to the knowledge of my reading.

Jacobus of Teramo, a canon of Aprutium, archdeacon of Aversa, a very celebrated jurist, an excellent doctor of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, clear and well-composed in speech, whose authority among the professors of this faculty was great in his time, published in that discipline certain outstanding volumes, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these I have found only the dialogue On the Redemption of the Human Race, commonly called Belial, which the author entitled:

The Consolation of Sinners, 1 book. “And afterwards through the tree of knowledge.” He is said to have written On the Clementines, 1 book. And certain other things.

He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and of the new Pope Boniface, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Wilhelmus of Oppenbach, a German by nation, an eminent doctor learned in the sacred Scriptures, and nobly exercised in scholastic philosophy, sharp and vigorous in intellect, well fitted for disputing and untying questions of the Scriptures, wrote in the theological faculty little works not to be rejected, by which he made his name known in the Parisian school. Of these I have found:

On the Sentences, 2 books. Disputed Questions, 1 book.

Of Ecclesiastical Writers.

He is also said to have written sermons and certain other treatises, and to have worked out readings in the schools, which have not come to my knowledge.

Henricus of Langenstein, called “of Hesse,” a German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect, abundant and expansive, since, after spending many years in lecturing on Genesis, scarcely reaching the fourth chapter of the book, he completed as many volumes. For he was ready in all things, copious in judging and writing, so much so that for him it was a matter of greater difficulty to keep away things worthy of remembrance that occurred to him of their own accord than to find new things to say. This man, as I found from a certain letter of his, I should believe to have been a canon of the church of Worms. He flourished first in the University of Paris, where he earned the laurel of the doctorate; then, for the adornment of the newly planted University of Vienna, he betook himself there, and both by teaching and by writing acquired great glory for his learning. Of his little works the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. A Prologue on Genesis, 5 books. On the Schism of Antichrist, 1 book. On the Instruction of the Priesthood, 1 book. On the Contemplative Soul, 1 book. On Contemplation, 1 book. Mirror of the Soul, 1 book. On the Canonical Hours, 1 book. Against the Astrologers, 1 book. On the Lord’s Prayer, 1 book. On the Hail Mary, 1 book. On the Creed of the Apostles, 1 book. On Contempt of the World, 1 book. Against Brother Telesphorus, 1 book. Against a Certain Wycliffite, 1 book. To the Canons Regular, 1 book. On the Property of Monks, 1 book. Sermons on the Season, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. On the Song of Songs, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. Various Questions, 1 book. 1 book. 1 book. book

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He also published many other things that have not come to my knowledge. He flourished in the times of Rupert the Bavarian Palatine, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1400.

Johannes de Bromyard, of the Order of the Friars Preachers of St. Dominic, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and learned through long practice, not ignorant also of secular letters, excellent in talent and an outstanding preacher, wrote certain distinguished volumes by which he secured the memory of his name among posterity. Among these the following are reported:

The Summa of Preachers, one book. “The life of preachers,” etc.

The Summa of Moral Law, one book. “What in the following work [unclear].”

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He is said to have written many other things besides, which have not come to my knowledge.

Johannes Gluel, German by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Cologne, born in Aachen, an imperial city, a man excellently learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, of excellent and distinguished talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, among the other little works of his study, a volume not to be rejected by devotees of this religious order, on the origin and advancement of his order, which he entitled:

Mirror of the Carmelites, one book.

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Lenten Sermons, one book. “Store up for yourselves.”

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

He flourished in his convent at Cologne, writing and composing various little works, where at last, failing, he passed his day and was buried in peace.

Henricus Euta, or Oyta, German by nation, the unique ornament of the University of Vienna in Austria, [unclear] from the beginning, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, nobly learned in Aristotelian philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, an outstanding preacher of sermons, wrote many distinguished volumes, of which very few have so far come into our hands. For I have read only:

On the Sentences, four books. “Concerning the prologue of the first [unclear].” “On [unclear].”

On Contracts, one book. “Love justice, you who [unclear].”

On the Conception of Saint Mary, one book. “A virgin shall arise from Israel.”

And certain sermons.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished in the University of Vienna, under Emperor Wenceslaus, together with Henricus de Hasia, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Henricus de Andernaco, German by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and an outstanding interpreter of Aristotelian philosophy, excellent in talent and famous among all men of his time as a preacher of sermons, published little works of no slight authority, of which the following are reported:

A distinguished work On the Sentences, four books.

Sermons on the Season, one book.

Sermons on the Saints, one book.

Questions of Philosophy, one book.

And certain other things that have by no means come to the notice of our reading.

He flourished especially in the convent at Cologne, where he is also said to have been buried.

Blaius Andernarius, French by nation, of the Order of the Friars of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the holy Scriptures and nobly trained in the arena of scholastic discipline, clear in talent and an outstanding disputant, wrote several distinguished volumes, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Among these an illuminating and notable work excels:

On the Sentences, one book.

Questions and Collations, one book.

He is also said to have written some things in moral philosophy, but they have not come to me.

Bartholomaeus de Saliceto, the most celebrated jurist of all his time, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, whose sayings are held in great authority among professors of civil law, published certain illuminating little works on the laws, by which he consecrated the memory of his name to immortality among posterity. Of these the following are reported:

On the Code, one book.

On the Institutes, one book.

On the Use of Fiefs, one book.

And several other things.

He flourished in the times of Emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of the Lord 1390.

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of St. Bavo, of the Order of the divine father Benedict, German by nation, an outstanding doctor and professor of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent and compact in eloquence, and no less distinguished in religious way of life than in knowledge of letters, wrote

Abbot of Spanheim.

[He] wrote certain distinguished little works for the instruction of monks, of which the following are extant: On the Eating of Meat, book 1; Declarations on the Rule, book 1; Questions on the Sentences, book 1.

In addition, he is said to have written various and numerous treatises, but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands, except that little book which he wrote on the eating of meat, in which he beautifully sets forth and soundly concludes that, for a healthy monk professed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the eating of meat is unlawful, and therefore altogether forbidden.

Richard Lavinham, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, a man excellently learned in the Holy Scriptures, an outstanding expounder of secular philosophy, and also of excellent talent in delivering sermons to the people, wrote several volumes as well, of which these are reported: Against the Lollards, book 1; On the Foundation of His Order, book 1; For the Book of Bridget, book 1; Various Sermons, book 1; On Logic also, book 1; and Various Questions, book 1.

He flourished at the University of Oxford, especially at the time when the heresy of John Wycliffe, that of the Lollards, began in Bohemia.

Johannes de Werdena, of the order, as they say, of the Friars Minor, a German by nation, a man studious and learned in the sacred writings, rich in reading of the ancients, and sufficiently learned in natural philosophy, excellent in talent, composed in speech with scholastic simplicity, and in his time a most celebrated deliverer of popular sermons, wrote, among the other monuments of his talent, little works very necessary for preachers of the word of God, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity. Of these there are extant: Double Sermons on the Temporale, book 1, “Let us put on,” see; Double Sermons on the Saints, book 1.

But the other things which he composed have by no means come to our knowledge.

Jacobus, who is called Magnus, a native of Toledo, of the order of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine, a man learned in the divine writings, distinguished in knowledge of natural philosophy, and abundant in reading of the ancients, is said to have issued various treatises and commentaries on the divine books, which have not yet come into our hands. I have found one outstanding and distinguished volume of his, on discourse in the inquiry of wisdom, entitled *So-

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

phologium*, 3 books, “Of the most illustrious prince.”

Concerning the others I have seen nothing. He flourished in the times of the emperor Wenceslaus and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Johannes Campsceñ, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, an Englishman by nation, long practiced in the Holy Scriptures and in continual reading of the ancients, rich in talent, an excellent deliverer of sermons, is said to have fashioned certain distinguished little works, by which he transmitted his name with glory to the knowledge of posterity. Of their number, they report that there are extant very notable Sermons on the Temporale, book 1; Sermons on the Saints, book 1.

But of the other things which he composed I have not been able to find the titles of the works.

Thomas Gualensis, of the order of the Friars Preachers, an Englishman by nation, a man learned and very studious in the divine Scriptures, and nobly learned in secular letters, especially in scholastic philosophy, subtle in talent and clear in eloquence, also an outstanding deliverer of sermons and an acute disputant in scholastic lectures, wrote many distinguished little works on the Holy Scriptures, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of posterity; of these, however, few have come into our hands. For I have found only the following: On the Whole Psalter, book 1, “Blessed is he who keeps”; On the Proverbs of Solomon, book 1, “In hidden places I shall prepare”; book 1; On Augustine’s City of God, 10 books, “The force of the river makes glad”; On the Song of Songs, book 1.

He flourished at the University of Oxford, where he is said to have composed many volumes, and especially various lectures on several books of the Bible.

Philippus, abbot of the monastery of Otterburg, in the diocese of Worms, of the Cistercian order, a German by nation, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, learned through long practice, and not ignorant of secular literature, published for the edification of readers volumes not to be despised; by soundly exercising his talent in them, he also left to posterity the memory of his name. Of their number the following are reported: a distinguished and notable work On the Song of Songs, book 1; Sermons on the Temporale, book 1; Sermons on the Saints, book 1; Letters to Various Persons, book 1.

If he published anything more, it has still by no means come to my knowledge.

Abbot of Spanheim.

Nicolaus, a physician of outstanding learning, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, a man highly learned not only in medicine but also in the other letters of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, polished in eloquence; how great his learning is among the physicians of this time is proved not by my words, but by their testimonies. He published certain notable little works in that faculty, among which an excellent work is reported:

Summa medicinae, one book.

And certain other things.

He died in the times of Rupert, king of the Romans, and of Pope John the twenty-third, in the year of the Lord 1412, in the fifth indiction.

Johannes de Duren, of the Order of Friars Minor of St Francis, German by nation, a man studious and nobly practiced in the Holy Scriptures, of great and distinguished reputation in delivering sermons to the people, is reported to have composed certain little works for the direction of simple priests as preachers, by which he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive:

Sermones de tempore, one book.

Sermones de sanctis, one book.

Quadragesimale, one book. “Sanctificate ieiunium.”

De septem peccatis mortalibus, one book. “Cum confessor idoneus.”

De occultis vitiis, one book. “Est via quae videtur ho-”

De confessione, one book.

He is also said to have written many other things, which have not come to my knowledge.

Tilmannus de Hachenberg, of the Order of Friars Minor, German by nation, from the diocese of Trier, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, learned through long practice, having a tongue polished by use in speaking, shone forth as great and most renowned in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote certain little works not to be despised by simple people, by which, profitably applying his talent, he left the memory of his name to posterity. Of these there survive:

Sermones de tempore, one book. “Erunt signa hic praedi-”

Sermones de sanctis, one book.

Sermones per quadragesimam, one book.

And certain other things.

He flourished in his convent at Koblenz, where he died and was buried.

Johannes de Ligniano, a very celebrated jurist, well instructed in the disciplines of the philosophers, outstanding in talent, distinguished in eloquence, is reported to have composed certain excellent little works in canon law,

On Ecclesiastical Writers

[unclear], applying himself to which, he both spent his time usefully and left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these, as Franciscus de Zabarellis testifies in the prologue on the Clementines, there are extant Comportationes on the Clementines, one book, and certain other works.

He flourished under Rupert the Bavarian, king of the Romans, and Pope Boniface IX, in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1400.

Hugo of Schlettstadt, a German by nation, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and notably learned in the disciplines of the philosophers, subtle in intellect, and a distinguished disputant of scholastic questions, wrote, as they say, certain excellent volumes, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these there is extant a work of Questions on the Sentences, four books.

And certain other works.

He was, moreover, a follower and clear interpreter, in his determinations, of the holy father Bonaventure, of the Order of Minors, explaining those things which in that man’s distinctive philosophy might have seemed obscure and rather rare to the simple.

Paulus Venetus, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and, in Aristotelian philosophy, second to none in Italy in his time, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, and an outstanding declaimer, composed many little works, especially in philosophy, by which he left to posterity the memory of his name. Of these are reported:

Against the Jews, one book. Summary on Natural Things, one book. Sermons on the Season, one book. Sermons on the Saints, one book. Sermons for Lent, one book. On the book of the Posterior Analytics, [two?] books. On the Physics, [two?] books. On the Metaphysics, [twelve?] books. On the Soul, [two?] books. Summary of Philosophy, one book. A Double Logic, [two?] books. On Generation and Corruption, [two?] books. On the book of Porphyry, one book. On the book of the Categories, one book. On Strode’s Consequences, one book. And many other works.

“Every doctrine,” etc. “Natural philosophy” “With you, most wise king” “So great a body of letters,” etc. “A conversation [unclear],” etc. “Considering,” etc. “Of human and divine things” “Greatest and strong,” etc. “As I was asking,” etc. “Jesus, God and man”
