On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the conception of Saint Mary, one book. Many counsels also, one book. And certain other small works. He died under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction.

John of Dorsten, German by nation, of the Order of the Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, well suited to disputing and resolving scriptural questions, and also of excellent reputation in delivering sermons to the people; he was held in esteem at the Erfurt school for teaching and preaching. He wrote works not to be despised, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there are reported:

Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished in the convent at Erfurt, under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, pope, in the year of the Lord 1475.

Angelus Saxo of Brunswick, German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, keen in intellect, distinguished in life, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people; after obtaining the mastership for teaching at the Erfurt school, he held the office of preacher at Mainz for a long time. Among other things he wrote a certain notable work:

On the Canon of the Mass, one book. Various sermons, one book. Diverse questions, one book. And certain other works.

He died at Strasbourg, and was buried in the monastery of the penitents, under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the fourteenth indiction.

Franciscus Philelphus, born from the ancient town of Tolentino, a knight decorated with gold and poet laureate, a very celebrated philosopher and orator, formerly in his youth at Venice a pupil of Chrysoloras the Byzantine philosopher, from whom he learned Greek and Latin eloquence most perfectly; a man so zealous and so indefatigable a lover and cultivator of the good arts that, like another Pliny, amid the continual occupations of wars he was always either reading something for himself or dictating something to others. For he wrote in both languages, both in prose and in verse, many splendid volu

lights, by which he left to posterity the memory of his most celebrated genius. Of these the following are extant:

Euthyphro, on piety, 1 book. On moral discipline, 8 books. The life of Pope Nicholas V, 2 books. A consolation addressed to a friend, 1 book. “Since I, desiring something ...” “How many laws [unclear]” On the diversity of laws, 4 books. Satires in the same meter, 9 books. “How nothing with me [unclear]” On jokes and serious matters, in hexameter, 10 books. Lyrics in every kind of meter, 6 books. Various orations, 60; 1 book. “If I thought it could be done ...” Of Latin letters, 16 books. The Rhetoric of Aristotle to King Alexander, 1 book. From Plato, 2 books. Hippocrates, on winds and bodily affections, 39 books. In Greek verses, by odes, 4 books. Of profane banquets, 2 books. Also on exile, 5 books. Also apophthegms, 2 books. And many other things. 2 books.

Moreover he translated many things into Latin, of which the following are reported. Among the Venetians, afterwards among the Florentines, the Sienese, the Bolognese, and finally the Milanese under four dukes, with an annual stipend, he taught Greek and Latin letters gloriously to very many. He died at Bologna, a nonagenarian and poor, indeed as a Christian philosopher, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the fourteenth indiction, in the year after the death of his son Marius.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

and made an end of his life and study. He wrote, among other things, a distinguished work:

Three books of Precepts of the Art of Rhetoric. I had already long ago resolved. One book of Elegant Orations. One book of Letters to Various Persons. [Songs?] and rhythms.

But he also composed many other works in meter and prose, which have not come to me. He died at Mantua under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480, in the thirteenth indiction.

Theoderic of Herxen, a German by nation, visitor of the order of the Brethren Clerics Living in Common, a devout man, studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, ready in intellect, clear in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, wrote many devout volumes for the edification of simple brothers. By usefully exercising his talent in them, he left remembrance of himself to posterity. Among these are reported:

On the Whole Psalter, one book. On the Lord’s Prayer, one book. On the Ave Maria, one book. On the Passion of the Lord, one book. On the Desire of Dying, one book.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1476.

Dominicus de Dominicis, a Venetian by homeland, first bishop of Torcello and afterward bishop of Brescia, and apostolic referendary, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, excellently adorned with studies of philosophy, dialectic, astronomy, and eloquence, who, because of his great virtues, was held in high esteem by the Roman pontiffs Pius, Paul, and Sixtus, and often fulfilled the office of legation, wrote several small works of excellent talent, but I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands. His elegant works are reported:

Orations on Various Subjects, one book. Various Sermons also, one book. And many treatises.

He died at Brescia under Emperor Frederick III and Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1478, in the eleventh indiction, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the sixtieth year of his age.

Lu[unclear]

The Abbot of Sponheim

Ludovicus Donatus, Venetian patrician and bishop of Bergamo, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of scholastic philosophy, also notable for piety, religion, clemency, and gentleness, subtle in intellect and clear in eloquence, wrote certain splendid small works, by which he left remembrance of himself to posterity. Of these I have never deserved to see anything anywhere. An outstanding work of his to Pope Paul II is reported:

On the Sentences, four books. Various Orations also, one book.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction, and was buried in the church of Saint Vincent the Martyr.

Conrad of Rodenberg, a German by nation, abbot of the monastery of St. John the Baptist of Rheingau, in the diocese of Mainz, of the order of the divine father Benedict, a devout and learned man, and an especially zealous guardian and lover of regular observance, who previously for many years held the office of prior at St. Matthias the Apostle in Trier and St. Martin in Cologne: since he was a most ardent lover of the Blessed Mary ever virgin, he wrote in her honor, in plain discourse, a very celebrated volume, taking from each of her members, under the figure of a cluster of grapes, the material of praise; to it he gave the very apt title:

On the Vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, one book. Its foundations are in the mountains. The Exercise of Novices, one book. Consider your calling. On Preparation before Mass, one book. Our Lord Jesus Christ. On the Ruin of the Order, an oration, or one book. The crown has fallen from the head. On the Causes of Ruin, an oration, one book. Catch us the little foxes. On Pastoral Care, an oration, one book. Blessed is the servant whom he finds. And various conferences in chapters.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1486, in the fourth indiction, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, and was buried in the right apse of the choir before the altar of Saint Benedict, toward the ambulatory.

Stephen of Gaeta, a Neapolitan, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures and a most learned professor and interpreter of both laws, sharp in intellect and sufficiently capable for debating and resolving questions of the Scriptures, clear and composed in speech, wrote to Giovanni Battista Bentivoglio of Sassoferrato, counsellor of Ferdinand, king of Sicily, a very celebrated work:

De quibus extant: Sermones de tempore lib.i. Sermones de sanctis lib.i. Sermones per adventum lib.i. Sermones de poenitentia per quadragesimam lib.i. Sermones de peccatis lib.i. Sermones de io. praeceptis, lib.i. Et quedam alia, Claruit sub Frederico imperatore tertio anno domini 1480. Et sub Innocentio papa octauo moritur. S lxtus papa quartus, natione Ligur, ex Sauona vrbe maritima natus, Frâciscus antea vocatus, ordinis fratrũ Minori mi- nister generalis, sedit post Paulum secūdum in cathedra Petri annis tredecim, vir in diuinis scripturis eruditꝰ, &amp; disputator egre- gius, amator cleri, religiosoꝝ ꝓmotor et amp; benefactor singularis, eo rum maxime quos vita obseruantialis commendabat, quem Pau- lus papa semel disputantem audiens, tantum admiratus est, vt eum car= y y iij

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Sacraments, 7 books. To the thresholds of blessed Peter. And certain other works.

He flourished in the time of Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1470.

Georgius Molitoris of Nuremberg, a German by nation, a man long practiced in the divine Scriptures and excellently learned, and not moderately instructed in scholastic philosophy, which they call Aristotelian, keen in intellect, distinguished in life, who for many years publicly taught theology in the academy of Erfurt and won great praise for his learning, wrote certain excellent little works of his talent, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

On the Sentences, 4 books. On the Passion of the Lord, 1 book. Many Sermons, 1 book. Various Questions. And several other works.

He died under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

Bartholomaeus, otherwise Baptista, surnamed Platina, by birthplace a Cremonese, once an apostolic abbreviator, a man most learned in every respect, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, subtle and forceful in intellect, eloquent and pleasing in speech, steadfast and strong in spirit, suffered many calamities at the hands of Pope Paul II, so that, stripped of all his goods and dignity, after suspension on the rack he was most cruelly thrust into prison and detained until the death of Paul himself. Soon freed by Sixtus, in imitation of Eutrandus, deacon of Pavia, who suffered similar things from Berengar, king of Italy, he wittily marked Paul’s character and vices by antiphraxis. For he wrote to Pope Sixtus IV:

On the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, 1 book. On the Natures of Things, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And certain other works.

His also is the Panegyric in praise of Bessarion, bishop of Sabina, etc.; an Oration to Paul II, Supreme Pontiff, on establishing peace in Italy and on declaring war on the Turks; On Honorable Pleasure, 10 books; On the False and True Good, 5 dialogues; Against Loves, 1 dialogue; On True Nobility, 1 dialogue; On the Best Citizen, 2 dialogues; [unclear]

The Abbot of Sponheim

He died at Rome of plague, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1481, in the fourteenth indiction.

Nicolaus de Wachenheim, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in intellect and clear in eloquence, who in the academy of Heidelberg for almost fifty years, teaching, lecturing, and disputing, was held in the highest esteem as though the prince of theologians, wrote little works of reading not to be despised, by which he also commended the memory of his name to posterity. Of these, few have come down to me:

Questions on the Sentences, 1 book. Many Sermons, 1 book. Several Collations and Orations, 1 book. Since with the approval of the sacred [unclear] And certain other works.

He flourished at Heidelberg under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1480, already very old, and under Pope Sixtus IV he died almost seven years before this.

Michael of Milan, of the Order of Friars Minor, devoted to and learned in the holy Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, subtle in intellect, distinguished in life and conduct, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, wrote, for the use of those who devote themselves to declamations, little works not to be despised, by which he also made his name known to posterity. Of these there are extant:

Sermons on the Temporale, 1 book. Sermons on the Saints, 1 book. Sermons for Advent, 1 book. Sermons on Penance for Lent, 1 book. Sermons on Sins, 1 book. Sermons on the Ten Commandments, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III in the year of the Lord 1480. And he died under Pope Innocent VIII.

Sixtus IV, pope, a Ligurian by nation, born from the maritime city of Savona, formerly called Franciscus, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, sat after Paul II in the chair of Peter for thirteen years; a man learned in the divine Scriptures and an outstanding disputant, a lover of the clergy, a singular promoter and benefactor of religious, especially of those whom an observant life commended. When Pope Paul once heard him disputing, he admired him so much that he

made [him] worthy of the honor of the cardinalate. Before his pontificate he wrote certain distinguished little works, among which the following are reported:

On Future Contingents, 1 book. On the Power of God, 2 books. On the Blood of Christ, 1 book. On the Conception of St. Mary, 1 book. And certain others.

He died under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

Johannes Consobrinus, Portuguese by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature and canon law, excellent in talent, of very celebrated reputation in delivering sermons to the people, first in England and then in Portugal uttered great and effective denunciations against the enemies of the faith; by disputing, preaching, and writing he reproved and refuted very many heresies and errors. At the urging of the provost of the royal college of blessed Mary of [Amhten] in England, he wrote a distinguished work in three parts, on contracts and exchanges, which he entitled

On Commutative Justice, 4 books. Various Sermons, 1 book. And certain others.

He abbreviated the Conflatum of Franciscus Maro in a pleasing compendium.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 1475. And under Pope Sixtus IV he died at Lisbon, poisoned for the faith.

Henricus, surnamed Prudens, of the order of the Carthusians, prior of the house of the valley near Bruges in Flanders, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, renowned in talent, devout in life and conduct, and singularly dedicated to God, wrote for the instruction of religious certain distinguished little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Among these there is extant a very celebrated work, especially suited to devotion, divided into three parts according to the distinctions of states, namely beginners, the progressing, and the perfect, in the manner of a dialogue, in which speakers are introduced: an angel and a monk, Jesus and the heavenly Father, Mary, the loving mother-in-law of holy souls. He entitled it

Tetralogue of Devotion, 5 books. And certain others.

He died in the new house of St. Sophia of Constantinople near ’s-Hertogenbosch, in which he had held the office of prior for some years, under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1484, in the second indiction.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Franciscus Diedus, a noble Venetian patrician, a man exceptionally learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a philosopher and rhetorician, distinguished in doctrine and eloquence, a very celebrated interpreter of pontifical and civil law, and an indefatigable lover and defender of the Venetian republic, wrote certain distinguished little works both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Among these the following are reported:

History of Saint Roch the Confessor, 1 book. Orations and various letters, And certain others.

He died at Verona under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1483, in the first indiction.

Rudolphus Agricola of Groningen, Frisian by nation, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, rhetorician, and the most celebrated poet of all of his time, skilled in Greek and Latin speech and not ignorant of the Hebrew language, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, once the teacher of Johannes Camerarius of Dalburg, bishop of Worms, likewise a most learned man, easily obtained first place in the Heidelberg school in teaching and writing, even among all doctors of whatever faculty. He wrote certain most excellent little works of his talent, by which he consecrated his name to immortality and left it to posterity. Among these the following are extant:

Life of Francesco Petrarca, 1 book. Poem on Saint Anne, 1 book. “Anna, parent of the highest [unclear]” A Most Subtle Dialectic, 3 books. Various Letters and Orations, 1 book.

In addition he produced various and most elegant poems, in which he showed his almost divine talent. He translated the Psalter from Hebrew, and certain works of Plato from Greek. Having begun to translate the volumes of Dionysius the Areopagite, he was forestalled by an untimely death and left them unfinished. He also wrote other things.

He died at Heidelberg, his mind most fully directed toward God, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1485, in the third indiction. Hermolaus Barbarus, patriarch of Aquileia, wrote this epitaph for him:

Envious fates have enclosed beneath this marble Rudolphus Agricola, the hope and glory of Frisian soil. Namely, while he lived, Germany earned whatever praise Latium has, whatever Greece has

Tillmannus, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, provost of the monastery of the holy martyr Christopher in Ravengirsburg, at the edge of the diocese of Mainz, near the Hercynian forest, which from the river Rhine extends its tail toward the Mediomatrices and the Treveri, in a place which from antiquity is called Recesius of the Huns, a German by nation, studious in the divine Scriptures, devout in life and conduct, wrote, in a simple and plain style for the edification of the brethren, certain little works full of devotion and charity, in which he exercised his talent. Of these the following are extant:

On the Spiritual Vineyard, one book. On the Instruction of Novices, one book. And certain small exercises.

He died old and full of days, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1485, in the third indiction.

[unclear]

Henricus Arnoldi, a Saxon by nation, by profession a Carthusian monk of the Basel house, a man devout in religion, distinguished in talent, sincere in affection, weighty in morals, sweet in speech, affable in conduct, pious, gentle, shining in example, very much exercised in sacred letters and not ignorant of pontifical law; when for many years he held the office of notary in the holy Council of Basel, he was approved by the testimony of all as faithful, just, and prudent. At length, seeing that all things are vanity, he despised everything for the love of Christ, choosing and entering the Carthusian enclosure; there, appointed prior of the same house, for many years he laudably ruled in peace and tranquility the monks subject to him, the conversi, and the rest, treating them with paternal love. He wrote many very devout and salutary little works, of which those that have come to our knowledge are set out below:

Many devout sermons on various saints, one book. Several sermons, one book. Histories of various saints, one book. A concordance of the Evangelists on the Passion of the Lord, one book. Meditations on the Life of Christ, one book. On the Conception of the Immaculate Virgin Mary, one treatise. A Dialogue between Jesus and Mary, one treatise. Dia[unclear] The following prayers, one treatise. [unclear], one treatise. [unclear], one treatise.

A Dialogue on holy exercises, between Saint Margaret and her little servant, one treatise. Another dialogue between the same persons on the cross, one treatise. On the Commendation of Charity, one treatise. The excellence of charity [unclear] On holy humility in the form of a prayer, one treatise. Of perfect humility [unclear] Again on humility, one treatise. Most beloved brothers, hu[unclear] A chronicle of the house of the Carthusians in Basel, one treatise.

He happily departed from this life under Frederick III, emperor of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1487.

Jodocus de Calwe, a German by nation, a Swabian by homeland, a man exercised by long study in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of scholastic philosophy, prompt and forceful in talent, was for many years held in esteem in the school of Heidelberg by lecturing and preaching, where also, according to custom, for some time he held the office of preacher in the church of the Holy Spirit. He wrote certain treatises, as they say, not to be rejected, but they have not come to the knowledge of our reading. There are extant from him various sermons on diverse subjects, one book; A Vocabulary of Preachers, one book; and various treatises.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. And under Pope Innocent VIII he died before this three-year period.

Nicolaus de Crutzenach, a German by nation, from the diocese of Mainz and the county of Sponheim, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, distinguished in life, an acute disputant and an outstanding declaimer of sermons, who for many years publicly taught theology in the school of Vienna, and both among the scholars there and with Emperor Frederick III obtained great praise and reward for his learning, wrote certain excellent little works, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

Questions on the Sentences, one book. Various sermons, two books. Many conferences and orations, one book. On the Conception of Saint Mary [unclear]

And many other things, which, since he concealed them until his death, could not yet come to the knowledge of our reading; nevertheless they will come day by day. He died at Vienna in Austria under Emperor Frederick III,

Peter Scotus, German by nation, from Strasbourg by homeland, a canon of Saint Peter there, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, most learned in both laws, and very well instructed in the other arts of humanity, a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, and poet, excellent in talent and distinguished in life and conduct, wrote certain modest and most elegant little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended himself to posterity. On Saints John the Baptist, John the Evangelist, and Chrysostom, he wrote a beautiful and pleasing work in elegiac verse, one book. The Praises of John Gerson, one book. Most elegant letters, [unclear], one book. In addition, he composed poems and various pieces, not contrary to the reader’s compunction, but properly apt and fitting, in various kinds of meter. He died at Strasbourg, buried in the church of Saint Peter, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the ninth indiction, and in the thirty-first year of his age. Having been perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many times, and he was taken away lest wickedness alter his understanding.

Nicasius de Voerda of Mechelen, German by nation, Brabantine by homeland, deprived of his sight from the third year of his age, and for that reason also naturally and completely ignorant of the alphabet of all letters, displayed, as it were, a great miracle, a second Didymus of Alexandria in our time, since he became most learned in every doctrine and science, both divine and human. For in the school of Cologne, where he also died, he publicly taught law: the books of both laws, which he had never seen, he learned by hearing, retained in memory, and recited openly. In the University of Leuven he first received the degree of master in arts; afterwards he governed schools for some time in Mechelen; then, having returned to Leuven, he was appointed licentiate in sacred theology, and by a singular apostolic dispensation was ordained priest. He preached publicly, heard confessions, served at the altar, and, though blind, recited the Gospel before all, using his mind as a book; only he did not celebrate the divine rites at the altar by himself. Lastly, in the academy of Cologne, by the agreement of all the doctors, he was made doctor of canon law, and also a careful interpreter of the imperial laws. He published a very celebrated work, which he read extraordinarily in the same University of Cologne, with many taking it down. On the Institutes, book one. Because those things which well in

The Abbot of Sponheim.

On the Sentences, 4 books. Various sermons, 1 book. Various questions.

He wrote to me some not inelegant letters, in each one of which, at considerable length, he wove together the whole history of his fortune; and, when I had asked him some time before, he humbly confessed that he had made the aforesaid little works.

He died at Cologne, buried in the greater church, under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1491, in the tenth indiction, on 26 August.

Christophorus Porsena, a Roman, prior of St Albina in the City, of the order of the hermit brothers of St William, a man most devoted to the divine Scriptures and very learned, highly skilled in the Greek and Latin languages, since from earliest youth he had imbibed those literatures in Greece itself and under Greek teachers, so that he seemed to have been born from Greece; subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech; wrote, among other things, 1 book:

Letters to various persons,

and many other works.

He translated into Latin Origen’s eight books Against Celsus the Philosopher, dedicated to Pope Sixtus IV; also moral sermons of the blessed John Chrysostom, twenty-five in number, which he dedicated to Marco Barbo, cardinal of St Mark. He also translated quite finely certain little works of Theophylact, archbishop of Bulgaria, with others, and gave them to the Latins to read.

He also translated the volumes of the following writers:

Procopius of Caesarea, On the Gothic War, 3 books.

And Agathias Scholasticus of Smyrna, On the Gothic War and other foreign histories, 5 books.

He also translated certain works of Athanasius.

He died at Rome, carried off by plague, under Frederick III, emperor, and Innocent VIII, pope, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1486, in the fourth indiction.

Hermolaus Barbarus, Venetian by nation, patrician by family, archbishop and patriarch of Aquileia, and at last cardinal-bishop of the most holy Roman Church; a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters; a very celebrated philosopher, rhetorician, poet, astronomer, and geometer; highly skilled in Greek and Latin speech; subtle in intellect, eloquent in expression, devout and distinguished in life and conduct, and most worthy of every ecclesiastical honor. From adolescence he devoted zeal and effort to good letters and holy morals, and proved such and so great a man that he left no one his superior. Beginning to write from the eighteenth year of his age, he composed many most elegant little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of their number the following are reported:

On Celibacy, 1 book.

Castigations on Pliny, 1 book.

Against the Barbarian Philosophers, 1 book.

On Marriage, in verse, 1 book.

Questions of Geometry, 1 book.

The Agreement of Astronomy and Medicine, 1 book.

Precepts for Writing History, 1 book.

Compendium of Philosophy, 1 book.

Compendium of Galen, 1 book.

Letters to various persons, 1 book.

Multiple Orations, 1 book.

More than twelve thousand verses of poems, 1 book.

And many other works.

The Castigations on Pliny, a great work which he began as Venetian legate at Rome and completed as patriarch, he dedicated to Pope Alexander VI; in it he healed nearly five thousand wounds of copyists. Once, in the year of the Lord 1486, when he was passing through Cologne on his way to Mainz, at the request of Theodericus Flas, physician of Neuss, he composed a little book, How Far Astronomy Agrees with Medicine. To Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, the historiographer, he published a book on the precepts for writing history. He also interpreted Aristotle’s Rhetoric, the whole Dialectic, and Dioscorides; and he composed elegies, letters, and metrical orations, up to twelve thousand verses of poems, as we have said. He translated into Latin the responsive treatise on the Catholic faith by the patriarch of Constantinople, to the question of Mahomet the great Turk; also Plutarch On Isis and Osiris, and the same author’s Why the Oracles Ceased; to Arnoldus Bostius, the Carmelite of Ghent, a certain little work of Dionysius the Areopagite. He translated many other things as well. His work On Marriage contains about six hundred verses, in which he argues most elegantly whether it is expedient for a wise man to take a wife, concluding that it is not. He died, not without the very great loss of the studious, under Frederick III, emperor, and Alexander VI, pope, in the year of the Lord 1495, in the thirty-ninth year of his age, in the second indiction.

Junianus Maius, a Parthenopean, Neapolitan, certainly a man most devoted to secular letters and outstandingly learned, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician,

The Abbot of Sponheim.

... outstanding in ability and renowned for eloquence, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these there is extant a large and distinguished volume addressed to Henry, archbishop of Acherontia [Acheruntia?], confessor of Ferdinand, king of Naples, and principally to the king himself, which, gathering from the books of the ancients, he entitled:

On the Property of Ancient Words, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I am uncertain whether he is still alive.

Benedictus Capra of Perugia, a man most celebratedly learned in both laws, and well exercised both in the divine scriptures and in the precepts of the philosophers, subtle in ability and an outstanding disputant, distinguished for knowledge of many ancient and modern matters, taught law publicly for a long time in the Perugian school and acquired a great reputation for his learning. Among other things he wrote:

On the Decretals, 5 books. Also several Counsels, 1 book. And certain other works.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480.

Johannes Andreas, bishop of Aleria, secretary of the apostolic library, formerly a companion of Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa; a man devoted to the divine scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a jurist and most eloquent orator, excellent in ability, distinguished in life and conduct, skilled in both Greek and Latin speech, wrote certain little works of no slight authority, by which he transmitted the memory of his name with glory to posterity. Among their number the following are given:

On the Fourth Book of the Decretals, 1 book. On the Use of Fiefs, 1 book. On Appeals, 1 book. Letters to Various Persons, 1 book. And very many others.

He died under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1493, in the eleventh indiction.

Johannes Campeius of Bologna, a most celebrated jurist, and not moderately learned both in the divine scriptures and in secular philosophy, excellent in ability and renowned for eloquence, taught law publicly for a long time in the Bolognese school, where, training many and very distinguished pupils, he gained great fruit and praise from his learning. In that faculty he wrote many outstanding commentaries and treatises, as they report, by which he commended his name to posterity. But none of them has come into our hands. A distinguished work of his is reported:

On Dowry, a treatise, 1 book. And very beautiful Counsels, with many other works.

He flourished under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484. And I do not know whether he is still alive.

Dominicus Bolanus, Venetian by nation, a man exercised in the divine scriptures and excellently learned in secular letters, a philosopher and rhetorician not to be rejected, sharp and vigorous in ability, composed in speech, published some distinguished little works of his ability, by which he showed himself a devout and faithful worshipper of the Christian name and commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only a distinguished little work against detractors of Marian purity, which he dedicated to Nicolò Marcello, the seventy-first doge of the Venetians:

On the Conception of Saint Mary, 1 book. Not with small grief...

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He flourished at Venice under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1484. I hear that he is still held to be alive.

Franciscus Niger, a Venetian priest, a man [unclear] in the divine scriptures, a poet and orator not worthless, outstanding in ability and eloquent in speech, wrote various little works of his ability, by which he made his name known to posterity. Of these there is extant a work not to be despised, but to be raised up with great praises, addressed to Leonardo Botta, a Milanese knight, entitled:

Grammar, 14 books. From Annaeus Seneca [unclear]

His letters are also reported. And certain other works.

He flourished at Venice under the emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480. I do not know whether he is still alive.

Jacobus de Stralen, a German by nation, a man most learned in the divine writings and excellently learned in secular philosophy, excellent in ability and renowned for eloquence, taught theology gloriously for many years in the Cologne school and earned great praises from all for his learning. He wrote many distinguished little works, lectures, and various questions, of which I have seen only:

On the Apocalypse of John, 1 book. Jacob saw in his sleep...

Of the others I have seen nothing. He flo-

The Abbot of Sponheim.

He flourished in Cologne under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490, a very old man, being about eighty years of age. And I believe that he is still counted among the living.

Marsilius Ficinus, an Italian by nation, a Florentine by homeland, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, most skilled in both languages, the singular glory, ornament, and crown of Platonic theology: he wrote in an ornate style many excellent little works, by which he showed to posterity the vein of his excellent intellect. Of these the following are reported:

A notable Theology, one book. “In what manner in [unclear]...”

On Intellect and Intelligence, one book.

On Plato’s Symposium, one book. “Plato, first among philosophers...”

Letters, several books.

And many other things.

From Greek, moreover, he translated many works into Latin. For Piero de’ Medici of Florence he translated fifty-six treatises of Plato. Also Hermes Trismegistus, On the Power and Wisdom of God. The book of Xenocrates the Platonist On Death, for the same Piero de’ Medici. For Giovanni Cavalcanti he translated the little works of Speusippus, Alcinous, and Pythagoras. For the same man, the book of Alcinous the Platonist On the Doctrine of Plato. He wrote, besides, many other things, which have by no means come to the knowledge of our reading.

He flourished at Florence under Emperor Frederick III and the Roman pontiffs Sixtus IV and Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still among men.

Rupertus of Lecce, bishop of Aquila of the Marsi, or of the city of Abruzzo, of the Order of Friars Minor, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in intellect, sweet and composed in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, a very celebrated declaimer of sermons, famous throughout the whole Christian world, who by word and example converted many from iniquity: he wrote, for the edification of readers, especially preachers of the divine word, certain excellent volumes, of which the following are reported:

Sermons on the Temporale, one book. “The night has passed...”

On the Praises of the Saints, one book. “Let not the wise man glory in...”

On Penance through Lent, one book. “Many are called... because...”

Also On Sins, one book.

And certain other things.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick III and Popes Sixtus and Innocent, in the year of the Lord 1486. I do not know whether he is still living.

Johannes Pheffer of Widenberg, a German by nation, an East Frank by homeland, a man learned through long study in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, excellent in intellect, devout, gentle, and outstanding in life and conduct; sent from the University of Heidelberg, he illuminated by his learning the beginning of the Freiburg school, in which he has already for many years gloriously taught theology and has properly instructed many of his hearers. He wrote certain excellent little works, among which there exists a notable work on the Epistles of Paul, which, read publicly, he entitled

Priestly Directory, thirteen books. “Concerning the reader of the epistle...”

And many other things.

He flourished still among men under Emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1490. He may still be alive.

Johannes Britannicus, born from Palazzolo, a town of the Brescian district, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a distinguished philosopher, notable poet, and lucid rhetorician, who today is held in esteem among his own people of Brescia, whom by inestimable learning, teaching, and writings he makes daily more illustrious: he wrote many and various works, by which he made his name known to posterity and venerable to those present. Of these the following are reported: a very celebrated work of commentaries

On Persius, one book.

Also On Statius, one book.

On Ovid’s Metamorphosis, one book.

Also various Letters.

And many other things.

He is flourishing in the city of Brescia and composing various little works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1495.

Baptista of Ferrara, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine writings and excellently instructed in secular literature, excellent in verse and prose, and skilled in both languages, very celebrated and of almost divine intellect in declaiming sermons to the people: he wrote many excellent volumes, by which he rendered himself useful to those present and known to posterity. Of these the following are reported: a most lucid work of histories from the times of Christ down to us, which he entitled

Florida, one book.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Chronicle of his order, one book. On the fall of the impious Roman, one book. On Mount Sinai, one book. Life of Mechtild, one book. Chronicle of Ferrara, one book. Various Sermons, one book.

He also published very many and varied epigrams, which we hope will be published day by day. He also translated from Greek into Latin several sermons of Blessed John Chrysostom, and many other things unknown to us. He is still living at Ferrara, and is writing various works under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

[Unclear], most learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular letters, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct. Skilled in the Hebrew and Latin languages, who for confirmation always carried off contests as victor; among other little works of his talent he wrote, to the senate of Vicenza, a very celebrated and distinguished work, copiously furnished with authorities of sacred Scripture:

Against the Jews, one book. “As I read, to me many...”

And certain other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1485. And I do not know whether he is still living.

Ubertinus Clericus of Crescentino, a man most learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, rhetorician, and distinguished poet, and most skilled in both languages, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, who in the very celebrated school of Pavia lectured publicly for seven years, on a stipend, with the greatest attention and benefit of his hearers, wrote many excellent little works both in verse and prose, of which the following are extant:

On the Letters of Cicero, sixteen books. “The letters of this volume...”

On the Duties of the same, one book.

On the Metamorphoses of Naso, one book.

Also Letters, one book. Many Poems, one book.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, in the year of the Lord 1480. And I do not know whether he is still living.

Wilhelmus of Aachen, German by nation, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, subtle in talent, scholastic in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, who once held the office of preacher in the church of Basel, wrote many commendable little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these he publicly lectured on some in the school of Erfurt, with the attention and praise of all. He wrote:

On the Gospel of John, one book.

On the Canon of the Mass, one book.

On the Passion of the Lord, one book. “Jesus handed over willingly...”

Disputed Questions, one book.

Itinerary of the Holy Land, one book.

Various Sermons, one book.

And several other things.

He flourished under Frederick III, emperor, and Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1483. And I believe that he is still living.

Johannes de Lapide, German by nation, of the Carthusian order, a monk of the Basel house, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct: once, in the school of Paris, he obtained the mastership in the faculty of arts, governed in the same for several years, and, diligently pursuing the study of sacred letters by teaching, lecturing, and disputing, deserved to be adorned with the dignity of doctor in the school of the theologians. He first transferred to the University of Basel the teaching of those Parisians who are called Realists, and there planted, strengthened, and increased it. He was also one of the principal initiators and authors of the studies of Tübingen. Finally, after freely resigning several benefices, he was called to the canonry and office of preaching of the distinguished church of Basel, and at last, after a few years [unclear], leaving everything for the love of Christ, he put on the habit of the sacred Carthusian order. He wrote many excellent little works, by which he made himself useful to the present and memorable to the future. We have obtained copies of few of these. Yet the following are extant:

Introduction to Grammar, one book. “Since grammar...”

Dialogue on the Art of Punctuation. “The disciple [unclear]...”

On Exponible Propositions, one treatise. “As by a young man...”

On the Art of Resolving Sophistical Arguments, one treatise. “Since for every...”

Explanation of All the Books of Aristotelian Logic, one book. “To investigate...”

Explanation of the Books of Physics of the same.

Explanation of the Six Books of Metaphysics of the same, one book. “Because first...”

On Those Things Which They Require for a Worthy Priest, one treatise. “Man to the image...”

Resolution of Doubts Occurring about the Mass, one treatise. “The office, how great...”

Abbot of Sponheim.

A summary of the Passion of Jesus Christ, one tract. “At night Jesus ...”

On the Ascension of the Lord, among the sermons of Meffret, one sermon. “Rise up, Lord ...”

On the sermons of Meffret concerning the immaculate conception of the Virgin Mary, one tract. “[unclear] ...”

Very many sermons, both to the clergy and to the people, one book.

Various orations and letters, one book.

Also many other things, of which no mention is made here, one book.

Moreover, he divided many books of various authors into treatises and chapters, prefixing arguments to each, by which the writer’s intention in them can clearly be recognized. Among these are Cicero’s books On Duties, On Friendship, On Old Age, and On the Dream of Scipio. Likewise Aristotle’s books of logic; the same author’s books On the Soul; the books of the Metaphysics. Likewise the books of Ephrem the deacon; John Chrysostom’s books On Compunction of Heart; Saint Augustine’s books On Contrition of Heart; the same author’s book of letters; and almost all the books of Saint Ambrose the bishop. He is still living in the charterhouse of Basel, composes various works, and by his example urges many, through writings, to holy studies, under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Angelus de Clavasio, an Italian by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated jurist, outstanding in intellect, distinguished in speech, devout in life and conduct, is said to have produced certain excellent little works by which he made his name known far and wide. Of these there is extant the notable Summa on cases, very useful and necessary for simple confessors, and no less for learned but occupied men, now dispersed everywhere, which is entitled from the name of its author:

The Angelic Summa, one book.

Additions to the same, one book. “Of an angelic spirit ...”

And certain other things.

He completed this Summa under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV. And I hear that he is still alive, while Maximilian governs the kingdom of the Romans and Germans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

Jason de Mayno, Milanese by country, ducal senator, a man most learned in both laws, very learned both in the divine Scriptures and in the other secular disciplines, a distinguished philosopher, a very celebrated orator, subtle in intellect, eloquent in [unclear], outstanding in counsel and action, is said to have produced certain excellent little works, by which, exercising his talent, he also commended the memory of himself to posterity. But apart from the oration which he is said to have delivered at Rome before Pope Alexander VI, and which is also circulated in print, I do not recall that any of them have come into our hands. Yet, as I have learned for certain, he wrote elegantly:

On the title De actionibus in the Institutes, one book.

Also on the Code, nine books.

On the Digest he wrote various works, fifty books.

Orations and letters.

And certain other things.

He is distinguished today among the Milanese princes, held in the highest esteem, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1493, in the eleventh indiction.

Laurentius Burellus of Dijon, of the Order of the Brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently taught in secular letters, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in speech, practiced in meter and prose, wrote in both kinds certain excellent volumes by which he made his name known. Of these the following are reported: a very celebrated work in praise of Elijah, patriarch of the Carmelites, which he entitled:

The Heliad, one book.

On the illustrious men of his order, one book.

And many other things.

He is still living, held in great esteem among his own, writing and composing many things under Maximilian, unconquered king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Christophorus Landinus, an Italian by nation, a citizen of Florence, a man especially learned in secular letters and not ignorant of philosophy or of sacred Scripture, for many years presided over the chair of the Muses and by public office taught poetry, distinguished in intellect. He wrote works held in great esteem by all, especially:

Commentaries on Publius Vergilius Maro.

The Camaldulensians.

Ethics.

He is said still to flourish among his Florentines, whom he adorns with the flowers of every literature.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Jacobus of Bergamo, of the Order of the Hermit Friars of St. Augustine, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and nobly instructed in the disciplines of secular letters, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, distinguished in life and conduct, a most celebrated historiographer, wrote certain very lucid little works by which he made posterity beholden to his memory. Of these there is extant a work of histories from the beginning of the world down to the year of the Lord 1486, a great and distinguished volume, which, compiling it from various sources with much and long labor, he entitled Supplement of Chronicles, in fifteen books. For Cicero’s [unclear]. I have seen nothing of the others.

He is still living among his own people of Bergamo, held in esteem, nearly sixty years old, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Baptista de Sancto Blasio of Padua, a man very skilled in both laws and distinguished by philosophical learning, subtle in talent and ornate in speech, who taught law publicly and excellently in the Paduan gymnasium, where he instructed a great number of pupils, wrote in that faculty certain distinguished little works, by which he showed the force of his talent to those present and to posterity. Of these I have read:

On Dowry Privileges, one book. Since concerning dowries many things.

Also The Correlative, one book. In this correlative work.

Questions on arbiters, [unclear]. In the name of Christ, [unclear]. Since [unclear].

On the First Rubric of the Decretals, one book. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

He also wrote other things.

He also wrote on the difference between an arbiter and an arbitrator.

He completed these very works in the Paduan gymnasium, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, in the year of the Lord 1480, indiction 13. And I believe that he is still alive.

Marcus Antonius Sabellicus, a man most learned in every respect, the most celebrated philosopher, orator, and poet of all our age, adorning Venice with his learning and books, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, skilled in both languages, for whom Hermolaus Barbarus, Venetian archbishop and patriarch of Aquileia, once composed a book on the precepts for writing history, wrote certain distinguished volumes both in meter and in prose, by which he secured everlasting remembrance for his name among posterity. Of these I have seen the following: three great volumes of histories from the beginning of the world. To the Senate, a most celebrated work, containing from the beginning of the city 33 books.

The History and Deeds of the Venetians. And if from every writing.

On the Antiquity of Aquileia, His Fatherland, one book. It pours forth with Illyrian [unclear]. Where headlong fortune.

On the Sontian Fortification, a poem, one book. Now, the wheels having been spread, she set out. The kindly vessel tosses.

On the Sontian Slaughter, a poem, one book. Among the pleasing suns of study. These things of one walking upon the ground.

On the Burning of the Carni, one book. The kindly vessel tosses.

On the Shipwreck of Peter’s Boat, one book. Among the pleasing suns of study.

On the Inventors of Things and Arts, one book. These things of one walking upon the ground.

On the Origin of Udine, a poem, one book. The gracious day of the Virgin.

In Praise of St. Mary, 14 elegies.

I have seen nothing of the rest.

He is distinguished today among the Venetians, held in the highest esteem, composing many and various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we are writing these things, 1494.

Hubertus Leonardus, bishop of Darien, of the Order of the Friars of the Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, excellent in talent and clear in eloquence, who once taught theology excellently in the Parisian gymnasium, wrote many highly commendable little works, by which he made his name known with glory. Of these the following are reported:

On the Genealogy of the Nobles of the Franks and Their Deeds, to Ludovicus, bishop of Liege, one book.

On the Gospel of Luke, one book.

On the Government of Princes, three books.

On Ecclesiastical Immunity, five books.

Against the Heretics of Nivelles, one book.

Various Sermons, one book.

A Notable Lenten Collection, one book.

And several other works.

When he was inquisitor of heretical depravity against certain heretics of Nivelles throughout the diocese of Liege, he confuted and defeated them with the sword of the Holy Spirit, writing the aforementioned very celebrated work, containing twenty-eight principal propositions; in it, vigorously and eloquently attacking just as many of their erroneous articles, he refuted them.

He flourished in Germany, from which he also came, under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still alive.

Abbot of Spanheim.

Gabriel Biel, German by nationality, of the order of those who call themselves Brothers of the Common Life, or those living in common: a man learned in the divine Scriptures and excellently instructed in secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct. From the beginning of its foundation he presided for many years over the university at Tubingen, where he instructed many pupils both in philosophy and in sacred letters. He wrote certain little works of no contemptible authority, by which he made his name known. Among these he ordinarily lectured in the aforesaid university:

On the Canon of the Mass, one book. Praemissa in cubiculo. On the Passion of the Lord, he wrote one book. Various sermons also, one book. And certain other things. Likewise an epitome and collection on the four books of the Sentences.

He is renowned today, an old man of advanced age, in the highest esteem with the count of Wurttemberg, and is said to be writing certain things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

George of Gemmingen, German by nationality, provost and canon of the distinguished church of Speyer, a learned and noble man, professor of both laws and a very celebrated interpreter, and excellently skilled in the other disciplines of the liberal arts; a distinguished philosopher and rhetorician, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, excellent in meter and prose. He wrote certain distinguished little works, in which, laudably exercising his talent, he also made his name known to posterity. Yet he conceals what he writes, so that he may avoid the semblance of vain glory, or may correct what he has written with the file of more mature examination. Of these, nevertheless, the following have become known to us:

On the Method of the Duel, one book. On Engines of War, one book. On the Care of Horses and Soldiers, one book. Certain orations.

Moreover, he has published many letters both to me and to others; from these, how much he is capable of, both in learning and in eloquence and in experience of many matters, is readily perceived by anyone who has read them. He is renowned in manhood in the city of Speyer, intent upon sacred letters and writing various things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear] John the Venetian, of the Carthusian order, of the house of Saint Andrew the Apostle de Littore near Venice: a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent, devout in life and conduct, and an eminent cultivator of regular observance. He wrote little works for the instruction of the simple, not to be despised, by which he made his name known. Among these there is an excellent work, which he entitled:

Know Thyself, three books. On Patience and Humility, one book. The Mirror of the Dying, five books. The Crown of Old Men also, one book. Various sermons, one book. Several devout letters, one book. And certain other things.

He flourished at Venice under Emperor Frederick III and Pope Sixtus IV, and completed the works written above in the year of the Lord 1480, in the thirteenth indiction. And I am uncertain whether he is still living.

[unclear] John of Muhlbach, German by nationality: a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and also not ignorant of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech. Formerly, in the university of Erfurt, he taught theology gloriously for a long time, and instructed very many pupils in that faculty. He wrote several distinguished little works, in which he exercised his talent magnificently and commended knowledge of himself to posterity. Among these he ordinarily lectured:

On the Epistles of Paul, one book. Various sermons, one book. In Praise of Saint Jerome, one book. Various questions. And certain other things.

He is renowned at Erfurt, old and weak, a prebendary in the monastery of Saint Peter, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

[unclear] John of Artundine, German by nationality, bishop of [Usbita?], of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, vicar in pontificals of David of Burgundy, bishop of Utrecht; a man learned in the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular philosophy, an excellent preacher of sermons, subtle in talent, distinguished in life and conduct. He wrote many distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these the following are reported:

A notable lecture on the Book of Wisdom, one book. On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, one book. On Be

The Abbot of Sponheim.

On “Blessed are the undefiled,” sermons, one book. Sermons on the season, one book. Sermons on the saints, one book. And certain other works.

He flourished at Utrecht under Frederick III, emperor, and Pope Innocent VIII, in the year of the Lord 1490. And I believe that he is still living.

Georgius Valla of Piacenza, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, rhetorician, and very celebrated poet, excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech, who now adorns all Italy with his learning, teaches both languages most flourishingly at Venice; he wrote many distinguished volumes, by whose elegance and usefulness he may deservedly feel that all learned men are indebted and obliged to him. Of these the following are extant:

On orthography, two books. On the quantity of syllables, one book. On the figures of orators and poets, one book. On Cicero, On the Universe, one book. On the same author, On Fate, one book. [unclear] On the Topics, a book of the same author, one book. “Long since foreseen by me” [incipit]. On the Rhetoric to Herennius, one book. On Juvenal, one book.

Also of the very acute Josephus, On the Resurrection. Also the book of Brisso on dialectic. Moreover the treatise of Galen the physician on the sects of physicians. The same author’s Introduction to Medicine. Also four books of the Problems of Allendrus. And many other works.

Johannes Camerarius of Dalburg, bishop of Worms, German by nation, a very celebrated jurist, most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, once a hearer of Rudolf Agricola, most skilled in both languages, a very distinguished rhetorician and poet, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, notable for much experience of affairs, magnificently illustrating the nobility of his family by his character and learning, has written and is writing, both in verse and in prose, certain little works of excellent talent, which he has not yet allowed to come to light, because, being occupied with the affairs of the commonwealth, he has not been able to bring them so far to completion as had been his intention. Yet some of these have become known to us:

A Sapphic poem On the Death of Rudolf Agricola, one book. Also On Coinage, one book. An Oration before Pope Innocent VIII, one book. Various poems and orations. And several most elegant letters.

He is distinguished today, in his manly age, in the chair of the church of Worms, a bishop worthy of God, and he is composing various works, under Maximilian, most clement king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we are writing these things concerning him, 1494.

Baptista Guarinus of Verona, son of the most learned man Guarinus, whom we mentioned in his proper place, a man certainly not inferior to his father, but most learned in every literature and discipline of the liberal arts, a philosopher, orator, and poet most celebrated among all, most skilled in the Greek and Latin tongues and very eloquent in both, wrote and translated many distinguished little works, by which he commends the force and keenness of his almost divine intellect both to those present and to posterity. Of these the following are reported:

A very beautiful work of dialogues On the Sect of Epicurus, one book. On the Order of Teaching, one book. [unclear] On Governing a Kingdom, one book. On the Letters of Cicero, one book. On Ovid’s Fasti, one book. On Lucan’s Pharsalia, one book. On the poet Catullus, one book. Letters to various persons, [four?] books. Also several orations, one book. And poems of various kinds.

He translated into Latin the following: from Xenophon, the Praise of Agesilaus, which he also dedicated to the elder Ermolao Barbaro, bishop of Verona. Also certain orations of Demosthenes and of Dio the historian. But also some prayers of Gregory Nazianzen to Christ and Mary. And

The Abbot of Sponheim.

And he published and translated many other works, which have not come to my knowledge. He is renowned down to the present day at Ferrara, where, succeeding his father, he has now for thirty-three years taught both languages most flourishingly, and writes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, the twelfth indiction. He himself has a son learned in the Greek and Latin language, following his ancestral discipline.

Angelo Poliziano, a man skilled and most learned in every respect, a celebrated grammarian, philosopher, orator, and distinguished poet, perfectly instructed in Greek and Latin eloquence, excellent in talent, who for a long time illuminated Italy by his learning and teaching, wrote various illustrious volumes, by which he commended the memory of his name to posterity. Among them the following are reported:

Certain Centuries, one book.

On Errors of the Latin Language, one book.

Various letters to diverse persons, two books.

And he is said to have written certain other things, which have not come to my knowledge. He dared to present Homer’s Iliad in verse for Latins to read. He is still renowned in Italy, as I have heard, writing various works, under the king of the Romans Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Baptista Mantuanus, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures, second to none in knowledge of secular letters, doctor of sacred theology, distinguished philosopher, very celebrated poet and orator, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, an ornament of the Latin language, a renowned interpreter of Greek, excelling in verse and prose, wrote in both styles many excellent volumes, by which he acquired for his name a celebrated reputation throughout the whole Christian world. Among these the following are reported:

To his father:

On the Blessed Life, a dialogue, one book. “Brother Baptista, to Peter …”

Suburbanum, on the Bucolics, two books. “Faustus approaches the fields …”

The life of Parthenice, three books. “Holy [Palestine?] …”

On Saint Catherine, one book. “[unclear] having begun [unclear] …”

The life of Albert the Carmelite, in Sapphic meter, one book. “Greatest of pontiffs …”

On the Calamity of His Times, one book. “The month of August returns …”

Panegyric of Robert, one book. “We are forced by the evils of this …”

A Dream Concerning the Same, one book. “The ancients [marked?] the demigods …”

To Falco, of epigrams, one book. “Greatest worshipper of justice …”

Consolation on Death, one book. “I owe it, but cares prevent …”

Delights of the Sacred Font [unclear]. “Delights of the sacred font …”

On Contempt of Death, one book. “Why do you grieve, and fear fate …”

Against Foul-Mouthed Poets, one book. “There are those to whom eloquence is given …”

On the Conquest of Granada, four books.

On Patience, in prose, one book.

On the Origin of Religions, one book.

Apology for Brother Peter, five books.

Introduction to the Subtle Scotus, one book.

Most elegant orations, one book.

Many letters to diverse persons, one book.

Poems of various kinds.

And many other things.

He is still living in Italy, everywhere named with a very celebrated reputation, and is writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we completed these things, 1494.

Johannes Bertram of Neuenburg, German by nation, formerly a pupil of Georgius Molitoris of Neuenburg, a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular philosophy, distinguished in talent, scholastic in speech, first at Erfurt and then in the school of Mainz publicly teaching theology and instructing many, wrote in that faculty certain illustrious little works, by which he made his name known. Among these there is a large work:

On the Prologue of the Bible, one book. “As I was thinking in [unclear] …”

Many addresses to the clergy, one book.

On the Value of Masses, one book. “Most reverend in Christ …”

Various questions.

And certain other things.

He is renowned in his manly age in the school of Mainz, teaching theology in ordinary course and composing various works, under the most illustrious Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Robert Gaguin, French by nation, minister general of the Order of the Holy Trinity, distinguished doctor of decrees, and most learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular letters, a renowned poet and a most eloquent orator, who often rendered the Italians stupefied by his eloquence, excellent in talent, devout in life and conduct, wrote in both kinds many illustrious little works, by which he made his name known far and wide. Laurentius Bonicontrius, an eminent philosopher and astronomer, and excellently learned also in the other disciplines of the liberal arts, outstanding in intellect and distinguished in eloquence, strong in verse and prose, is said to have produced many splendid little works, by which he transmitted his name to the knowledge of many; but I have not yet been able to see any of them. His notable work over the cycle of the year is said to be:

The Fasti, with preliminary notes, 1 book.

And certain commentaries.

And certain other things.

He is still living in Italy, writing many and various works, both in verse and in prose, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Sermons to the people, 1 book.

The Abbot of Sponheim.

Various orations to the clergy, one book. And certain other things.

At great expense and with long labor he collected the works of Johannes Gerson, many of which he at last brought to us from France, dividing them into three parts in a very fine order, and compiling a very useful table; he gave that whole work to the press. He is still living in the German city of Strasbourg, and composes various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Johannes Picus, an Italian by nation, count of Mirandola, lord of Concordia, a man most devoted to every kind of good literature, and, just as most noble in distinguished blood, so also in almost divine talent, surrounded by a great household throng trained in all sorts of arts, with whom he exercises himself in the arena of letters and studies, Latin as well as Hebrew and Greek; most worthy and deserving, one whose journey the Muses should follow; the most learned philosopher of our age and a very keen disputant: he wrote, in a most elegant style, some works which our age will both approve and, above all, admire, by which he has not unworthily made the memory of his glorious name everlasting. Of these there are extant the works that have already appeared:

The Heptaplus on the beginning of Genesis. Likewise, nine hundred philosophical conclusions. An apology. Likewise, on the Psalms, one book. And several other works which have not yet presented themselves to our sight.

He is still living today among the Italians, amid the flock of his talented young men, and he does not cease either to write higher things or to do good to posterity, under Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, and Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Johannes Capnion, otherwise Reuchlin, a German by nation, from the town of Pforzheim in Swabia, an excellent doctor of imperial laws, counselor of the illustrious count Eberhard of Württemberg, both most eloquent and wholly upright in law and faith, a most diligent investigator of all the most ancient philosophy and literature, a most learned interpreter of the three principal languages, namely Hebrew together with Chaldean, Greek, and likewise Latin; also especially renowned in French and in our more polished vernacular tongue; and most learned both as secretary in divine writings and in secular letters. Indeed, in every kind of learning he is foremost at this time, since for many years he has most earnestly penetrated the secret mysteries of the Greeks and Hebrews.

On Ecclesiastical Writers

Worthy indeed to devote himself to letters alone, and not also to the noisy popular court. For not only Italy, but not even our own age, could set before us anyone equal to so great a man. He wrote a number of works, by which he commended his memory to those now living and to posterity. To the bishop of Worms, Camerarius Dalburg, he wrote a dialogue, in which he explains all the secret, wonder-working words of Greek, Hebrew, and Christian philosophy, which he entitled

Capnion, or On the Wonder-Working Word, five books. On the Preliminary Exercises of the Orator, one book. It is from the ancients. On the Diversity of the Four Idioms of the Greek Language, one book. A funeral oration on the death of Rudolf Agricola. A book of epigrams and elegies, one book. Epistles and scholastic orations, many without number.

Besides these, he translated for our common use many small works from Greek into Latin: Xenophon’s Apology for Socrates; Nestorius the heretic; the Confession of Cyprian; Proclus on the Blessed Virgin; some dialogues of the dead by Lucian; by the same author a dialogue on the council of the gods; the Monomachia of Homer’s Iliad, on the duel of Paris and Menelaus, in the German language, in verse; Epiphanius on the life and death of the prophets; Maximus Tyrius, the Platonic philosopher, in the oration, If God Made Good Things, Whence Do Evils Come? He is living still today, devoted to letters, under King Maximilian and his own prince Eberhard of Württemberg, whose illustrious name that distinguished Capnion makes still more illustrious by his talent, in the year in which we write these things, 1494.

Conradus Leonorius, commonly called de Leonberg, a German by nation, a monk of the monastery of Maulbronn, of the Cistercian order, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally learned in secular subjects, a philosopher, orator, and poet not to be dismissed, skilled, as they say, in the three principal languages, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote some small works in verse and prose, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a volume of

Letters to various persons, one book. Various orations. Many poems. And certain other things.

He is living still today among the Cistercians, and persists in the study he has begun, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

The Abbot of Spanheim.

A poet laureate, also not unacquainted with the divine Scriptures, skilled in both languages, excellent in talent, eloquent in speech, he wrote certain distinguished little works both in verse and in prose, by which he commended the memory of himself to posterity. Of these he recently read the following to me:

To Maximilian, most illustrious King of the Romans, on both rhetorics of Marcus Tullius Cicero, an Epitome, that is, a Breviary, 1 book. On the Praises of Eloquence, 1 book. On the Art of [Versifying?], 1 book. On Composing Letters, 1 book. On the Site of Nuremberg, 1 book. The Sarmatian Pilgrimage, 1 book. Poems, 4 books. Of Loves, which in German are entitled According to the Four Sides, 4 books. A Panegyric to the Duke of Bavaria, 1 book. On the Life of Saint Sebald, 1 poem. The Site of Germany, 1 book. Various Orations, 1 book.

He has published many very elegant letters to various persons in verse and prose, and various epigrams. In cosmography, of which he is very knowledgeable, he has written various works, which we trust will hereafter come to light. He is still living, being thirty-five years of age, and is writing various things under Maximilian, most illustrious King of the Romans, when Alexander VI was supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494.

Petrus Bonomus of Trieste, protonotary of the imperial court, a man very learned in the Latin tongue, both very fluent and very practiced in composing poems of every kind, as though the tuneful Muses poured forth from his storehouse, and for that reason most celebrated by the fame of a great name, wrote very many works in prose and in verse of various kinds. Of these the following are especially extant:

Books of Epigrams. A tireless accumulation of Letters.

Nor does he ever cease writing. He is still living under his king Maximilian, devoted to letters and cultivating his talent with the good arts, in the year in which we write these things, 1494, the twelfth indiction.

Sebastian Ticio, otherwise Brant, a native of Strasbourg, German by nation, an eminent professor of both laws, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in the other disciplines of secular literature, by no means unskilled in poetry, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, outstanding in counsel and action, who by his learning and night-labour wonderfully adorns Basel, a renowned city of Germany, wrote certain little works, both in verse and in prose, of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name well known. Of these the following are extant:

On the Titles of Both Laws, 1 book. A Sapphic Rosary of the divine Mary. In Praise of the Virgin, Enigmas of the Old Testament. He Proves the Virginal Conception Possible. The Wondering of Mary When the Angel Arrived. The Salutation of the Angel. On the Miraculous Places of the Blessed Virgin. The Virginal Compassion. The Consolation of Christ to His Mother. On the Blows Given to Christ. On the Ingratitude of Those Eating Manna. In Praise of Saint Sebastian. The Life of Saint Onuphrius. In Praise of Saint Valentine. In Praise of Saint Ivo. The Life of Saint Bernard. In Praise of the Carthusian Order. On Contempt of the World. Praises of Blessed Christiana near Basel. Against Slanderous Advocates. On the Captivity of King Maximilian. He has moreover compiled, with wonderful art and talent, though in the common and vernacular language, a certain little book which he called the Ship of Narragonia. In it he has so elegantly expressed the cause and root of all folly, censures the morals of men, and gives certain salutary remedies to individuals, that he would rightly have called that work not the book of fools, but rather a divine satire. For I do not know whether anything could be read more wholesome or more pleasant for the needs of our time. They say that he is striving greatly so that in Latin, in verse
