He still lives at Basel, being thirty-six years of age; and printers make very great use of his labor and diligence in adorning their books. For he writes various works under Maximilian, King of the Romans, whom he loves in a singular way; he has composed many poems about him and to him, including, as they say, most delightful secrets, in the year in which we write this, 1494.

Jacob Wimpheling of Schlettstadt, a German by nation, priest of the church of Speyer, a man most learned in divine matters and excellently instructed in secular letters, a very celebrated theologian, philosopher, orator, and the most outstanding poet of all, first at Erfurt and then in the school of Heidelberg publicly expounding philosophy and sacred Scripture, acquired great glory for his learning. A man, I say, most learned in every respect, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, excelling both in verse and in prose, he wrote in both kinds some distinguished little works, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these the following are extant: to Berthold, archbishop of Mainz, a very celebrated work in hexameter and pentameter verse, most elegantly composed, which he entitled On the Threefold Whiteness, one book. [Incipit:] “Our greatest hope...” In Praise of the divine Mary, one book. [Incipit:] “I do not know whether your Theod[unclear]...” Precepts of Rhetoric, one book. An Oration on the Holy Spirit, one book. [Incipit unclear:] “In what way [unclear]...” An Oration to the King of France, one book. [Incipit:] “Eight five-year periods now [unclear]...” On the Art of Poetry, one book. Many poems of various kinds.

He composed many elegant letters, both to me and to others, whose number is uncertain. At the request of Ludwig, bishop of Speyer, he composed an office on the Compassion of the blessed Mary ever virgin, which is solemnly performed every year throughout that same diocese. To this Jacob we long ago dedicated the book On the Luminaries, or Illustrious Men, of Germany.

He lives in manly age, being almost forty-three years old, in the renowned city of Speyer, and writes various works under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Baptista de Salis, of the Order of Friars Minor, of the Genoese province, a man studious and learned in divine Scriptures, excellently instructed both in both laws and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, scholastic in speech, devout in life and conduct, and distinguished in the observance of regular discipline, published certain little works necessary for the instruction of simple priests, by which he spread his name far and wide. Of these there is extant the Summa on Cases, very useful in the forum of conscience, which after the author’s name is called the Summa Baptistiniana, one book. And some other works.

He completed the same Summa under Emperor Frederick III. And he still lives while Frederick’s son Maximilian holds the kingdom, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Egelhard Funk of Schwabach, an East Franconian, German by nation, a learned man and skilled in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, orator, and poet, not ignorant of divine Scriptures and canon law, outstanding in intellect and eloquent in speech, excelling in verse and prose, is said to have fashioned certain little works in both kinds of style, by which he made his name known. In elegiac verse: On the Praise of His Fatherland, one book. On a Ring Given to Him, one book. Various epigrams. And several other works.

He is renowned at Rome as a pleader or advocate in cases, and he composes various works under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

John Langer of Bolkenhain, a priest of Wrocław, a man studious and learned in divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in intellect and eloquent in speech, excelling in verse and prose, worthy of the priesthood in life and conduct, wrote many distinguished little works in both kinds of style, by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a notable work addressed to George de Lapide, lord of Steinau, which he entitled On Revenues and the Commonwealth, one book. [Incipit:] “Today I am oppressed by a great...” Letters to Various People, one book. Many poems. And several other works.

He still lives in Wrocław and writes various works under Maximilian, King of the Romans, and Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Werner Rolevinck of Laer, German by nation, Westphalian by homeland, of the Order of Carthusians, of the house of St. Barbara in Cologne, a man most studious in divine Scriptures and very learned, excellent in intellect, devout in life and conduct, published many distinguished little works, by which he [made] himself useful to those of the present day,

[unclear], and made [him] memorable to future generations. Of these the following are extant:

A large work on all the epistles of Paul, which he entitled The Teaching of Paul, in 14 books. “The teaching of Paul the apostle...” Also On the Life of Paul, in 7 books. “As I was with Moses, so...” On the Value of Masses, 1 book. On the Governance of Princes, 1 book. On the Study of Theology, 1 book. Bundle of Times, 1 book. “Generation...” Paradise of Conscience, 1 book. “The Lord God took the man...” Many sermons, 1 book. And many other things.

I once saw in his cell some small treatises, but several useful ones, whose titles oblivion has now carried from my memory. He is still living in the Carthusian house at Cologne, of advanced age, and writes various works, under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

Arnoldus Bostius, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of Blessed Mary ever Virgin of Mount Carmel, of the convent of Ghent, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, exceptionally well taught in secular letters, a theologian, philosopher, orator, and outstanding poet, keen in intellect, eloquent in speech, devout in life and conduct, of whom several letters to me are extant, wrote in verse and prose many distinguished little works, of which the following are extant: a notable volume composed in verse and prose, in which he clearly shows the prerogative, origin, and progress of his order in view of Marian protection; for this reason he was pleased to entitle it

On the Patronage of Mary, 1 book. “You asked, most distinguished man...” On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusians, 1 book. Against Vincentius of Nieuwpoort, 1 book. “Brother Arnoldus Bostius...” Letters to various persons, 1 book. “How long always...” On the Four Last Things, 1 book. Various poems. And many other things.

He is still living at Ghent in manly age, composing various works, and by his example and writings urging many on to holy studies, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Henricus Euticius, an East Frank, an excellent professor of both branches of medicine, has published many things which he is preparing for posterity. Also, in diverse and elegant script, a very beautiful little work of poems, which he entitled

Scommata, or Urbane and Witty Jests of Young Men. Several little works in medicine. A satire against sophists and dialecticians, and enemies of the study of humane letters. In praise of the Blessed Virgin. And many other things.

He is still living when we wrote these things, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Etelwolfus de Lapide, a noble man, a German by nation and a Swabian, a man of great talent and a zealous emulator of Roman eloquence, and for that reason having obtained great honor with the Margrave of Brandenburg, wrote to Georgius de Lapide, his maternal uncle, a man most devoted to letters,

On the Praises of Heroes and Illustrious Men, 1 book. A most polished letter collection. And other things, by which he will win great praise for Germany among cultivators of the Roman tongue. He is still living today under King Maximilian, in the year in which we wrote this, 1494.

Rodulphus Langius, a German by nation, canon of the church of Munster in Westphalia, a man studious in the divine Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a philosopher, orator, and very celebrated poet, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, wrote, both in verse and in prose, many distinguished little works, by which he spread his name far and wide with immense glory. Of these the following are extant: To Hermannus Langius, dean of the same church,

On the City of Jerusalem, 2 books. “Once most splendid...” To the dean of Cologne, poems, 1 book. “Whom bright virtue...” On the Siege of the City of Neuss, 1 book. A poem On the Three Magi, 1 book. Several letters to various persons. Also various poems. And many other things.

He is still living, very old, in the city of Munster, composing many things under Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Ebastianus Murrho Colmariensis, natione Teutonicus, pre- sbyter et canonicꝰ in Colmaria, vir in diuinis scripturis studi- osus et eruditus, & in secularibus literis doctissimus, philoso- phus, orator, poeta et cosmographus insignis, trium linguaꝝ, He- braicae, Graecae ac Latinae peritissimus, legum et canonum notitia celebris, in architectura, musica et toto quadruuio nulli secundūt̃ scripsit inter alia, ad Iacobum Vuimphelingum Sletstetēsem (cul- us supra meminimus) breue, sed per pulchrum, Epitoma de laudibꝰ Germanoꝝ lib.1. In Baptista Mantuani opera lib.1. Epistolas plures ad diuersos. Et quaedam alia. Viuit hodie in Colmaria, vbi canonicus est, & varia cōscribit, quae indies publicanda speramus, sub Maximiliano Romanorum re- ge, anno domini quo nos ista scripsimus, 1494. Crolus Phernādus, natione Teutonico, Brugis oppido Flan- driae ortus, à parua aetate captus oculis, & ob id elementorũ quoqƺ penitus ignarus, tantum sui miraculum praebet, vt ve- lut alter Homerus, poeta, musicus, philosophus et orator celeberri- mus euaf̃erit, diuinarum quoqƺ scripturarum sagacissimus inter- pres, carmine excellens et profa, ingenio subtilis, eloquio difertus, vita et conuerfatione integerrimus, qui à rege Gallorum publico et amp; perpetuo donatus stipendio, in celebrerrimo gymnasio Parisieñ multo tēpore literas humanitatis egregie docuit, &amp; authores com- plures pulcherrime exposuit. Demum contemptis omnibus, mun dum cum suis stipēdijs deseruit, & ante biennium ferme ordinem diui patris nostri Benedicti intrauit, in monasterio probe reforma to, quod Cafale Benedictum appellatur, situm in quadā sylua den- fissima, decem à Bituricensi ciuitate ferme millibus distāte, in quo vfꝙ hodie perfeuerat, magno feruens zelo animaꝝ, adeo vt dispen satione apostolica Leuita ordinatus, verbū Dei cum maximo oīm fructu et admiratione publice praedicet, scripsit tam metro ꝗ̃ psa multa praeclara volumina, qƺbus nomen suum posteritati cōmanda uit. In decertationẽ metricam Ruperti Gaguini de purissima con ceptione facrae Dei genitricis et virginis Mariae, aduerfus Vincen- tium de Castronouo ordinis Praedicatorum, opus elegātissimum, Commentariorũ lib.1. Nõ ambigimꝰ ab Apl̄o Laudes ordinis Carmelitarum lib.1. Dum tela vertit Parthꝰ Oda- 392 DE SCRIPTORIBVS ECCLES. Odarum in laudem Christi lib.4. De conceptione contra Vincentium lib.I. Carmen iambicũ de eadem lib.I. Orationẽ de cõceptione, ad Carthusiẽ lib.I. De sancta Catharina orationem lib.I. Epistolarum multarum lib.Z. Carmina ferme innumera lib.I. Elegias de contemptu mundi lib.I. Et alia multa. Viuit hodie caecus, sed doctissimus, in praefato coenobio, multa ac varia cõponens, sub Maximiliano Rom.rege, summo pontifice Alexando 6. anno dñi qͦ ista scripsimus, I494. indictione etz. I Ohannes Phernãdus, frater praedicti Caroli, natione ipse Teutonicus, vir vnde cunque doctissimus philosophus, orator poeta celeberrimus, diuinarum scripturarum nō ignarus, ingeniꝰ subtilis difertus eloquio, quem rex Gallorũ perpetuo stipendio donans, fitibi in musicum desumptis scripsit tam metro ꝗ̃ prosa multa vtilia deuotioni congrua opuscula, quibus nomen suū ad multoꝝ notitiā deduxit, E ꝙbus extant subiecta: De S.Iohanne Baptista lib.I. H Ieronymus Donatus, patritius Venetus, vir clarissimus, in diuinis scripturis studiosus, in secularibus literis eruditiffimus, vtriusque linguae celeberrimus interpres, ingenio excellēs difertꝰ eloquio, qui licet vxoris filiorum cura iam difftrahatur, mirabili tamen diligentia incredibili studio feruet litteraꝝ, mul ta indies scribens, e Gręco multa transferens: quae si alius, etiā om̃i cura solutus, conderet, posset esse miraculo. E ꝙibus extant: Oratio ad regem Lusitaniae lib.I. Orationes quoque variae lib.I. Epi-

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Sebastian Murrho of Colmar, a German by nation, priest and canon in Colmar, a man zealous and learned in the divine Scriptures, and most learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, orator, poet, and cosmographer, most skilled in the three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, renowned for his knowledge of laws and canons, second to none in architecture, music, and the whole quadrivium, wrote, among other things, to Jakob Wimpheling of Sélestat, whom we mentioned above, a brief but very beautiful work:

An epitome on the praises of the Germans, 1 book. On the works of Baptista Mantuanus, 1 book. Several letters to various persons. And certain other things.

He lives today in Colmar, where he is a canon, and is writing various works, which we hope will be published day by day, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Carolus Fernandus, a German by nation, born at Bruges, a town of Flanders, deprived of sight from early childhood, and for that reason utterly ignorant even of the elements of learning, displays so great a marvel of himself that, like another Homer, he has become a most celebrated poet, musician, philosopher, and orator, also a most acute interpreter of the divine Scriptures, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, most upright in life and conduct. Having been granted a public and perpetual stipend by the king of the French, he taught humane letters excellently for a long time in the very celebrated school of Paris, and gave most beautiful expositions of numerous authors. At length, having despised everything, he abandoned the world together with its stipends, and almost two years ago entered the order of our holy father Benedict, in a well-reformed monastery called Casale Benedictum, situated in a certain very dense wood, about ten miles distant from the city of Bourges. In it he perseveres to this day, burning with great zeal for souls, so much so that, ordained deacon by apostolic dispensation, he publicly preaches the word of God with the greatest fruit and admiration of all. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, many excellent volumes, by which he commended his name to posterity. On the metrical contest of Robert Gaguin concerning the most pure conception of the holy Mother of God and Virgin Mary, against Vincent de Castronovo of the Order of Preachers, a most elegant work:

Commentaries, 1 book. “We do not doubt from the Apostle...” Praises of the Order of Carmelites, 1 book. “While the Parthian turns his weapons...”

Concerning Ecclesiastical Writers.

Odes in praise of Christ, 4 books. On the conception against Vincent, 1 book. An iambic poem on the same subject, 1 book. An oration on the conception, to the Carthusian, 1 book. An oration on Saint Catherine, 1 book. Many letters, 2 books. Almost innumerable poems, 1 book. Elegies on contempt of the world, 1 book. And many other things.

He lives today blind, but most learned, in the aforesaid monastery, composing many and various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494, in the [unclear] indiction.

Johannes Fernandus, brother of the aforesaid Carolus, himself a German by nation, a man most learned in every respect, a philosopher, a very celebrated orator and poet, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech. The king of the French, granting him a perpetual stipend, took him into his service as a musician. He wrote, both in meter and in prose, many useful little works suited to devotion, by which he brought his name to the knowledge of many. Of these the following are extant:

On Saint John the Baptist, 1 book. “With what fitting plectrum, what...” Many various orations, 1 book. Letters to various persons, 1 book. Several poems and epigrams. And many other things.

He also wrote the Hours of the Holy Cross and of the compassion of Saint Mary the Virgin in elegant verse, which, recently printed at Paris, are in circulation.

He lives to this day with the king of France, in the highest esteem, and composes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Hieronymus Donatus, a Venetian patrician, a very distinguished man, zealous in the divine Scriptures, most learned in secular letters, a very celebrated interpreter of both languages, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech. Although he is now distracted by care for wife and children, nevertheless with wonderful diligence and incredible zeal for letters he is fervent, writing many things day by day, translating many from Greek; if another man, even released from every care, produced these, he could be regarded as a marvel. Of these there are extant:

An oration to the king of Portugal, 1 book. Various orations also, 1 book. Letters—

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Of letters to various persons, one book. And many other things. He translated into Latin John Damascene on the immaculate mysteries; also Dionysius on the divine names, and certain letters of his; also the volume On the Soul by Alexander of Aphrodisias the philosopher; and many other things.

He lives to this day at Venice, thirty-seven years old, writing and translating various works, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Jodocus Badius of Ghent, a German by nation, a man most learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, rhetorician, and most distinguished poet, excellent in intellect, eloquent in speech, who formerly at Ferrara heard Baptista Guarinus teaching Greek letters and in that science also became learned, now adorns Lyons with his learning, reads the poets publicly and privately, instructs several sons of magnates, and has written in verse many distinguished little works, of which the following are extant: a notable metrical work against the vices, which he entitled

The Moral Wood, one book. And many other things. Also Against Vincentius, one book. “Unhappy Vincentius, which …” The Psalter of Mary in sapphics, one book. “What the chorus of bards …” Also On Grammar, one book. Several epigrams, one book. Various letters.

He lives to this day, thirty-two years old, composing many different things under Maximilian, the renowned king, in the year of the Lord 1492, indiction 12.

Elias Regnier, a very celebrated jurist, excellently learned both in the divine Scriptures and in secular philosophy, subtle in intellect, distinguished in speech, cautious in counsel, who for a long time publicly taught law in the university of Poitiers, wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these I have seen only the following: a celebrated work which contains

Cases of the Sixth Book of the Decretals, one book. “Boniface VIII [unclear] …” Cases of the Clementines, one book. “John, bishop [unclear] …”

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He is still living in the University of Poitiers, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Rutgerus Venray, a German by nation, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine, of the monastery of the divine apostle Peter, which, situated not far from Worms, is called Heyne, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature, practiced in metre and prose, wrote in both kinds certain little works not to be despised, of which the following are extant: a Tetralogue, which he entitled

On the Instruction of Children, two books. “When boys [unclear] …” On the Inquiry into the Blessed Life, two books. “In the year in which Ceres [unclear] …” Of Hymns on Saint Mary, two books. “Behold, to the Mother of God Mary …” On the Varied Appearance of Letters, two books. “Although, excellent Peter …” On a Marvelous Thing, two books. “For knowing [unclear] in verse …” On New Things, two books. “I say that very many things [unclear] …” On the Kinds of Metres, one book. “Most familiarly in [unclear] …” On the Accents of the Latins, two books. “This Tetralogue, which on …” A Panegyric to Me, one book. “To the reverend [unclear] …” Various epigrams. And certain other things.

I hear that he is fashioning for me a work on the calamities of these times, which I have not yet seen.

He has written very many letters, both to me and to others, in verse and in prose, not inelegant.

He lives to this day and composes various things, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Jodocus Beisselius, patrician of the royal city of Aachen, a German by nation, a man devoted to the holy Scriptures and most learned in secular letters, a distinguished philosopher, fluent orator, and notable poet, who, although he is necessarily distracted by care for his wife and household property, nevertheless burns with incredible love for the Scriptures, writing and composing many things daily, by which he spreads his name everywhere with great glory. Of these the following are extant: a most beautiful dialogue addressed to Hermolaus Barbarus, in the manner of the Platonists,

On the Best Kind of Musicians, one book. “I have led you, O Hermolaus …” On Christian Ambition, one book. “And if all things are available to you …” Epitome of The Spur of Love, one book. “Since through these, Christ [unclear] …” On the Rosy Crown of Mary, one book. “The most august rosy …” A Metrical Rosary, one book. “Whoever loves the rosy …” On the Mysteries of the Rosary, one book. “Go forth, daughters of Sion …” A Rosary on the Sacrament of the Altar, one book. “Beneath this small bread …” The Deeds of the Flemings, one book. The Abbot of Spanheim

He lives to this day at Aachen, a most distinguished interpreter of both laws, and is writing various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Hieronymus Balbus, a man of very celebrated reputation, and excellently learned in all the disciplines of the liberal arts, a distinguished philosopher and eloquent rhetorician, excellent in verse and prose, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, who by teaching, reading publicly, and writing earned great glory among the French and the Parisians, wrote certain distinguished little works of his talent, by which he commended his name to posterity. Of these I have so far seen only a volume seasoned with great wit of eloquence, in which he responds to the slanders of a certain Guillaume Tardif, a rhetorician, in the manner of a dialogue, under the names of himself, Charles Fernand, Pierre Cohard, and the assailant himself; to it he gave the title The Glorious Rhetorician, one book.

Among those offices by which

I have seen nothing of the others.

He still lives in France, writing and composing various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Aegidius Nettelet, dean of the church of Cambrai, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, and not ignorant of secular literature, outstanding in talent, distinguished in life and conduct, and conspicuous for singular devotion, published certain distinguished volumes, by which he made his name known. Of these there exists a very celebrated work, necessary for every estate, which with remarkable industry and very beautiful sequence he gathered into one from the epistles of St. Jerome the priest, four books.

The rest are unknown to me.

He lives to this day in the city of Cambrai, very celebrated for life and learning, and is composing various works, under Maximilian, the most distinguished king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Philippus Callimachus, Italian by nation, Florentine by homeland, secretary of the king of Poland, most learned in every respect, a distinguished philosopher, eloquent orator, and notable poet, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, is said to have produced many distinguished little works, by which he left remembrance of himself to posterity. Of their number the following are reported: A notable work on the deeds of the impious king Attila, which he entitled Attila, one book.

Polish History against the Turk, one book.

The Abbot of Spanheim

On Ecclesiastical Writers

On the Customs of the Tartars, one book. Love Poems in Various Metres, one book.

And very many others.

He lives to this day with the king of Poland, in the highest esteem, and writes various works, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1490, the twelfth indiction.

Paulus Niauis, German by nation, a man excellently learned in humane letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a very celebrated philosopher and rhetorician, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, by teaching and writing various things acquired great fame for his name in the gymnasium of Leipzig. For he wrote certain distinguished little works, the reading of which should not be despised. Of these the following are reported: A little work for religious novices,

On Instruction in Latinizing, one book. “When I have very often thought”

The Vision of a Certain Hermit, one book. “A great grove clearly”

The Colors of the Art of Rhetoric, one book. “Once you wished, eleg...”

The Dialogue of the Idiot, one book. “When I often recalled, nu...”

Short Formal Letters, one book. “A great force is wont”

Letters to the Same, of Moderate Length, one book. “I promised, good man”

Also Longer Letters, one book. “I conceive great and in...”

And certain others.

He lives to this day in Germany, composing various works, under Maximilian, the most illustrious king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Bohuslaus of Hassenstein, German by nation, a noble man and most learned in every respect, a notable orator and poet, who, contrary to the custom of the other nobles of this age, both handles arms and cultivates letters with remarkable zeal; he fosters and celebrates them, so that, like a second Pliny the Younger, even while serving as a soldier he composes books and poems. He wrote certain distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he made his name known. Of these the following exist: A distinguished work on the proper inventions of the Germans and Italians, one book.

Also Poems, one book.

Various letters.

And very many others.

He lives to this day in his castle Hassenstein, and writes various works, under Maximilian, the most excellent king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494, the twelfth indiction.

Abbot of Spanheim.

Henricus Northeimensis, German by nationality, a man studious and learned in secular letters, not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, subtle in talent, eloquent in speech, excellent in verse and prose, wrote certain little works of reading not to be despised, by which he commended his name to posterity with glory. Of these I have seen only that distinguished work which he composed in verse and prose for Frederick, margrave of Meissen and duke of Saxony, entitled Dinetromachia:

On the conflict of virtues and vices, one book. “Tu mea laurigeros.”

Concerning the rest that he composed, nothing has come to my knowledge. He lives even to this day, writing various things, under Maximilian, most illustrious king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Aquinus, of the order of the Friars Preachers, deriving the origin of his life from Sweden, a man studious in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular literature, a celebrated philosopher, a distinguished mathematician, excellent in talent, polished in speech, in imitation of Boethius wrote a most commendable work on the proportions of numbers and sounds, one book.

Certain letters.

And certain other things.

He lives to this day, held in esteem by Otto, duke of Bavaria; he writes various things, under Maximilian, most unconquered king, in the year of the Lord 1494, the twelfth indiction.

Albertus de Prusa, Polish by nationality, a member of the college of the University of Cracow, a man studious and learned in the divine writings, also excellently instructed in secular letters, a theologian, philosopher, and distinguished astronomer, praised in verse by Conrad Celtis for his knowledge of the stars, outstanding in talent and renowned in eloquence, wrote several little works of reading not to be despised, by which he made his name known. But few of them have come to my knowledge.

On the Theoricae of Georgius Burbachius, one book of commentaries.

On the ephemerides of Konigsperg, one book.

And certain other things.

He is still living in the University of Cracow, composing various things under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, the twelfth indiction.

On Ecclesiastical Writers.

[unclear]

Theodericus de Ofenbruck, German by nationality, of the order of the Friars Minor of the province of Cologne, a man practiced in the divine Scriptures, a most famous declaimer of popular sermons, whose life all who know him proclaim at this time to be most holy: in delivering sermons to the people he is illumined by God with such grace, and in short moves his hearers with such compunction and sweetness, that he has had no equal among the Germans. Hence he has also been appointed general preacher throughout the whole province. Recently, when he was with me at Cologne, he read to me a notable little work, suited to devotion, which he had composed at the request of Hermann, archbishop of Cologne:

On the Passion of the Lord, one book.

Manual for simple people, one book. “Quia sicut Augustin.”

On interior exercise, one book. “Qui perseveraverit.”

And certain other things.

He is still living in the province of Cologne, vigorously applying himself to the office he has begun, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1494.

[unclear]

Bartholomaeus Coloniensis, German by nationality, a man excellently learned in secular letters, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, a distinguished philosopher and poet, whose poems even the most learned poets both admire and extol with praises, wrote in both styles some little works worthy of celebration, by which he made his name known. Of these I have so far seen only a little work on the praises of philosophy, composed in verse, which he entitled:

Sylva of poems, one book. “Cur Plutoni aurum prae.”

Defecta Diogenis, one book. “Quisquis avet cynice.”

A mythological letter.

Of the others I have seen nothing.

He lives to this day at Deventer, composing various things, under King Maximilian and Pope Alexander, supreme pontiff, the sixth, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

[unclear]

Johannes Thurotz, a Pannonian, a man studious and practiced in secular letters, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent and renowned in speech, is said to have written some little works by which he made his name known. Of these there is extant a volume not to be rejected, which he assembled with much industry, containing:

A Chronicle of Hungary, one book. “Iugi ocio his annis no.”

And certain other things.

Abbot of Sponheim.

He is said still to be living and to be composing various works under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Hieronymus of Padua, an Italian by nation, a man devoted to the divine Scriptures and remarkably learned in secular letters, a philosopher and distinguished poet, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote certain little works of no contemptible reading, by which he commended his memory to posterity. Of these there is extant a very fine little book, entitled Iesuida, addressed to Petrus Donatus, bishop of the city of Padua, in verse, one book: “Greatest of the heavenly ones, [unclear].”

Other works of his are also extant.

He is said still to be living and to be composing various works under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Franciscus Mataracius of Perugia, a man learned in secular letters and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, a philosopher, orator, and most celebrated poet, and highly skilled in both languages, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote certain distinguished little works, by which he left his memory to posterity. Of these there is extant a very celebrated little work addressed to the young Petrus Paulus Cornelius, On Composing Verses, one book: “The poetic art the ancients...”

Letters to various persons, one book.

Many epigrams.

And several other works.

He flourished under Emperor Frederick and Pope Sixtus IV.

Dominicus Mancinus, a man very learned in the divine writings and remarkably learned in secular letters, excellent in verse and prose, subtle in talent and distinguished in eloquence, wrote certain approved little works, by which he made his name known. Of these I have read only that treatise which he composed in elegant verse, On the Passion of the Lord, one book: “Not the praises of men, nor...”

He also wrote other works.

He is said still to be living and to be writing various things under Maximilian, most noble king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote these things, 1494.

Ludovicus Brunus, an Italian by nation, from the marquisate of Montferrat, a man most learned in every respect, a professor of each law and a very celebrated interpreter, a laureate poet, a distinguished philosopher and orator, and not ignorant of the divine Scriptures, excellent in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote many distinguished little works in both kinds of writing, but I do not remember that any of them came into our hands except that treatise which he set out in elegant verse, On the Coronation of King Maximilian, one book: “Holy through the eternal [unclear].”

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He is still living; he is said to be writing various works under the same King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Jacobus Sprenger, a German by nation, of the Order of Friars Preachers, provincial of Cologne, a man studiously learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, outstanding in talent, clear in eloquence; since he had previously been appointed by Pope Innocent VIII as inquisitor of heretical depravity, together with Henricus Institoris, a theologian of the same order, he gathered together and wrote, with the help of the same colleague, a volume against witches, those little women who are instruments of the devil, for the precaution of the simple, which he entitled The Hammer of Witches, three books: “Whether to assert [unclear] witch...”

If he wrote anything further, I do not know.

He is still living today in his convent at Cologne, under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we wrote this, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

Johannes Tholofus, a German by nation, originating from East Francia, which is called Franconia, canon of Regensburg, provost of Forchheim, a man studiously learned in the divine Scriptures, remarkably learned in secular letters, a distinguished doctor of pontifical law, an astronomer, cosmographer, and most celebrated poet, subtle in talent and eloquent in speech, wrote certain distinguished little works, both in verse and in prose, by which he commended his name to posterity. But I do not remember that any of them came into our hands. Those who have known the man well report that there are, by him, on various subjects:

Elegant Letters, one book.

And certain works on mathematics.

And certain other works.

He is still living today in the city of Regensburg in the province of the Norici, and is writing various works; he is a very great patron of learned men, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and Pope Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord 1493, in the twelfth indiction.

[unclear], a very distinguished interpreter, outstanding in talent and eloquent in speech, writes various things, playing in verse and prose, by which he has made his name known far and wide. Many of his very elegant poems are extant here and there on diverse things and subjects.

Of poems addressed to me, one book. “To the reverend father in Christ ...” Also many letters. He has composed for me one book on Saint Anne. In addition he has written, and writes daily, many other things to be published.

He lives to this day at Heidelberg, tutor of young princes, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord in which we composed these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

Johannes of Düsseldorf, a German by nation, of the order of the brothers of blessed Mary ever virgin of Mount Carmel, prior of Strasbourg, a man studious and learned in the divine Scriptures, not ignorant of secular philosophy, a very celebrated interpreter of the theological faculty, outstanding in talent and illustrious in life, is said to write many things, but to conceal them. I have seen certain treatises of his, whose titles I have not now been able to recall to memory.

He lives to this day at Strasbourg, under Maximilian, most merciful king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord in which we write these things, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

Theodericus Ulsenius, a Frisian man, of singular learning and skill in poetry and oratory, has published some things, among which there are extant his

Polished elegies. And certain epigrams. And many other things, which will come down to posterity.

He is still living under Maximilian, king of the Romans, in the year of the Lord 1494.

Hartmann Schedel of Nuremberg, a German by nation, doctor of arts and medicine, not ignorant also of the divine Scriptures, outstanding in talent and distinguished in eloquence, compiled and wrote, among other little works of his talent, adding some things from Jacobus of Bergamo and other historiographers, especially on the affairs of the Germans, a large and notable work, which contains

Histories of the times, one book.

Of the rest I have seen nothing.

He lives to this day at Nuremberg, under King Maximilian, in the year of the Lord 1494.

402 On Ecclesiastical Writers

Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin the bishop, in Spanheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict, of the diocese of Mainz, a German by nation, a Mosellan by homeland, born from the village of Trittenheim in the diocese of Trier: although I am not worthy that my name should be placed among the ecclesiastical writers, on account of the poverty of my talent, nevertheless, compelled by urging friends, I have been forced at the end of this catalogue to place the titles and beginnings of my own lucubrations also, after the example of the holy fathers Jerome, Gennadius, Honorius, priest of Autun, and Sigebert, monk of Gembloux, who also placed themselves at the end of their treatises published on these same matters. I have therefore written, besides this work, also the following. And first, by command of the presidents of the general chapter, I abridged

The statutes of the same chapter, one book. On the visitation of monks, one book. On the manner of holding a chapter, two books. On the Rule of Saint Benedict, two books. An exhortation to monks, two books. On temptations, two books. On the life of priests, one book. On the vice of ownership, one book. On the misery of this life, one book. On the ruin of our order, one book. On the illustrious men of our order, four books. Praises of the Carmelite order, two books. On the praise of scribes, one book. On the luminaries of Germany, one book. Letters to various persons, one book. On Saint Anne, one book. Various sermons, one book.

As for conferences, whether delivered in general chapters, or in observantial ones, or elsewhere, they are without fixed number; some are preserved, some have been removed. These, then, are the works, besides those which are still unfinished in my hands, which I presently recall having written, in the thirty-fourth year of my age, the tenth of my assumption of the office of abbot, and the twelfth of my monastic life, under Maximilian, king of the Romans, and the supreme pontiff Alexander VI, in the year of the Lord in which I have now for the third time corrected, enlarged, and completed this catalogue, having labored on it for almost seven years, 1494, in the twelfth indiction.

ABBAS SPANHEMENSIS. 495 PERORATIO. AM nunc igitur post multos tandem labores, operi nostro finem imponamus: quoniam et si multi restant Scriptorum illustrium catalogo digni, nobis tamen impossibile fuit, omnium vel sola nomina iuuenire. Eos vero, quoque certitudinem habere potui, diligenter confignauit: nec quem quam sciēter omisi, cuius opufcula, ingenium et tempora īcirre poutissem. Neque ignoro, quàm multi eruditissimi viri hodie superfint, varia componētes: quorum ego nullam feci mentionem, non qđ eos iudicauerim indignes nostrō Catalogo, sed ꝓpterea qđ opufcula sua vel celare maluerunt, vel non vsgadeo multiplicata funt, vt in notitiam meam venire potuerint, feci quantum potui, nonquantum volui;quippe qui omnes quotquot funt vel vnquam fu-erunt, si licuiset, Scriptores mihi conciliassem. Relinquo pofteris eam prouinciam, vt de sua vena addant, vbi ego fatigatus defliti. Caeterum vos oro, Patres Conscripti, qui coelica regna tenetis, quihunc nostrum Catalogum vestris nominibus, ingenijs et lucubrationibus exornatis, quatenus si vera, si iusta, si digna, si denique grantionibus exornatīs, quatenus si verā, si iūsta, si digne gra ta de vobis scripsimus, omnipotentis Dei clementiā pro nobis exoretis, vt culpas ablatas, veniam tribuat, sanctium propositum confirmet, intellectum illuminet, affectum purificet, participes gaudio-rum vestroque clementer efficiat. Quod si in aliquibus minus quàm res ipsa requirebat, potui mus, veniam nobis o sacratissimi donate:quoniam ficubi erratum est, vitium est ignorantiae, non volūtatis.Vos etiam o clarissimi viri Scriptores, qui adhuc vitam terrenawem mortalem agitis, vos interpello, vos obtestor et oro, si quid minꝰvestris meritis, ingenijs vel lucubrationibus dignum in hoc Catalogo peregi mus, non volūtati, sed imperitiae nostrae adscribatis, veiniam quam petimus, non negantes:quoniam ficubi defecimus, eo rum culpa fuit, qui nobis aliter quàm se res habet, opufcula vestravel ingenia descripferunt. Lectorem deinde huius Catalogi monemus et obfearamus, ne facile cōtra nos moueatūr, si Scriptorumnomina, dignitates, patriami, vel opufcula fecus exarata iuenerit,quàm ipse forfitan alibi legit, cum historiarum transacti temporisdiffonantiam nemo vnquam potuerit conciliare.Nequē nos aliqdscripsimus, quod non multis locis vel testimonijs fuerit comprobante.Verum sicut in principio huius operis professi sumus, libentercedimus opinioni cuiuscunque beneuoli correctoris, quam et ccc ij vee 404 IN ABBATE SPAN. DE SCRIP. veritas solidam, & charitas reddiderit syncerã. Nouissime vero nobis deridendi sunt aemuli, qui more canum ex consuetudine pessima latrantes, omnia damnant, omnia vituperant, omnia lacerant, quae vel ipsi nõ fecerint, vel suis opinionibus inuenerint esse cõtraria. Mox enim vt vel modicum legere coeperint, stoma chantes, il-lud non verum esse dicunt, iudices temerarij prius, quàm examinatores veritatis effectũ. Sed quae nobis causa cum ipsis, qui nihil vituperant nisi bonum, nihil laudant nisi malum? Contemnandi sunt igitur inuidi canes, non docendi. Nos autem etsi displacere maleuolis, existimemus gloriosum, bonis tamen et eruditis viris placuisse, multo gloriosus arbitramur: à quibus, sicubi erratum effet, libenter corripimus: correcti, fructuosi emendamur. Excufet nos amor scripturaꝝ, pro qbus onus graue intrepida ceruice subiuimus. Libri de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis, authore Dn. Iohanne Tritthemio Abbate Spanheimensi, Finis. Augustini, theologus consultissimus, ac totius ordinis generalis Prior, hoc quo nostro tanquam lucifer et quidam fol perfulgudus, suis exquisitissimis declamationibus, & nouo quodã concionandi genere emicuit, ac veluti alter electionis vas mundo oblatus, tantam ingenij vim et docendi robur de se ostendit, vt dice re ausim, nemine̓ in hoc seculo inueniri vn-quam potuisse, qui cum eo exquireret comparari. Erat profectotalis ac tantus, vt nihil ex eo effet in omni politiore disciplina frustra defiderandum. Nam in suis declamationibus ad populum, ita verbis

The Abbot of Spanheim.

Peroration.

Now therefore, after many labors at last, let us set an end to our work; for although many remain who are worthy of the catalogue of illustrious writers, nevertheless it was impossible for us to find even the bare names of them all. Those, however, concerning whom I was able to have certainty, I have diligently recorded; nor have I knowingly omitted anyone whose little works, talent, and times I could have known.

Nor am I unaware how many most learned men survive today, composing various works; of these I have made no mention, not because I judged them unworthy of our catalogue, but because they either preferred to conceal their little works, or they have not been so widely multiplied that they could come to my knowledge. I have done as much as I could, not as much as I wished, since, had it been permitted, I would have brought together for myself all writers, however many there are or ever have been. I leave this province to posterity, that they may add from their own vein where I, wearied, have left off.

Moreover I beseech you, enrolled Fathers, who hold the heavenly kingdoms, who adorn this catalogue of ours with your names, talents, and lucubrations, that if we have written true, just, worthy, and finally pleasing things about you, you may entreat the mercy of almighty God on our behalf, that, our faults being taken away, he may grant pardon, confirm our holy purpose, illuminate our understanding, purify our affection, and mercifully make us sharers in your joys. But if in some matters we have been able to do less than the thing itself required, grant us pardon, O most sacred ones; for wherever there has been error, it is the fault of ignorance, not of will.

You also, O most distinguished men, writers who still live a mortal earthly life, I address you, I adjure you and beg you: if in this catalogue we have done anything less worthy of your merits, talents, or lucubrations, ascribe it not to our will but to our lack of skill, not refusing the pardon we ask; for wherever we have failed, it was the fault of those who described your little works or talents to us otherwise than the matter stands.

Next we admonish and beseech the reader of this catalogue not to be readily moved against us if he finds the names, dignities, native lands, or little works of writers set down otherwise than perhaps he himself has read elsewhere, since no one has ever been able to reconcile the discordance of histories of time past. Nor have we written anything that had not been confirmed in many places or by testimonies. But, as we professed at the beginning of this work, we willingly yield to the opinion of any benevolent corrector, which truth shall have made solid and charity sincere.

Finally, however, we must laugh at our rivals, who, like dogs barking from the worst habit, condemn everything, disparage everything, tear apart everything that they themselves have not made, or that they have found to be contrary to their own opinions. For as soon as they begin to read even a little, grumbling, they say that it is not true, having become rash judges before they are examiners of the truth. But what have we to do with those who disparage nothing but the good, and praise nothing but the bad? Therefore envious dogs are to be despised, not taught. We, however, although we think it glorious to displease the malicious, consider it much more glorious to have pleased good and learned men; by them, wherever there has been error, we are gladly corrected; once corrected, we are fruitfully amended. Let the love of writings excuse us, for whose sake we have taken up a heavy burden with fearless neck.

The End of the Books on Ecclesiastical Writers, by Lord Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

How great, moreover, this man’s learning was, how great the force and majesty of his eloquence, anyone can clearly gather partly from the sermons, partly from the letters and orations most learnedly published by him.

For he wrote various sermons. One book of orations. One book of letters.

He died, with great loss to the Christian commonwealth, in the year of the Lord 1500.

Felinus Sandeus, of the most noble family of the Sandei, a native of Ferrara, a most accomplished doctor of both laws, and not ignorant of the other good letters, first at Ferrara, then at Pisa, in the public academies of those cities, professed canon law to the great admiration of all. Summoned to Rome by Innocent VIII, while he was occupied in the college of the Rota, where difficult affairs of the greatest importance are treated, both there and in the consultations of the supreme pontiff, nevertheless, since he was of almost divine talent and of most accomplished prudence in both laws, he published many little works and commentaries in that field. And these indeed so clearly, so learnedly, so exactly, that he untied all the knots of this discipline, restored obscure matters to the light, and, with right judgment applied, rendered doubtful matters easy and accessible; in this he brought no small assistance to our jurists. What he published is appended:

First, on the books of Gregory’s Decretals. On constitutions. On rescripts. On the office of the ordinary. On majority and obedience. On truce and peace. On joinder of issue. On proofs. On witnesses. On compelled witnesses. On the credibility of instruments. On presumptions. On oath-taking. On exceptions. On prescriptions. On sentences and res judicata. On appeals. On accusations and inquisitions. Additions to the Decree, to the work begun by the abbot. One treatise on the right of patronage. A sermon on plenary indulgence, whose theme is: Today you will be with me in paradise, etc. In history, one little book on the Neapolitan kings. There are also other commentaries of his. He flourished at Rome under Innocent VIII and Alexander VI.

Matthaeus Bossus, a native of Verona, of the order of the canons regular of Blessed Augustine, a man exceptionally learned in every kind of erudition, but still more learned in elegance and gravity of speech, was held in great esteem among all, both because of the office of preaching and teaching, in which he was long engaged, and because of the various works composed by him, in which he so adorned and polished ecclesiastical doctrine with oratorical pigments that you will find nothing more refined or more elegant. He wrote the following little works:

A Dialogue on Enduring Adversities, divided into two books. On Conducting Magistracy and Cultivating Justice, to Giovanni Ludovico Bosso, jurisconsult and golden knight, two books. One book of orations. Books of letters to various persons.

He published certain other things; in all of them, although he overflows with varied learning and is everywhere brilliant, nowhere did he belch forth the smoke of arrogance, but, as befits a religious man, he was everywhere most devoted to holiness and divine wisdom.

He died at Padua in the year of the Lord 1502.

Antonius Cornazanus, a native of Ferrara, a most brilliant orator and poet, so polished, copious, and sweet, especially in poetry, that many think he received poetry from the mouths of angels. For among other things he sang the life and death of the Virgin Mother of God so devoutly, piously, copiously, brilliantly, and holily that all proclaim that the poetry in them is not mortal, but altogether divine. He inscribed and dedicated that work to Hippolyta, queen of the Neapolitans, while she was still a virgin.

He published certain elegies and various poems. He wrote in prose the life of Bartolomeo Colleoni, the great commander of the Venetians. Also very many orations, and certain other things.

Georgius Merula, a native of Alessandria, an orator and philosopher most learned in both languages, always served letters well by teaching and writing. He wrote, in many volumes, the deeds of Ludovico Sforza and of his ancestors.

Commentaries on Juvenal. On Statius and very many others. He published certain centuries. Many books of letters.

He died at Milan in the year of the Lord 1494. Hi-

Jerome of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers, a most ardent declaimer and a man of much learning, was exceedingly erudite; relying on this, he embraced ambition, damnable in religious men, which he ought most earnestly to have strangled in himself. This contagious plague indeed proved to be the cause of his ruin and most bitter death, and no small scandal to his order. For since he attempted many things, presumed much, and raised his horns against the leading men of his profession, he stirred up no small schism throughout all Italy. It could not be extinguished except by the death of his accomplices, a loss indeed to be lamented in so great a man, if he had applied those gifts of mind which he displayed to edification, and not to the ruin and destruction of himself and his own people; since, filled with every kind of learning, he would have brought great aid to Christian letters. Alas, that crafty tempter, going about and always seeking whom he may devour, begrudged us this one man. He wrote one Lenten book, book 1.

A commentary on the penitential Psalms.

He also commented on many prophets.

He also issued a prophecy, in which he foretold many things about this our age, the kingdom, and the disturbance.

At length, condemned under Alexander VI, in the year of salvation 1499, he was burned in the Florentine marketplace with two companions.

Bernardinus Gadolus of Brescia, a Camaldolese abbot, a man of good letters, exceedingly learned in philosophy and canon law, renowned for holiness of life and religion, left us many monuments of his learning, in which he shows himself most erudite. He wrote commentaries on all the books of the Bible.

On fleeing the world and embracing religion, one treatise.

Against pride and ambition.

Also many letters.

And certain other things scattered here and there.

Having ended his life, he is honorably buried in the Camaldolese monastery.

Marius Sanutus, a Venetian patrician, not only a man learned in good letters, but also skilled in administering the commonwealth, was very powerful in eloquence, as can easily be discerned from his little works. For he wrote the following:

Philippus Beroaldus, a Bolognese by birth, most skilled in both languages, and easily the foremost of all grammarians, rhetoricians, and orators of his age, left no ordinary testimonies of his very fertile genius.

Orations delivered in the exposition of various authors.

A panegyric to Lodovico Sforza.

One oration on the marriage of the Bentivoli.

The story of Gisippus and Titus.

Also that of Galesus and Simon.

One proverbial oration.

One little book on the sayings of the seven sages.

Symbols of Pythagoras, book 1.

On the best state, book 1.

On happiness, book 1.

A declamation of the philosopher, physician, and orator.

A declamation of the drunkard, whoremonger, and gambler.

A lamentation on the Lord’s Passion.

A poem on fortune.

A poem on two lovers.

A poem on Cupid, the god of love.

A poem against a slanderous woman.

Various epigrams.

Annotations on Servius; annotations on civil law.

Commentaries on Propertius; on Suetonius.

On the Tusculan Questions; on Apuleius.

Annotations on Titus Livy; on Cicero’s Rhetoric.

On Horace Flaccus; on Persius.

He wrote many other things which have not yet reached us. He died at Bologna, not without great loss to the republic of letters, in the year of the Lord 1510.

Ambrosius Calepinus of Bergamo, of the Order of Saint Augustine, flourished in this age, a most zealous investigator of divine and human letters. Hence by his own industry and great labor he made common to us a very large work, collected from almost countless authors, on the knowledge of words and the interpretation of Greek and Latin prepositions, with the attestation of authors. In it he explained, learnedly enough and elegantly, not only the words that contribute very much to literature and to the knowledge of poets and orators, but also those that pertain to physicians, philosophers, and also ecclesiastical doctors; and, having explained them, he left them to be read in a truer light than in certain other similar books. These certainly brought no small assistance to learned and unlearned alike. For by this it has come about that things which among the barbarians had already become barbarous are made Latin, while those that among the learned were being called into doubt now lie open, the cloud of uncertainty having been dispelled.

419 On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

Petrus Burrus, a Belgian, by country a man of Bruges, canon of Amiens, distinguished in divine and human letters, flourished at Paris under Charles VIII, king of the Franks. There he grew to such renown for good disciplines, virtues, most approved morals, piety, and religion, that very many, and especially the family of the Gandincourts, wished to use this one man alone as teacher for the instruction of their children and of very many other more noble youths. Nor indeed is it at all to be wondered at, since he was one among the few in this our age who taught how to join eloquence, poetry, and the other good arts with wisdom, and professed neither arts without morals nor morals without letters. His works indeed show this; in them you would not know what to admire most: the weight of his very grave and most holy sentiments, or the variety of his style and poetry, or the propriety of things and words, or his skillful joinings, or the charming diction and texture, or the ever-recurring flower and harmony of his verse, or finally hundreds of other ornaments, so that you would rightly say that all the graces, charms, delights, and elegances of speech have been most abundantly granted here, while nevertheless nothing swollen or inflated is observed. Therefore, if this Burrus had written in Quintilian’s time, he certainly would not have said that, of the lyric poets, Horace alone is almost worthy to be read. For this man too is most worthy to be read even by holy nuns. For since he is wholly chaste, which that other is not, and wholly Christian, and sweetly redolent of the Christian religion, he nevertheless rises at times no less than that other, full of delight and grace, and most happily bold in varied figures and words, as it is easy for anyone to discern from his works written below and published. These are the monuments of that most fertile genius:

Odes, 4 books.

Apologues, 1 book.

Hexameters, 1 book.

Elegies, [unclear] books.

Epi-[unclear].

Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition I

One book of Epigrams. Songs on two feasts. On the vigil of the Lord. On the circumcision of the Lord. On fasting. On confession and the Eucharist. On the praise of the cross. On the Lord's resurrection. On the finding of the cross. On Pentecost. On the body of the Lord. On the face of the Lord. On the feast of blessed Mary. There are also certain other works. Moral works. On the advent of the Lord. On the nativity of the Lord. On Epiphany. On the entry into Jerusalem. On the Lord's Supper. On the Lord's Passion. On Easter communion. On the ascension of the Lord. On the Trinity. On the exaltation of the cross. Hymns on all the saints. Not a few letters and prayers. He died at Amiens in the year 1507.

Jacobus Faber Stapulensis, a most celebrated philosopher of our age, the unique ornament of Belgium, indeed of all Gaul, given in our time by a certain divine gift as a remedy for the republic of letters, rescued all parts of philosophy from the murky barbarism of certain sophists. And those things which by now had altogether disdained to speak Latin, and had gone far away from the mind of Aristotle and of the rest who truly philosophize, he restored to their former majesty both of language and of doctrine, with such structure and sequence that nothing is lacking that should be added, and nothing offers itself to be removed without fault; with so great industry, so much art in all his works, so great dignity in speaking, that anyone even moderately learned, together with philosophy, could most richly attain eloquence, which had not been possible before. For he was the first among the Gauls, as Cicero was among the Romans, to join philosophy, still rough and unpolished, with eloquence. For what had previously been wandering as a stranger at Paris he endowed with citizenship. Hence those who are untrained not only in philosophy but also in learning think that they have acquired something, both for judging and for adjudging. For in speaking he is lofty, in his thoughts weighty, in invention refined, in composition careful and exacting, and [unclear] not only his own resources but also those of others. To this one purpose indeed he seems to have been born: to look after the literary [palaestra?], restore the good arts, and bring them back to their ancient splendor. Such is this man's care, such his delight, this the study toward which all my thought directs itself, toward which his mind, toward which his spirit directs itself. So that this might be done more freely, he not only, like Demetrius, gave over to his own people the patrimony, not to be despised, which he had at Etaples, but also cast aside dignities, offices, benefices, and honors,

On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers

honorific and rich, thinking with Crates of Thebes that such things rarely cling together with virtues. Finally, to sum everything up in a short verse: Faber has enriched our age with wisdom. There follow, moreover, the things that were composed by him in the liberal arts. The first is:

A Paraphrase on Aristotle's Logic, elaborated with marvelous art. An Introduction to Aristotle's Physics. And a Paraphrase composed in a not unlearned style. An introductory Paraphrase on the Ethics of the same author. A Commentary on the Economics. An introductory Commentary on the Politics. A Commentary on Jordanus's Arithmetic; Demonstrations. An Epitome of the arithmetical books of Severinus Boethius. Certain Elements on Music. A Commentary on the astronomical Introduction of Johannes de Sacrobosco. Two books of astronomical theory of the heavenly bodies. An Introduction to the six Metaphysical books of Aristotle; a Commentary on the same.

Other, greater works in the faculty of the liberal arts are indeed awaited. But not content with these, this most religious man has directed his mind to divine matters, and has given himself wholly to them; he is about to bring a great ornament and aid to our theologians, searchers of the divine word, as one who explains what is tangled, illuminates what is obscure, unties what is knotted, and everywhere restores what is broken and mutilated with his craftsman's skill. This can easily be perceived from the things which, in this most sacred discipline of divine wisdom, he has either translated, or written, or caused to be printed more correctly and more accurately. They are written below:

A translation of Johannes Damascenus. Commentaries on Richard. On the Trinity. Commentaries on Ecclesiastes. Commentaries on the four Gospels. Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul. Scholia on the works of Dionysius the Areopagite. On the adornment of spiritual nuptials. Commentaries on Hugh of Saint Victor.

He lives at Paris, daily forging certain new works on his craftsman's anvil. Born a historian, poet, philosopher, and most eloquent orator, not

Tanta rei literariae sitis, tantus amor, tan ta cura, tantum studium. not only most splendidly endowed with gifts of fortune, but also with gifts of mind, in this our age he is renowned throughout all Italy, not to mention throughout Gaul, on account of his incredible knowledge of all branches of wisdom; daily most learned in both languages, of almost divine talent, of weighty and polished eloquence, most learned in every kind of discipline; besides his singular learning, a man certainly very humane, affable, modest, and worthy of much veneration. He wrote very many orations and letters,

elegies, various epigrams.

He published annotations on twenty-four books of the Pandects or Digest, and will publish them on the remaining books, as he himself testifies in the letter which he writes to Johannes de Ganayo, great chancellor of France. How great the learning and doctrine of the annotations may be is left for each person to consider.

He lives at Paris, to the great expectation of all; from him greater works will soon come to light.

Wilhelmus Castellus ([Ieiunio Castalius?]), a Frenchman, a most distinguished poet and orator, of Tours, was born at Tours in the year of the Lord 1468, his father being Christianus Castellus, a doctor [Paxisien?] and royal physician, and his mother Martina of Bourges. There, after being taught the first rudiments of letters, he was sent to Paris, as is customary, to take up more fruitful and more solid disciplines, to his maternal brother Johannes Anglicus, a man excellently learned in divine and human letters, to enter the Navarre bursary, as the ordinary word has it. There he devoted such labor to liberal studies, especially the humanities, that in a short course of time he not only equalled all his companions who preceded him in age and learning, but even far surpassed them. So great was his thirst for letters, so great his love, so great his care, so great his zeal. Hence, suddenly known by fame above the heavens, he was summoned to the Burgundian college, to instruct youth in the better and more polished letters, by Bernardus Roillete, a man richly furnished with all good disciplines, the chief rector of that college, and was put in charge of the first class in the humanities. Then, after enduring the contest of dialectic and after his pupils had been presented with the laurel, he returned to the Navarre college, intending to join divine studies, for which he had always yearned, to human disciplines. At last, having obtained the doctorate in the most sacred faculty of theology, he withdrew to Tours, where, honored with honorable benefices of the church, the archdeaconry and a canonry, he lives with his own people, intent on prayer and preaching. ...he imparts to the disciplines, consulting for his name and for posterity, as he has already begun, by the many works which he has brought to light. Their titles are set down below:

A Sibylline poem on the Last Judgment. An eclogue, named Eumorphus. A poem on the foolish vows of women. A dialogue in praise of Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples, book 1. Elegies, book 1. Epigrams, book 1. Many various letters to different persons. Far greater works are expected.

Johannes Bartholus of Paris, a doctor of medicine, the most excellent of all men of this age, and for that reason specially endowed by various most devoted and expert lovers of every discipline with the name of Apollo and Aesculapius, is of such authority and learning among all that, whether you seek what belongs to his own profession or what belongs to any other doctrine, you will find absolutely no one to compare with him. Indeed, most accomplished in every kind of discipline, he discusses everything so learnedly, so elegantly, so skillfully and readily, and has so deep a knowledge, that he alone seems to have embraced most eagerly all arts, both divine and human.

Antonius [Sylviolus?] of Paris, a distinguished poet and orator, although he knows many kinds of languages, nevertheless excels in three, namely French, Latin, and the common Italian tongue. By these, among all men, and especially among the most learned and most noble men, and above all among the lords of the house of Amboise, the greatest and most renowned family of France, he has won for himself such fame and favor that no disparagement of the envious can dissolve it, no decay of devouring age can abolish it, since by this threefold gift of language he has already sought immortality for himself, and among our people, for this most pleasing fluency in the French language, he is held in no less esteem than Dante among the Florentines. How great an eloquence he possesses, how much he is endowed with the light of his genius, with what subtlety of invention he stands out, in what skill of arrangement he excels, with what richness of variety he abounds, and finally with what weight of things and sentiments he proceeds: his distinguished works give the fullest testimony. For he wrote many excellent works, first of all several comedies in his own vernacular, in which he showed how varied, how abundant, how eloquent, how elegant, how witty, and finally how urbane he was; in Latin, however, he issued the following:

Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition I.

[unclear], book 1. Epigrams, book 1. Several weighty dialogues. A Triumph concerning the Venetians.

He wrote, and day by day writes, other far greater works, by which he may show that the French have their own poets and orators, not inferior to the Italians, indeed superior to them, if they devote constant, unwearied labor to these coverings of language, by which every Italian either flatters or catches at favor. He still lives and breathes the ethereal air, the orator of the reverend father in Christ, George of Amboise, archbishop of Rouen.

Wilhelm Cop of Basel, a most learned philosopher, highly skilled in Latin and Greek, in this our age excels at Paris in the art of medicine, of which he is a most eminent doctor and professor. To his house not only Parisians flee, as to the sole remedy of health, but even those who rule over this kingdom of ours, having heard the man’s reputation, send for him most swiftly and summon him, and experience his aid. Hence he alone among all the chief men of this profession has won himself a name, I do not know whether immortal or rather envied. This Wilhelm is subtle in intellect, polished in expression, eloquent in speech, admirable in learning, and to be placed after no one in knowledge of natural things. He lives at Paris under Louis the Twelfth of that name, with great renown and expectation of himself among all. For he is forging things for posterity to read, among which we already have:

The healthful precepts of Paul of Aegina, clothed by him in Latin elegance. Likewise the Praenotastica of Hippocrates.

Jodocus Clichtoveus of Nieuwpoort, a most consummate doctor of theology, a most elegant philosopher, and so distinguished an orator that he brings the savage manners of men, and the whole mortal race, into order by eloquence divine rather than mortal. He was born for these duties: to guide those ignorant of letters with straight reins, to instruct [unclear] with polished eloquence, and to illuminate, with the darkness driven far away, those deprived of the splendor of philosophy with a most brilliant radiance. Mother Nature marked this man with these most noble gifts and dignity of soul, so that whatever he undertakes in this world of sensible things he adapts to the propagation of learning. For he strives with all his might to polish whatever is rough, foul, gaping, and barbarous, to restore to philosophy its own brilliance, and he resolves in mind and soul to devote his zeal for interpretation especially to sacred utterances. Divine utterances so adorn him, and the [unclear] of things above the world...

416 On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers

recognitions, so that, while he still breathes mortal life on earth, they associate him with the most brilliant choirs of the heavenly ones; he has left to us and to future posterity outstanding monuments of his most abundant learning in a great number of volumes, and will in time leave still greater ones. For he wrote the works set down in this order:

A commentary on the Elegantiae of Augustinus Dathus. Commentaries on the Introduction to Arithmetic of D. Severinus Boethius. A compendium On the Practice of Numbering. A commentary on John Damascene. An excellent book On True Nobility. Scholia on the paraphrase of Aristotle's Physics. A commentary on the prepared introduction to Aristotle's Physics. A commentary on the prepared introduction to the books of Aristotle's Metaphysics. A commentary on the elaborated introduction to Aristotle's Ethics. He also published three books of sermons, namely on the saints and on other extraordinary matters.

Carolus Bovillus Beromundius, of Samarobriva, a man adorned with rhetorical richness, poetic variety, and the most [unclear] splendor of all philosophy, and an outstanding geometer: indeed nature is believed to have brought him forth rather to investigate the divine secrets of things and the breadths and essences of all beings, than that, enclosed in a mortal body, he should lead a human life. For he was endowed with such an elevated keenness of intellect that not only did he bring into the light the natures of earthly beings, formerly covered in blind darkness, but also, with philosophy as his guide, he penetrated most deeply the star-bearing spheres and the open structure of the heavens; by the philosophical proportion of worldly things he foreshowed the ineffable trinity of the heavenly court, and exactly prefigured it by the philosophical [display?] of numbers and by the most unified investigation of earthly things. He was so wholly and especially devoted to contemplative philosophy and geometrical abstractions that often for nine hours, leaning on the trunk of a tree, with unmoving eyes and unmoving body, forgetful of himself, his own people, and human sustenance, and freed from the mass of the body, he seemed to contemplate the natures of things, so that his soul seemed rather, released from the body, to dwell in heaven than, bound by human chains, to draw vital breaths in this sensible world.

Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition I.

He discovered many things by the sharpness of his intellect, unseen in earlier ages. For, by means of his geometrical devices, he constructed the quadrature of the circle, which none of the philosophers before had discovered with sufficient exactness. With great wonder on the part of all, he wrote with marvellous ingenuity a book On Nothing, and he left to posterity very many other philosophical works which none of mortals in past ages had foreseen.

Six introductory books on geometry. One book On the Quadrature of the Circle. An introduction to the science of perspective. A book On the Divine, Angelic, and Human Intellect. A book On Sense. A book On Nothing. The Art of Opposites. A book On the Twelve Numbers. A book Of the Divine Darkness. Several philosophical letters.

Guilhelmus de Quercu, an outstanding doctor of theology, most eminent in our age in sacred eloquence; when that majesty of the French was being oppressed by the dreadful assault of the supreme pontiff, the English, and the Spanish, and by the grim preparation of wars, he alone, by his counsel and sound judgment of mind, most graciously came to the aid of the distress and necessity of the French. For he crossed the Alps and came to the city of Pisa, where by the sole sagacity of his mind he strengthened the very great assembly of cardinals and bishops, wavering over the French matter and over so great a portent of wars, and claimed for himself the more eminent roles in so great a council. Nor was he of less power in the people, when they had to undertake divine offices, by his eloquence. For he was cultivated with such gravity of judgment and knowledge of divine counsels that by his easy eloquence he set right the untamed manners of mortals and barbarous peoples, and easily led them back to the bright recognition of the supreme creator, with a kindly voice, gracious eyes, measured gesture, and pleasing comparisons.

Renatus Garnerius of Luxeuil, a doctor of both laws, most skilled in our age; because of his distinction in every kind of discipline, and then especially in the excellent faculty of laws, he spread his reputation and honor through various regions of the earth, and deservedly, in establishing and interpreting laws everywhere, easily claimed for himself the roles of Lycurgus and Socrates. With the eloquence of a more polished voice, with a tested profession, a keen mind, and calm gesture, he solved the riddles of the laws,
