418 [unclear], Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers

... lived, so that he adorned the borders of Poitiers with perpetual honor, and day by day ennobled all Gaul by his eminence.

Christophorus Longolius, a Parisian, a most ingenious philosopher and a very distinguished orator of our age: as mother nature adorned him with the greatest gifts of mind and marked him out with a natural equipment for investigating the natures of things, so fortune bestowed on him most abundantly the vastest accumulations of goods and a most pleasing dexterity. Reflecting in his mind that kindly nature had breathed into him the noblest gifts of the soul, he so increased nature’s gifts by labor and practice that he emerged as the most distinguished philosopher and most copious orator of our age. He lectured on Pliny in the renowned academy of Poitiers with an inexpressible structure of style, so that he seemed, without distinction, to belong to all, not relying on mortal eloquence but rather strengthened by a variety of thoughts drawn from the inner chambers of the heavens. The Parisian academy, nurse of the disciplines, trained him not inelegantly in morals, in oratorical savor, and in philosophical letters; nevertheless, not satisfied with Gallic eloquence, he hastened to Italian households, judging that he would attain greater things there. There, instructed by ready experience of affairs and polished eloquence, he at last returned to the borders of Gaul, where he gave testimonies of his eloquence and learning. For scarcely passing his twenty-fourth year, consulting posterity with an innumerable variety of volumes, he published monuments of his learning and left them to his followers in this arranged order:

An oration on the praises of Saint Louis, king of the Franks, and of the nation of the Gauls, addressed to Francis of Valois, the Dauphin.

Nearly innumerable orations and letters.

Various elegies and epigrams.

Commentaries on Pliny, which he learnedly and elegantly interpreted publicly at Poitiers, to the highest admiration of all.

Certain writings on civil law, while he was publicly professing it at Poitiers.

Johannes Stephanus flourished in this our age; by nation an Italian, bishop of Vercelli, cardinal of Bologna, a most exacting cultivator of literary learning. The more fortune raised him to the most excellent and eminent dignities, the more nature adorned him with nobler gifts of mind. He, indeed, always placed all things, even the most illustrious heights of dignities, after literary leisure and the investigated natures of things. And finally by his own tireless labor and diligence he brought it about that Aristotle’s Great Ethics, never before known in earlier ages...

[unclear] known, has made common to us, which Jacques Lefevre, the most eminent philosopher of our age and a most vigorous defender of philosophy, committed to the press under his auspices, likely to bring no small fruits once set forth.

William de Mara flourished at this time, a Neustrian by nation, born in the deserted district of Coutances, begotten by parents of noble lineage and most holy life, now canon and treasurer of the cathedral church of Coutances, a distinguished orator and poet. When he was still a boy, the distinguished theologian Doctor Jean Boucard, formerly bishop of Avranches and royal confessor, took him up to be educated in learning, on account of the excellent gifts of mind which he perceived in the boy. Nor did he only see to having him instructed by others, but also taught him himself whenever he had leisure, taking no little delight in the cultivation of so fertile a field. And he hoped so much from his excellent natural ability that he did not hesitate to endow him with a benefice in tender age, and certainly would have given greater things if he had lived longer. Finally William himself went off to the famous study at Paris, and in a short space of time advanced so far that no one was held more celebrated than he in the art of oratory or poetry. Hence Robert Briconnet, formerly archbishop of Reims and chancellor of France, hearing the reputation of so great a man, summoned him to himself as secretary. When this Robert died, Charles VIII gave this William to his chancellor, Guy de Rochefort. For Charles loved William himself because of the not unpolished rhymes which he knew how to compose most elegantly in the French tongue, and also because of his skill in writing in every kind of letters, in which he found no one equal to him. Afterwards the most reverend cardinal of Saint-Malo, Guillaume Briconnet, obtained this man from Guy de Rochefort to be his confidant; with him he remained for a long time. But at last, weary of the misery of courts and ill bearing the loss of time, he withdrew to the study at Caen, where he was granted the dignity of rector, and afterwards the doctoral laurel in both laws. And in that study he professed law for many years, and at length was taken up as canon and treasurer of the cathedral church of Coutances, where he resides, serving God alone and good letters, with which he is to enrich posterity. These are the testimonies of his learning which now exist:

The Conflict against the Chimera, to Jean de Ganay, great chancellor of France, a truly excellent and holy work, in which he elegantly attacked those three chief vices by which the whole world is infected and poisoned, namely pride, lust, and avarice.

A little work on the most holy eucharist, to Guillaume, bishop of Coutances.

A paraphrase on Musaeus, On Hero and Leander, to Nicolas de Cerisay, dean of Saint-Germain of Paris.

One book On Loves, to the same man.

One book On Praises, to Jean Briconnet, president of the royal accounts.

One book On Reproaches, to Charles Guillart, president of the Parlement of Paris.

One book of dirges and epitaphs.

One book On Divine Things.

Besides these he wrote many things in prose discourse which have not yet come to light.

Matthew of Evreux, a Norman, of the Order of Friars Preachers, a very profound investigator of the Scriptures, a man certainly full of religion and letters, made an excellent postil on the Pentateuch, Isaiah, and very many other books of the Old and New Testament, which is kept deposited in the common library of the convent of Evreux of the aforesaid order, of which he had been an alumnus. He flourished, however, as appears from certain writings of his, around the times of Charles VI, king of the Franks. When his books had been scattered in gatherings, Brother Robert Baiguard, doctor of theology and confessor of the Most Christian king of the Franks Charles VII, of the same order and convent, gathered them together again and deposited them in the common library of the same house.

Guy of Evreux, a compiler of excellent sermons, is believed to have flourished around these same times, a brother of the same order, who also, besides the rules of Tyconius, gave certain very apt instructions for grasping the meaning of sacred Scripture, showing from ignorance of what matters it often happens that one errs in the exposition of sacred doctrine; these are found gathered together among the rest of his works in the libraries of certain convents.

Laurence Gervais, of the convent of Lisieux, of the Order of Preachers in Normandy, in the reign of Louis XI, king of the Franks, was held distinguished at Paris, a doctor of theology, a man

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition I.

certainly a man most famous for knowledge and learning, who, because of his outstanding wisdom, since he was especially skilled in the doctrine of the most holy doctor Thomas Aquinas, was sent to reform the Cologne studium for the better; and when he had made extraordinary progress there, returning from there, he gave up his spirit at Dijon, a town of Burgundy. There, buried with the brothers of his order, he left very useful works, which are called the Copulata of Master Laurentius Gervasius, on the whole Summa of Theology of the Angelic Doctor, of whose doctrine, indeed, while he lived, he was called the repository.

Sylvester of Prierio, a Bolognese, of the Order of Preachers, a venerable doctor and certainly a most renowned expounder and likewise very keen defender of the doctrine of Saint Thomas Aquinas, flourished in Lombardy around the times of Pope Innocent VIII. For he wrote a Defence of the doctrine of Saint Thomas on the questions of Johannes Capreolus, abridging the writings and demonstrating more clearly than light the irrefragable doctrine of the most holy doctor, dissolving from that doctor’s own sayings all the subtleties of his opponents. He also wrote an Introduction to Logic.

Also a Summa of Sermons, which is called the Golden Rose.

Also a Summa on cases of conscience.

Also on the four books of the Sentences.

He continued writing down to these times, living at Bologna, that is, to the year of the Lord 1512.

Dominicus of Flanders, a most renowned doctor, of the same Bolognese order, in the same times as the preceding, wrote Metaphysical Questions. Questions on the Soul. Also on the books of the Posterior Analytics. He died while Alexander VI, supreme pontiff, presided in the chair of Peter.

Paulus Soncinas, of the same order, in these times wrote Metaphysical Questions. Also on the predicables and categories. He died at the same time as, or about the same time as, the preceding.

In Abbot Spanheim, On Writers. Second Addition of Some Notable Writers, partly ancient, partly recent, now added for the first time in the manner of an index to those previously compiled by Trithemius and others, by F. Balthazar Werlin of Colmar.

A certain abbot of Ursperg, whose proper name is hidden, wrote a volume of Chronicles. Its beginning is from Ninus, great king of the Assyrians, down to Frederick II, emperor of the Romans. The last year is counted by him as 1229 from the salvation of the world. Ursperg, moreover, is a monastery of the Premonstratensian institute, almost halfway between Ulm and Augsburg of the Vindelici.

Abba Abraham and Abba Patritius, holy fathers [unclear], translated the ascetic sermons of Isaac, the Syrian monk, into the Greek language. This work is extant at Rome in the Vatican Library.

Adrianus Barlandus, a Zeelander by nation, a man of rare learning, published several dialogues, together with a little work on the notable towns of Lower Germany.

Five books of the same author’s old and recent jests, illustrated with scholia, are extant. And a little work on all the bishops of Utrecht.

Also a poem on the location and pleasantness of Louvain.

The same man described the instruction of a Christian man in aphorisms.

He also composed concise institutes of the art of oratory.

He also selected proverbial verses from Virgil with the greatest zeal.

He wrote many other things unknown to us.

He flourished at Louvain around the beginning of the reign of Charles V, 1520.

Aegidius Bellamera, a remarkably learned man, wrote counsels in law, of which 148 survive at Rome in the Palatine Library.

The same man published several other little works, namely those which follow:

On plurality of benefices. On the Roman Rota.

He also wrote on De foro competenti, c. Romana. And on the paragraph Contrahentes. And

Floruit circa tempora Zenonis et Anastasii imperatorum. Interijt autem circa annum salutis 538. Agnellus episcopus scripfit epistolam ad Arminium de ratione fidei, in qua praecipue Arianam haeresim refusat, Dei patris et filij consubstantiali et coaeua natura. Initium tale est: Frater Martinus exegit literas ad tuam charitatem mittendas etc. Alanus Porretanꝰ vir doctus, regulas iuris celestis vel maximas, id est axiomata theologiz cum interpretatione conscripsit. Alardus Aemstelredamus, natione Hollandus, omnia Rodolphi Agricolae opera emendauit, & diectis scholijs illustrauit, Idem scripsit epitomen in librum Rodolphi Agricolae de inuentione dialectica. Descripsit etiam Ecclesiasten iuxta omnes Rod. Agricolae locos. Extant et quaedam alia eiusdem opufcula, nempe Similia facra, & paraphrasis epistoleae Hippocratis Coei ad Damagetum, quam para phrasice e Graeco in Latinum transfudit. Superfunt eius et multa epigrammata, epiftolle, praefationes, annontationes, commētariola in alios diuerfos authores, nobis per typographiam nondum cognita. Eius est et Teutonico in Latinum versio libelli de miraculis per venerabilem Eucharistiam Bruxellae in Belgio factis. Albertus Crantz, politioris literaturae mirus amator, Suediam, Daniam, & Saxoniā descripsit. Albertus de Ferrarijs Placentinus, scripsit de horis canonicis. Item de celebratione Missarum, in primum c. tertij Decretal. q̄ incipit, Presbyter. Albertus Florētinus sub Nicolao V. egregios de architectura libros conscripsit, vt testat Aeneas Syluius in descrip. Europę cap. 58. Albertus Pius, comes et princeps Carporum, atqꝫ styli Cicero niani fedulus imitator, scripsit epistolam paraeneticam instar libri, ad Des. Erasmum Roterodamū. Albertus Pighius, patria Campenfis, natione Germanus, de eq̃ noctiorum folstitiorum; inuentione scripsit, ad D. Fran. Molinif abbatem S. Maximini, à secretis et consilio regis Francoꝝ etc. Item de ratione Paschalis celebrationis, deqꝫ restitutione Ecclesiastici Calendarij ad Leonem X. pontificem max. Eiusdem Pighij astrologiae defensio, & liber quidam in prognosticatores editus est. Insu

Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

Aegidius Maserius of Paris, a man by no means moderately versed in the liberal arts, wrote commentaries on the poems of Valerius Flaccus Setinus Balbus, the Argonautica, in 8 books.

Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis, Spanish by nation, highly learned, made himself famous in his age by certain excellent books, of which these are extant:

On Cosmography.

A lexicon of civil law, against certain notable errors of Accursius.

Commentaries on the satires of Aulus Persius.

Exegeses on some passages of sacred Scripture.

Expositions on the Paschal work of Coelius Sedulius.

On Grammar.

Aeneas the Christian Platonist wrote a golden dialogue on the immortality of the soul and on the resurrection of bodies, which is entitled Theophrastus. It was translated from Greek into the Latin language by Ambrosius Camaldulensis. He flourished around the times of the emperors Zeno and Anastasius.

Agapetus, deacon of the great and most holy Church of God, wrote in Greek 72 paraenetic sentences to Justinian Caesar, which the Greeks call the royal schedule; for it discusses the office of a king. He died about the year of salvation 538.

Agathius Guidacerius, royal professor of sacred theology at Paris, wrote a Mirror, whose subject will be learned from the author’s own letter, which is approximately as follows:

Although, being bound by the public lectures on the holy Scriptures in their original languages, I have not yet completed the commentaries which I had undertaken to write on the holy tongue, nevertheless I wished at present to publish at least its first precepts. Wherefore, behold, from the most approved Hebrew teachers, Moses Kimhi, Pethah Debarai, the Michlol, and others, in whose writings I think I have done enough to write Latin commentaries, since I was born of Christian parents and from tender childhood, as they say, was instructed in Latin and Greek, and not in Hebrew, we now give this first little book, on letters, on points, on the quantity of syllables, on accents, and finally on the perfect method of pronunciation, in which all the beauty and sweetness of this heavenly language consists. We shall soon give, with Christ’s help, if I understand that these things are pleasing to you, a second book on the eight parts of speech; and thereafter we shall proceed to work out and publish those matters which are most copiously handed down in the very learned David Kimhi’s Michlol, for the practice of this art’s dikduk (that is, subtle consideration; for thus the Hebrews call that which we call grammar).

Agnellus the bishop wrote a letter to Arminius on the principle of faith, in which he chiefly refutes the Arian heresy by the consubstantial and coeternal nature of God the Father and the Son. Its beginning is as follows: Brother Martin demanded that letters be sent to your Charity, etc.

Alanus Porretanus, a learned man, wrote rules, or maxims, of heavenly law, that is, theological axioms, with interpretation.

Alardus Aemstelredamus, a Hollander by nation, corrected all the works of Rodolphus Agricola and illustrated them with learned scholia.

The same man wrote an epitome on Rodolphus Agricola’s book On Dialectical Invention.

He also described Ecclesiastes according to all the passages of Rodolphus Agricola.

There are also extant certain other small works of the same man, namely Sacred Similitudes, and a paraphrase of the letter of Hippocrates of Cos to Damagetus, which he rendered paraphrastically from Greek into Latin.

Many epigrams, letters, prefaces, annotations, and little commentaries on various other authors by him also survive, not yet known to us through printing.

His too is the translation from German into Latin of a little book on the miracles performed through the venerable Eucharist at Brussels in Belgium.

Albertus Crantz, a remarkable lover of more refined literature, described Sweden, Denmark, and Saxony.

Albertus de Ferrarijs of Piacenza wrote on the canonical hours. Likewise on the celebration of Masses, on the first chapter of the third book of the Decretals, which begins Presbyter.

Albertus Florentinus under Nicholas V wrote excellent books on architecture, as Aeneas Sylvius testifies in the Description of Europe, chapter 58.

Albertus Pius, count and prince of Carpi, and a zealous imitator of the Ciceronian style, wrote a paraenetic letter, in the form of a book, to Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.

Albertus Pighius, of Kampen by homeland, German by nation, wrote on the discovery of the equinoxes and solstices, to Dom Franciscus Molinis, abbot of Saint Maximin, secretary and councillor of the king of the Franks, etc.

Likewise on the method of celebrating Easter and on the restoration of the ecclesiastical calendar, to Leo X, supreme pontiff.

A defense of astrology by the same Pighius, and a certain book against prognosticators, has been published.

Moreover he also published other books, namely: On Composing Disputes, and On the Controversies at the Diets of Regensburg.

Aldus Manutius, a Roman, very skilled in the liberal arts, wrote Institutions of Greek Grammar in pure Greek speech; On the Various Inflections of Every Kind of Nouns and Verbs. The same man wrote four books of Institutions of Latin Grammar. He also published another volume, On the Kinds of Days, and at the same time On Shadows and Hours, which are mentioned in Palladius. There are also extant his very elegant annotations on Quintus Horatius, and prefaces not to be despised, prefixed to many books printed by him. One letter of the same man to Angelo Poliziano. He composed several other little works, and translated not a few from Greek into Latin phrasing, among which he rendered Homer's poem on the battle of the frogs and mice in Latin words in prose, so that verse answers to verse. He translated in the same way also the compunctive poems of Damascenus, and well. He flourished at Venice under Maximilian, and died around the year of the Lord 1514.

Alexander the monk, by no means moderately instructed in the liberal arts, wrote the historical discourse, which is extant at Rome in Greek, On the Discovery of the Holy and Life-Giving Cross.

Alexander ab Alexandro, a distinguished jurist of Naples, published six books of Genial Days. He was illustrious in the time of Francesco Filelfo, Niccolo Perotti, and Ermolao Barbaro.

Alfonsus Ferrus of Naples, a notable physician, chief surgeon of Pope Paul III, brought to light four books On the Manifold Medicine of the Holy Wood, and on the Administration of Wine.

Aloisius Marlianus of Milan wrote an elegant letter on the disastrous voyage to Spain of Philip, king of the Spaniards.

Aloisius Mundella, a distinguished physician at Brescia in Italy, wrote twenty-three medical letters, containing an exposition of various questions and, besides, of difficult passages of Galen.

Alphonsus, a man most illustrious in every kind of good letters, made himself famous in his age by an excellent volume, which is inscribed Against Heresies.

Alphonsus, archbishop of Toledo, wrote several questions on Aristotle's books On the Soul.

Alvarus Gomes, a Spaniard, a man not unlearned, rendered the Proverbs of Solomon in verse.

most practiced in sacred and profane letters, and the most vigilant preacher of the most reverend arch-prelate of the Church of Trier, published many distinguished little works against heresies, of which I have found only the following.

On the sacrifice of the Mass, a little disputation of the pious man and the misoliturgist.

Again on the sacrifice of the Mass, both in Latin and in German, to the senate of Basel.

Against the Eleutherobaptists, book 1.

A refutation of the counsel of Oecolampadius concerning the postponing of the baptism of little children until that age at which they will already begin to babble, book 1.

Against the iconoclasts, book 1; and

Whether it is right to take action against Anabaptists, inasmuch as they are heretics, book 1.

Desserts of letters sent in turn to Erasmus of Rotterdam.

He also wrote annotations on sayings brought forward by Erasmus of Rotterdam in an unorthodox manner.

A little book On Death Not to Be Feared, not yet committed to the press.

A dialogue, not yet printed, of men and women, standard-bearers of the Lutheran sect.

The same man rendered into Latin the liturgy of Saint Chrysostom.

There is added a Doxology in Greek and at the same time in Latin, which was also in use among the ancients both in the Mass and in morning prayers.

Likewise the Nicene Creed, made Latin from the Greek by the same man.

All according to the exemplar of the library of the monastery of Saint Simeon, which is held to be very ancient at Belgian Trier, with brief annotations by the same Ambrose.

On the celibacy of priests he published a little book filled with learning.

Besides these works that have been enumerated, he also wrote innumerable sermons, and very learned exegeses on various books of the Bible, but not yet brought to light.

He enjoys the air above in the year of the Virgin birth 1546, intending to write many more things for the sake of students.

Ambrosius Spiera of Treviso, of the order of the brethren of Saint Mary, wrote a Lenten book On the Flowers of Wisdom.

Amedeus, bishop of Lausanne, wrote eight homilies on Mary the virgin mother, filled with much learning.

Anacletus, Roman pontiff, a man of most holy life and of learning not to be despised, published decrees and a letter, which is found in the volume of councils.

To the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

Five Greek sermons of Saint Anastasius of Antioch, perhaps bishop or presbyter, are preserved there:

  1. On the correct dogmas of truth among us.

  2. παρ᾽ ἐκπεμψθαι, that is, On the uncircumscribed.

  3. On the divine economy or dispensation.

  4. On the suffering or impassibility of Christ.

  5. On the resurrection.

Anastasius, monk of Mount Sinai, wrote commentaries on the sixth psalm. He also published other things, of which the following are held:

An oration at the beginning of Lent.

On the diverse ways of the soul's salvation.

All these, the catalogue of the Palatine library bears witness, are preserved in Greek at Rome.

Andreas Albius, a physician of Bologna, published an excellent book on medicine, and, if the powers above favor him, will soon give six dialogues on waters. He is still flourishing in the year of the Lord 1546.

Andreas Alciatus, jurisconsult, most famous in our age, wrote a book of Emblems, which contains about one hundred various pictures as if hieroglyphics; their meaning, which follows each one, is acutely explained by elegiac epigrams. The inscriptions are of this kind: The insignia of the duchy of Milan. The treaties of the Italians. On silence. That even the fiercest are tamed. That gratitude is to be returned. Concord. Love the most powerful passion.

On weights and measures, book 1.

Of the same man, Paradoxes to Pratus, 6 books.

Corrections on the first 3 books of the Code, 3 books.

Things Passed Over, book [unclear]. Punctuations, 4 books.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

On the prescription of five feet, one book. On magistrates and civil and military offices, one book. Parergon of law, three books. The process of law. An apology against Ludovicus. On presumptions. On things entrusted. On single combat. Commentaries on the title If a fixed sum is claimed. An opinion on the matter of the duel, taken from book 5 of the responses. On book 1 of the second book of the Code, On judgments which; on C. 4 of the second book of the Decretals, On trials. And many other things, by which he endowed himself with immortality.

Andreas, archbishop of Rhodes, wrote a demonstrative apology, from the writings of St Thomas, to Bessarion of Nicaea, on the divine essence and operation; it is extant in Italy.

Andreas Barbatias, most skilled in the laws, wrote many distinguished little works; among them the following are reported:

On [z.?] ff. novi. Four volumes of opinions. On the Clementines. On the first [book] of the Infortiatum. On cardinals. On book 2 of the Decretals, rubric On witnesses, chapter Testimonium. On book 2 of the Decretals, rubric On sureties, chapter Dilectorum. On book 2, chapter, rubric [unclear], chapter Quae admit. On [z.?] C. De fideicommissis, law Cum acutissimi.

Andreas Brentzius of Padua translated into Latin Hippocrates’ book On the Nature of Man, and also the same author’s book On Dreams, with a preface to Sixtus, the supreme pontiff, in which he discusses dreams at length. To this little book is appended an epistle by the same author to Ni. Gupalatinus, in which he explains the words of Hippocrates by which he assigns the internal parts of the body to the Moon, the middle parts to the Sun, and the external parts to the Stars; and why Hippocrates commands supplication to be made to the Sun, to celestial Jupiter, to terrestrial Jupiter, to terrestrial Minerva, to Mercury, to Apollo, to Earth, and to the Heroes.

Andreas Camutius, a physician in Cisalpine Gaul, published certain propositions in philosophy and medicine, to which he promises that he will respond, and a certain little work in which he attempts to reconcile philosophy and theology. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1545.

Andreas, bishop of Crete, wrote several notable sermons, which are entitled:

A sermon on Lazarus four days dead.

430 In the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

Sermon 2 on the divine resurrection of the Lord. And thereafter he published other homilies on the feasts of the saints. All these are preserved in Greek in Italy.

Andreas ab Exea, doctor and interpreter of both laws in the Academy of Valencia, wrote a little book on the treasury and fisc, and on the prefecture of the accounts of both.

Andreas Gratiolus of Tusculum, from Benacus, translated into Latin the commentaries of Eustratius, bishop of Nicaea, on the second book of Aristotle’s Posterior Analytics.

Also the concise expositions of an uncertain author on the same work.

Andreas Janus Lascaris Rhydacenus excerpted certain things from the histories of Polybius on the military affairs of the Romans, and especially on the laying out of camps. He rendered the same into the Latin language.

Greek and Latin epigrams by the same man.

Andreas à Lacuna, a Spanish physician of Segovia, wrote on the method of recognizing, preventing, and driving off pestilential fever.

There is also extant by the same man an anatomical method, or contemplation on the dissection of the human body.

I also translated not a few works, concerning which the following are given:

A little book of Aristotle On Virtues, translated from the Greek and illustrated with many scholia and examples.

From the commentaries On Agriculture, formerly ascribed to the divine Emperor Constantine, the last eight books, in which the nature, habits, and nurture of very many animals are described, translated into Latin according to the authority of very ancient codices.

One book of Galen of Pergamum On Philosophical History, turned into Latin.

By the same interpreter, that work of Aristotle On the Nature of Plants.

He poured Aristotle’s book On the World into Latin.

He also wrote other little works, namely, on the regimen of diet and exercises to be observed, especially in old age.

And Europe Lamenting Herself.

Andreas de Novo Castro, skilled in scholastic theosophy, published an excellent volume on the four books of the Sentences.

Andreas Stiborius, a Bavarian, canon at Vienna in Austria and a distinguished professor of mathematics, wrote many books, of which only the following have come down to us:

A book of astronomical instruments of the first and second movable [heaven], with their proper old canons.

Ecclesiastical [writers], Addition II.

The Austrian Shield with canons, in which the face of the astrolabe shines forth at every moment.

A little book on various clocks: spherical, concave, columnar, pyramidal, and annular.

A little book on various compasses.

A little book on various quadrants.

An Introduction to sensible astronomy, with various astronomical pictures and an astronomical calendar.

The Arms of Stiborius’s Piety.

A Contemplation of the Mirror of Piety.

A Contemplation of the Face of the Savior.

A Contemplation on Different Marriages.

A little book on the authors of mathematics.

Prefaces to various books in mathematics, lectured on by himself.

Determinations of certain quodlibetal questions.

Andreas Thurinus of Pescia, apostolic physician, a man most learned in medical matters, wrote a letter against Matteo Curti of Pavia, physician, on the vein to be cut in the treatment of pleurisy.

And likewise to Paul III, On the Perfection of the Treatment of Pleurisy.

Responses by the same author against Matteo Curti, on the place of the vein to be cut in disease of the ribs.

The same man wrote On the Goodness of Waters, of spring-water and cistern-water, which is [unclear]; and a dissertation on the new embrocha, or artificial shower-bath.

There is also extant, by the same author, a Defense of Hippocrates and Galen against Girolamo Fracastoro, on the causes of critical days.

Andreas Vesalius of Brussels, public professor of the school of physicians at Padua, composed paraphrases on the ninth book of the very famous Arab physician to King Almansor, on the treatment of affections of the individual parts of the body.

There survives a letter of the same man, which teaches that the axillary vein of the right elbow is to be cut in pain of the side, and that melancholic juice is purged from the branches of the portal vein pertaining to the seat.

There are also extant seven books, On the Fabric of the Human Body, with most elegant figures of all kinds, by the same author.

Angelo Andrea Resende, Portuguese by nation, composed a learned and elegant poem against the foolish barkers at more polished literature. An-

In the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers

Angelo Aretino, J.C. (whom they otherwise call Angelo Gambiglioni, or de Gambiglioni of Arezzo), wrote two volumes of commentaries on the Institutes of civil law, addressed to Leonello d’Este, marquis of Ferrara.

Likewise:

On Testaments, and the Clauses of Testaments.

On Crimes in Law, and the Clauses of Inquisitorial Procedure.

On the three books of the Code.

Two volumes of Counsels. Certain singularia.

A Repertory of Law.

A repetition, for the third time, on C. De bon. vac., book 10, l. Si vacantia.

Angelo Bolognini publicly taught surgery from Avicenna at Bologna, and wrote two books on the care of external ulcers, in an uncultivated style. In the first part of these are set forth the things that impede consolidation, what and how many they are, how they do harm, and how they are recognized. In the other, medicines are administered both generally and individually.

The same man composed a book on common ointments, in the solution of continuity.

Angelo Cospi of Bologna, a man thoroughly learned in both Greek and Latin literature, translated the sixteenth and seventeenth books of Diodorus Siculus.

Antiochus Tibertus of Cesena, professor of the liberal disciplines, wrote three books on chiromancy to Ottaviano Ubaldini, count of Mercatello.

Antipater, bishop of Bostra, composed a sermon on the Nativity of Christ. It is extant in Greek in Italy.

Antoninus, bishop of Constantina, driven into exile under Arcadius by Genseric, king of the Vandals, wrote an exhortation.

Antonius of Brescia worked out a learned work of sermons, which is extant in Italy.

Antonius Broekwey (which word may be rendered in Latin as Paludopascuus), of Königstein, guardian of the Regular Observance of St. Francis at Nijmegen, composed elegant expositions on the four Gospels. The same man also wrote commentaries on several epistles of St. Paul,

On Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

[Unclear] that very thing and all the rest, if he had lived somewhat longer; on the road between Brula and Deventer, for a most just cause of his Brulensian convent at that time, not far from the town of Restanum in Cleves, in the lodging of a certain little village, he died unexpectedly from pain in the sides contracted from cold humors and excessive fatigue, and this in the winter after that famous plague which raged most fiercely at Cologne through the summer and autumn of the year 1541.

The same man wrote, by means of figures, a brief Monotessaron of the Gospels, which is wonderfully useful to preachers of the word of God for aiding the memory; printed at Cologne in the year of the Lord 1542.

Antonius Cermisonus, a man fully instructed in healing bodies, the teacher of Savonarola, is said to have written many little works on medicine, which have not yet come into our hands. I have read only that notable work which he wrote in the form of counsels, one book. He wrote On Urines.

Antonius Codrus Urceus, a man of distinguished learning, was born at the little town of Herberia in the territory of Reggio, which is about seven miles distant from Modena, in the year of salvation 1446. He left to posterity several immortal monuments of his mind; although he was by no means able to put the final hand to them, nevertheless for the most part they show how great was his faculty of expression, how great his talent, and finally how great his learning. In composing and arranging poems, both in Greek and in Latin, he was very ready; in this kind there survive very many of his elegies, epigrams, and Sylvae. Those who read them will see how highly the acuteness of his wit and his judgments are to be valued. To the Greek vocabulary he added many things of his own and corrected many things. He wrote sermons or orations filled with much learning, etc., and many other works, which you have appended below.

Letters, two books. Sylvae, two books. Satires. One Eclogue.

Antonius Eparchus of Corcyra teaches Greek literature at Venice. He translated into the Latin tongue several books of Polybius’s Histories, not yet published either in Greek or in Latin.

He is still living in the year of the Lord 1546.

Antonius Fumanellus of Verona, a physician, by far the most practiced in the use of the art throughout all Italy, published a complete method for diagnosing and curing all fevers.

By the same man there is a surgical counsel on fracture of the skull, a wound of the breast and lung, and inflammation.

A history and method of cure for difficulty and constriction in passing urine.

Likewise:

Whether mineral water is suitable for difficulty of urination. On the powers of the iron-bearing bath and on the nature of iron. On the baths of simple water.

Antonius Gazius of Padua, an illustrious physician, in the year 1490, as he himself testifies at the end of his book, wrote a book On Preserving Health, which he entitled The Flowering Crown, evidently because from the chief opinions of physicians, as though from little flowers, he arranged this work like a certain garland.

He flourished under the dominion of the Venetians in the year of salvation 1504.

Antonius Goveanus, a Portuguese, wrote certain epigrams and four letters.

The same man restored not a few things to their former splendor, among which Virgil and Terence are especially reckoned.

On the same Terence he published very elegant commentaries. He also translated Porphyry’s Introduction on the Five Predicables very elegantly. And he brought to light an exposition on Cicero’s speech Against Vatinius the Witness; the critical part of logic.

Antonius Lodovicus, a physician of Lisbon, a most learned man, composed certain works on medical matters; among these the following are the chief:

On Occult Properties, five books. Problems, five books.

Antonius Mancinellus, a distinguished grammarian, flourished and wrote many works at Venice around the year of the Lord 1490. All his works are comprised for those who choose them in these verses:

The Government of Words, Variation, Ear of Grain, Figure, Thesaurus, Flowers, these first kept vigil here, that is, in his homeland. Afterwards Rome gave the Gymnasium, the commentaries on Maro, Then on the Satirist, thence on Flaccus, and the Versilogus likewise. Brought to the Venetian shores at the urging of Pomponius, You write the file of Laurentius, and thence the Method. You explain the Dreams, who were seen greater, Scipio; And at the same time the Rhetorician, or the work of Cicero.

Antonius Marinarius, of the Carmelite profession, a most celebrated theologian, composed three books On the Consonance of Jesus Christ and the Prophets. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1545.

On Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

[the names?] of all simple medicaments whose use is in the workshops, especially in Italy and at Ferrara; he also wrote, in eight books, an exposition of the Aphorisms and Prognostics of Hippocrates and Galen, commentaries and annotations with two very full indexes, and many other works, by which he endowed himself with immortality.

Antonius Panormita was master of letters to Alfonso of Aragon, king of Sicily, and wrote his memorable sayings and deeds in four books.

Antonius de Prato, of Trent, wrote a book On the Commonwealth, On Fiefs, On Second Marriages, and a Repertory on Bartolus.

Aquilius Severus, in Spain, of the family of that Severus to whom Lactantius’s two books of letters are written, composed a volume, containing, as it were, the [unclear] state of his whole life, both in prose and in verses, which he called [unclear] or [unclear]. He died under the emperor Valentinian.

Armandus de Bellovisu, of the Order of Preachers, wrote an explanation of difficult terms, both of theology and of philosophy and logic.

Arnoldus Peraxylus Arlenius, a man learned beyond his years even in youth, is still, unless I am mistaken, in the household of the most noble Lord Diego Hurtado de Mendoza, ambassador of the imperial majesty among the Venetians, a singular pillar of the literary commonwealth, and one who has deserved exceedingly well of every kind of study and wisdom, while he has diligently sought out ancient authors, especially Greek ones, in the libraries of Italy, and restored them to the light and use of mortals. We expect from him, if God prolongs his life, certain treatises from Plutarch on morals, not yet translated by anyone; also seven books of Dio Cocceius’s Roman History, rendered purely into Latin speech; and the commentaries of Olympiodorus, the great Platonic philosopher, on Aristotle’s Meteora.

From the sacred writers Chrysostom, Theodoret, and others, he will give most beautiful sermons, commentaries, and orations hitherto unseen. In addition, he has resolved to publish certain little notes on Lactantius Firmianus, in which he attempts to refute the trifling superstition and vanity of the ancients, and to establish that our own doctrines are much more certain and true by law.

Arnoldus de Villanova, by nation a Frenchman from Provence, or, as others will have it, a Catalan, since Villanova is a town four miles distant from the city of Girona in Catalonia, was most devoted to astronomy, and certain men asserted that he had been a heretic. Sent by King Frederick from Sicily to the pope, he died at sea and was buried at Genoa.

He expounded very many volumes in every branch of learning, from the excellence of his own intellect, without a teacher.

A certain principal work of his on medicine is in circulation.

He also wrote an elegant letter on alchemy to the king of Naples.

On Abbot Spanheim, On Writers.

Arnoldus Haldrenius of Wesel, a man conspicuous for singular holiness of life and exact knowledge of sacred scripture, and most skilled also in the three languages, Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, equally strong in verse and in prose: he was of such humility that the various works, as we have learned from his friends, which he both composed and corrected, he did not publish to the public, apart from these few:

While still rather young he corrected Macrobius, adding, so far as could be done, those things that were missing from the Greek sources.

He applied the same labor to restoring Diomedes, the ancient grammarian, and likewise certain others less well known.

He published a little book on the Ten Commandments of the Decalogue, on that Gospel saying: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.

Likewise another, against the hagiomastiges; and others, which, as we have said, still lie hidden.

He wrote several prefaces or letters, placed before various authors partly in his own name, partly in another’s.

Also many epigrams, either purely Greek or translated from Greek into Latin. Among these the chief are those in Heresbach’s translation of Herodotus; when the translator, for I know not what reason, unless perhaps terrified by their majesty, had left them untouched in translating, this Arnoldus of ours, for the sake of public usefulness, rendered them into Latin no less splendidly than they had formerly been in Greek.

His too are those summaries prefixed to the individual distinctions of the commentary of Dionysius the Carthusian on the four books of the Sentences, expressed almost in individual distichs, although several of these, especially in Books I, III, and IV, left in passing by Haldrenius, were supplied by a certain Noviomagus, as the copy of Arnoldus preserved up to now in the Carthusian house at Cologne clearly bears witness to this very fact.

He died in the year of the Lord 1534, on the thirtieth day of October. For him, in the chief church at holy Cologne, where he was a canon and where he is buried, students of his piety and learning placed this epitaph:

To the Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

Whoever you are, if you wish to enter blessed rest, and so enjoy everlasting peace with Christ, you must listen to the words of God and follow them. Therefore, while it is granted to live here, learn to die. Death is a passage to life, if you believe in him who, seized by love of us, bore death.

Arsenius, archbishop of Monemvasia, collected apophthegms of philosophers, emperors, rhetoricians, and poets.

The same man collected Greek scholia on seven tragedies of Euripides, namely on Hecuba, Orestes, the Phoenissae, Medea, Hippolytus, Alcestis, and Andromache.

There is also a little book compiled by him, containing various witty poems, and several fables and poetic explanations, and certain passages from the Stromata of Clement concerning the thefts of writers.

And he is said to have collected many other things. He flourished under Charles V, the most unconquered Roman emperor.

Asianus, bishop of Sardis, a man of no common learning, delivered to the emperor Antoninus an Apologeticum for Christians, both pious and catholic.

Audbertus, wonderfully practiced in divine letters, published certain most learned homilies, which Alcuin the Levite collected.

Augustinus Dathus of Siena, philosopher and orator, highly skilled in both sacred and profane literature, composed various little works, of which the following are extant:

On the immortality of souls, ten treatises. Latin orations, 222. Letters, 3 books. A fragment of the history of Siena, 3 books. A little book of the history of Plumbino. A work of elegances, On the Flowers of Eloquence. A discourse On Pleasure. An introductory little book On the Order of Learning, addressed to his son Nicolaus. A little book addressed to his dearer pupils, against the common opinion of many concerning the nine words, namely: Manes, Lucus, Bellum, Officium, Parca, Ludus, Ocium, Coelum, Eumenides. A little book On the Genius and the [unclear] genialis.

438 On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

The first lecture, when he had begun publicly to explain Virgil’s Aeneid. A little book On the Blessed Life. Plato’s book On the Bird Halcyon, translated from Greek speech into Latin. A treatise On the Seven Virtues, namely faith, hope, charity, also prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance. On the sacraments of bread and water, 1 book. On the marriages of the saints, 1 book. A little book of Flosculi, which explains in alphabetical order the force and usage of several words.

Augustinus Dodo, a Frisian, canon at Saint Leonard’s in Basel, once first collected the works of Saint Augustine; for the individual works he had learnedly prepared arguments and judgments on the works, since he was most studious, but plague carried him off at an untimely age in the year in which the work was to be begun, namely [unclear].

Augustinus Iustinianus of Genoa, of the Order of Preachers, bishop of Nebbio, arranged an Octaple Psalter in a handsome order, and rendered both Testaments from the Hebrew, Greek, and Chaldean truth into purer Latin expression.

He flourished under Leo X, Supreme Pontiff.

Augustinus Niphus, philosopher of Sessa, translated many little works of Aristotle and wrote not a few commentaries on them. He wrote a book On the Infinity of the First Mover, addressed to Cardinal Dominicus Grimanus.

And another book On the Immortality of the Human Soul, against the little book of the philosopher Petrus Pomponatius, and the following other little works:

On the Active Sense, 1 treatise. On the Beautiful, 1 book. On Auguries, 1 book. On the Calamities of Our Times, 1 book. On Courtly Affairs, 1 book. On the Comparison of Arms and Letters. On the Profit of Enmities. The Apology of Socrates. Aristotle’s Rhetoric. On the French Disease, 1 book. On the [unclear] figures of the stars, 1 book. On critical or decretory days, 1 book. On the false prediction of a flood, which was spread abroad from the conjunction of all the planets that will occur in Pisces in the year 1524, 1 book.

On Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II

Instructions on Ptolemy’s Apotelesmata, one book. A playful Dialectic; and he composed very many other works, a man worthy of immortality, under Charles V, emperor of the Romans.

Augustinus Steuchus of Gubbio, a canon regular of Saint Saviour, distinguished in every kind of wisdom, produced elegant annotations on the Pentateuch of Moses. Besides these he composed other works, of which he has the following:

On perennial philosophy, ten books, together with a little book on the name of Gubbio, his own city. Against the Lutherans, [unclear] books. The same man’s Cosmopoeia, or exposition on the fabric of the world from the three chapters of Genesis. The same man wrote very learned commentaries on forty-seven Psalms. He is still alive and is meditating many things under the most unconquered emperor of the Romans, Charles V, and Pope Paul III.

Avitus, a priest, a Spaniard by birth, translated into Latin Lucian’s book, written in Greek, on the revelation of the tomb and relics of the body of Saint Stephen, and, with his own letter added, gave it to the westerners through Orosius the priest.

[unclear]

Bachylus, bishop of Corinth, regarded as illustrious under the emperor Severus, wrote, in the person of all the bishops who were in Achaia, a book full of learning on Easter.

Bacciauius, a man of Christian philosophy, unencumbered and ready, deciding to devote himself to God, also chose pilgrimage in order to preserve his integrity. He is said to have published pleasing little works, but of them I have read only one, on faith, in which he satisfies the pontiff of the city against the querulous slanderers of his pilgrimage, declaring that he undertook the pilgrimage not from fear, in the manner of men, but for the sake of God, so that, going out from his land and from his kindred, he might become a co-heir of the patriarch Abraham.

Baptista Fulgosus wrote an incomparable work, arranged in nine books, on the memorable sayings and deeds of emperors, princes, dukes, bishops, priests, private persons, etc.; drawn partly from all the historiographers who exist anywhere, and partly illustrated by examples that occurred in his own age, of which there is the greater part, so that he can deservedly be called another Valerius Maximus, both on account of his native eloquence and on account of the variety of matters which he inserts everywhere.

In the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers

Barlaam, a Calabrian, a monk of Saint Basil, flourished at almost the same time as Francesco Petrarca. Learned in both languages, he gathered into one volume many things that pertain to the disciplines. Certain Greek little works of the same man are extant in Italy, namely: several letters; Logic, five books (elsewhere six); Geometry.

An arithmetical demonstration, or geometrical demonstration, on numbers. A theological speculation on the discovery of the feast of Easter. Sermons against the Latins on the Holy Spirit are extant at Rome. Little works by the same man and by various others on the procession of the Holy Spirit are there also.

Bartholomaeus Argentarius, an Italian by nation, a physician by profession, indeed an excellent and very learned man, proficient in both languages, collected an outstanding work of medical matters from Galen’s books for the use of students.

He is still illustrious in the year of salvation 1546, while Charles V, the most unconquered emperor of the Romans, is reigning.

Bartholomaeus Arnoldus of Usingen wrote a compendious summary of the whole of logic.

The same man’s Little Book of Natural Philosophy, or interpretation by figures and tables, in an epitome of the Physics, completed in three treatises. To these is appended a question on the quiddity of continuous quantity.

Bartholomaeus Cocles of Bologna, a distiller of medicine, surgeon, physiognomist, chiromancer, and geomancer, collected a revival of chiromancy and physiognomy from many, indeed almost innumerable, authors.

Bartholomaeus Latomus of Arlon was for a long time royal professor at Paris, and is now chief counsellor of the most reverend archbishop of Trier. He devoted much labor to students, both by dictating and by writing. Certain proofs of this distinguished talent are extant; of these the following are reported:

An oration on the praises of eloquence. A funeral oration at the obsequies of Richard, archbishop of Trier. A congratulatory poem on the coronation of the king of the Romans, addressed to Charles V Caesar and King Ferdinand, the august brothers. An oration on his departure for Italy. An epitome of the commentaries on the dialectical invention of Rudolph Agricola.

On ecclesiastical writers, Addition II.

The Dialectic and Rhetoric of the same man.

Commentaries on several speeches of Cicero.

Annotations on Cicero's Paradoxes, and on the books On Duties, On Friendship, On Old Age, On the Dream of Scipio, on Cicero's Topics addressed to Trebatius, and on the Oratorical Partitions of the same author.

He also wrote in the year of salvation 1544 to Martin Bucer, in the form of a little book, a lengthy letter. Then in the following year he published an elegant book against the same Bucer, in which the following headings are treated:

On the administration of the Eucharist. On the invocation of the Church. On the celibacy of priests.

And he is still meditating certain other works, renowned under Charles V, emperor of the Romans.

Bartholomaeus Merula of Mantua, apostolic protonotary and very skilled in sacred and profane letters, wrote learned commentaries on Ovid's books from Pontus.

Bartholomaeus Vespuccius of Florence, distinguished doctor of arts and medicine, composed some scattered annotations on the Sphere of Johannes de Sacrobosco. A very elegant oration by the same man is extant.

Basilius Zanchus of Bergamo, canon of the Lateran order, composed an epitome of Latin words from various authors.

By the same man, an appendix of the words which are lacking in the observations of Marius Nizolius on Cicero.

By the same author, commentaries on epithets have appeared.

Bassianus Landus of Piacenza, a learned young man, composed Iatrologia, or two dialogues, addressed to Hercules Este, duke of Ferrara, in which is contained a method for recognizing and curing diseases.

The same man wrote two books On Human History.

And he rendered several speeches of Demosthenes into Latin.

Beatus Rhenanus of Selestat, a man abundantly learned in secular letters and very well instructed in the divine Scriptures, reviewed many books of the orthodox fathers, worn away by age, and himself composed not a few volumes, among which these are reported:

On German Affairs, 3 books.

Annotations on the extant books of Titus Livius.

Annotations on Cornelius Tacitus, with a preface.

He revised the two books of P. Velleius Paterculus' Roman History.

Very lucid commentaries on the works of D. Tertullian, together with arguments and a preface.

442 Against the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

He prefixed a letter to the works of Origen.

On all the works of Erasmus of Rotterdam, a letter to Charles V, most unconquered emperor.

Commentaries on Seneca's play on the death of the emperor Claudius.

The Life of Johannes Geiler of Kaysersberg, written by the same man.

A preface to the Theophrastus of Aeneas, and to the gnomology of Xystus.

He translated two letters of Gregory Nazianzen to Themistius.

Preface and correction in the books of Pliny's Natural History.

He is still living today in his own homeland, namely in the year of salvation 1546, already an old man, and perhaps, as we hope, he will still deserve even more credit for good letters.

Beda Natalis, a Parisian theologian, wrote against certain false opinions of D. Erasmus of Rotterdam, and also of the Lutherans.

By the same author there appeared certain books on the single Magdalene, against Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples.

He flourished under Paul III and Charles V, in the year of the Lord 1536.

Benedictus Aretinus de Accoltis, a man greatly adorned with more polished learning, composed four books on the war waged by Christians for many years against the barbarians, for the recovery of Judaea and the holy sepulchre of Christ.

Benno the cardinal, archpriest of the Roman church, wrote the life and deeds of Hildebrand, who afterwards, having been made Roman pontiff, was called Gregory VII, in whose time he lived. There it is narrated why he was deposed, and certain other things are reported which no historian has yet published, neither Platina nor anyone else.

He flourished under Gregory VII, in the year of the Lord 1080.

Bernardinus Carvajal, bishop of Badajoz, a learned man and distinguished orator of the king of Spain, delivered at Rome, in the church of Saint Peter, before the senate of cardinals, after the death of Innocent VIII, an oration on electing the supreme pontiff.

Bernardus de Busti, a pious and learned man, wrote the Defence of the Mount of Piety, and the things that follow:

A counsel on buying back.

On the pact of buying back, in the first part of the Rosary.

Bernardus Lutzenburgus, monk of the Order of Preachers and prior of Cologne, wrote a catalogue of almost all the heretics who down to these times have everywhere been handed down in literary monuments, indicating their names, errors, and the times in which they lived, in [unclear] books.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

At the end he also makes mention of Martin Luther, the heresiarch. He flourished under Emperor Charles V, in the year of salvation 1531.

Bernardus Saracenus, a Venetian, a learned man, was the first of the more recent writers to write explanations and corrections on Plautus. He lived at the time of Georgius Valla.

[Bertrucius?] of Bologna composed a method for recognizing diseases, both particular and universal, in which he briefly explains the causes, signs, differences, and accidents of diseases.

Brigitta, a most holy widow, accustomed to divine converse and united to God by the perfection of inward charity, and also very famous for the prophetic spirit and for miracles, founded, at Christ’s command, a new religious order, called by her own name. She wrote on her prophecies and revelations a distinguished work, most edifying for all orders of the Church, and in every respect consonant with Catholic doctrines. She flourished in Sweden and at Rome around the year of the Lord [1350?].

Alisius of Piacenza, a canon regular, a learned and pious man, composed several excellent books, of which those set below report: two books. On Free Will against Luther, two books. And certain other works known to students.

Carolus Aretinus, formerly chancellor of Florence, learned in both languages, wrote certain comedies, from which Albertus de Eyb selected some sayings in his Poetic Pearl.

Carolus Verardus of Cesena, papal chamberlain, wrote the Baetican History, addressed to Raphael Riario, cardinal-deacon of St George, in several dialogues, about 20. He flourished while Innocent VIII presided, in the year of the Lord 1492.

Catharina of Siena, a nun of the Order of St Dominic, was the cause, through letters written to Gregory XI and by undertaking a journey, that he returned to Rome. Her writings, together with her prudence in speaking, can be compared with the great learning of theologians.

Christodulus, a monk, a man of most holy life, composed nine sermons against the Jews, which are extant in Greek at Rome in the Palatine library.

Christophorus Richerius Torichneus of Sens, royal chamberlain and secretary-chancellor of France, wrote five books on Turkish affairs, addressed to Francis, king of the French. He is still flourishing in the year 1546.

Chronicle

Chromatius, bishop of [Aquileia?], a man of rare integrity and, what is rare, as blessed Jerome testifies, a most learned bishop, composed a dissertation on the fifth and sixth chapters of Matthew, and an elegant declamation on the same fifth chapter.

Claudianus, priest of the church of Vienne, a man skilled in speaking and subtle in disputation, composed three books On the State, or On the Substance, of Souls, in which he pursues the intention of showing that there is something incorporeal besides God. Thus Gennadius.

Claudius of Auxerre, very skilled in scholastic theology, wrote a Summa and commentaries on the epistles of Paul.

Commodianus, while among secular writings he was also reading ours, received the occasion of faith; and so, having become a Christian and wishing to offer some gift of his studies to Christ, the author of his salvation, he wrote in a middling style, as if in verse, against the pagans. And because he had touched upon the writings of our fathers, he was better able to destroy their doctrines than to establish ours. Hence, when treating against them concerning the divine promises, he discoursed in a sufficiently mean and coarse sense, so to speak, striking amazement into them and despair into us. Following Tertullian, Lactantius, and Papias as authorities, he pursued sound moral doctrine, and especially love of voluntary poverty, very well, and impressed it upon students. He flourished before Gennadius.

Conradus Collin of the Order of Preachers, formerly prior and distinguished governor of the convent of Cologne, from his tender years imbibed no small learning in scholastic theology. He composed very lucid commentaries on the Prima Secundae of St Thomas Aquinas. He also wrote four books against Luther’s Epithalamium, and a seventh book on opinions or quodlibetal questions, and he would have published certain other works had not hostile death taken so great a man from us. He flourished in the year of restored salvation 1536. He died in the year 1536.

Conradus à Mure, first cantor and canon of the church of Zurich, a man of great knowledge, wrote the Fabularium, where he reviews the fables of the poets in alphabetical order, explaining chiefly the names of men and gods which are found among the poets, in a fairly large volume, which is preserved in manuscript in the library of the greater church at Zurich.

He also testifies that he wrote in verse on the natures of animals, emended the New Graecismus, and wrote several other things, which, as I found them at the end of the Fabularium, I shall append here.

Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

The New Graecismus has about 10,560 verses. A little book On the Sacraments, about 4,000. The Passion of the holy martyrs Felix and Regula and Exuperantius, about 3,000. A little book On the Proper Names of Rivers and Mountains, about 1,500. The Seats of the Romans, about 1,150. Praises of the Blessed Virgin, about 900. The [Clipearium?] of the Teutons, about 160. A Catalogue of the Roman Popes and Emperors, about 1,640. A Commendation of Rudolf, King of the Romans, about 800. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1275.

Conrad Peutinger, doctor of both laws, wrote Table-Talk Sermons, in which many things concerning the wondrous antiquities of Germany are related. The same man published an epitome On the Emigrations of Certain Peoples.

Conrad Summerhart of Calw, a Swabian, principal founder of the University of Tübingen and a theologian, wrote many works most pleasing to the learned, among which these are reported: Commentaries on the whole of physics. On Contracts, a large volume. Conclusions on the Sentences of Peter Lombard. Treatise I: That God Willed to Become Man. An oration to the fathers in the Hirsau chapter of the Order of Saint Benedict, On the Twelve Monastic Abuses. He flourished in the year 1501.

Cosimo Pazzi, archbishop of Florence, a man powerful in both languages, made Latin the 41 discourses of Maximus Tyrius the Platonist.

Cuthbert Tunstall, bishop of London, singular ornament and pillar of good letters, composed four books On the Art of Calculation. He flourished under Charles V Caesar.

Cinthio Giovanni Battista Giraldi of Ferrara, a man suited to the making of poems, wrote certain poems, and they are these: An Epicedion on the death of Lord Alfonso d’Este, prince. Hercules d’Este hailed as duke. One book of Elegies. Two books of Silvae. An Epithalamium on the marriage of Johann Sinapius. Three Eclogues.

On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

Certain things On the Parts of the Human Body. A letter On Change. And many other things which have not come down to us.

Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, often driven from the Church and received back, at last under the emperor Theodosius held the episcopate unshaken for eight years. His Catecheses are extant, which he composed in his youth.

Cyrus Theodorus Prodromus, a man zealous and learned in the divine scriptures, composed ancient and pious Greek epigrams. Arguments or chapters of each testament were composed by the same man in iambic tetrastichs of six-foot verses, and in heroic tetrastichs, which everywhere are joined beneath the iambics of the same meaning, not indeed on all the books, but on the Pentateuch, Joshua, Judges, and Kings. Likewise on the four Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles. And he composed very many other things, of which I shall append certain ones which have come down to us: Iambic and heroic tetrastichs on the three holy hierarchs, Gregory, Basil, and Chrysostom. Elegies in which he addresses the apostle Paul. Similar ones to Gregory the Theologian. Others on Basil the Great. Others on Chrysostom. Others to Gregory of Nyssa. Others on Saint Nicholas. He wrote An Exile of Friendship in six-foot iambics. Expostulatory verses On Providence. On Bareus, by whom he had rashly been called a heretic. On the Image of Life. Admonitory verses to the envious.

Daniel Barbaro, a Venetian patrician, doctor of arts, great-nephew of Ermolao, recently wrote refined commentaries on the five words of Porphyry. Likewise he published commentaries on the three books of Aristotle’s Rhetoric to Theodectes. Elegant letters of the same man to various persons are also extant. He is still flourishing in the year 1546.

On Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

Endowed with Greek and Latin eloquence, leaving his homeland, he came to Milan, where he applied himself equally to Latin letters and to theology.

He translated the books of Thomas Aquinas into the Greek language, which are preserved today in the Vatican Library.

He wrote Against Eunomius, on the Divinity of the Son. Finally returning, he stopped in Crete, where, having distributed his goods to the poor, he lived most holy in a certain monastery there, though without profession, and there likewise died, about two hundred years ago.

He also wrote On the Procession of the Holy Spirit, against Cabasilas, who had drawn his pen against St. Thomas Aquinas.

He rendered from Latin into Greek the book of Richard, a monk of the Order of Preachers, against the Mohammedan sect.

He similarly translated certain works of St. Augustine.

He published a book against a certain Palamas.

Sermons on Pentecost.

Also letters and dialogues, all of which survive in Greek in Italy, especially at Rome.

Desiderius Erasmus was born at Rotterdam, which is a town in Holland, a province of Lower Germany, in the first years of the reign of Frederick III, emperor; the restorer of the republic of letters and its foremost illuminator, he spent his life in the most celebrated cities and schools of Germany, France, England, and Italy. After countless labors expended for the sake of students, correcting ancient authors corrupted by the injury of time, translating Greek works, illuminating and explaining the New Testament and certain other things, and finally composing very many new works, he died at Basel in the year 1536.

Whoever wishes to know all his volumes should read his own letter written to Johannes Botzheimus Abstemius.

Dexter, son of Pacianus, famous among the learned and devoted to the faith of Christ, is said to have woven, for me, a comprehensive history, which I have not yet read. Thus St. Jerome.

Diego Hurtado de Mendoza, an illustrious man both by hereditary nobility and by learning and hidden wisdom, ambassador of Caesar’s Majesty among the Venetians, although occupied with the administration of the greatest affairs, nevertheless does not abandon his former studies of letters and philosophy. Especially well taught in philosophical and mathematical matters, he undertook a lucid paraphrase of the whole of Aristotle. He was likewise not only the author of the history of the Tunis expedition, but also, in good part, took charge of it together with his brothers. Many offspring of the most celebrated writers have, by his labor and industry, been restored to their former beauty, among which we have all the works of Flavius Josephus in Greek. He is still living in the year of salvation 1546, intending to restore several Greek copies to students.

Diodorus, bishop of Tarsus, was more renowned while he was a presbyter at Antioch. His commentaries on the Apostle are extant, and many other works, belonging rather to the style of Eusebius of Emesa; although he followed his sense, he could not imitate his eloquence, because of his ignorance of secular letters. He flourished in the time of St. Jerome.

Dominicus Nanus Mirabellius, a citizen of Alba and doctor of arts, wrote the Polyanthea, a very useful work, which partly, after the manner of a lexicon, explains not a few words in alphabetical order, and partly brings forward the opinions of every kind of writer on virtues, vices, and other commonplaces.

Donatus Acciaiolus, a citizen of Florence, translated from Plutarch’s Lives Hannibal and Demetrius. Nothing sweeter than his style could be wished for; its ease and ornament display the man’s most agreeable character.

Not only his learning is praised, but also the justice of his life.

He came forth from the school of Argyropylus; he died while on an embassy.

He left complete commentaries on Aristotle’s Ethics to Nicomachus, written learnedly and elegantly.

Donatus Bossius, a citizen of Milan, wrote chronicles, or books on the changes of human conditions, from the beginning of the world down to his own times.

Also on the bishops and archbishops of Milan down to the year 1489.

Dorotheus, a man distinguished by rare holiness, composed nineteen sermons in Greek, together with the lives of the holy fathers Antony, Sabbas the Younger, Euthymius, and Athanasius; on the martyrdom of Saints Eustratius, Auxentius, Eugenius, Mardarius, and Orestes. By the same author there is a certain Greek book without a title, and another On Love, and twenty-one chapters of teachings.

Also a monastic work. All survive in Greek at Rome in the pontifical library.

A certain Durandellus, a monk of the institute of St. Dominic, wrote against Durandus, of the same order, an opponent of St. Thomas; he began thus: “You thought that I would be wickedly like you; I shall rebuke you, I shall set it before your face.”

Edward Lee, an Englishman, wrote annotations against the annotations of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam on the New Testament,

To the Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II

He flourished at the time when Erasmus himself did, certainly at Louvain in the year 1520.

Clarundus, a man wonderfully experienced in affairs and in knowledge of the times, made this age illustrious with a splendid volume, which is entitled On the Genealogy of the Dukes of Burgundy, Brabant, Flanders, Holland, etc., from Hector the Trojan down to Charles V.

Ephraim, Greek by nation, a man well instructed in the liberal arts, wrote the lives of the emperors of Constantinople in iambic verse. He flourished 200 years ago.

Epiphanius, prelate of Selybria, or Olybria, a man not a little practiced in sacred letters, published a very useful book against the burners of images.

Erveus, a monk of the order of St. Dominic, very skilled in philosophy, composed commentaries, in a rough style but learned, on the logic and philosophy of Aristotle.

Eusebius, a Sardinian by nation, and, from being reader of the city of Rome, bishop of Vercelli, banished for confession of the faith by the emperor Constantius to Scythopolis and thence to Cappadocia, returned to the church under the emperor Julian and published commentaries on the Psalms by Eusebius of Caesarea, which he had translated from Greek into Latin. He died in the reigns of Valentinian and Valens.

Euthymius Zygadenus, a monk, a diligent compiler of sacred literature, wrote expositions on all the Psalms, which are extant in Greek at Rome. The same man carefully collected an interpretation of the epistles of Paul from Chrysostom and various other fathers.

Euzoius, while a youth, was educated at Caesarea under the rhetor Thespesius together with Gregory Nazianzen the bishop; and, as bishop of that same city, with very great labor he attempted to restore on parchment the corrupted library of Origen and Pamphilus. At the last he was driven from the church under the emperor Theodosius. Various and manifold treatises of his are reported, which were extant in the time of St. Jerome.

Fabianus of Monte San Savino, having a certain exact knowledge of jurisprudence, wrote on the alienation of ecclesiastical property in the treatise On Purchase. Likewise, On Buying and Selling.

Felix Malleolus, a Swiss of Zurich, doctor of decrees, once cantor of the church in his homeland, composed many little works not unworthy of the learned, of which we shall add the catalogue here:

Against the Strong Mendicants. A Recapitulation of the same.

Against anchorites, Beghards, and woodland Beguines.

A Description of the Lollards. On the Business of Monks.

A Gloss on the Bulls Obtained by the Beghards.

On Parish Priests and Mendicant Religious.

On Religious Proprietors, Preaching the Lord’s Precepts.

The Tenor of a Letter Sent from Heaven by the Patrons of the Church of Zurich, against those negligent in divine worship.

A Treatise on the Institution of New Divine Offices.

On Money Offered and Paid for Receiving a Prebend or Benefice in Churches or Monasteries.

A Dialogue on the Jubilee Year.

On Blessings of the Air to be Performed with the Sacrament.

A Treatise on Exorcisms. Another Treatise of Exorcisms.

On Credence to be Given to Demons.

On Drawing the Press-Tree on a Feast Day.

On Marriage or Betrothals.

On the Theft of Relics and Other Things Recently Miraculously Committed and Carried Out by Three Persons in the Monastery of the Blessed Virgin of the Place of the Hermits, and Finally Found and Recovered.

A Letter against a Certain Proud Cleric.

A Form of Appeal against a Certain Cardinal Who in Germany Wished to Enter a Cathedral Church.

On Ecclesiastical Liberty. On the Occasion of Good and Evil.

On Buying and Selling One for Twenty.

On Contracts Which Are Called Hostageships, and in the Vernacular Gisel.

A Doctorate in Folly. The Tenor of the Letter of Doctorate in Folly.

Against Unjust Judges.

A Dialogue on the Consolation of Those Unjustly Oppressed.

The Passionale of the same man. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1454.

Felix Petantius, chancellor of Segna, wrote a book to Vladislaus, king of Hungary and Bohemia, on the routes by which the Turks should be attacked. This book ought to be read by our princes in this unhappy age, so that the bloody enemy of Christians may be attacked to greater advantage than up to now.

Florentius Volusenus, a young man of keen intellect, wrote a theological oration, or a pious and learned commentary.

A certain celebrated work of the same man is extant, entitled On Tranquillity of Mind,

Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

He is still living in the year of the Lord 1546; from him we expect great usefulness that will come to scholars, if the powers above prolong his life.

Franciscus de Accoltis of Arezzo, well trained in jurisprudence, wrote on the whole civil law.

He also wrote Consilia.

On the Difference between an Interlocutory and a Definitive Sentence.

He rendered the Letters of Diogenes into Latin.

He dedicated to Pope Pius a little book by an uncertain author, On the Baths of Pozzuoli and the Neighboring Ones, found and published by him in Italy.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 1300.

Franciscus Capuanus of Manfredonia, formerly public professor of astronomy in the University of Padua, wrote commentaries on the Theoricae planetarum of Georgius Purbachius.

Franciscus Craneveldius of Nijmegen, J.C. and councillor of the Imperial Majesty, in his preface to the books On the Truth of the Christian Faith by Ioannes Lodovicus Vives, discusses a number of matters concerning the excellence of those volumes, the manner of writing, and also the author himself.

The same man translated into Latin style the six books of Procopius the rhetor and historiographer On the Buildings of the Emperor Justinian.

He is still living under Emperor Charles V, in the year of the Lord 1546.

Franciscus Emericus of Opava, a Viennese physician, having exact knowledge of the medical art, among other things published a book On the Proper Use of Medical Aids, according to the true mind of Hippocrates and Galen.

Franciscus Macerata, of the Order of Minors, composed summaries of the individual chapters in the seven books of Josephus On the Jewish War, which serve in place of an epitome.

Franciscus Maturancius of Perugia, highly skilled in every kind of liberal art, wrote commentaries on the Philippic orations of M. Tullius Cicero, and on the books On Duties, also on the Paradoxes and the books of Rhetoric.

Franciscus Romeus of Castiglione, of the Order of Preachers, who, having concern for his profession, imbibed sacred letters from his earliest years, wrote a learned and elegant book On the Freedom and Necessity of Works, against Christian pseudo-philosophers.

The same man published a brief annotation concerning the immortality of the soul, derived in a Christian and Peripatetic manner, as the title of the book has it.

Franciscus Titelmannus of Hasselt, of the Order of the Friars Minor, a most vigilant professor of sacred Scripture among the Louvain scholars, commended himself to posterity by many excellent books, among which we have been able to find these:

An Apologetic Epistle.

A Compendium of Natural Philosophy, gathered into twelve books.

On Dialectical Consideration, 6 books.

Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans.

Paraphrases on all the epistles of Saint Paul.

Most lucid commentaries on the whole Psalter.

And he published very many other things, which are found here and there in booksellers’ shops.

He flourished at the time of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam.

Franciscus Valleriola, a very celebrated physician of Avignon, wrote commentaries on the six books of Galen On Diseases and Symptoms. He is still living under Francis of Valois, king of the French, composing many things.

Franciscus Vatablus, royal professor of the Hebrew language at Paris, a man most adorned with liberal arts, rendered into Latin Aristotle’s Little Natural Works, as they are called. He also revised the paraphrases on all the physical works of Aristotle published by Jacobus Faber.

The same man wrote annotations on the Pentateuch of Moses.

He is still living in the year 1546.

Fridericus Nausea, theologian and J.C., now bishop of Vienna in Austria, an outstanding cultivator of profane letters and sufficiently learned in sacred letters, wrote many little works. Among them these are reported:

Lenten sermons, earlier, later, and Advent sermons.

Prague sermons.

A homiliary of four centuries, on the season and on the saints.

Commentaries on Tobias.

The Life of the Apostles.

On Marvels.

Fragments.

Continuations.

What Councils Are, and Whence.

Panegyrics.

A Monody on D. Erasmus of Rotterdam, together with a catalogue of all Erasmus’s lucubrations, and his life and death.
