Gaius, under Zephyrinus, bishop of the city of Rome, that is, under Antoninus, son of Severus, held a very notable disputation against Proculus, a follower of Montanus, accusing him of rashness in defending the new prophecy; and in the same volume, enumerating only thirteen letters of Paul, he says that the fourteenth, which is said to be to the Hebrews, is not his; and even among the Romans down to the present day it is not regarded as being, as it were, by Paul the apostle.

Gaspar Sasgerus, otherwise Schatzgerus, a Minorite, having early acquired no slight learning in sacred Scripture, drew his pen, as befits a soldier of Christ, against the pestilential offspring of the Lutherans. And although he showed himself a strong antagonist in many works, he did this especially in two books, which are entitled On the Dissolubility of Marriages and On the Sacrifice of the Mass.

I know that the man labored over many other works, but I do not have the titles of the books; therefore I would rather play the Angerona in this matter than ascribe false titles of books.

He flourished under Emperor Charles V.

Geminus, priest of the Church of Antioch, composed a few monuments of his talent, flourishing under the emperor Alexander and Zebennus, bishop of his city, especially at that time when Heraclas was ordained pontiff of the Alexandrian church.

Gemma Frisius, physician and distinguished professor of mathematics among the Louvain scholars, wrote a method of arithmetic, and certain things on the description of places and on finding their distances.

Likewise, booklets on the use of the astronomical ring, recently enlarged by the same man. He also wrote a chart, which they commonly call a map, more elegant than those which we have seen up to now.

He is still distinguished under Emperor Charles V, 1546.

Gennadius Scholarius, a man well learned in divine letters, wrote certain excellent little works. Those which follow are extant with the illustrious man Diego, for thus the Italians call Jacobus, Hurtado [unclear] de Mendoza, the emperor’s ambassador among the Venetians.

George, a certain Greek monk, distinguished in knowledge of histories, wrote Chronicles from the creation of the world down to the reign of Nicephorus Botaniates, under whom he flourished; these exist in manuscript at Venice in the library of Saints John and Paul.

George Wicelius, a German, a man, besides his other innumerable gifts of mind, learned even to a marvel, highly skilled in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin languages, excelling in outstanding talent and renowned for rare learning, throughout his whole life does and meditates nothing except that, both by writing and by teaching publicly in the schools from the pulpit, he may instruct and educate the holy people of Jesus Christ.

It has seemed good to append a catalogue of the works which he wrote, for the benefit of students.

In Defense of Good Works, against the new Evangelists.

The cause of the so long-lasting calamity of the ecclesiastical estate in Germany.

He is still living in the year of the Lord 1546, intending, if God gives him a longer life, to write certain other works for students.

Germanus, archbishop of Constantinople, adorned himself with sacred letters while he was still a boy; whence it came about that he published many little works not unworthy of reading.

A Greek sermon of the same man, on the limits of life, is extant in Italy.

Germanus Brixius of Auxerre, canon of Paris, a man learned in both languages, wrote many things, of which the following are reported:

Antimorus, a poem against Thomas More, the Englishman.

Four congratulatory letters.

An elegy on the death of Francis Deloinus.

And certain poems and letters.

He translated the dialogue of St. John Chrysostom on the dignity and burden of a bishop, in 6 books.

Eight homilies on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.

He is still flourishing under Francis, king of the French, in the year 1546.

Gertrude, a learned virgin, joined familiarly to God by the perfection of outstanding holiness and accustomed to heavenly revelations, published, at the institution of the Holy Spirit, the Book of the Insinuations of Divine Piety, very consolatory to pious minds, divided into 5 books.

And she flourished in the monastery of Helfede at Eisleben, about the year of the Lord 1300.

Gervasius Riccobaldus of Ferrara, as a man in his time most devoted to antiquity, wrote a history of the pontiffs down to his own times, that is, to the year of the Lord 1300.

Gratiadeus, a monk of the Order of St. Dominic, and skilled in sacred Scripture and philosophy, wrote a summa of the whole of logic. The same man also wrote great and small questions in physics.

Gregory, archbishop of Constantinople, since he had imbibed sacred Scripture from the cradle, in mature age offered a brilliant proof of this matter. He wrote 29 elegant sermons, and 18 other addresses.

In the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

A collection and exposition by the same man, [unclear], are extant in Greek at Rome in the Vatican Library.

Gregory Baeticus, bishop of Elvira, composed various treatises in a moderate style up to extreme old age, and an elegant book on faith.

He flourished in the time of St. Jerome, about the year of the Lord 400.

Gregory, patriarch of Cyprus, collected proverbs in alphabetical order; these are extant at Rome in the Vatican Library.

By the same man: Against Beccus Joannes, The Tome of the Holy Synod, or Pillar of Orthodoxy; On Measures; On Faith; On the Predicaments.

Gregory, bishop of Antioch, a most learned man and of a certain singular integrity, wrote certain sermons in Greek, namely: On the Burial of Christ; On Joseph of Arimathea; On the divine resurrection of the Lord after three days. They are preserved at Rome.

Gregory, metropolitan of Corinth, wrote on the canons of the κοιμήσων of the divine Virgin and of the Annunciation, moreover on the feast of the Lord’s Antipascha, that is, on the touching by Thomas, on the assumption of the great God and Savior Jesus, and on Pentecost.

A poem by the same man on the first feast of the venerable death of Cosmas the monk.

A Greek volume with this inscription is preserved at Rome in the Vatican Library.

Gregory Olympiadas, a man well learned in Greek literature, left to posterity splendid monuments of his talent, among which there is extant a Greek exposition on the Song of Songs and the Proverbs of Solomon, which is still found in Italy, not yet printed.

Guido Bonatus, otherwise Bonacius, a mathematician of Forlì, learned in the knowledge of the stars, wrote ten treatises on astronomy. He flourished under Martin IV, supreme pontiff, in 1282.

Guido of Ravenna, a priest six hundred years ago, wrote a history of the pontiffs.

A history by the same man on the war of the Goths is extant.

Guilhelmus Puteanus Blangiacus, a physician and citizen of Grenoble in France, a man of much learning and excellent talent, wrote a defense of John Mesue the physician, that aloe opens the mouths of the veins, and no few other similar things to be said, against John Manardus and Leonardus Fuchsius and many other newer physicians, a work not a little useful for knowing the powers of simple medicines. On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

Hadrianus, priest-cardinal of the title of St. Chrysogonus, [Batonien̄], composed many very distinguished books, since he was a man of great learning; of these the following circulate:

On Latin speech, or modes of speaking Latin, one book. A Hunt addressed to Cardinal Ascanio, in Phalaecian verses. The Journey of Julius II, Roman pontiff, in heroic verses. On True Philosophy, four books, compiled from the four doctors of the Church.

He flourished under Julius II, supreme pontiff, and Maximilian.

Haymo and Strabo, brothers of Bede, also learned men, of whom the one wrote certain not unlearned homilies, the other on Genesis.

Heliodorus of Antioch, priest, extraordinarily practiced in sacred letters, published an excellent volume on virginity, furnished with holy Scriptures.

Henricus Bebelius of Justingen, German by nation, poet laureate, wrote an art of composing poems, corrected and enlarged by him, together with his [racamationes] or observations to be followed in verse. By the same: The Instruction of Boys; The Triumph. And many other things, among which are those scurrilous jests, by no means worthy of a free, much less a Christian and learned, man.

He flourished under Emperor Maximilian, in the year 1514.

Henricus Glareanus, a Swiss from the district of Glarus, poet laureate, was the first, or among the first, of the men of our nation successfully to learn good letters, and to teach them publicly. He professed for some time at Basel; then he moved to Freiburg, a town of Breisgau, where he is still living today, a very old man, if I am not mistaken, and still teaches. He is to be praised on this account, that he cultivated several liberal arts, antiquity, and histories excellently, and illustrated them by writings. Of those which have come into our hands, these are:

Scholia on Aelius Donatus’s method concerning the eight parts of speech. An Introduction to Arithmetic. A Description of the Situation of Switzerland and the Neighboring Peoples. A Panegyric on the League of the Four Swiss Peoples. A Panegyric for the Most Just League of the Swiss. An Introduction to Music. On Geography, one book. A Judgment on the verses of P. Terentius throughout all the comedies.

In Abbot Span[heim], On Writings.

Annotations on Horace. Annotations on Ovid’s Metamorphoses. Annotations on Cicero’s book On Old Age. Annotations on the fragments of Sallust’s Histories. Annotations on the commentaries of C. Julius Caesar. Annotations on Titus Livius. Chronology for the whole of Roman history. He revised Dionysius of Halicarnassus and illustrated him with annotations, and added a chronography of the times comprised in Dionysius’s history. Two books of elegies. And he is said to have published certain other things.

He flourishes under Emperor Charles V, in the year 1546.

Henricus Suso, a Swabian, of the Order of St. Dominic, an excellent preacher, renowned for holiness of life and also for miracles, wrote some works both in Latin and in German which powerfully kindle the mind to the love of God. Of these there is extant in Latin:

The Clock of Eternal Wisdom. And One Hundred Articles on the Passion of the Lord.

He flourished around the year of the Lord 1350.

Hermannus Torrentinus, a German, almost the most learned among the grammarians of his age and nation, wrote commentaries on the first part of Alexander’s Doctrinale, with the interpretation of words, some faulty, superfluous, and obscure verses being either rejected or changed into truer and clearer ones.

There are also extant by the same man commentaries on Virgil’s Bucolics and Georgics. He also published a Poetic Elucidarium.

He flourished under Maximilian in the year of the Lord 1500.

Hermas, whom the apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans, “Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas,” etc., is said to be the author of the book which is called The Shepherd, and in certain churches of Greece it is even read publicly. It is truly a useful book, and many of the ancient writers have employed testimonies from it; but among the Latins it is almost unknown.

Hieronymus Cardanus of Castiglione, a Milanese physician, a man not unlearned, composed two books On Consolation.

There is extant by the same man a most complete Arithmetic.

Hieronymus Bagolinus of Verona, skilled in the philosophical art, wrote annotations on Averroes’s compendium on Aristotle’s Prior Analytics. He translated the commentaries of John the Grammarian Philoponus on Aristotle’s books On Generation and Corruption. Trans

Honoratus Massiliensis ecclesiae episcopus, vir eloquens et amp; abs- que vllo linguae impedimento, ex tempore in Ecclesia declama- tor, &amp; quia à pueritia in timore Dei crescens, etiam in negocijs ec- clesiasticis exercitus est, os suum quasi armarium scripturarum aperit, &amp; in homiliarum modum, ad vtilitatem legentium multa componit, maximèqƺ ad colẽdam fidei rationem, &amp; reuincendam hereticorum peruersitatem, Sanctorum patrum vitas ad aedificationem posteriorum coaptat ipse legendas, praecipue nutritoris sui sancti Hilarij Arelatensis epi- scopi, litanias ad supplicandum Dei clemētiā cum plebe sibi cre dita pro viribus agit. Iacobus Locher Philomusus,natione Germanus,vtriusqƺ lin- guae peritissimus,varia carmine et amp; pedestri oratione scripsit,ex q̃- bus,quae nos in lucem edita vidimus,haec sunt: Compendium Rhetorices. On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

He also translated Alexander of Aphrodisias's moral and natural questions, and those on fate.

Hieronymus Fracastorius, physician, very elegantly wrote in heroic verse three books of Syphilis, or On the French Disease, addressed to Pietro Bembo. By the same author: Homocentrica; and On the Causes of Critical Days, Through Those Things Which Are in Us. He is still distinguished under Emperor Charles V, in the year 1546.

Hieronymus Gaebuilerus, outstanding in knowledge of sacred and profane letters, composed many excellent works, of which a great many are still extant, namely an Exhortation to Holy Communion; an Epitome of the Royal and Most Ancient Origin of Emperor Charles V and of Ferdinand, King of Hungary and Bohemia, and of all the Archdukes of Austria and Counts of Habsburg. He flourished in the year 1530.

Honoratus, bishop of the church of Marseille, an eloquent man and without any impediment of speech, an extempore declaimer in the Church, and, because from boyhood he grew up in the fear of God and was also practiced in ecclesiastical affairs, opens his mouth like an armory of the Scriptures, and, in the manner of homilies, composes many things for the profit of readers, and especially for cultivating the reasoning of faith and refuting the perversity of heretics.

He adapts the lives of the holy fathers to be read for the edification of later generations, especially that of his nurturer, Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles; he performs litanies for supplicating the clemency of God with the people entrusted to him, as far as he is able. He flourished at the time when Gennadius lived.

Jacobus Hochstratus, of the order of St. Dominic, Prior of Cologne and a most diligent inquisitor of heretical depravity, brought forth several productions against the enemies of the Church. He wrote an Apology and Destruction of the Cabala against Johannes Reuchlin. The same man wrote On Faith and Works, 1 book; On Purgatory, 1 book; On the Veneration of the Saints, 1 book; On Christian Liberty, 4 books, against Luther; Against Concubinary Priests, 1 book; also the Pearl of Moral Philosophy; and many other little works against heretics. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1512; he died in 1527.

Jacobus Monachus, a pious and learned man, wrote certain Greek sermons which are preserved in Italy, namely: On the [unclear]; On the Conception of the Virgin Mary; On the Twelve Tribes of Israel; again, On the Conception and Generation; On the Holy of Holies; “[unclear],” etc.

462 On the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

Jacobus Henrichmannus of Sindelfingen, at the rebirth of good letters, published Grammatical Institutes for the benefit of students, with an exhortation to tender youth that it eliminate barbarism and study eloquence. He flourished in the year of salvation 1506.

Jacobus Locher Philomusus, a German by nation, highly skilled in both languages, wrote various works in verse and prose. Of those which we have seen published, these are: Compendium of Rhetoric; Syntax on Composing a Funeral Oration; Epode on the Death of Pluto and the Other Demons; Poem on Night, Wine, and Woman; Dialogue on the Eminence of the Four Doctors of the Church. He flourished at the time when Reuchlin lived.

Jacobus Picoloninus, Cardinal of Pavia, wrote very elegant letters, very full of recondite matters, together with most lucid commentaries containing the events of his own time, along with certain other works not previously printed.

Jacobus, Count of [Purililiatum?], a most learned man, wrote a little work on the generous education of children, no less delightful than useful. He flourished around the year of the Lord 1480.

Jacobus Sadoltus, bishop of Carpentras, a most learned man and no ordinary imitator of the Ciceronian style, wrote On the Right and Liberal Instruction of Children, and published both other books and commentaries, which learned men love exceedingly and turn over with diligent labor. They are these: On the Praises of Philosophy, 1 book; On the Kingdom of Hungary, Oppressed by the Turkish Enemies, 1 homily; Hortatory Oration on Undertaking War against the Turks, addressed to Louis, King of the French; Commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans, 3 books; Interpretation of Three Psalms, namely 50, 93, and 95; On

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

On the death of Cardinal Federico Fregoso, one homily. He also wrote very many letters. He flourished under Emperor Charles V, in the year of salvation 1530.

Jacobus Spiegel of Schlettstadt, German by nation, skilled in both laws and in languages, by many nights of study commended himself to posterity as one to be admired; among these works, the following are reported under his name:

An Explanation on Johannes Reuchlin's Progymnasmata.

An exposition on the poem of Gianfrancesco Pico on the mystery of the Lord's Cross, recently come down into Germany.

Scholia on the twelve books of Richard Bartholinus's Austrias and on the poet Gunther's work on the deeds of Emperor Frederick.

Scholia on the four books of Antonius Panormita, On the Sayings and Deeds of Alfonso, King of Aragon.

A Lexicon of Civil Law.

He is still living in the year of the Lord 1546.

Jacobus Tusanus, French by nation, public professor of the Greek language at Paris, translated certain parts of Theodore Gaza's grammar into Latin.

Likewise the Greek passages which are found in Angelo Poliziano's books.

He also translated the Greek letters of Guillaume Budaeus and added scholia from Budaeus's own replies.

He flourishes under Francis of Valois, king of the French, 1546.

Jacobus Peretz of Valencia, bishop of Christopolis and a most observant member of the order of the Hermits of Saint Augustine, wrote expositions on all the Psalms of David.

Likewise on the official Canticles, or, as he himself calls them, the ferial and evangelical together, and the remaining ecclesiastical canticles.

To these were added treatises against the Jews, and an exposition on the Song of Songs of Solomon.

Janus Parrhasius, also called Neapolitanus, of Cosenza, Italian by nation, flourished and taught at Milan around the year of the Lord 1500. He wrote a compendium of rhetoric excerpted from the best authors of both languages.

Commentaries by the same man on Claudian's work On the Rape of Proserpina.

Janus Vitalis of Palermo, a man exquisitely learned in divine scripture, wrote hymns to the Holy Trinity. Likewise The Triumph of Ferdinand Francesco d'Avalos of Aquino, the great marquis of Pescara.

The Laments of the same man on that same commander, and a certain poem entitled Archangelus. Some epigrams of his are also extant.

In the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

Idacius, a distinguished Spaniard, a very great defender of the Catholic faith against the Arians, wrote a book against Varimadus the Arian. There was also added an explanation of certain very difficult passages concerning the Trinity.

Ignatius, deacon and skeuophylax of the Great Church of Constantinople, who was metropolitan of Nicaea, a grammarian, wrote lives of the holy and blessed patriarchs Tarasius and Nicephorus, funeral elegies, letters, iambics, against Thomas Antartes, the so-called [unclear], and many other things.

Pope Innocent VIII wrote two letters to Angelo Poliziano: one in which he thanks him and sends him two hundred gold pieces for the dedication of the translated Herodian.

The other to Lorenzo de' Medici, in commendation of Poliziano himself.

Joachimus Perionius of Cormery, French by nation, a monk by profession, translated into Latin certain books of the ancient Greeks, especially of Aristotle, with such polish and elegance of style, rivaling Cicero, that no one seems to have taken this praise away from him. Day by day we expect more monuments of so great a talent; but the works we have seen up to now were all written at Paris, where the author resides. He is still flourishing in the year of salvation 1546.

Johannes Atrocianus, German by nation, a learned Catholic man of our time, published certain grammatical commentaries on the common book of Macer On the Powers of Herbs.

An elegy by the same man on the Peasants' War.

Some more select epigrams.

No Evangelical, a little book written in verse. He is planning many other things under Emperor Charles V.

Johannes Baptista Egnatius of Venice, a priest and public professor of humane letters in his native city, wrote three books on the Roman princes or Caesars, from Caesar the Dictator to Constantine Palaiologos, and then from Charlemagne to Emperor Maximilian.

Likewise annotations on the lives of the Caesars whom Suetonius mentions.

On the Origin of the Turks, one book.

Observations on Ovid.

A panegyric on the king of the French.

Gleanings, which interpret some of the more obscure passages of authors.

On Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

Johannes Bernardus Felicianus, a Venetian, a man learned in Greek and Latin, translated many things from Greek physicians, philosophers, and theologians, and is still continuing in translation, namely in the year 1546. For he has almost finished that “golden chain,” as they call it, or the Greek interpretation of Oecumenius on the Acts of the Apostles, on Paul’s epistles and those of others. He translated Galen’s books On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato.

On the anatomy of the womb, one book.

On the formation of fetuses, one book.

He translated book 6 of Paul of Aegina, on surgery.

He made Latin Alexander of Aphrodisias’s explanation on the first book of Aristotle’s Prior Analytics.

Likewise he endowed with Latin Aristotle’s ten books of Ethics, with the explanations of Eustratius, Aspasius, Michael of Ephesus, and some other Greeks.

Johannes Caesarius of Julich, a German by nation, helped the cause of letters not inconsiderably by his studies, and entered into great favor among all students. He is still living, in the year 1546, a very old man, in Cologne. The catalogue of all his books and commentaries is this:

A learned Dialectic. A most elegant Rhetoric.

Commentaries on Jodocus Clichtoveus’s Introduction to the Knowledge of Terms. A geometrical epitome.

He corrected the work of Diomedes the grammarian.

He corrected and illustrated with scholia the books of C. Plinius Secundus on the medicine of fishes.

Likewise Paulus Jovius’s book on Roman fishes.

He rescued the whole work of C. Plinius Secundus’s Natural History from innumerable errors.

He revised the five books of Severinus Boethius On the Consolation of Philosophy.

And many other works still unknown to us.

Johannes Chrysostomus Zanchus, an Italian by nation, brother of Basilius Zanchus, wrote five books On the Origin of the Orobians or Cenomani, addressed to Pietro Bembo, and a panegyric to Charles V, emperor, in an elegant style.

Johannes Cochlaeus of Nuremberg, a German by nation, applied himself to theology in Italy, where he also obtained the insignia of the doctorate, as they call it. He was once dean at Frankfurt, at the church of the Blessed Virgin, in the year 1520. Today he resides in the city of Eichstatt, now advanced in age.

In the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

I hear that many works have been written and published by him. But those which I have seen are these:

Rudiments of grammar.

An expostulation against the new reformation in the Church of the senate of Bern among the Swiss.

A little book On the Authority of Canonical Scripture and the Catholic [Church], against Heinrich Bullinger.

A brief reply against Heinrich Bullinger’s lengthy response on the authority of Scripture and the Church.

A defense of the priesthood and sacrifice against the gnawings of Wolfgang Musculus.

A skirmish against Andreas Osiander’s four conjectures about the end of the world.

On the purgatory of souls, one book.

Six Philippics against Philip Melanchthon.

A discussion on the new Hebrew translations of Holy Scripture.

One little book On the Power of a General Council.

A refutation of the fifty articles that were disputed at Wittenberg.

Seventy propositions in a general council.

Nycticorax.

He is still living as an old man, composing many things, in the year of salvation 1546.

Johannes Cono of Nuremberg, a German by nation, a monk of the Dominican order, added Greek to Jerome’s books when they were first being printed at Basel. He translated Gregory Nazianzen’s oration on Gregory of Nyssa, and Basil the Great’s little book On the Difference between Essence and Hypostasis, and restored Gregory of Nyssa’s book On Man to its native splendor.

Johannes Despauterius of Ninove, a German by nation, published a most elegant grammar and a Recrimination against an adversary. He flourished in the year of salvation 1539.

Johannes Dietenberger, a most profound professor of theology, for so the inscription has it, and inquisitor of heretical depravity, brought to light the Phimositomum or Confutatory of the Scripturarians and Lutheran brethren. A treatise of the same man on divorce was added to it. He also translated the Bible into German. He flourished in the year of salvation 1527.

Johannes Driedo, once an outstanding professor of Holy Scripture among the Louvain scholars, published many volumes against the Lutherans, of which learned men circulate the following:

To the Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

On grace and free will, book 1. On the harmony of free will. On the captivity and redemption of the human race, 4 books. On ecclesiastical writings. He flourished in our century under Charles V, around the year of the Lord 1550.

John Eck, a Swabian, German by nation, doctor and sincere and indefatigable defender of theology, died recently after writing and publishing many things in Latin and German, among which are these:

Homilies throughout the whole year, on the temporal cycle and the saints.

A commentary on Haggai.

On the primacy of Peter, or of the supreme pontiff, against Luther.

A letter on the method of his studies.

On the sacrifice of the Mass, to Sigismund, king of Poland, 2 books.

The same, on the sacrifice of the Mass. A handbook of commonplaces against Luther.

Chrysopassus, or On Predestination, 6 centuries.

He also translated the Bible into the German language.

He also wrote many letters to various persons.

Reply.

An apology by the same against the filth of Bucer.

He is said to have written certain other innumerable works, a man worthy of immortality, and one who would have published several more, had not jealous death denied him to us. He died in the year of the Lord 1543.

John Fabri, German by nation, bishop of Vienna, a very learned man, who died a few years ago, wrote many excellent works, of which this is the catalogue:

Commentaries on the Institutes.

On books 1 and 2 of the Code.

On faith and works, book 1.

Against Doctor Balthasar Pacimontanus, the first author of the Anabaptists of our age, a defense of the orthodox Catholic faith.

A little book on the victory won among the Swiss.

A refutation of the six articles of Huldrych Zwingli.

A German letter to Huldrych Zwingli, book 1.

On the Eucharist. The Hammer of Heretics.

Sermons on the Eucharist, Victory against the Turks, Patience, and the Baptism of Little Children.

In the Abbot of Sponheim, On Ecclesiastical Writers.

A funeral oration by the same in praise of Lady Margaret, duchess of Austria, etc.

He composed very many other works, which were consigned to Vulcan by the heretics. He flourished, if I am not mistaken, in the year of the Lord 1536.

John Fisher, bishop of Rochester in England, a very learned man and a most keen champion of the Catholic faith, endowed also with the crown of martyrdom under Henry VIII, king of the English, and made famous because of his constant profession of the Catholic faith, wrote against Oecolampadius for the truth of the body and blood of Christ in the Eucharist, and against Luther for the Mass, and against Jacques Lefevre d'Etaples on the single Mary Magdalene.

And many other works, although not yet brought to light because of the savagery of the storms of the present age. He flourished in the year of Christ's birth 1535.

John Hoffmeister, a Swabian by homeland, of the institute of Saint Augustine, and a well-deserving provincial of the same order, commended himself to our age by innumerable little works. From these the following are listed:

A dialogue against the followers of the Lutheran gospel.

On the sacrifice of the Mass, book 1.

Commentaries on two epistles of Paul addressed to the Corinthians.

Expositions on Paul's Epistle to the Philippians.

Commentaries on Matthew.

Exegeses on Tobias.

Three sermons, in German.

And certain other works, which, if those above prolong his life, he will publish for the benefit of students. He is still living, a man worthy of ambrosia and nectar, in the year of Christ 1546.

John Ulrich of Basel, of the Order of Preachers, a man whom you would call learning itself and sincerity of faith, while still a young man acquired such knowledge of Greek expression as scarcely one or another of his age possessed.

He detected innumerable errors in the translation of Theophylact.

He also wrote Greek commentaries on Paul's Epistle to the Hebrews.

He died at Colmar in the year of salvation 1536, a young man.

John Lanspergius, a Bavarian, a member of the Cologne Carthusian house, and for some time vicar there, and afterwards prior at Cantave near Julich, a man devoted to God and learned, and excellently instructed in the spiritual life, and enlightened by the Holy Spirit, wrote in an elegant and devout style:

Sermons on the temporal cycle for the whole year. Ser-

Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

Capitular sermons on the principal feasts of the whole year. On the struggle, or passion, of the Lord, 3 books. On the true Christian religion, addressed to the divine Charles, the fifth emperor of this name, ever Augustus, 1 book. The Handbook of Christian Warfare, 1 book. The Scholastic Quiver, 1 book. The Mystical Quiver of Divine Love, 1 book. A work of letters to various persons, 1 book. A Dialogue between a Monk and a Soldier, 1 book. The Mirror of Christian Perfection, 1 book. The Life of the Savior, with various rosaries. He also wrote some things in German against the Lutherans. He further published learned dedicatory letters, although under the names of others, before the books of D. Dionysius the Carthusian. At length he died in the Cologne Charterhouse, on the very day of Saint Tiburtius, after long and most patiently endured severe illnesses, in the year of the Lord 1539.

Johannes Ludovicus Vives of Valencia, Spanish by nation, within a few years published several very distinguished works, written learnedly and with full polish; in them he so joined wisdom to eloquence that no one, even an erudite man, would not admit that he had read them with some profit. He died recently, leaving behind a great longing for him among students. Moreover, whatever I have found published under his name are these:

Two letters On the Method of Boys’ Studies. Introduction to True Wisdom. A golden little book On Writing Letters. On the Method of Studying, Reading, and Interpreting. On the Method of Instructing Pupils. On the Method of Collecting Examples. Exercise in the Latin Language. An interpretation of Vergil’s Bucolics, chiefly allegorical. A preface and exposition on the Dream of Scipio, which he entitled The Vigil. Rhetoric, 13 books. On the Disciplines, 20 books. And he produced very many other vigils, which are known to the learned.

Johannes Manardus, a physician of Ferrara, a man in his own age the most celebrated, and most deserving, of all professors of medicine throughout Italy in Galen’s doctrine and in his censure of the Arabs, composed eighteen books of medical letters.

His annotations, with censure, on the simple and compound medicines of Mesue. He also composed commentaries on the first book of Galen’s Little Art. He flourished in the year of salvation 1539.

Johannes Murmellius of Roermond wrote many little works, especially grammatical ones, not unlearned, and the following other works:

An Isagoge on Aristotle’s Categories. Sentences drawn from the elegies of Tibullus, Catullus, Propertius, and Ovid. Tables of Grammar. Tables on the rudiments of the art of composing verses. Three little works of tables. Commentaries on the Satires of A. Persius. Commentaries on the five books of Boethius On the Consolation of Philosophy. And many other things, namely various epigrams, Scoparius Pappa. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1504. He died in 1517 at Deventer.

Johannes Nauclerus, provost of Tübingen, wrote Chronicles briefly comprising the memorable affairs of all ages and peoples, from the beginning of the world down to the year 1500 from the birth of Christ, with an addition by Nicolaus Basellius from the year of the Lord 1501 to the year 1514, and with a new appendix, briefly noting the events meanwhile carried on from the year 1515 down to the year 1544, the compilers being partly Conrad Tigemann and partly Bartholomaeus Laurens.

Johannes Pesselius Tilanus, by homeland a Geldrian, an outstanding professor of sacred scripture and a most worthy provincial of the institute of D. Dominic, both restored certain works of doctors from errors and himself composed works of his own, of which this is the catalogue:

He revised certain works of the divine Augustine corrupted by our heretics. Gorra’s Expositions on the Four Gospels. A Compendium of the New Treasury, on the Temporale and the Sanctorale. And certain other things, if heaven favors, he will publish. The pious orthodox man is still living in the year of Christ 1546.

On Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

[unclear] by topics whatever very many authors have in various disciplines, which can in any way contribute to the knowledge of things, histories, and words.

By the same man, A Specimen of Epithets, very useful to all students of the poetic art.

He is still flourishing, as I think, namely in the year of the Lord 1546.

Johannes Ruellius, a physician of Soissons, by nation a Frenchman, wrote three books On the Nature of Plants, than which, in this subject, nothing, so far as I know, has appeared down to this day more learned or more copious.

He also translated not a few works, of which you have the following:

He translated the six books of Pedanius Dioscorides On Medical Matter, and one book of Actuarius On the Composition of Medicines.

He rescued from decay, with very great diligence, Scribonius Largus’ book On the Composition of Medicines.

The same man gave Latin form to two books of veterinary medicine collected from Apsyrtus and others.

He flourished in the year of salvation 1539.

Johannes Simoneta, by nation a Calabrian, a most diligent man in composing histories, wrote thirty-one books on the deeds of Francesco Sforza, duke of the Milanese.

He flourished around the year 1486.

Johannes Stella, a priest in rank, but a Venetian by homeland, diligent in writing the lives of the supreme pontiffs, wrote a book on the life and morals of the Roman pontiffs, from Peter the Apostle down to Julius II, that is, to the year of the Lord 1503.

Johannes Tagautius Ambianus Vimacus, a Parisian physician, very celebrated in our age, published six books On Surgical Instruction.

The same man wrote two books On Purgative Medicines.

And certain other works known to physicians.

He is flourishing in the year of the Lord 1546.

Isaac, a monk by profession, highly skilled in Greek literature, composed a Greek scholium on the first figure of a description on a plane, and verses on the twelve winds.

He wrote out certain other things, the catalogue of which I shall append:

Various astronomical works in Greek, and The Apparatus of the Astrolabe.

A Method of Geodesy, that is, of the division of the earth.

The Solution of a Certain Palamedic Question, [unclear].

On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

An encomium of the martyr Demetrius. And on the saying, “These things I command you, that you love one another.”

At what time he flourished, I have nothing to offer.

Johannes Thaulerus, of the Order of Saint Dominic, a most profound theologian and a support of the city of Cologne, excellently illuminated by the anointing of the Holy Spirit in delivering sermons, wrote sermons on the perfection of the inner life, very useful.

A treatise on the virtues.

And various letters, redolent of the spirit of devotion.

And with prophetic spirit he foretold the scourges and heresies against the sacraments and doctrines of the Catholic Church that would arise, which now in our times are devastating the Church.

He flourished at Cologne around the year of the Lord 1350.

His works, now translated into Latin, are expected to appear any day.

Lambertus de Monte wrote a sufficiently acute magisterial question, showing by the authorities of divine Scripture what, according to the sounder opinion of the doctors, can more probably be said about the salvation of Aristotle the Stagirite.

Landulphus de Columna, a Roman, canon of Chartres, a man not idle in collecting histories, wrote a history of the Pontiffs, not long after Vincent of Beauvais.

Lazarus Baynius, by nation a Frenchman, in our age ambassador among the Venetians in the name of Francis, king of the French, a very learned man, wrote Annotations on the Second Law, On Captives Returned by Right of Postliminium.

By the same man, annotations on the treatise On Gold and Silver Bequeathed, in which the kinds of garments and vessels are explained.

The books are altogether most learned, philological, and very useful for the knowledge of authors in both languages, especially historians.

Leonardus Iacchinus, or Giachinus, formerly a Florentine physician, but now, as I hear, a professor at Pisa, an exceptionally learned man, wrote a book On the Number and Being of Indications.

Also a treatise against Avicenna, Mesue, and all the common physicians.

He also translated Galen’s little book On Prognosis, to which is added an apologetic oration.

On ecclesiastical writers, second addition.

…a very old man, distinguished by knowledge of various things, is said to have made many things Latin from Greek; of these I have as yet seen nothing except Symeon Seth, On the Powers of Foods. He is also reported to have written other things, which you have below:

Certain poems. The Life of Hercules. A treatise on the Muses. On years and months, and the other divisions of time: an easy and clear dissertation on this material, difficult and obstructed up to this point. The Roman Calendar. On tombs and the various rite of burial, one book. Some dialogues on poetry and the history of poets. On nautical matters, one book. On the vessels that pertain to the sacrifices of the gods and their ceremonies, one book. He flourished in the year of the Lord 1543.

[On the authority of the printed text “Lilium,” which the OCR places at the head of the following entry:] Aegidius [Lilius?] Libellius of Città di Castello, a disciple of Gregorius Tifernas and teacher of Raphael Volaterranus, endowed with Latinity four volumes of the works of Philo the Jew. Likewise Dio on kingship, and some books of Chrysostom.

Lippus Brandelinus Aurelius, an Augustinian Hermit, published Christian Paradoxes. The same man wrote a dialogue on the condition of human life and on enduring bodily sickness, to Matthias Corvinus, king of Hungary. Some poems by the same man on the death of Platina are extant. He flourished under the emperor Frederick III, around the year of the Lord [1480?].

Lucianus Mantuanus, a monk of the order of Saint Benedict, a man learned in Greek and Latin, made Latin the commentaries of Saint John Chrysostom on the Epistle of Paul to the Romans, and wrote a defense of Chrysostom against those who suspect and accuse Chrysostom of having weakened divine grace and exalted freedom of choice beyond measure.

Lucius Ioannes Scoppa, an Italian by nation, a grammarian, published at Naples Grammatical Collectanea. By the same man, a Spicilegium, and collectanea on various passages of authors. He flourished around the year of the Lord 1512.

Ludovico Bigo Pittorio of Ferrara, a man renowned for remarkable learning and excellent dexterity of character, composed an elegant book on heavenly hymns and epitaphs. Likewise two books of epigrams.

Against the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

[Agentinus?], metropolitan or archbishop of Mytilene, a man deeply skilled in sacred scripture and philosophy, published a most learned exposition on Aristotle’s book On Interpretation. Commentaries by the same man on the two books of Aristotle’s Prior Analytics.

Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, flourished under the rulers Constans and Constantine, and wrote many volumes on various subjects, especially against the Arians. The books of Asterius and Apollinarius are carried about against him, accusing him of the Sabellian heresy.

Marcus Antonius Antimachus, a man powerful in both languages and at this time professor of Greek letters at Ferrara, wrote an oration in praise of Greek letters. The same man translated two books of Gemistus Pletho on the deeds of the Greeks after the battle at Mantinea. The precepts of Dionysius of Halicarnassus on panegyric, nuptial, birthday, and epithalamic oratory. Likewise the precepts of Demetrius of Phalerum on clauses and incises, on periods, on composing letters, on characters of speaking, and the preface of Polyaenus on military matters. He himself also composed eight books of epigrams, and some things in Greek prose.

Marcus Hieronymus Vida of Cremona, poet and bishop of Alba, a man skilled and learned in composing verse, published certain poetical works, of which the following circulate among the learned: The Christiad, that is, on the life, deeds, and death of Christ, six books. On the art of poetry, three books. On the care and use of silkworms, two books. On the game of chess, one book. Hymns. Bucolics. Odes. A letter to Giovanni Matteo Giberti. Likewise some epigrams.

Marcus Marulus, or Marullus, of Split, published an Evangelistarium divided into seven books, six books. And on instruction in living religiously.

Marcus Vigerius, priest of Santa Maria in Trastevere, wrote two books on the Christian decachord to Julius II, supreme pontiff. A dialogue by the same man on removing the abuses of the Church, Mar…

Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

Martinus Gregorius, a physician at Paris, a man skilled in both languages, corrected according to Greek exemplars several translations of Galen's books; among them there is extant Method of Healing, and the following:

Introduction to Pulses. On the Motion of the Muscles, 2 books. On the Use of the Parts, 17 books. On the Faculties of Foods, 3 books. On the Regimen of Attenuating Diet, 1 book. He flourished two years ago.

Martinus Polichius Mellerstadius, a most learned professor in the university of Wittenberg thirty years ago, published collected notes of commentaries for a course in logic, on all Aristotle's books of logic and the book On the Six Principles.

Collected notes of the same man's excellent course in physics.

Matthaeus, monk of Aula Regia, a man of notable life and by no means ordinary learning, often disputed at Prague with Ioannes Huss and his followers.

He also wrote on the four books of Peter Lombard. On the Psalter. On the Gospel of Matthew. Commentaries on the hymns, and many other things.

Matthaeus Curtius of Pavia, a physician by far the most learned in Italy, an excellent instructor in the old method of healing according to Hippocrates and Galen, wrote on venesection in pleurisy, twice, I think. He died, as I hear, in the year of salvation 1544.

Matthaeus of Philadelphia, metropolitan at Ephesus, a learned and honorable man, wrote prayers, in the first place laying out a compendious path to repentance, and contributing not a little to the reception of the Lord's body. They were translated by Alardus Aemstelredamus.

Michael Ritius of Naples, skilled in both laws, a very celebrated councillor of the king of the French, composed three books On the Kings of the Franks, and is said to have written very many other volumes, of which these are extant:

On the Kings of Spain, 5 books. On the Kings of Jerusalem, 1 book. On the Kings of Naples and Sicily, 4 books. On the Kings of Hungary, 2 books. And certain other things.

Mechtildis, a learned and devout virgin of the order of St. Benedict, familiarly united in friendship with her heavenly bridegroom, and renowned for divine revelations, published a book abundantly full of the new wine of the divine sweetness of spiritual grace.

And she flourished in the monastery of Helfta in Eisleben, otherwise Isleben, a town of the county of Mansfeld, around the year of the Lord 1300.

On the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

Nemesius, philosopher and bishop, adorned with excellent learning in sacred letters, wrote summary discourses On the Nature of Man. They are extant in Greek in Italy. They have also been printed in Latin, with Georgius Valla as translator.

Nicephorus Blemmydes, who was both monk, solitary, and priest, surnamed [unclear], a man learned in good letters, wrote many and various works, whose titles we have seen; they are these:

An inquiry On the Five Words, and why they are only five, neither more nor fewer. A Method concerning the Compendious Art of Disputing. A Summary, or Introductory Epitomes to Logic, 2 books. Epitome of Philosophy. A commentary On Sophistical Refutations. Book of Laws; On the Soul; On the Body. Thirty-two chapters On Meteors. On Natural Principles and Causes. A discourse, What Sort of Man a King Ought to Be. Canons on Urines. [unclear Greek title]. A demonstration that life is not predetermined for individuals. Forty-one chapters; I do not know on what subject. And he is said to have elucidated many other things.

Nicolaus Beraldus Aurelius, a man most ardently devoted to more refined literature, wrote a very elegant dialogue in which certain methods are explained by which the ability to speak extemporaneously can be acquired, and also concerning that extemporaneous faculty itself.

He composed an elegant oration On Old and New Jurisprudence, with a learned exhortation to the reading and study of the ancients.

He is also said to have written on Politian's Nutricia.

He flourished in the year of salvation 1533.

Nicolaus Borbonius Vandoperanus, a man learned in both languages,

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II

An elegant poet, he wrote grammatical tables.

By the same man, Paedologia, or a little book on the conduct of boys.

Under his name there are also circulated Nugae, epigrams.

He flourished at Paris in the year of the Lord 1533.

Nicolaus Clenardus of Mechelen, a man most skilled in the three languages, for many years publicly taught humane letters at Mechelen, and, in order to benefit everyone, even those absent, brought to light certain works in Latin, Greek, and also Hebrew, among which the following are recorded:

Most complete and very brief Institutions in the Greek language.

To these have been added Greek meditations, for the benefit of those who lack the living voice of a teacher.

By the same man, a Hebrew grammar, or rather tables of that language.

I think that he is still alive.

Nicolaus Dathus, son of Augustinus Dathus, wrote a book On the Praises of Eloquence, and a life of his father, which is found prefixed to the works of Augustinus; but, overtaken by death, he did not complete it.

There are certain poems in that book in praise of his father; others are On the Duty of a Scribe.

Nicolaus Saguntinus, most eloquent in both languages, equally ready in talent and fluency, was an interpreter at the council which, under Eugene IV, was held between the Greeks and the Latins, both on other articles of the faith and on the procession of the Holy Spirit, at Ferrara and Florence.

He translated Plutarch’s book On Civic Precepts, and Onosander the Platonist’s On the Best Commander.

Nilus, a holy man, exactly learned in Greek, wrote monastic orations, together with fifteen theological little works, in φωτικοῖς chapters.

By the same man, a book to Charicles the bishop, too harsh toward sinners, who said that repentance alone did not suffice for confession.

Some works are extant at Rome, and others in Italy in Greek.

Nicolaus Villagogus, a Rhodian knight, published, in the form of a little book, a notable letter on the armed expedition of Charles V against Algiers, depicting that campaign, in which he himself took part, so graphically that the matter seems almost to be taking place, not merely to be narrated.

Because this letter was most elegant and bore before it, as it were, a certain majesty, it was inserted, together with other events done around that time, into the chronicles of Nauclerus printed at Cologne in the year 1544.

The author Nicolaus himself flourished under the emperor Charles V, in the year of the Lord 1541, perhaps still living, and likely hereafter to become more famous through the publication of similar monuments.

Octavianus Mirandula, an Italian by nationality, a regular canon of Saint Augustine of the Lateran, a man renowned for no common honesty and learning, collected the flowers of illustrious poets from the best and ancient poets, twenty-five in number.

The work is no less useful than laborious.

Olympiodorus, an outstanding paraphrast of sacred Scripture, wrote most learned scholia on Ecclesiastes, inserted with a new translation, unfamiliar to Latin ears, namely that of Aquila, Theodotion, and the Septuagint.

Olympius, a Spaniard by nationality, a bishop, a man learned in sacred letters, wrote a book on faith against those who blame nature and not free choice, showing that evil was implanted in nature not by creation, but by disobedience.

Orontius Fineus of Dauphine, royal professor of the liberal disciplines in the Academy of Paris, wrote Protomathesis, a varied work, no less useful than pleasant to know.

By the same man, a universal astrolabic quadrant.

Demonstrations on the first six books of Euclid.

A recent and complete description of the whole world, in the likeness of the human heart.

A new description of all Gaul.

He flourished, if I am not mistaken, in the year of salvation 1543.

Paduanus de Grassis of Barletta, master of sacred theology, regent in the school of the great house of Venice, wrote a scholastic Enchiridion of the quodlibetal contradictions of the subtle doctor Scotus.

Pacianus, [or?] Tatianus, father of Dexter, to whom Saint Jerome wrote the book On Illustrious Men, bishop of Barcelona in the ridges of the Pyrenees, distinguished for chastity and eloquence, and as much by life as by speech, wrote various little works, among which is [unclear], and Against the Novatians.

He died under the emperor Theodosius, already in extreme old age.

Panthaleon of Vercelli, chief physician of the duke of Savoy, coming from Lombardy and Savoy into the Touraine region of Gaul, was held in high esteem. Contrary to the custom of the Gauls, pills before

food, at every age, illness, and season, according to the nature of the disease, committing it to writing, so that nothing could have been sweeter to them for long-lasting health than to take a pill before food. Of his writings these are extant:

On Pills, one book.

On Dairy Foods, one book.

I think that he flourished in our century, that is, in the year of salvation 1542.

Paulus Belmissenus, physician, lecturer and doctor of Bologna, and a man fully learned in all the arts, rendered the first two books of Aristotle On Animals in Latin elegies, which correspond to their chapters.

Of the same man, three elegies: one to Francis, king of the Gauls; another on the pope’s departure into Gaul; the third to Clement, supreme pontiff, on undertaking war against the Turks.

An epithalamium for Henry, brother of King Francis.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 1543.

Paulus Cortesius, apostolic protonotary, a remarkable lover of the liberal arts, used a style beyond measure elegant in the commentaries which he wrote on the four books of the Sentences.

It is also reported that he wrote certain letters.

He flourished in the time of Julius II, supreme pontiff.

Paulus Ricius, an Israelite, a very learned man converted to the Christian faith a few years ago, and physician of Emperor Maximilian, composed many excellent little works, of which these are extant:

The Balance of the Wise.

A book On the Six Hundred and Thirteen Ordinances of the Mosaic Sanction or Pentateuchal Edict.

A Prophetic, Philosophical, and Talmudic Disputation on Behalf of Christian Truth.

An Introduction to the Learning of the Kabbalists or Allegorists, with a letter against the letter of Stephen the priest, detractor of the Kabbalah.

A Compendium on the Nine Orders of Doctrines and the Connection of the Whole Peripatetic Dogma.

A Resolutive Oration on the Threefold Order of Doctrine.

Conclusions by Which You Will Be Able to Judge That Aristotle Practiced a Threefold Doctrine and to Discern the Connection of His Whole Dogma.

On Celestial Agriculture, book 1, [unclear], to Emperor Charles V and Ferdinand his brother.

On the Common Principle of the Sacraments, a sermon.

On the Hidden Providence of God, on the Psalm Blessed is the man.

A Compendium on the Soul of Heaven, According to the Tradition of the Holy Philosophers.

On the Method of the Parts of the Proem According to the Rhetoricians.

On the Method of Investigating and Establishing the Subject of Any Science.

A Learned and Elegant Oration Against the Virulent and Most Savage Frenzy of the Turks, to the Princes, Magistrates, and Peoples of Germany.

A Medley Excerpted from the Talmudic Code, at the Request of Emperor Maximilian.

He flourished, as is clear, under Charles V, most unconquered emperor of the Romans.

Petrus de Alvernia, of the Order of Preachers, a disciple of Saint Thomas Aquinas, a man learned in the divine Scriptures by long study and acute in intellect, wrote commentaries on several books of Aristotle, namely:

On the Motions of Animals.

On Length and Shortness of Life.

On Youth and Old Age.

On Respiration.

On Death and Life.

Additions to the Commentaries of St. Thomas Aquinas on Aristotle’s Books On Heaven.

Petrus Bembus, a Venetian cardinal, now an old man, is still living at Padua, unless I am mistaken; a man highly adorned with the liberal arts, the greatest imitator of Ciceronian eloquence, he commended the acuteness of his intellect to mortals in numerous little works, of which they report these:

Quite a few letters.

On the Imitation of Speech, one book.

Benacus, a heroic poem.

A little book On Aetna.

I hear that at this time he is committing the history of the Venetians to writing.

Petrus Blomevenna, by homeland of Leiden, by nation a Hollander, a man sufficiently learned in sacred letters, nobly illumined by the inward anointing of the Holy Spirit, preserving himself clean from the contagions of the age and the flesh from his earliest youth, betook himself to the contemplative life in the Charterhouse of Cologne; in it he advanced so sublimely that often in Masses and spiritual exercises, from the sweetness of divine love, he would grow wholly aflame,

Petrus Victor, aliàs Victorius, vir nostro seculo doctissimꝰ, Romae agens, edidit libellum de regionibus &; locis vrbis Romae. Idẽ castigauit: Cicerōis libros, &; adiecit explicatiões castigationũ. [On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II]

[unclear], and was transported above himself. Having been made prior and visitor of the whole province along the Rhine, he governed the house and province entrusted to him successfully for many years.

Under his auspices the books of D. Dionysius the Carthusian, and many other pious and learned books, were brought to light. He himself wrote:

An Introduction to the Contemplative Life, 1 book.

On the Outpouring of the Heart, 1 book.

A Handbook for Priests, 1 book.

On Divine Goodness, 4 books.

Exhortations to Convents of Monks for the Chief Feasts of the Whole Year, 1 book.

The Evangelical Candle, 1 book.

And some other works against the Lutherans.

He died in the year of the Lord 1536, on the very day of St. Michael.

Petrus Crinitus, a very learned man, distinguished for an approved life, left to posterity works not to be despised; from these I shall set down certain ones:

On Honest Discipline, 25 books.

On the Latin Poets, 5 books.

He also wrote numerous letters.

He flourished in the year of restored salvation 1505.

Petrus Galatinus, of the Order of Minors, a most accomplished doctor of arts and sacred theology, and a member of the household of Cardinal Laurentius Puccius, composed a work, in the manner of a dialogue, On the Secrets of Catholic Truth Found in the Hebrew Books, especially in the Talmud, in defense of the most excellent man Johannes Capnio, against the Jewish obstinacy of our age.

He flourished under Maximilian, emperor of the Romans, and Leo X, supreme pontiff, in the year of salvation 1516.

Petrus Gylius, a Frenchman by nation, a man exquisitely learned in Greek and Latin, very highly deserving of good letters, translated Theodoret’s commentaries on the Twelve Prophets; he also promises this in the preface to Philo, book 36.

He gave Latin form to Aelian’s sixteen books On the History of Animals, and everywhere added corollaries in their proper places from Porphyry, Heliodorus, and Oppian.

There is also his book on the French and Latin names of the fish of Marseille. He flourished in the year of salvation 1542.

Petrus Martyr of Anghiera, a Milanese orator, formerly [unclear] of Ferdinand and Elisabeth, monarchs of Spain, composed five Decades on the lands recently discovered, or on Oceanic matters and the New World; in these, whatever has been handed down about the lands recently discovered is taught copiously, faithfully, and learnedly, so as to hold the reader eager for new things.

In addition, there are three books of his Babylonian Embassy.

He flourished in the year of the redeemed human race 1516.

Petrus Mosellanus of Proteg, a German by nation, and, as I think, to be counted among the foremost restorers of the more polished literature in our age.

Among his writings I found the following:

A Paedology written for the use of boys. There are 57 dialogues.

Tables on figures and tropes.

Precepts on the first exercises before the rhetor.

An oration on acquiring knowledge of various languages.

Annotations on Aulus Gellius’ Attic Nights, and on book 7 of M. Fabius Quintilianus’ Rhetorical Institutes.

He wrote scholia on the Dialectic of Georgius Valla.

From Greek he made Latin: Gregory Nazianzen’s sermon on the feast of Christ’s Nativity, and Isocrates’ oration on avoiding war and preserving peace.

He flourished at Leipzig around the year of the Lord 1518.

Petrus Numagen of Trier, a priest at Zurich around the year of the Lord 1483, wrote about Nicolaus Subsylanus, a Swiss, who is piously believed to have lived holily as a solitary for a long time without food.

The same man composed a treatise on apparitions of spirits and phantoms.

Petrus Tataretus of Paris, a man excellently learned in secular philosophy and endowed with remarkable talent, wrote on almost the whole philosophy of Aristotle: on logic, physics, On the Heavens and the World, generation and corruption, the Meteorology, On the Soul, On Sense and the Sensible, memory and recollection, sleep and waking, length and shortness of life, and certain matters of metaphysics.

Likewise an exposition on the Summulae of Petrus Hispanus with the text, together with additions.

He flourished in the year of the Lord 1509.

Petrus Victor, otherwise Victorius, a very learned man in our age, living at Rome, published a little book on the districts and places of the city of Rome.

The same man corrected Cicero’s books, and added explanations of the corrections.

His annotations on Cicero’s familiar letters, on the books On

Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

On the Orator, Brutus, The Perfect Orator, and the Rhetoric to Herennius. He also published annotations on Cato, Varro, and Columella, and commentaries on Aristotle’s Rhetoric. He is still living in the year of the Lord 1546.

Philippus Decius of Milan professed publicly in many places and for many years, more than any other jurisconsult ever in Italy, namely for about 65 years. He left most learned writings in both laws, and besides these four books of counsels, and commentaries on the rules of law, and on the first and second of the Old Digest and the first and [unclear] of the Code.

Philotheus, patriarch of Constantinople, a man learned in Greek beyond what can be said, famous for the keenness of a happy intellect, published a notable book against the writings of the philosopher Gregoras. By the same Philotheus: [unclear Greek].

Encomia of Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom, and on All Saints.

Epitome of Christ Incarnate.

These and certain other works are preserved in Greek at Rome in the Vatican Library.

Photius, patriarch, a man diligent in collecting the books of authors, wrote in Greek two volumes of description and enumeration of the authors, as many as he himself had read.

By the same, a purgation and defense addressed to the Council.

Against those of old Rome, thirteen chapters.

Other works also circulate under his name, which are in Greek, namely:

Letter to the eastern thrones,

On the procession of the Holy Spirit,

On the Holy Spirit,

On the Seven Synods, one book.

Pinytus of Crete, bishop of the city of Gnossus, wrote to Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, a very elegant letter, in which he teaches that peoples must not always be nourished with milk, lest, as little children, they be overtaken by the last day, but that they should also feed on solid food, so that they may advance to spiritual old age.

He flourished under Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus, around the year of the Lord 170.

Polycarp, disciple of the apostle John, and ordained by him bishop of Smyrna, was the foremost man of all Asia. He wrote to the Philippians a very useful letter, which is read even to this day in the assembly of Asia.

On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

He also wrote to the great Dionysius the Areopagite, and to other churches.

Polydorus Virgilius of Urbino, collector for the Roman pontiff in England and archdeacon of Wells, wrote three books of dialogues on prodigies, and also a work of Adages, both sacred and profane.

By the same, twenty-six books of English History, and eight books On the Inventors of Things.

He flourished in the year of salvation 1499.

Pomerius, a Moor by nation, ordained priest in Gaul, in answer to the questions and requests of Bishop Julian and the priest Verus, replying in the manner of dialogues, with dialectical art and a style suited to his talent, composed eight books on the nature of the soul, its quality, and the special character of its resurrection in this life for the faithful, and the general resurrection of all human beings. I remember that I once read his dictation to a certain man named Principius, an exhortation on contempt of the world and the passing away of things, and another entitled On Vices and Virtues. He is said to have written other things too, and still to be writing, which have not come to my knowledge. He is certainly living to this day, in a manner of life worthy of God, suited to his rank and profession. Thus Gennadius.

Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, a man possessing exact knowledge of sacred letters, wrote a letter on the faith to the venerable and holy bishops, priests, and archimandrites throughout Armenia.

Very many words by the same are reported by Epiphanius himself.

He flourished under the consulship of Theodosius for the fifth time and Valentinian for the fourth.

Prosper Calanus, from Sarzana, a city of Etruria, a very learned man, practiced medicine for many years at Rome and then at Bologna, and indeed by the best and most exact method. He shared with students the lucubrations entitled:

A Commentary on Preserving Health.

A Paraphrase on Galen’s book On Natural Faculties.

An Enchiridion on Guarding against Poisons.

Eighteen commentaries, through which he himself gave counsel to the same number of illustrious and powerful men concerning various illnesses.

A Paraphrase on Galen’s little book On Unequal Distemperament.

Very many letters, sent to various friends on the cure of certain illnesses.

He flourished under Clement VII, supreme pontiff.

Publius Faustus Andrelinus of Forlì, poet laureate, wrote proverbial and moral letters no less learned than pious. By him

Richardꝰ frater ordinis Praedicatoꝝ, patria Florētinus, abhinc annis 200. non contemnenda doctrina, cum in Asia peregrinare- tur, Alcoranū doctus linguam Arabicam conuertit, contraque com PPP iij men 486 IN ABBATEM SPAN. DE SCRIP. mentarium edidit, quem Demetrius Cydonius in Graecum postea transfudit sermonem. Richardus Perusinus, politioris literaturae mirum in modum ardens amator, Austriados libros duodecim non ineleganti carmine hexametro composuit. Claruit sub Maximiliano Augusto. Robertus Ketenensis, aliàs Remensis, ex Anglosaxonibus Bri- tannus, &; tandem Archidiaconus Papilonen̄, Alcorani libros qua tuor in Epitomen redactos, ex Arabico transtulit in sermonem La tinum. Petri abbatis Cluniacensis hortatu, Codex authenticus doctrinae Machumeticae, ab eodem versus. Claruit tempore Adelfonsi imperatoris. Rudbertus à Mosham, doctor infignis, ac decanus Patauiensis, Ferdinandi Romanorum regis consiliarius, librum edidit, cuius incriptio prima, talis est: Microsynodus Norimbergen̄, Romana non Germanica, quā Rud bertus à Mosham, cum senatū ecclesiastis Norimbergen̄, sum- mo pietatis veritatis studio, corrigendi emendandi Lutheri- smi gratia celebrauit. Qua denique Babylonica meretrix magna, illiusqꝫ primogenitus Antichristus, in doctrina ecclesia Luthe- ranorum sedens regens, reuelatur gladio spiritus iugulatur, simusque Norimbergen̄ Ecclesiastarum epiftole respondetur. Eiusdem liber de summo articulo iustificationis, aliàs de fide mo- narcha, monacha. Considerationes axiomata, qꝫ que madmodum poenitentia non debet separari à remiffiōe peccatorum, verbum Charitas à fide, crux ab Euāgelio, sic etiam nec lex indiscriminatim debet separa ti à iustificatione. Claruit anno Christi 1540. Robertus Stephanus, natione Gallus, Typographus Parisien̄, hac tempestate quàmplurimos ex sua calchographia libros politis characteribus, emendatissime elaboratos, itudiosis proposuit. Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

Of the same author: four Eclogues, and certain Distichs.

Raphael Volaterranus, a man of varied learning, widely extending among others, carefully wrote thirty-eight books of the Urban Commentaries.

The same man published one book, On the Office of a Prince and Leader, and gave Latin form to not a few books of both sacred and profane authors; among these the following are said to have been translated by him:

Xenophon’s Oeconomicus.

Gregory Nazianzen’s Monody.

Ten short orations of Basil, and the Institutes of Monks.

Two books of Procopius of Caesarea On the Persian War, and the same number On the Vandalic War.

He flourished in the time of Julius II, Supreme Pontiff.

Raymundus of Barcelona, chaplain and penitentiary of Gregory IX, Supreme Pontiff, was a man most skilled in theology and pontifical law; with his assistance, as Platina testifies, he compiled the Decretals. He also wrote a Summa called On Penance and Betrothals.

Raymundus Lullius, a man learned in medical matters and long exercised by study in sacred and divine letters, became a hermit, and afterward an outstanding preacher of the divine word; he wrote many things in theology.

And various other little works; those which we have seen are these:

On the Praises of Mary, book 1.

A wondrous and very celebrated work On Fevers.

New Metaphysics, and a Remonstrance of Philosophy against the Averroists.

Proverbs, 3 books.

On the Cabalistic Art, or Introduction to All the Sciences, 4 books.

Isagoge into Rhetoric.

Astrology.

On the Secrets of Nature, or the fifth essence, which they commonly call distillation, 2 books.

Lily of Understanding.

The Great General and Ultimate Art, the attainer and key-bearer of whatever arts and sciences.

He flourished in the year of Christ 1311.

Richard, a brother of the Order of Preachers, a Florentine by homeland, about 200 years ago a man of no contemptible learning, when he was traveling in Asia, learned the Qur’an and translated the Arabic language; and against it he published a commentary, which Demetrius Cydonius afterward rendered into the Greek tongue.

On the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

Richardus Perusinus, a wonderfully ardent lover of more polished literature, composed twelve books of the Austriad in not inelegant hexameter verse.

He flourished under Maximilian Augustus.

Robertus Ketenensis, otherwise Remensis, a Briton from the Anglo-Saxons, and finally archdeacon of Pamplona, translated into the Latin language the four books of the Qur’an, reduced into an epitome, from Arabic.

At the urging of Peter, abbot of Cluny, the authentic codex of the doctrine of Muhammad was translated by the same man.

He flourished in the time of the emperor Adelfonsus.

Rudbertus of Mosham, a distinguished doctor and dean of Passau, counselor of Ferdinand, king of the Romans, published a book whose first inscription is as follows:

The Little Synod of Nuremberg, Roman, Not German, which Rudbertus of Mosham celebrated with the ecclesiastical senate of Nuremberg, with the highest zeal for piety and truth, for the sake of correcting and amending Lutheranism. In it at last the great Babylonian whore, and her firstborn Antichrist, sitting and ruling in the doctrine and church of the Lutherans, is revealed and slain with the sword of the spirit, and [unclear] reply is made to the letter of the Nuremberg ecclesiastics.

A book by the same man On the Supreme Article of Justification, otherwise On Faith the Monarch, the Nun.

Considerations, Axioms, that just as penance ought not to be separated from the remission of sins, nor the word Charity from faith, nor the cross from the Gospel, so also the law ought not indiscriminately to be separated from justification.

He flourished in the year of Christ 1540.

Robertus Stephanus, a Frenchman by nation, a Parisian printer, in this age has offered to students very many books from his press, worked out with elegant type and with the greatest correctness.

And indeed he not only printed, but also by his own diligence composed very noble volumes, which are named here:

Dictionary, or Thesaurus of the Latin Language.

Latin-French Lexicon. Elu-

Ecclesiastical [Writers], Addition II.

The Poetic Elucidarius, not the former one, but an entirely different work, and so enlarged and polished that a studious youth could lack nothing among those matters that pertain both to the understanding of poets and to oratory.

Romulus Amasaeus, a man learned in both languages with few equals and endowed with a distinguished intellect, translated Xenophon’s seven books on the expedition of Cyrus the Younger.

I hear that Pausanias has been translated by him, but has not yet been published.

He flourished in the year of Christ 1543.

Rusticus the deacon, a man, as is clear from the books which he wrote, well practiced in divine letters, composed an excellent book against the Acephali.

He defends the definition of faith of the Synod of Chalcedon, through a dialogue between an orthodox man and a heretic.

Salmonius Macrinus of Iuliodunum, a Gaul by nation, by profession a distinguished poet, and chamberlain of King Francis of Valois, excelling greatly in keenness of intellect, composed and sported with many splendid poems, among which these are counted:

Six books of Hymns.

Three books of selected hymns by the same.

One book of Poems.

Four books of Poems or Odes.

He flourished, as has been said, under Francis of Valois, King of the French.

Santes Pagninus of Lucca, of the Order of Preachers, apostolic preacher, a man learned in Hebrew beyond measure, published most complete Institutions of the holy language, divided into four books. But this is the index of the other works which he published:

An Isagoge to the sacred writings, one book.

An Isagoge to the mystical senses of Sacred Scripture, eighteen books.

An abridgment of the Hebrew Institutions.

A new translation of both Testaments from the Hebrew and Greek truth, almost word for word.

Added to these is a book on the interpretations of Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek names.

A Treasury of the Holy Language, or Hebrew Lexicon.

He wrote Hebrew Meditations on Psalm 50.

He flourished under Clement VII, Supreme Pontiff.

Saxo Grammaticus the [Zealander?], a man wholly devoted to writing histories, wrote sixteen books of Danish History to Andreas, bishop of Denmark, three hundred years ago, with such elegance of diction and such variety of deeds performed that they may seem able to vie with all antiquity.

In the Abbot of Spanheim, On Writers.

Sebastianus Aquilanus, a follower of Galen, a man most expert in medicine, composed for Lodovico de Gonzaga, bishop of Mantua, a book full of learning on the French disease; all physicians have borrowed from this author the treatments of it which they use in our time.

By the same, a question on sanguine fever.

Phoebadius, bishop of Agen in Gaul, a man not moderately versed in sacred and humane letters, published against the Arians a book excellent indeed in my opinion. They say that there are other little works of his, which I have not yet read.

He flourished in the time of St. Jerome.

Sophronius, a very learned man, while still a boy composed the Praises of Bethlehem, and recently an outstanding book on the overthrow of Serapis.

He also translated into Greek, in elegant speech, my little works On Virginity to Eustochium and the Life of Hilarion the monk; also the Psalter and the Prophets, which we translated from Hebrew into Latin. These are the words of St. Jerome.

The same man rendered from Latin into Greek St. Jerome’s Lives of Ecclesiastical Writers.

By the same, a paraphrase on Aristotle’s books On the Soul.

Likewise on the little book On Memory, the following [unclear].

Stephanus Doletus of Orléans, a Gaul by nation, wrote not a few works within a few years, for the instruction of the Latin language, in a most correct style.

Among these, the following are known to me:

On Naval Matters, to Badius, one book.

A Dialogue on Ciceronian Imitation, for Christophe de Longueil, against D. Erasmus.

Two Orations against Toulouse.

Two books of Letters.

Two books of Poems.

One book of Letters of friends to Dolet himself.

Other Poems, four books.

On the Deeds of Francis of Valois, King of the French, two books.

Two volumes of Commentaries on the Latin Language.

A Formula of the More Illustrious Latin Expressions.
