Ecclesiastical [writers], Addition II.

Tables on Galen’s books On Diseases and Symptoms. And he wrote certain other works, which have not come into our hands. He flourished in the year of Christ 1543.

Symphorianus Campegius, otherwise Champerius, of Lyon, a Frenchman by birth, a knight, and distinguished chief physician of the Lorrainers, divided into four books the Castigations or Emendations of the apothecaries and of the Arab physicians Mesue, Serapion, Rasis, Alpharabius, and other more recent physicians. To these is added the workshop of apothecaries and more recent physicians. Various minor works by the same man. These are: On Famous Writers of Medicine, Ancient and More Recent, one book. On the Founders of the Divine Laws, together with a Refutation of the Mohammedan Sect, or of the Koran, one book. A dialogue on the Mohammedan law. On Diseases and Remedies of Bodies and Souls, [two?] books. A confirmation of the evangelical and Christian religion from the writings of gentiles, poets, and philosophers. Medical aphorisms. The Gallic Garden, a book on medicine so entitled. The Monarchy of the Gauls. He also excerpted four books from all the books of Galen. On dialectic, rhetoric, geometry, arithmetic, astronomy, music, natural philosophy, medicine, theology, likewise on laws, politics, and ethics. By the same man, [two?] books on an apologetic dispute between Andreas Thurinus and Matthaeus Curtius.

Synesius of Pentapolis in Africa, a Christian philosopher, made bishop of Ptolemais, wrote books on grammar and philosophy, royal, panegyrical, or demonstrative speeches. An encomium of baldness. He composed a remarkable discourse, in Greek style, On Providence, and very many other books of diverse kinds, and admirable letters. Of these the following are extant in Italy in Greek: On the Interpretation of Dreams, one book. Letters peri ten pistin, that is, concerning the faith. Scholia on the book of Democritus. Greek discourses on kingship, on the household, on his own life. Two monostichs. And he is said to have published many other works. Suidas mentions him. At what time he flourished, however, I could not easily say.

Theodoricus Adamaeus Salembergius published annotations on the six books of Procopius the rhetorician concerning the buildings of the emperor Justinian. By the same man, a congratulatory panegyric on the concord of the Christian world. A book on the island of Rhodes and the institution of the military orders. Likewise he rendered the Tablet of Cebes into Latin.

Theodorus the deacon, a man not ignorant of the liberal arts, with the utmost zeal composed an excellent book of the sacred canons, both of the Apostles and of synods, both ecumenical and particular, and of other holy fathers, etc. It is extant in Italy.

Theophanes, bishop, otherwise metropolitan, of Nicaea, since he was a very great lover of the Christian religion, composed certain chapters against the impious Jews. Two letters of his are also extant in Greek: one of them, which is called didascalic, he wrote to priests and the rest of the clergy; the other to the Nicaeans, in which he teaches how a Christian ought to hold all present things, both pleasant and troublesome, of no account.

Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, which was formerly called the Tower of Strato, under the emperor [Seno?], composed, together with the other bishops, a very useful synodical letter against those who celebrated Easter with the Jews on the fourteenth moon.

Theophylactus, archbishop of Bulgaria, a man most accomplished in every kind of letters and of a more sincere life, published in Greek most elegant expositions on the four Gospels and all the epistles of Saint Paul. Commentaries by the same man on the prophet Hosea and on all of Micah, recently discovered, have been brought from the island of Patmos.

Theotimus, bishop of Tomi in Scythia, a man distinguished by very elegant talent, published short and concise treatises in the manner of dialogues and of ancient eloquence. And he was writing certain other works in the time of Jerome, as Jerome himself testifies.

Thomas Branduandinus, otherwise Brauardinus, an Englishman, an outstanding theologian, wrote On the House of God, otherwise On the Causes of God, and On the Virtue of God, the Cause of Causes, against the Pelagians. And certain other works. He flourished in the year of the Lord 157.

Thomas de Vio Cajetan, cardinal of San Sisto, published many excellent minor works against the Lutherans, namely

Confilium de commenda Beneficiorum, cuius initium est: Qui- dam Vrbanus in tractatu suo de etc. V Alescus de Taranta, protomedicꝰ regis Fraciae, vir (vt fertur) in re medica exercitatissimus, scripsit tractatulum de peste et amp; Epidimia. Et Practicum, vulgo dictam Philonium, de curatione morborum omnis generis. Viuit (vt audio) adhuc anno Christi 15.46. Varinus Phauorinus Camertinꝰ episcopus, vir et amp; Grae- ci et amp; Latini idiomatis exactam habens notitiam. Dictionarium Graecum, &amp; commentaria ex multis varijsqꝫ autho ribus collegit. Eiusdem thesaurus fiue Cornucopię, &amp; horti Adonidis, Trāstulit etiam apophthegmata q̃dam, ex Io. Stobaei locis selecta. Vi=

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

On faith and works, On communion, On satisfaction, On the invocation of saints.

By the same man there is also a Little Summary on sins.

Thomas Linacre, English by nation, a professor of medicine, a man most highly skilled in both languages and of a very polished style, earned great praise and favor among the learned by his writings, so that he is regarded as an excellent grammarian and the most distinguished of Galen’s interpreters.

Rudiments of grammar. On the Corrected Structure of Latin Speech, 6 books. From the works of Claudius Galen he rendered into Latin: On Temperaments, 3 books. On Unequal Distemper, 1 book. Method of Healing, or On Curing Diseases, 14 books, to Henry VIII, king of England. On Preserving Health, 6 books. On Natural Faculties, 5 books. On the Use of Pulses, 1 book. He also translated the Sphere of Proclus.

Thomas More, English by nation, notably learned both in Greek and in Latin, and a man of upright life, because of the remarkable dexterity with which he was endowed, was condemned to death by Henry VIII, king of the English, and became famous among posterity not only by martyrdom but also by many little works, of which I have seen the following:

Several dialogues of Lucian translated by him. Utopia. Many excellent epigrams by him are extant. He flourished in the year, if I am not mistaken, 1535.

Thomas Murner of Strasbourg, bachelor of sacred letters at Krakow, of the Order of Minors, published many little works, full of jokes and witticisms, against the Lutherans, and certain others, namely these:

A Worthy Praise of Honorable Poems, a Wonderful Chastisement of Shameless Ones. He wrote very many sermons; a Calendar, in which he graphically depicts the customs of the Lutherans according to the zodiac, namely in which sign someone could conveniently seize the goods of the Church, or deflower nuns. He flourished in the year of salvation 1536.

Timothy, bishop, an elegant writer, very learned in [unclear] of all antiquity, wrote four books to the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world, in which he asserts that it is the duty of a Christian man, while he is in this life, to expend the riches of this world for the honor and name of God.

Against the Abbot of Sponheim, On Ecclesiastical Writers.

Tilmannus Sibergensis, of the Order of Preachers, prior of Cologne, a most diligent inquisitor of heretical depravity and an outstanding professor of sacred scripture, a man acute in resolving questions, published many excellent little works displaying the acuteness of his talent, of which the following are reported:

On the Seven Sacraments, 1 book. Annotations and Appendix to the Enchiridion of Johann Eck. And certain other things he will write, if God grants him a longer life. He is still living, a very old man, in the year of Christ 1546.

Torellus Sarayna of Verona, doctor of laws, wrote On the Origin and Antiquity of the City of Verona. Also:

On the Illustrious Men of Ancient Verona. On Those Who Held Dominion over the City of Verona. On the Monuments of the Ancients, arranged in alphabetical order, from which, with assistance, one may read most old inscriptions without difficulty.

Troilus Malvitius, jurist, wrote On Play, On Offerings, On [unclear], On the Dignity of a Bishop, On the Canonization of Saints.

An Opinion on the Commendation of Benefices, whose beginning is: A certain Urbanus in his treatise on etc.

Valescus de Taranta, chief physician of the king of France, a man, as is reported, very experienced in medical matters, wrote a little treatise On Plague and Epidemic Disease.

And a Practicum, commonly called Philonium, on the cure of diseases of every kind. He is still living, as I hear, in the year of Christ 1546.

Varinus Phavorinus, bishop of Camerino, a man having exact knowledge of both the Greek and the Latin idiom.

He compiled a Greek Dictionary and commentaries from many and various authors. By the same man there is a Thesaurus or Cornucopia and Gardens of Adonis. He also translated certain apophthegms selected from the passages of Joannes Stobaeus.

On Ecclesiastical Writers, Addition II.

Victor, the fifteenth bishop of the city of Rome, a holy and learned man, wrote on the question of Easter and certain other little works. Among them the following are recorded:

Certain decrees.

An account of the faith, rendered to Huneric, king of the Vandals, when he demanded it.

He flourished under the emperor Severus, around the year of the Lord 200.

Victor, bishop of Utica, wrote three books of a History of the Vandal Persecutions, which Christians formerly endured in Africa around the times of blessed Augustine, about the year of the Lord 430, under Genseric and Huneric, kings of the Vandals.

Vigilius, martyr and bishop of Trent, published five pious and elegant books, about a thousand years ago, against Eutyches and other heretics, who thought with too little piety about the property of Christ’s natures and the unity of his person.

Vigilius, a bishop most skilled in divine letters and a most ardent emulator of martyrdom, wrote to a certain Simplicianus a little book in praise of martyrdom, and a letter containing the deeds of the martyrs of his time among the barbarians.

I think he is the same man who, a thousand years ago, wrote against Eutyches and other heretics, who thought with too little piety about the property of Christ’s natures and the unity of his person.

Vitus Amerbachius, German by birth, a very learned man of our own time, a few years ago a most vigorous champion of the Lutheran sect, now led by repentance, has betaken himself to the Catholic Church; and he succeeded Johann Eck, a man worthy of immortality, in the academy at Ingolstadt. He composed distinguished little works of learning and doctrine, some of which are entitled as follows:

Antiparadoxa, with orations on the praises of his homeland and on the method of studies.

Commentaries on the three books of Cicero On Duties.

A paraphrase of Cicero’s speech for Archias the poet.

A double interpretation of the poems of Pythagoras and Phocylides.

An interpretation of the Meteora of Joannes Jovianus Pontanus.

On the Soul, four books.

He is still living under Charles V Caesar, in the year of salvation 1546, and will compose many things for the benefit of students.

Ulpius Franekerensis, a Frisian, a man most learned in both languages, rendered Hesiod’s Works and Days in verse, in such a way that he expressed each Greek verse with a corresponding Latin one.

On the Abbot of Sponheim, On Writers.

He also wrote certain collections of proverbs not noticed by Erasmus.

Urbanus of Belluno, a Franciscan monk, instructed in the Latin and Greek languages to no ordinary degree, learnedly and accurately wrote two books of Grammatical Institutes for the Greek language.

Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome, a learned and upright man, describing in a volume the decree of the synod held against Nestorius, sent it to the churches of East and West, confirming that, while two natures remain perfectly in Christ, one person of the Son of God is to be believed.

Likewise also Xystus, the successor of Celestine, sent opinions on the same matter to Nestorius himself and to the bishops of the East, to cut down his error.

(What agreement there may be between these two Xystuses, let Gesner’s Bibliotheca see to it; from there these things, with many others, have been taken.)

Zacharias Scholasticus, otherwise called the Sophist, bishop of Mytilene, renowned for his knowledge of human and divine letters, made known to posterity the sharpness of his talent in certain little books, namely in a Dialogue, which is inscribed Ammonius, or The Philosopher. It is reported that something in Greek under his name is extant at Rome.

To the Reader.

Somewhat above, where Heinrich Herp is treated, namely on page 331, let the following be inserted, if you please, not because they were carelessly omitted there, but because, after Herp’s section had been completed, they were meanwhile incidentally suggested to us by certain studious and pious men:

On the Song of Songs of Solomon, concerning the virtues formed like Christ, one book. “Let him kiss me with the kiss...”

Directory of Contemplatives, one book. “Who [unclear] of our Lord Jesus Christ...”

Conferences on the Perfection of Life.

Eden, or The Paradise of Contemplatives, one book. “Friend, come up more often...”

The End.

Cologne, from the Quentel printing-house, in the month of March of the year 1546.
